nodes.name: Characteristic function
nodes.statement: The characteristic function of a measure $\mu$ on a normed space $E$ is the function $E^* \to \mathbb{C}$ defined by \begin{align*} \hat{\mu}(L) = \int_E e^{i L(x)} \: d\mu(x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Characteristic function of a measure on a normed space, evaluated at dual elements $L \in E^*$.
nodes.label: def:charFunDual

nodes.name: Uniqueness of characteristic function (Banach space)
nodes.statement: In a separable Banach space, if two finite measures have same characteristic function, they are equal.
assumptions: In a separable Banach space
two finite measures have same characteristic function
conclusions: they are equal
nodes.label: thm:ext_of_charFunDual

nodes.name: Characteristic function
nodes.statement: The characteristic function of a measure $\mu$ on an inner product space $E$ is the function $E \to \mathbb{C}$ defined by \begin{align*} \hat{\mu}(t) = \int_E e^{i \langle t, x \rangle} \: d\mu(x) \: . \end{align*} This is equal to the normed space version of the characteristic function applied to the linear map $x \mapsto \langle t, x \rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Characteristic function of a measure on an inner product space, as a function of $t \in E$.
nodes.label: def:charFun

nodes.name: Uniqueness of characteristic function (Hilbert space)
nodes.statement: In a separable Hilbert space, if two finite measures have same characteristic function, they are equal.
assumptions: In a separable Hilbert space
two finite measures have same characteristic function
conclusions: they are equal
nodes.label: thm:ext_of_charFun

nodes.name: Characteristic function of a pushforward by a linear form
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $F$ and let $L \in F^*$. Then \begin{align*} \widehat{L_*\mu}(x) &= \hat{\mu}(x \cdot L) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: $\mu$ be a measure on $F$
$L \in F^*$
conclusions: \widehat{L_*\mu}(x) &= \hat{\mu}(x \cdot L)
nodes.label: lem:charFun_map_eq_charFunDual_smul

nodes.name: Characteristic function of a pushforward by a linear map
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a normed space $E$ and let $L$ be a continuous linear map from $E$ to $F$. Then for all $L' \in F^*$, \begin{align*} \widehat{L_*\mu}(L') = \hat{\mu}(L' \circ L) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: $\mu$ be a measure on a normed space $E$
$L$ be a continuous linear map from $E$ to $F$
conclusions: \widehat{L_*\mu}(L') = \hat{\mu}(L' \circ L)
nodes.label: lem:charFunDual_map

nodes.name: Ambient Banach and Hilbert spaces
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a Banach space and $E$ be a Hilbert space.

nodes.name: Covariance
nodes.statement: The covariance bilinear form of a measure $\mu$ on $F$ with finite second moment is the continuous bilinear form $C_\mu : F^* \times F^* \to \mathbb{R}$ with \begin{align*} C_\mu(L_1, L_2) &= \int_x (L_1(x) - L_1(m_\mu)) (L_2(x) - L_2(m_\mu)) \: d\mu(x) \\ &= \int_x L_1(x - m_\mu) L_2(x- m_\mu) \: d\mu(x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Covariance bilinear form on the dual: integral of centered products $L_1(x-m_\mu)L_2(x-m_\mu)$.
differentia: $C_\mu : F^* \times F^* \to \mathbb{R}$
nodes.label: def:covarianceBilin

nodes.name: Covariance on the diagonal is the variance
nodes.statement: For $\mu$ a measure on $F$ with finite second moment and $L \in F^*$, $C_\mu(L, L) = \mathbb{V}_\mu[L]$.
assumptions: $\mu$ a measure on $F$ with finite second moment
$L \in F^*$
conclusions: $C_\mu(L, L) = \mathbb{V}_\mu[L]$
nodes.label: lem:covarianceBilin_same_eq_variance

nodes.name: Covariance in a Hilbert space
nodes.statement: The covariance bilinear form of a finite measure $\mu$ with finite second moment on a Hilbert space $E$ is the continuous bilinear form $C_\mu : E \times E \to \mathbb{R}$ with \begin{align*} C'_\mu(x, y) = \int_z \langle x, z - m_\mu \rangle \langle y, z - m_\mu \rangle \: d\mu(z) \: . \end{align*} This is $C_\mu$ applied to the linear maps $L_x, L_y \in E^*$ defined by $L_x(z) = \langle x, z \rangle$ and $L_y(z) = \langle y, z \rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Covariance bilinear form on a Hilbert space, $C'_\mu(x,y)$ = covariance of $\langle x,\cdot\rangle$ and $\langle y,\cdot\rangle$.
nodes.label: def:covInnerBilin

nodes.name: Covariance of a pushforward measure (Hilbert)
nodes.statement: Let $E$ and $F$ be two Hilbert spaces with $F$ finite dimensional, $\mu$ a finite measure on $E$ with finite second moment, and $L : E \to F$ a continuous linear map. Then the covariance bilinear form of the measure $L_*\mu$ is given by \begin{align*} C'_{L_*\mu}(u, v) &= C'_\mu(L^\dagger(u), L^\dagger(v)) \: , \end{align*} in which $L^\dagger : F \to E$ is the adjoint of $L$.
nodes.statement_short: Covariance of the pushforward by $L$ is the covariance composed with the adjoint $L^\dagger$.
assumptions: $E$ and $F$ be two Hilbert spaces with $F$ finite dimensional
$\mu$ a finite measure on $E$ with finite second moment
$L : E \to F$ a continuous linear map
conclusions: C'_{L_*\mu}(u, v) &= C'_\mu(L^\dagger(u), L^\dagger(v))
nodes.label: lem:covInnerBilin_map

nodes.name: Proof of Covariance of a pushforward measure (Hilbert)
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} C'_{L_*\mu}(u, v) &= (L_*\mu)\left[\langle u, x - m_{L_*\mu}\rangle \langle x - m_{L_*\mu}, v \rangle\right] \\ &= \mu\left[\langle u, L(x) - L(m_\mu)\rangle \langle L(x) - L(m_\mu), v \rangle \right] \\ &= \mu\left[\langle L^\dagger(u), x - m_\mu\rangle \langle x - m_\mu, L^\dagger(v) \rangle \right] \\ &= C'_\mu(L^\dagger(u), L^\dagger(v)) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation: rewrite the pushforward integral and move $L$ to the adjoint.

nodes.name: Covariance matrix
nodes.statement: The covariance matrix of a finite measure $\mu$ with finite second moment on a finite dimensional inner product space $E$ is the positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma_\mu$ such that for $u, v \in E$, \begin{align*} \langle u, \Sigma_\mu v\rangle = \mu[\langle u, x - m_\mu \rangle \langle x - m_\mu, v \rangle] \: . \end{align*} This is the covariance bilinear form $C'_\mu(u, v)$, as a matrix.
differentia: \langle u, \Sigma_\mu v\rangle = \mu[\langle u, x - m_\mu \rangle \langle x - m_\mu, v \rangle]
nodes.label: def:covMatrix

nodes.name: Covariance matrix of a pushforward measure
nodes.statement: Let $E$ and $F$ be two finite dimensional inner product spaces, $\mu$ a measure on $E$ with finite second moment, and $L : E \to F$ a continuous linear map. Then the covariance matrix of the measure $L_*\mu$ has entries \begin{align*} \langle e_i, \Sigma_{L_*\mu} e_j\rangle &= \langle L^\dagger(e_i), \Sigma_\mu L^\dagger(e_j)\rangle \: , \end{align*} in which $L^\dagger : F \to E$ is the adjoint of $L$.
assumptions: $E$ and $F$ be two finite dimensional inner product spaces
$\mu$ a measure on $E$ with finite second moment
$L : E \to F$ a continuous linear map
conclusions: \langle e_i, \Sigma_{L_*\mu} e_j\rangle &= \langle L^\dagger(e_i), \Sigma_\mu L^\dagger(e_j)\rangle
nodes.label: lem:covMatrix_map

nodes.name: Proof of Covariance matrix of a pushforward measure
nodes.statement: On the left-hand side we have $$\langle e_i, \Sigma_{L_*\mu} e_j\rangle = C'_{L_*\mu}(e_i, e_j) = C'_\mu(L^\dagger(e_i), L^\dagger(e_j)),$$ where the last equality comes from Lemma~\ref{lem:covInnerBilin_map}. On the right-hand side we have $$\langle L^\dagger(e_i), \Sigma_{L_*\mu} L^\dagger(e_j)\rangle = C'_\mu(L^\dagger(e_i), L^\dagger(e_j)),$$ which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Compute both sides as $C'_\mu(L^\dagger e_i, L^\dagger e_j)$ using the pushforward covariance lemma.

nodes.name: Index set and probability space
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be an index set and $\Omega$ a measurable space, with measure $\mathbb{P}$.

nodes.name: Stochastic process
nodes.statement: A stochastic process is a function $X : T \to \Omega \to E$, where $E$ is another measurable space, such that for all $t \in T$, $X_t : \Omega \to E$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable.
differentia: for all $t \in T$, $X_t : \Omega \to E$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable

nodes.name: Law of a stochastic process
nodes.statement: The law of a stochastic process $X$ is the measure on the measurable space $E^T$ obtained by pushing forward the measure $\mathbb{P}$ by the map $\omega \mapsto X(\cdot, \omega)$.
nodes.label: def:processLaw

nodes.name: Modification
nodes.statement: We say that a stochastic process $Y$ is a \emph{modification} of another stochastic process $X$ if for all $t \in T$, $Y_t =_{\mathbb{P}\text{-a.e.}} X_t$.
differentia: for all $t \in T$, $Y_t =_{\mathbb{P}\text{-a.e.}} X_t$
nodes.label: def:modification

nodes.name: Indistinguishable
nodes.statement: We say that a stochastic processes $Y$ is a \emph{indistinguishable} from $X$ if $\mathbb{P}$-a.e., for all $t \in T$, $X_t = Y_t$.
differentia: $\mathbb{P}$-a.e., for all $t \in T$, $X_t = Y_t$
nodes.label: def:indistinguishable

nodes.name: Indistinguishable implies modification
nodes.statement: If $Y$ is indistinguishable from $X$, then $Y$ is a modification of $X$.
assumptions: $Y$ is indistinguishable from $X$
conclusions: $Y$ is a modification of $X$
nodes.label: lem:Indistinguishable.Modification

nodes.name: Proof of Indistinguishable implies modification
nodes.statement: Obvious.
nodes.statement_short: Asserted obvious.

nodes.name: Modifications have the same finite-dimensional distributions
nodes.statement: Let $X, Y : T \to \Omega \to E$ be two stochastic processes that are modifications of each other. Then for all $t_1, \ldots, t_n \in T$, the random vector $(X_{t_1}, \ldots, X_{t_n})$ has the same distribution as the random vector $(Y_{t_1}, \ldots, Y_{t_n})$. That is, $X$ and $Y$ have same finite-dimensional distributions.
assumptions: $X, Y : T \to \Omega \to E$ be two stochastic processes that are modifications of each other
conclusions: for all $t_1, \ldots, t_n \in T$, the random vector $(X_{t_1}, \ldots, X_{t_n})$ has the same distribution as the random vector $(Y_{t_1}, \ldots, Y_{t_n})$
nodes.label: lem:map_eq_of_modification

nodes.name: Proof of Modifications have the same finite-dimensional distributions
nodes.statement: By the modification property, almost surely $X_{t_i} = Y_{t_i}$ for all $i \in [n]$. Thus the function $\omega \mapsto (X_{t_1}(\omega), \ldots, X_{t_n}(\omega))$ is equal to $\omega \mapsto (Y_{t_1}(\omega), \ldots, Y_{t_n}(\omega))$ almost surely, hence the maps of $\mathbb{P}$ by these two functions are equal.
nodes.statement_short: The finite-dimensional maps agree almost surely, so their pushforwards of $\mathbb{P}$ coincide.

nodes.name: Same finite-dimensional distributions iff same law
nodes.statement: Let $X, Y : T \to \Omega \to E$ be two stochastic processes. Then $X$ and $Y$ have same finite-dimensional distributions if and only if they have the same law.
assumptions: $X, Y : T \to \Omega \to E$ be two stochastic processes
conclusions: $X$ and $Y$ have same finite-dimensional distributions if and only if they have the same law
equivalent_conditions: $X$ and $Y$ have same finite-dimensional distributions
they have the same law
nodes.label: lem:map_eq_iff

nodes.name: Proof of Same finite-dimensional distributions iff same law
nodes.statement: TODO: consider the $\pi$-system of cylinder sets.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch only (TODO): use the $\pi$-system of cylinder sets.

nodes.name: Continuous modifications are indistinguishable
nodes.statement: Let $T$ and $E$ be topological spaces and suppose that $T$ is separable Hausdorff. Let $X, Y : T \to \Omega \to E$ be two stochastic processes that are modifications of each other and are almost surely continuous. Then $X$ and $Y$ are indistinguishable.
assumptions: $T$ and $E$ be topological spaces
$T$ is separable Hausdorff
$X, Y : T \to \Omega \to E$ be two stochastic processes that are modifications of each other and are almost surely continuous
conclusions: $X$ and $Y$ are indistinguishable
nodes.label: lem:indistinguishable_of_modification_of_continuous

nodes.name: Proof of Continuous modifications are indistinguishable
nodes.statement: Since $T$ is separable, it has a countable dense subset $D$. Since $D$ is countable, \begin{align*} (\forall t \in D, \mathbb{P}\text{-a.e.}, X_t = Y_t) \iff (\mathbb{P}\text{-a.e.}, \forall t \in D, X_t = Y_t) \end{align*} Hence by the modification property we have that almost surely, for all $t \in D$, $X_t = Y_t$. Then almost surely $X$ and $Y$ are continuous functions which are equal on a dense subset of $T$: those two functions are equal everywhere.
nodes.statement_short: Agreement on a countable dense set holds a.s. simultaneously; continuity extends equality everywhere.

nodes.name: Countable dense subset
nodes.statement: Since $T$ is separable, it has a countable dense subset $D$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a countable dense subset $D$ of $T$.

nodes.name: Simultaneous a.s. agreement on D
nodes.statement_short: Swap 'a.e.' and the countable quantifier, then use the modification property.

nodes.name: Extend by continuity
nodes.statement: Then almost surely $X$ and $Y$ are continuous functions which are equal on a dense subset of $T$: those two functions are equal everywhere.
nodes.statement_short: Continuous functions equal on a dense set are equal.

nodes.name: Real Gaussian measure
nodes.statement: The real Gaussian measure with mean $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ and variance $\sigma^2 > 0$ is the measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with density $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \sigma^2}\right)$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure. The real Gaussian measure with mean $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ and variance $0$ is the Dirac measure $\delta_\mu$. We denote this measure by $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ on $\mathbb{R}$: normal density if $\sigma^2>0$, Dirac mass at $\mu$ if $\sigma^2=0$.
nodes.label: def:gaussianReal

nodes.name: Characteristic function of a real Gaussian
nodes.statement: The characteristic function of a real Gaussian measure with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ is given by $x \mapsto \exp\left(i \mu x - \frac{\sigma^2 x^2}{2}\right)$.
assumptions: a real Gaussian measure with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$
conclusions: $x \mapsto \exp\left(i \mu x - \frac{\sigma^2 x^2}{2}\right)$
nodes.label: lem:charFun_gaussianReal

nodes.name: Central moments of a real Gaussian
nodes.statement: The central moment of order $2n$ of a real Gaussian measure $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ is given by \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[(X - \mu)^{2n}] = \sigma^{2n} (2n - 1)!! \: , \end{align*} in which $(2n - 1)!! = (2n - 1)(2n - 3) \cdots 3 \cdot 1$ is the double factorial of $2n - 1$.
assumptions: a real Gaussian measure $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$
nodes.label: lem:centralMoment_two_mul_gaussianReal

nodes.name: Proof of Central moments of a real Gaussian
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[(X - \mu)^{2n}] &= \int_{-\infty}^\infty (x - \mu)^{2n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \sigma^2}} \mathrm dx \\ &= \int_{-\infty}^\infty x^{2n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2 \sigma^2}} \mathrm dx \\ &= 2 \int_{0}^\infty x^{2n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2 \sigma^2}} \mathrm dx \\ &= 2 \int_{0}^\infty {\sqrt{2 \sigma^2 x}}^{2n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} e^{-x)} \frac{\sigma^2}{\sqrt{2 \sigma^2 x'}} \mathrm dx \\ &= \frac{\sigma^{2n} 2^n}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{0}^\infty x^{n - 1/2} e{-x} \mathrm dx \\ &= \frac{\sigma^{2n} 2^n}{\sqrt{\pi}} \Gamma(n + 1/2) \\ &= \frac{\sigma^{2n} 2^n}{\Gamma(1/2)} \left( \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} (k + 1/2) \right) \Gamma(1/2) \\ &= \sigma^{2n} \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} (2k + 1) \\ &= \sigma^{2n} (2n - 1)!! \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute and reduce the Gaussian moment integral to a Gamma function, then expand $\Gamma(n+1/2)$.

nodes.name: Separable Banach space $F$
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a separable Banach space.

nodes.name: Gaussian measure
nodes.statement: A measure $\mu$ on $F$ is Gaussian if for every continuous linear form $L \in F^*$, the pushforward measure $L_* \mu$ is a Gaussian measure on $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.section: 3.1.2 Gaussian measures on a Banach space
differentia: for every continuous linear form $L \in F^*$, the pushforward measure $L_* \mu$ is a Gaussian measure on $\mathbb{R}$

nodes.name: Gaussian measures are probability measures
nodes.statement: A Gaussian measure is a probability measure.
nodes.section: 3.1.2 Gaussian measures on a Banach space
conclusions: A Gaussian measure is a probability measure.
nodes.label: lem:IsGaussian.IsProbabilityMeasure

nodes.name: Characteristic function characterization of Gaussian measures
nodes.statement: A finite measure $\mu$ on $F$ is Gaussian if and only if for every continuous linear form $L \in F^*$, the characteristic function of $\mu$ at $L$ is \begin{align*} \hat{\mu}(L) = \exp\left(i \mu[L] - \mathbb{V}_\mu[L] / 2\right) \: , \end{align*} in which $\mathbb{V}_\mu[L]$ is the variance of $L$ with respect to $\mu$.

nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:IsGaussian.charFun_eq} states that the characteristic function of a Gaussian measure has the wanted form. Suppose now that there exists $m \in E$ and $C$ positive semidefinite such that for all $t \in E$, $\hat{\mu}(t) = \exp\left(i \langle t, m \rangle - \frac{1}{2} C(t, t)\right)$. We need to show that for all $L \in E^*$, $L_*\mu$ is a Gaussian measure on $\mathbb{R}$. Such an $L$ can be written as $\langle u, \cdot \rangle$ for some $u \in E$. Let then $u \in E$. We compute the characteristic function of $\langle u, \cdot\rangle_*\mu$ at $x \in \mathbb{R}$ with Lemma~\ref{lem:charFun_map_eq_charFunDual_smul}: \begin{align*} \widehat{\langle u, \cdot\rangle_*\mu}(x) &= \hat{\mu}(x \cdot u) \\ &= \exp\left(i x \langle u, m \rangle - \frac{1}{2} x^2 C(u, u)\right) \: . \end{align*} This is the characteristic function of a Gaussian measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with mean $\langle u, m \rangle$ and variance $C(u, u)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:ext_of_charFun}, $\langle u, \cdot\rangle_*\mu$ is Gaussian, hence $\mu$ is Gaussian. By Lemma~\ref{lem:IsGaussian.charFun_eq}, we deduce that for any $t \in E$ we have $$\exp\left(i\langle t, m \rangle - \frac{1}{2} C(t, t)\right) = \exp\left(i\langle t, m_\mu \rangle - \frac{1}{2} C'_\mu(t, t)\right).$$ In particular, for any $t$ there exists $n_t \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $$i\langle t, m \rangle - \frac{1}{2} C(t, t) = i\langle t, m_\mu \rangle - \frac{1}{2} C'_\mu(t, t) + 2i\pi n_t.$$ We deduce that $n$ is a continuous map from $E$ to $\mathbb{Z}$, and thus must be constant because $E$ is connected. By looking at the value at $t = 0$, we deduce that for any $t$, $n_t = 0$. Looking at real and imaginary parts we obtain that for any $t$, $$\langle t, m \rangle = \langle t, m_\mu \rangle \quad \text{and} \quad C(t, t) = C'_\mu(t, t).$$ We immediately deduce that $m = m_\mu$. Moreover, because $C$ and $C'_\mu$ are symmetric, they are characterized by their values on the diagonal. Indeed, for any $x, y$, $$C(x, y) = \frac{1}{2} (C(x + y, x + y) - C(x, x) - C(y, y)).$$ We deduce that $C = C'_\mu$.

nodes.statement: Since the multivariate Gaussian measure is a Gaussian measure, we can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:IsGaussian.charFun_eq} to it. It suffices then to show that the mean and the covariance matrix of the multivariate Gaussian measure are equal to $m$ and $\Sigma$, respectively. This is given by Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_id_multivariateGaussian} and Lemma~\ref{lem:covMatrix_multivariateGaussian}.
