nodes.name: Gaussian process
nodes.statement: A process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is Gaussian if for every finite subset $t_1, \ldots, t_n \in T$, the random vector $(X_{t_1}, \ldots, X_{t_n})$ has a Gaussian distribution.
differentia: for every finite subset $t_1, \ldots, t_n \in T$, the random vector $(X_{t_1}, \ldots, X_{t_n})$ has a Gaussian distribution
nodes.label: def:IsGaussianProcess

nodes.name: Modification of a Gaussian process is Gaussian
nodes.statement: Let $X, Y : T \to \Omega \to E$ be two stochastic processes that are modifications of each other (that is, for all $t \in T$, $X_t =_{a.e.} Y_t$). If $X$ is a Gaussian process, then $Y$ is a Gaussian process as well.
assumptions: $X, Y : T \to \Omega \to E$ be two stochastic processes that are modifications of each other
$X$ is a Gaussian process
conclusions: $Y$ is a Gaussian process as well
nodes.label: lem:isGaussianProcess_of_modification

nodes.name: Proof of Modification of a Gaussian process is Gaussian
nodes.statement: Being a Gaussian process is defined in terms of the distribution of finite-dimensional random vectors. By Lemma~\ref{lem:map_eq_of_modification}, the random vector $(Y_{t_1}, \ldots, Y_{t_n})$ has the same distribution as the random vector $(X_{t_1}, \ldots, X_{t_n})$ for all $t_1, \ldots, t_n \in T$.
nodes.statement_short: Gaussianity depends only on finite-dimensional distributions, which modifications share.

nodes.name: Projective family
nodes.statement: A family of measures $P$ indexed by finite sets of $T$ is projective if, for finite sets $J \subseteq I$, the projection from $E^I$ to $E^J$ maps $P_I$ to $P_J$.
nodes.genus: family of measures $P$ indexed by finite sets of $T$
differentia: for finite sets $J \subseteq I$, the projection from $E^I$ to $E^J$ maps $P_I$ to $P_J$
nodes.label: def:IsProjectiveMeasureFamily

nodes.name: Projective limit
nodes.statement: A measure $\mu$ on $E^T$ is the projective limit of a projective family of measures $P$ indexed by finite sets of $T$ if, for every finite set $I \subseteq T$, the projection from $E^T$ to $E^I$ maps $\mu$ to $P_I$.
differentia: for every finite set $I \subseteq T$, the projection from $E^T$ to $E^I$ maps $\mu$ to $P_I$
nodes.label: def:IsProjectiveLimit

nodes.name: Kolmogorov extension theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a Polish space, equipped with the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and let $T$ be an index set. Let $P$ be a projective family of finite measures on $\mathcal{X}$. Then the projective limit $\mu$ of $P$ exists, is unique, and is a finite measure on $\mathcal{X}^T$. Moreover, if $P_I$ is a probability measure for every finite set $I \subseteq T$, then $\mu$ is a probability measure.
assumptions: $\mathcal{X}$ be a Polish space, equipped with the Borel $\sigma$-algebra
$T$ be an index set
$P$ be a projective family of finite measures on $\mathcal{X}$
$P_I$ is a probability measure for every finite set $I \subseteq T$
conclusions: the projective limit $\mu$ of $P$ exists, is unique, and is a finite measure on $\mathcal{X}^T$
$\mu$ is a probability measure
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); formalized in kolmogorov_extension4 by Degenne and Pfaffelhuber

conclusions: the projective limit $\mu$ of $P$ exists, is unique, and is a finite measure on $\mathcal{X}^T$

assumptions: $P_I$ is a probability measure for every finite set $I \subseteq T$
conclusions: $\mu$ is a probability measure

nodes.label: thm:kolmogorovExtension

nodes.name: Gram matrix
nodes.statement: Let $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ be vectors in an inner product space $E$. The Gram matrix of $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ is the matrix in $\mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ with entries $G_{ij} = \langle v_i, v_j \rangle$ for $1 \leq i,j \leq n$.
differentia: entries $G_{ij} = \langle v_i, v_j \rangle$ for $1 \leq i,j \leq n$
nodes.label: def:gramMatrix

nodes.name: Gram matrices are positive semidefinite
nodes.statement: A gram matrix is positive semidefinite.
nodes.label: lem:posSemidef_gramMatrix

nodes.name: Proof of Gram matrices are positive semidefinite
nodes.statement: Symmetry is obvious from the definition. Let $x \in E$. Then \begin{align*} \langle x, G x \rangle &= \sum_{i,j} x_i x_j \langle v_i, v_j \rangle \\ &= \langle \sum_i x_i v_i, \sum_j x_j v_j \rangle \\ &= \left\Vert \sum_i x_i v_i \right\Vert^2 \\ &\ge 0 \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the quadratic form as the squared norm of $\sum_i x_i v_i$.

nodes.name: Brownian covariance matrix is a Gram matrix
nodes.statement: Let $I = \{t_1, \ldots, t_n\}$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}_+$. For $i \le n$, let $v_i = \mathbb{I}_{[0, t_i]}$ be the indicator function of the interval $[0, t_i]$, as an element of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. Then the Gram matrix of $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ is equal to the matrix $C_{ij} = \min(t_i, t_j)$ for $1 \leq i,j \leq n$.
assumptions: $I = \{t_1, \ldots, t_n\}$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}_+$
let $v_i = \mathbb{I}_{[0, t_i]}$ be the indicator function of the interval $[0, t_i]$, as an element of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$
conclusions: the Gram matrix of $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ is equal to the matrix $C_{ij} = \min(t_i, t_j)$ for $1 \leq i,j \leq n$
nodes.label: lem:C_eq_gramMatrix

nodes.name: Proof of Brownian covariance matrix is a Gram matrix
nodes.statement: By definition of the inner product in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, \begin{align*} \langle v_i, v_j \rangle &= \int_{\mathbb{R}} \mathbb{I}_{[0, t_i]}(x) \mathbb{I}_{[0, t_j]}(x) \: dx = \min(t_i, t_j) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Compute the $L^2$ inner product of two interval indicators.

nodes.name: Brownian covariance matrix is positive semidefinite
nodes.statement: For $I = \{t_1, \ldots, t_n\}$ a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}_+$, let $C \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ be the matrix $C_{ij} = \min(t_i, t_j)$ for $1 \leq i,j \leq n$. Then $C$ is positive semidefinite.
assumptions: For $I = \{t_1, \ldots, t_n\}$ a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}_+$, let $C \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ be the matrix $C_{ij} = \min(t_i, t_j)$ for $1 \leq i,j \leq n$.
conclusions: $C$ is positive semidefinite
nodes.label: lem:posSemidef_brownianCov

nodes.name: Proof of Brownian covariance matrix is positive semidefinite
nodes.statement: $C$ is a Gram matrix by Lemma~\ref{lem:C_eq_gramMatrix}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:posSemidef_gramMatrix}, it is positive semidefinite.
nodes.statement_short: $C$ is a Gram matrix, hence positive semidefinite.

nodes.name: Projective family of the Brownian motion
nodes.statement: For $I = \{t_1, \ldots, t_n\}$ a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}_+$, let $P^B_I$ be the multivariate Gaussian measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with mean $0$ and covariance matrix $C_{ij} = \min(t_i, t_j)$ for $1 \leq i,j \leq n$. We call the family of measures $P^B_I$ the \emph{projective family of the Brownian motion}.
definiendum: projective family of the Brownian motion
differentia: mean $0$
covariance matrix $C_{ij} = \min(t_i, t_j)$
nodes.label: def:gaussianProjectiveFamily

nodes.name: Brownian projective family is projective
nodes.statement: The projective family of the Brownian motion is a projective family of measures.
nodes.label: lem:isProjectiveMeasureFamily_gaussianProjectiveFamily

nodes.name: Proof of Brownian projective family is projective
nodes.statement: Let $J \subseteq I$ be finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}_+$. We need to show that the restriction from $\mathbb{R}^I$ to $\mathbb{R}^J$ (denote it by $\pi_{IJ}$) maps $P^B_I$ to $P^B_J$. The restriction is a continuous linear map from $\mathbb{R}^I$ to $\mathbb{R}^J$. The map of a Gaussian measure by a continuous linear map is Gaussian (Lemma~\ref{lem:isGaussian_map}). It thus suffices to show that the mean and covariance matrix of the map are equal to the ones of $P^B_J$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:IsGaussian.ext_iff}. The mean of the map is $0$, since the mean of $P^B_I$ is $0$ and the map is linear. Let us turn to the covariance matrix. For any $i \in J$, the map $x : \mathbb{R}^I \mapsto \pi_{IJ}(x) i$ is equal to $x : \mathbb{R}^I \mapsto x i$. Let $i, j \in J$. The covariance of $x : \mathbb{R}^J \mapsto x i$ and $x : \mathbb{R}^J \mapsto x j$ with respect to ${\pi_{IJ}}_*P^B_J$ is equal to the covariance of $x : \mathbb{R}^I \mapsto \pi_{IJ}(x) i$ and $x : \mathbb{R}^I \mapsto \pi_{IJ}(x) j$ with respect to $P^B_I$, which is equal to the covariance of $x : \mathbb{R}^I \mapsto x i$ and $x : \mathbb{R}^I \mapsto x i$ with respect to $P^B_I$, which is equal to $t_i \land t_j$. But this is also the covariance of $x : \mathbb{R}^J \mapsto x i$ and $x : \mathbb{R}^J \mapsto x j$ with respect to $P^B_J$, so we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Restriction maps are linear, so the image is Gaussian; compare means and covariance matrices and conclude by Gaussian uniqueness.

nodes.name: Setup the projectivity goal
nodes.statement: Let $J \subseteq I$ be finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}_+$. We need to show that the restriction from $\mathbb{R}^I$ to $\mathbb{R}^J$ (denote it by $\pi_{IJ}$) maps $P^B_I$ to $P^B_J$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $J \subseteq I$ and state the restriction goal.

nodes.name: Reduce to mean and covariance
nodes.statement: The restriction is a continuous linear map from $\mathbb{R}^I$ to $\mathbb{R}^J$. The map of a Gaussian measure by a continuous linear map is Gaussian (Lemma~\ref{lem:isGaussian_map}). It thus suffices to show that the mean and covariance matrix of the map are equal to the ones of $P^B_J$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:IsGaussian.ext_iff}.
nodes.statement_short: The image is Gaussian; reduce to matching mean and covariance.

nodes.name: Mean is zero
nodes.statement: The mean of the map is $0$, since the mean of $P^B_I$ is $0$ and the map is linear.
nodes.statement_short: The image has mean 0.

nodes.name: Covariances match
nodes.statement: Let us turn to the covariance matrix. For any $i \in J$, the map $x : \mathbb{R}^I \mapsto \pi_{IJ}(x) i$ is equal to $x : \mathbb{R}^I \mapsto x i$. Let $i, j \in J$. The covariance of $x : \mathbb{R}^J \mapsto x i$ and $x : \mathbb{R}^J \mapsto x j$ with respect to ${\pi_{IJ}}_*P^B_J$ is equal to the covariance of $x : \mathbb{R}^I \mapsto \pi_{IJ}(x) i$ and $x : \mathbb{R}^I \mapsto \pi_{IJ}(x) j$ with respect to $P^B_I$, which is equal to the covariance of $x : \mathbb{R}^I \mapsto x i$ and $x : \mathbb{R}^I \mapsto x i$ with respect to $P^B_I$, which is equal to $t_i \land t_j$. But this is also the covariance of $x : \mathbb{R}^J \mapsto x i$ and $x : \mathbb{R}^J \mapsto x j$ with respect to $P^B_J$, so we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Covariance entries of the image equal $t_i \wedge t_j$.

nodes.name: Brownian projective limit
nodes.statement: We denote by $P_B$ the projective limit of the projective family of the Brownian motion given by Theorem~\ref{thm:kolmogorovExtension}. This is a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}_+}$.
nodes.label: def:gaussianLimit

nodes.name: Metric setting for the Kolmogorov-Chentsov theorem
nodes.statement: That theorem is about stochastic processes $X : T \to \Omega \to E$, where $\Omega$ is a measurable space with a probability measure $\mathbb{P}$, the index set $T$ is a metric space with distance $d_T$, and $E$ is also a metric space with distance $d_E$, on which we put the Borel $\sigma$-algebra.

nodes.name: Pseudo-metric space $E$
nodes.statement: Let $(E, d_E)$ be a pseudo-metric space.

nodes.name: $\varepsilon$-cover
nodes.statement: A set $C \subseteq E$ is an $\varepsilon$-cover of a set $A \subseteq E$ if for every $x \in A$, there exists $y \in C$ such that $d_E(x, y) \le \varepsilon$.
differentia: for every $x \in A$, there exists $y \in C$ such that $d_E(x, y) \le \varepsilon$
nodes.label: def:IsCover

nodes.name: External covering number
nodes.statement: The external covering number of a set $A \subseteq E$ for $\varepsilon \ge 0$ is the smallest cardinality of an $\varepsilon$-cover of $A$. Denote it by $N^{ext}_\varepsilon(A)$.
nodes.label: def:externalCoveringNumber

nodes.name: Internal covering number
nodes.statement: The internal covering number of a set $A \subseteq E$ for $\varepsilon \ge 0$ is the smallest cardinality of an $\varepsilon$-cover of $A$ which is a subset of $A$. Denote it by $N^{int}_\varepsilon(A)$.
nodes.label: def:internalCoveringNumber

nodes.name: Separated set
nodes.statement: A set $c \subseteq E$ is $\varepsilon$-separated if for all $x, y \in c$, $d_E(x, y) > \varepsilon$.
differentia: for all $x, y \in c$, $d_E(x, y) > \varepsilon$
nodes.label: def:IsSeparated

nodes.name: Packing number
nodes.statement: The packing number of a set $A \subseteq E$ for $\varepsilon > 0$ is the largest cardinality of an $\varepsilon$-separated subset of $A$. Denote it by $P_\varepsilon(A)$.
nodes.label: def:packingNumber

nodes.name: External covering number at most internal covering number
nodes.statement: $N^{ext}_\varepsilon(A) \le N^{int}_\varepsilon(A)$.
nodes.label: lem:externalCoveringNumber_le_internalCoveringNumber

nodes.name: Internal covering number at most packing number
nodes.statement: $N^{int}_\varepsilon(A) \le P_\varepsilon(A)$.
nodes.label: lem:internalCoveringNumber_le_packingNumber

nodes.name: Packing number bounded by external covering number
nodes.statement: $P_{2\varepsilon}(A) \le N^{ext}_\varepsilon(A)$.
nodes.label: lem:packingNumber_two_le_externalCoveringNumber

nodes.name: Internal covering number of a small set is one
nodes.statement: If $\mathrm{diam}(A) \le \varepsilon$ and $A$ is nonempty, then $N^{int}_\varepsilon(A) = 1$.
assumptions: $\mathrm{diam}(A) \le \varepsilon$
$A$ is nonempty
conclusions: $N^{int}_\varepsilon(A) = 1$
nodes.label: lem:internalCoveringNumber_eq_one_of_diam_le

nodes.name: Monotonicity of the external covering number
nodes.statement: For $B \subseteq A$, $N^{ext}_\varepsilon(B) \le N^{ext}_{\varepsilon}(A)$.
assumptions: $B \subseteq A$
conclusions: $N^{ext}_\varepsilon(B) \le N^{ext}_{\varepsilon}(A)$
nodes.label: lem:externalCoveringNumber_mono

nodes.name: Internal covering number of a subset
nodes.statement: For $B \subseteq A$, $N^{int}_\varepsilon(B) \le N^{int}_{\varepsilon/2}(A)$.
assumptions: $B \subseteq A$
conclusions: $N^{int}_\varepsilon(B) \le N^{int}_{\varepsilon/2}(A)$
nodes.label: lem:internalCoveringNumber_subset_le

nodes.name: Proof of Internal covering number of a subset
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} N^{int}_\varepsilon(B) &\le P_{\varepsilon}(B) \le N^{ext}_{\varepsilon/2}(B) \le N^{ext}_{\varepsilon/2}(A) \le N^{int}_{\varepsilon/2}(A) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Chain of comparisons between internal, packing and external covering numbers plus monotonicity.

nodes.name: Finite dimensional inner product space of dimension d
nodes.statement: In this section $E$ is a finite dimensional inner product space, with dimension $d$.

nodes.name: Volume bound from a finite cover
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq E$ and $C \subseteq E$ be a finite $\varepsilon$-cover of $A$. Denote by $V(A)$ the volume of $A$. Then $V(A) \le \vert C \vert V(B_\varepsilon)$, in which $B_\varepsilon$ is the closed ball of radius $\varepsilon$ in $E$.
assumptions: $A \subseteq E$ and $C \subseteq E$ be a finite $\varepsilon$-cover of $A$
conclusions: $V(A) \le \vert C \vert V(B_\varepsilon)$
nodes.label: lem:volume_le_of_isCover

nodes.name: Proof of Volume bound from a finite cover
nodes.statement: Since $C$ is a cover of $A$, $A$ is a subset of the union of the closed balls $B_\varepsilon(c)$ for $c \in C$. Then \begin{align*} V(A) \le V(\bigcup_{c \in C} B_\varepsilon(c)) &\le \sum_{c \in C} V(B_\varepsilon(c)) = \vert C \vert V(B_\varepsilon) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Cover $A$ by balls around the cover points and use subadditivity of volume.

nodes.name: Volume of a Euclidean ball
conclusions: V(B_\varepsilon) = \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2 + 1)} \varepsilon^d

nodes.name: Volume bound by external covering number
nodes.statement: If $0 < \varepsilon$ then $V(A) \le N^{ext}_\varepsilon(A) V(B_\varepsilon)$.
assumptions: $0 < \varepsilon$
conclusions: $V(A) \le N^{ext}_\varepsilon(A) V(B_\varepsilon)$
nodes.label: lem:volume_le_externalCoveringNumber_mul

nodes.name: Proof of Volume bound by external covering number
nodes.statement: If $A$ has no $\varepsilon$-cover, then $N^{ext}_\varepsilon(A) = \infty$, and because $0 < \varepsilon$, we have that $0 < V(B_\varepsilon)$, so the right-hand side is infinite and the inequality follows. Otherwise there exists an $\varepsilon$-cover which realizes $N^{ext}_\varepsilon(A)$. We can conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:volume_le_of_isCover}.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether a finite $\varepsilon$-cover exists; otherwise apply the cover volume bound.

nodes.name: No finite cover
nodes.statement: If $A$ has no $\varepsilon$-cover, then $N^{ext}_\varepsilon(A) = \infty$, and because $0 < \varepsilon$, we have that $0 < V(B_\varepsilon)$, so the right-hand side is infinite and the inequality follows.
nodes.statement_short: If no cover exists the right side is infinite.

nodes.name: Optimal cover exists
nodes.statement: Otherwise there exists an $\varepsilon$-cover which realizes $N^{ext}_\varepsilon(A)$. We can conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:volume_le_of_isCover}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the cover volume bound to an optimal cover.

nodes.name: Volume bound for a separated set
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq E$ and let $S \subseteq A$ be an $\varepsilon$-separated set. Then $\vert S \vert V(B_{\varepsilon/2}) \le V(A + B_{\varepsilon/2})$.
assumptions: $A \subseteq E$
$S \subseteq A$ be an $\varepsilon$-separated set
conclusions: $\vert S \vert V(B_{\varepsilon/2}) \le V(A + B_{\varepsilon/2})$
nodes.label: lem:le_volume_of_isSeparated

nodes.name: Proof of Volume bound for a separated set
nodes.statement: Since $S$ is $\varepsilon$-separated, the closed balls $B_{\varepsilon/2}(s)$ for $s \in S$ are pairwise disjoint. Furthermore, these balls are contained in $A + B_{\varepsilon/2}$. Thus, we have \begin{align*} \vert S \vert V(B_{\varepsilon/2}) &= \sum_{s \in S} V(B_{\varepsilon/2}(s)) = V(\bigcup_{s \in S} B_{\varepsilon/2}(s)) \le V(A + B_{\varepsilon/2}) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Disjoint half-radius balls around separated points fit inside $A + B_{\varepsilon/2}$; add their volumes.

nodes.name: Disjoint balls
nodes.statement: Since $S$ is $\varepsilon$-separated, the closed balls $B_{\varepsilon/2}(s)$ for $s \in S$ are pairwise disjoint.
nodes.statement_short: Half-radius balls around separated points are disjoint.

nodes.name: Balls inside enlarged set
nodes.statement: Furthermore, these balls are contained in $A + B_{\varepsilon/2}$.
nodes.statement_short: The balls lie in $A + B_{\varepsilon/2}$.

nodes.name: Compare volumes
nodes.statement:
Thus, we have
\begin{align*}
  \vert S \vert V(B_{\varepsilon/2})
  &= \sum_{s \in S} V(B_{\varepsilon/2}(s))
  = V(\bigcup_{s \in S} B_{\varepsilon/2}(s))
  \le V(A + B_{\varepsilon/2})
  \: .
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Add volumes of disjoint balls.

nodes.name: Packing number volume bound
nodes.statement: $P_\varepsilon(A) V(B_{\varepsilon/2}) \le V(A + B_{\varepsilon/2})$.
nodes.label: lem:packingNumber_mul_le_volume

nodes.name: Proof of Packing number volume bound
nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:le_volume_of_isSeparated} with $S$ an $\varepsilon$-separated set of maximal cardinality.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the separated-set volume bound to a maximal separated set.

nodes.name: Volume lower bound on internal covering number
nodes.statement: If $0 < \varepsilon$ then $\frac{V(A)}{V(B_\varepsilon)} \le N^{int}_\varepsilon(A)$.
assumptions: $0 < \varepsilon$
conclusions: $\frac{V(A)}{V(B_\varepsilon)} \le N^{int}_\varepsilon(A)$
nodes.label: lem:volume_div_le_internalCoveringNumber

nodes.name: Proof of Volume lower bound on internal covering number
nodes.statement: We have $\frac{V(A)}{V(B_\varepsilon)} \le N^{ext}_\varepsilon(A)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:volume_le_externalCoveringNumber_mul} and $N^{ext}_\varepsilon(A) \le N^{int}_\varepsilon(A)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:externalCoveringNumber_le_internalCoveringNumber}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the external covering volume bound with external $\le$ internal.

nodes.name: Volume upper bound on internal covering number
nodes.statement: If $0 < \varepsilon < \infty$ then $N^{int}_\varepsilon(A) \le \frac{V(A + B_{\varepsilon/2})}{V(B_{\varepsilon/2})}$.
assumptions: $0 < \varepsilon < \infty$
conclusions: $N^{int}_\varepsilon(A) \le \frac{V(A + B_{\varepsilon/2})}{V(B_{\varepsilon/2})}$
nodes.label: lem:internalCoveringNumber_le_volume_div

nodes.name: Proof of Volume upper bound on internal covering number
nodes.statement: We have $N^{int}_\varepsilon(A) \le P_\varepsilon(A)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:internalCoveringNumber_le_packingNumber} and $P_\varepsilon(A) \le \frac{V(A + B_{\varepsilon/2})}{V(B_{\varepsilon/2})}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:packingNumber_mul_le_volume}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine internal $\le$ packing with the packing number volume bound.

nodes.name: Lower bound on covering number of the unit ball
nodes.statement: $N_\varepsilon^{int}(B_1) \ge \frac{1}{\varepsilon^d}$.
nodes.label: lem:internalCoveringNumber_closedBall_ge

nodes.name: Proof of Lower bound on covering number of the unit ball
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:volume_div_le_internalCoveringNumber}, \begin{align*} N^{int}_\varepsilon(B_1) &\ge \frac{V(B_1)}{V(B_\varepsilon)} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon^d} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Volume lower bound with the ratio of ball volumes $V(B_1)/V(B_\varepsilon)$.

nodes.name: Upper bound on covering number of the unit ball
nodes.statement: $N_\varepsilon^{int}(B_1) \le \left(\frac{2}{\varepsilon} + 1\right)^d$.
nodes.label: lem:internalCoveringNumber_closedBall_le

nodes.name: Proof of Upper bound on covering number of the unit ball
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:internalCoveringNumber_le_volume_div}, \begin{align*} N^{int}_\varepsilon(B_1) &\le \frac{V(B_1 + B_{\varepsilon/2})}{V(B_{\varepsilon/2})} = \frac{V(B_{1 + \varepsilon/2})}{V(B_{\varepsilon/2})} = \frac{(1 + \varepsilon/2)^d}{(\varepsilon/2)^d} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Volume upper bound and the formula for ball volumes.

nodes.name: Bounded internal covering number
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{diam}(A)$ be the diameter of $A \subseteq E$, i.e. $\mathrm{diam}(A) = \sup_{x,y \in A} d_E(x, y)$. A set $A \subseteq E$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c>0$ and exponent $t>0$ if for all $\varepsilon \in (0, \mathrm{diam}(A)]$, $N^{int}_\varepsilon(A) \le c \varepsilon^{-t}$.
nodes.statement_short: $A$ has bounded internal covering number $(c,t)$ if $N^{int}_\varepsilon(A) \le c\varepsilon^{-t}$ for $\varepsilon \le \mathrm{diam}(A)$.
differentia: for all $\varepsilon \in (0, \mathrm{diam}(A)]$, $N^{int}_\varepsilon(A) \le c \varepsilon^{-t}$
nodes.label: def:HasBoundedInternalCoveringNumber

nodes.name: Unit interval has bounded internal covering number
nodes.statement: The unit interval $I = [0, 1] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $1$ and exponent $1$: for $\varepsilon \le 1$, $N^{int}_\varepsilon(I) \le 1/\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: lem:hasBoundedInternalCoveringNumber_unitInterval

nodes.name: Bounded internal covering number passes to subsets
nodes.statement: If $A$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c>0$ and exponent $d>0$, then for all $B \subseteq A$, $B$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $2^d c$ and exponent $d$.
assumptions: $A$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c>0$ and exponent $d>0$
$B \subseteq A$
conclusions: $B$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $2^d c$ and exponent $d$
nodes.label: lem:hasBoundedInternalCoveringNumber_subset

nodes.name: Proof of Bounded internal covering number passes to subsets
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} N^{int}_\varepsilon(B) &\le N^{int}_{\varepsilon/2}(A) \le c (\varepsilon/2)^{-d} = 2^d c \varepsilon^{-d} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Use the subset covering bound at scale $\varepsilon/2$.

nodes.name: Diameter bound from bounded internal covering number
nodes.statement: If $A$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c>0$ and exponent $d>0$, then $\mathrm{diam}(A) \le c^{1/d}$.
assumptions: $A$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c>0$ and exponent $d>0$
conclusions: $\mathrm{diam}(A) \le c^{1/d}$
nodes.label: lem:hasBoundedInternalCoveringNumber_diam_le

nodes.name: Proof of Diameter bound from bounded internal covering number
nodes.statement: If $\mathrm{diam}(A) = 0$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise $A$ is nonempty, so any cover of $A$ has at least one element, and applying the covering condition with $\varepsilon = \mathrm{diam}(A)$ gives $1 \le N^{int}_{\mathrm{diam}(A)}(A) \le c \, \mathrm{diam}(A)^{-d}$, hence $\mathrm{diam}(A)^d \le c$.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on zero diameter; otherwise apply the covering condition at $\varepsilon = \mathrm{diam}(A)$.

nodes.name: Nearest point in a finite set
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a finite set of $E$ and $x \in E$. We denote by $\pi(x, S)$ the point in $S$ which is closest to $x$, i.e. a point such that $d_E(x, S) = \min_{y \in S} d_E(x, y)$ (chosen arbitrarily among the minima if there are several).
nodes.label: def:nearestPt

nodes.name: Nearest point minimizes distance
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a finite set of $E$ and $x \in E$. Then for all $y \in S$, $d_E(x, \pi(x, S)) \le d_E(x, y)$.
assumptions: $S$ be a finite set of $E$ and $x \in E$
conclusions: for all $y \in S$, $d_E(x, \pi(x, S)) \le d_E(x, y)$
nodes.label: lem:dist_nearestPt_le

nodes.name: Proof of Nearest point minimizes distance
nodes.statement: By definition.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition of the nearest point.

nodes.name: Nearest point in a cover is close
nodes.statement: Let $C_\varepsilon$ be a finite $\varepsilon$-cover of $A \subseteq E$ (assuming such a finite cover exists). Then for all $x \in A$, $d_E(x, \pi(x, C_\varepsilon)) \le \varepsilon$.
assumptions: $C_\varepsilon$ be a finite $\varepsilon$-cover of $A \subseteq E$ (assuming such a finite cover exists)
conclusions: for all $x \in A$, $d_E(x, \pi(x, C_\varepsilon)) \le \varepsilon$
nodes.label: lem:dist_nearestPt_of_isCover

nodes.name: Chaining sequence
nodes.statement: Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $A \subseteq E$ with $C_n \subseteq A$ and $x \in C_k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$. We define the chaining sequence of $x$, denoted $(\bar{x}_i)_{i \le k}$, recursively as follows: $\bar{x}_k = x$ and for $i < k$, $\bar{x}_i = \pi(\bar{x}_{i+1}, C_i)$.
nodes.statement_short: Chaining sequence: start at $x \in C_k$ and repeatedly project to the nearest point of the coarser cover $C_i$.
nodes.label: def:chainingSequence

nodes.name: Chaining sequence stays in the covers
nodes.statement: Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $A \subseteq E$ with $C_n \subseteq A$ and $x \in C_k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for all $i \le k$, $\bar{x}_i\in C_i$.
assumptions: $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $A \subseteq E$ with $C_n \subseteq A$ and $x \in C_k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$
conclusions: for all $i \le k$, $\bar{x}_i\in C_i$
nodes.label: lem:chainingSequence_mem

nodes.name: Proof of Chaining sequence stays in the covers
nodes.statement: By definition.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition of the chaining sequence.

nodes.name: One-step distance in a chaining sequence
nodes.statement: Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $A \subseteq E$ with $C_n \subseteq A$ and $x \in C_k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for all $i < k$, $d_E(\bar{x}_i, \bar{x}_{i+1}) \le \varepsilon_i$.
assumptions: $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $A \subseteq E$ with $C_n \subseteq A$ and $x \in C_k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$
conclusions: for all $i < k$, $d_E(\bar{x}_i, \bar{x}_{i+1}) \le \varepsilon_i$
nodes.label: lem:dist_chainingSequence_add_one

nodes.name: Proof of One-step distance in a chaining sequence
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:dist_nearestPt_of_isCover} with $S = C_i$ and $x = \bar{x}_{i+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the nearest-point-in-cover bound to $C_i$ and $\bar{x}_{i+1}$.

nodes.name: Distance along a chaining sequence
nodes.statement: Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $A \subseteq E$ with $C_n \subseteq A$ and $x \in C_k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for $m \le k$, $d_E(\bar{x}_m, x) \le \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \varepsilon_i$.
assumptions: $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $A \subseteq E$ with $C_n \subseteq A$ and $x \in C_k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$
conclusions: for $m \le k$, $d_E(\bar{x}_m, x) \le \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \varepsilon_i$
nodes.label: lem:dist_chainingSequence_le_sum

nodes.name: Proof of Distance along a chaining sequence
nodes.statement: By the triangle inequality and Lemma~\ref{lem:dist_chainingSequence_add_one}, \begin{align*} d_E(\bar{x}_m, x) \le \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} d_E(\bar{x}_i, \bar{x}_{i+1}) \le \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \varepsilon_i \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality along the chain plus the one-step bound.

nodes.name: Distance between chaining sequences
nodes.statement: Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $A \subseteq E$ with $C_n \subseteq A$. Let $m, k, \ell \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \le k$ and $m \le \ell$ and let $x \in C_k$ and $y \in C_\ell$. Then \begin{align*} d_E(\bar{x}_m, \bar{y}_m) &\le d_E(x, y) + \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \varepsilon_i + \sum_{j=m}^{\ell-1} \varepsilon_j \end{align*}
assumptions: $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $A \subseteq E$ with $C_n \subseteq A$
$m, k, \ell \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \le k$ and $m \le \ell$ and let $x \in C_k$ and $y \in C_\ell$
conclusions: d_E(\bar{x}_m, \bar{y}_m) &\le d_E(x, y) + \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \varepsilon_i + \sum_{j=m}^{\ell-1} \varepsilon_j
nodes.label: lem:dist_chainingSequence_le

nodes.name: Proof of Distance between chaining sequences
nodes.statement: Triangle inequality and Lemma~\ref{lem:dist_chainingSequence_le_sum}.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality and the distance-along-chain bound for both points.

nodes.name: Distance between chaining sequences for geometric scales
nodes.statement: For $\varepsilon_n = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n}$, with the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:dist_chainingSequence_le}, we have \begin{align*} d_E(\bar{x}_m, \bar{y}_m) &\le d_E(x, y) + \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+2} \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For $\varepsilon_n = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n}$, with the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:dist_chainingSequence_le}
conclusions: d_E(\bar{x}_m, \bar{y}_m) &\le d_E(x, y) + \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+2}
nodes.label: cor:dist_chainingSequence_pow_two_le

nodes.name: Closed ball in a subset
nodes.statement: For $t \in V \subseteq T$ and $u\ge 0$, we denote by $B_V(t, u)$ the closed ball with center $t$ and radius $u$ in $V$. That is, $B_V(t, u) = \{s \in V \mid d_T(s, t) \le u\}$.

nodes.name: Log-size radius
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a finite subset of a metric space and let $t \in V$ and $a > 1$, $c > 0$. Let the \emph{log-size radius} of $t$ in $V$, denoted by $r_{V,t}$, be the smallest positive integer $r$ such that $\vert B_V(t, r c) \vert \le a^{r}$.
differentia: $\vert B_V(t, r c) \vert \le a^{r}$
nodes.label: def:logSizeRadius

nodes.name: Lower bound at the log-size radius
nodes.statement: $a^{r_{V,t}-1} \le \vert B_V(t, (r_{V,t}-1)c) \vert$~.
nodes.label: lem:card_logSizeRadius_ge

nodes.name: Upper bound at the log-size radius
nodes.statement: $\vert B_V(t, r_{V,t}c) \vert \le a^{r_{V,t}}$~.
nodes.label: lem:card_logSizeRadius_le

nodes.name: Log-size ball sequence
nodes.statement: Let $(T,d_T)$ be a metric space and let $J \subseteq T$ be finite, $a,c \in \mathbb R_+$ with $a \ge 1$ and $n \in \{1, 2, ...\}$ such that $|J| \le a^n$. An log-size ball sequence for $(J, a, c, n)$ is a sequence of $(V_i, t_i, r_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $V_0 = J$, $t_0$ is an arbitrary point in $J$, \item for all $i$, $r_i$ is the log-size radius of $t_i$ in $V_i$, \item $V_{i+1} = V_i \setminus B_{V_i}(t_i, (r_i - 1)c)$, $t_{i+1}$ is arbitrarily chosen in $V_{i+1}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Greedy sequence removing from $V_i$ the ball of radius $(r_i-1)c$ around $t_i$, where $r_i$ is the log-size radius.
nodes.label: def:logSizeBallSequence

nodes.name: Log-size ball sequence partitions J
nodes.statement: A log-size ball sequence gives a partition of $J$ into sets which are contained in balls of radius $(r_i - 1)c$ around $t_i$, and satisfy cardinality constraints.

nodes.name: Log-size radii are at most n
nodes.statement: The radius of a log-size ball sequence $(V_i, t_i, r_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ for $(J, a, c, n)$ satisfies $r_i \le n$ for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.label: lem:logSizeRadius_logSizeBallSequence_le

nodes.name: Proof of Log-size radii are at most n
nodes.statement: Since $|J| \le a^n$, we have $\vert B_{V_i}(t_i, n c) \vert \le \vert J \vert \le a^{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: The ball of radius $nc$ has at most $|J| \le a^n$ points, so the minimal radius is at most $n$.

nodes.name: Log-size ball sequence sets are decreasing
nodes.statement: The sets $V_i$ of a log-size ball sequence $(V_i, t_i, r_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ are a decreasing sequence of sets. That is, $V_{i+1} \subseteq V_i$ for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.label: lem:logSizeBallSequence_V_anti

nodes.name: Proof of Log-size ball sequence sets are decreasing
nodes.statement: $V_{i+1} = V_i \setminus B_{V_i}(t_i, (r_i - 1)c)$ hence $V_{i+1} \subseteq V_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the recursive definition $V_{i+1} = V_i \setminus B$.

nodes.name: Log-size ball sequence terminates
nodes.statement: For any log-size ball sequence $(V_i, t_i, r_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ for $(J, a, c, n)$, for all $k \ge \vert J \vert$, $V_k = \emptyset$.
nodes.label: lem:logSizeBallSequence_eq_zero

nodes.name: Proof of Log-size ball sequence terminates
nodes.statement: $V_{i+1} = V_i \setminus B_{V_i}(t_i, (r_i - 1)c)$ and since $t_i \in B_{V_i}(t_i, (r_i - 1)c)$, we have $\vert V_{i+1} \vert < \vert V_i \vert$ and the cardinal eventually reaches $0$, in at most $\vert J \vert$ steps.
nodes.statement_short: Each step removes at least $t_i$, so cardinality strictly decreases.

nodes.name: Log-size ball sequence balls are disjoint
nodes.statement: For $i \ne j$, the balls $B_{V_i}(t, (r_i-1)c)$ and $B_{V_j}(t_j, (r_j-1)c)$ of a log-size ball sequence $(V_i, t_i, r_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ are disjoint.
nodes.label: lem:logSizeBallSequence_disjoint_B

nodes.name: Proof of Log-size ball sequence balls are disjoint
nodes.statement: Assume w.l.o.g. that $i < j$. Then $B_{V_j}(t_j, (r_j-1)c) \subseteq V_j \subseteq V_{i+1}$. It suffices to show that $B_{V_i}(t_i, (r_i-1)c)$ and $V_{i+1}$ are disjoint. This follows from the definition of $V_{i+1} = V_i \setminus B_{V_i}(t_i, (r_i-1)c)$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $i<j$; the later ball lies in $V_{i+1}$, which is disjoint from the $i$-th removed ball.

nodes.name: WLOG i<j
nodes.statement: Assume w.l.o.g. that $i < j$. Then $B_{V_j}(t_j, (r_j-1)c) \subseteq V_j \subseteq V_{i+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $i<j$, so the $j$-th ball lies in $V_{i+1}$.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that $B_{V_i}(t_i, (r_i-1)c)$ and $V_{i+1}$ are disjoint.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to disjointness of the $i$-th ball and $V_{i+1}$.

nodes.name: By definition
nodes.statement: This follows from the definition of $V_{i+1} = V_i \setminus B_{V_i}(t_i, (r_i-1)c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition of $V_{i+1}$.

nodes.name: Pair set of a log-size ball sequence
nodes.statement: Let $(V_i, t_i, r_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a log-size ball sequence for $(J, a, c, n)$. For $i \in \mathbb{N}$, let $K_i = \{t_i\} \times B_{V_i}(t_i, r_i c)$ be the set of pairs $(t_i, s)$ for $s$ in the ball $B_{V_i}(t_i, r_i c)$. We define $K = \bigcup_{i=0}^{\vert J \vert-1} K_i$, set of all pairs from the log-size ball sequence.
nodes.statement_short: Pair set $K$: union over $i$ of pairs $(t_i, s)$ with $s$ in the ball of radius $r_i c$ around $t_i$ in $V_i$.
nodes.label: def:pairSet

nodes.name: Cardinality of the pair set
nodes.statement: The cardinal of the pair set $K$ of a log-size ball sequence for $(J, a, c, n)$ satisfies $|K| \le a |J|$.
nodes.label: lem:card_pairSet_le

nodes.name: Proof of Cardinality of the pair set
nodes.statement: Using Lemma~\ref{lem:card_logSizeRadius_le}, the cardinal of $K$ is bounded by \begin{align*} \vert K \vert &\le \sum_{i=0}^{m-1} \vert K_i \vert \le \sum_{i=0}^{m-1} a^{r_i} \: . \end{align*} Since the sets $B_{V_i}(t_i, (r_i-1)c)$ are disjoint by Lemma~\ref{lem:logSizeBallSequence_disjoint_B}, we can use Lemma~\ref{lem:card_logSizeRadius_ge} to get \begin{align*} \sum_{i=0}^{m-1} a^{r_i - 1} \le \sum_{i=0}^{m-1} \vert B_{V_i}(t_i, (r_i-1)c) \vert = \left\vert \bigcup_{i=0}^{m-1} B_{V_i}(t_i, (r_i-1)c) \right\vert \le \vert J \vert \: . \end{align*} We obtained the inequality $\vert K \vert \le a \vert J \vert$
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|K|$ by $\sum a^{r_i}$, then use disjointness of the removed balls and the log-size lower bound.

nodes.name: Bound by sum of a^{r_i}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|K|$ by $\sum a^{r_i}$.

nodes.name: Disjointness bound
nodes.statement_short: Disjoint balls give $\sum a^{r_i-1} \le |J|$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: We obtained the inequality $\vert K \vert \le a \vert J \vert$
nodes.statement_short: Combine to $|K| \le a|J|$.

nodes.name: Pairs in the pair set are close
nodes.statement: Let $(s, t)$ be a pair in the pair set $K$ of a log-size ball sequence for $(J, a, c, n)$. Then $d_T(s, t) \le c n$.
assumptions: $(s, t)$ be a pair in the pair set $K$ of a log-size ball sequence for $(J, a, c, n)$
conclusions: $d_T(s, t) \le c n$
nodes.label: lem:dist_le_of_mem_pairSet

nodes.name: Proof of Pairs in the pair set are close
nodes.statement: A pair $(t, s) \in K$ is of the form $(t_i, s)$ for $s \in B_V(t_i, r_i c)$ and satisfies \begin{align*} d_T(t_i, s) \le c r_i \le c n \: . \end{align*} The last inequality is from Lemma~\ref{lem:logSizeRadius_logSizeBallSequence_le}.
nodes.statement_short: Pairs lie in balls of radius $r_i c$ with $r_i \le n$.

nodes.name: Supremum over close pairs bounded via the pair set
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be the pair set of a log-size ball sequence $(V_i, t_i, r_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ for $(J, a, c, n)$. Then for any function $f : T \to E$ with $(E,d_E)$ a metric space, \begin{align*} \sup_{s,t\in J, d_T(s,t) \le c} d_E(f(s), f(t)) & \le 2 \sup_{(s,t) \in K} d_E(f(s), f(t)) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: $K$ be the pair set of a log-size ball sequence $(V_i, t_i, r_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ for $(J, a, c, n)$
any function $f : T \to E$ with $(E,d_E)$ a metric space
conclusions: \sup_{s,t\in J, d_T(s,t) \le c} d_E(f(s), f(t)) & \le 2 \sup_{(s,t) \in K} d_E(f(s), f(t))
nodes.label: lem:sup_dist_le_two_mul_sup_dist_pairSet

nodes.name: Proof of Supremum over close pairs bounded via the pair set
nodes.statement: Let $(s, t) \in J^2$ such that $d_T(s, t) \le c$. Then there exists a largest $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $s, t \in V_\ell$. Assume w.l.o.g. that $s \notin V_{\ell + 1}$. Then $s \in B_{V_\ell}(t_\ell, (r_\ell-1)c)$ (since $V_{\ell + 1} = V_\ell \setminus B_{V_\ell}(t_\ell, (r_\ell-1)c)$), which implies $d_T(s, t_\ell) \le (r_\ell - 1)c$. Since $d_T(s, t) \le c$, $d_T(t, t_\ell) \le d_T(t, s) + d_T(s, t_\ell) \le r_\ell c$, hence $t \in B_{V_\ell}(t_\ell, r_\ell c)$ and we have that both $s$ and $t$ are in $B_{V_\ell}(t_\ell, r_\ell c)$. Thus both $(t_\ell, s)$ and $(t_\ell, t)$ are in $K_\ell \subseteq K$. Finally \begin{align*} d_E(f(s), f(t)) &\le d_E(f(s), f(t_\ell)) + d_E(f(t_\ell), f(t)) \\ &\le 2\sup_{(s',t') \in K} d_E(f(s'), f(t')) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: For a close pair, locate the last set $V_\ell$ containing both; both points lie in the ball of $t_\ell$, then triangle inequality.

nodes.name: Fix a close pair
nodes.statement: Let $(s, t) \in J^2$ such that $d_T(s, t) \le c$. Then there exists a largest $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $s, t \in V_\ell$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a close pair and the last $V_\ell$ containing both.

nodes.name: s is in the removed ball
nodes.statement: Assume w.l.o.g. that $s \notin V_{\ell + 1}$. Then $s \in B_{V_\ell}(t_\ell, (r_\ell-1)c)$ (since $V_{\ell + 1} = V_\ell \setminus B_{V_\ell}(t_\ell, (r_\ell-1)c)$), which implies $d_T(s, t_\ell) \le (r_\ell - 1)c$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $s$ was removed at step $\ell$, so it is close to $t_\ell$.

nodes.name: Both pairs lie in K
nodes.statement: Since $d_T(s, t) \le c$, $d_T(t, t_\ell) \le d_T(t, s) + d_T(s, t_\ell) \le r_\ell c$, hence $t \in B_{V_\ell}(t_\ell, r_\ell c)$ and we have that both $s$ and $t$ are in $B_{V_\ell}(t_\ell, r_\ell c)$. Thus both $(t_\ell, s)$ and $(t_\ell, t)$ are in $K_\ell \subseteq K$.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality puts $t$ in the larger ball, so both pairs are in $K$.

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
nodes.statement:
Finally
\begin{align*}
  d_E(f(s), f(t))
  &\le d_E(f(s), f(t_\ell)) + d_E(f(t_\ell), f(t))
  \\
  &\le 2\sup_{(s',t') \in K} d_E(f(s'), f(t'))
  \: .
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality through $t_\ell$.

nodes.name: Pair reduction lemma
nodes.statement: Let $(T,d_T)$ be a metric space. Let $J \subseteq T$ be finite, $a > 1$, $c>0$ and $n \in \{1, 2, ...\}$ such that $|J| \le a^n$. Then, there is $K \subseteq J^2$ such that for any function $f : T \to E$ with $(E,d_E)$ a metric space, \begin{align} |K| & \le a |J| \:, \\ \forall (s,t) \in K, &\: d_T(s,t) \le c n \:, \\ \sup_{s,t\in J, d_T(s,t) \le c} d_E(f(s), f(t)) & \le 2 \sup_{(s,t) \in K} d_E(f(s), f(t)) \: . \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: A finite $J$ with $|J| \le a^n$ admits a pair set $K$ of size $\le a|J|$, with pairs at distance $\le cn$, controlling sup over $c$-close pairs.
assumptions: $(T,d_T)$ be a metric space
$J \subseteq T$ be finite, $a > 1$, $c>0$ and $n \in \{1, 2, ...\}$ such that $|J| \le a^n$
conclusions: there is $K \subseteq J^2$ such that for any function $f : T \to E$ with $(E,d_E)$ a metric space,
nodes.label: lem:pair_reduction

nodes.name: Pair set distance bound
nodes.statement: \forall (s,t) \in K, &\: d_T(s,t) \le c n \:,
nodes.label: eq:chain2

nodes.name: Pair reduction inequality
nodes.statement: \sup_{s,t\in J, d_T(s,t) \le c} d_E(f(s), f(t)) & \le 2 \sup_{(s,t) \in K} d_E(f(s), f(t)) \: .
nodes.label: eq:chain3

nodes.name: Proof of Pair reduction lemma
nodes.statement: Let $(V_i, t_i, r_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a log-size ball sequence for $(J, a, c, n)$. We show that its pair set satisfies the conditions of the lemma. Equation~\eqref{eq:chain1} is given by Lemma~\ref{lem:card_pairSet_le}. The second property~\eqref{eq:chain2} is Lemma~\ref{lem:dist_le_of_mem_pairSet}. Equation~\eqref{eq:chain3} was proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:sup_dist_le_two_mul_sup_dist_pairSet}.
nodes.statement_short: Take the pair set of a log-size ball sequence; the three properties are the three preceding lemmas.

nodes.name: Choose a log-size ball sequence
nodes.statement: Let $(V_i, t_i, r_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a log-size ball sequence for $(J, a, c, n)$. We show that its pair set satisfies the conditions of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Take the pair set of a log-size ball sequence.

nodes.name: Size bound
nodes.statement: Equation~\eqref{eq:chain1} is given by Lemma~\ref{lem:card_pairSet_le}.
nodes.statement_short: Cardinality from the pair-set lemma.

nodes.name: Distance bound
nodes.statement: The second property~\eqref{eq:chain2} is Lemma~\ref{lem:dist_le_of_mem_pairSet}.
nodes.statement_short: Distance bound lemma.

nodes.name: Supremum bound
nodes.statement: Equation~\eqref{eq:chain3} was proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:sup_dist_le_two_mul_sup_dist_pairSet}.
nodes.statement_short: Supremum bound lemma.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov condition
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a stochastic process, where $(T, d_T)$ and $(E, d_E)$ are pseudo-metric spaces and $(\Omega, \mathbb{P})$ is a measure space. Let $p, q > 0$. We say that $X$ satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$ if for all $s, t \in T$, $(X_s, X_t)$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable for the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $E^2$ and \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[d_E(X_s, X_t)^p] \le M d_T(s, t)^q \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: A process satisfies the Kolmogorov condition with exponents (p,q) and constant M if pairs are a.e. measurable and E[d(X_s,X_t)^p] <= M d(s,t)^q.
differentia: $(X_s, X_t)$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable for the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $E^2$
\begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[d_E(X_s, X_t)^p] \le M d_T(s, t)^q \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:IsKolmogorovProcess

nodes.name: Measurability condition in the Kolmogorov condition
nodes.statement: Remark: the measurability condition on the pair would be implied by the measurability of $X_t$ for all $t \in T$ if we assumed that $E$ is separable (\texttt{SecondCountableTopology} in Lean), which implies that the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on the product is equal to the product of the Borel $\sigma$-algebras. We follow \cite{kratschmer2023kolmogorov} and do not require separability.
nodes.statement_short: Pair measurability would follow from separability of E; following Krätschmer et al. separability is not assumed.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov process: a.e. equality at distance zero
nodes.statement: If $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$ and $s, t \in T$ are such that $d_T(s, t) = 0$, then $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. $d_E(X_s, X_t) = 0$.
assumptions: $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$
$s, t \in T$ are such that $d_T(s, t) = 0$
conclusions: $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. $d_E(X_s, X_t) = 0$
nodes.label: lem:IsKolmogorovProcess.edist_eq_zero

nodes.name: Proof of Kolmogorov process: a.e. equality at distance zero
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that $d_E(X_s, X_t)^p = 0$ almost everywhere, which is in turn implied by $\mathbb{E}[d_E(X_s, X_t)^p] \le M d_t(s, t)^q = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Markov-type argument: the p-th moment is bounded by M d(s,t)^q = 0, so the distance vanishes a.e.

nodes.name: Zero expected supremum on a countable zero-diameter set
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $T'$ be a countable subset of $T$ such that for all $s, t \in T'$, $d_T(s, t) = 0$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in T'} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &= 0 \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $T'$ be a countable subset of $T$ such that for all $s, t \in T'$, $d_T(s, t) = 0$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in T'} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &= 0 \: . \end{align*}
Let $T'$ be a countable subset of $T$ such that for all $s, t \in T'$, $d_T(s, t) = 0$.
conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in T'} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &= 0 \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:IsKolmogorovProcess.lintegral_sup_rpow_edist_eq_zero

nodes.name: Proof of Zero expected supremum on a countable zero-diameter set
nodes.statement: Since $T'$ is countable, we get from Lemma~\ref{lem:IsKolmogorovProcess.edist_eq_zero} that almost surely, for all $s, t \in T'$, $d_E(X_s, X_t)^p = 0$. In particular the expectation of the supremum is $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Countable union of null sets via the distance-zero lemma, so the supremum vanishes a.s.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov process is a.e. measurable
nodes.statement: If $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a function that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition, then for all $t \in T$, $X_t$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable.
assumptions: $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a function that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition
conclusions: for all $t \in T$, $X_t$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable
nodes.label: lem:IsKolmogorovProcess.aemeasurable

nodes.name: A.e. measurability of pairs in separable spaces
nodes.statement: If $E$ is separable and $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a process such that $X_t$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable for all $t \in T$, then for all $s, t \in T$, the pair $(X_s, X_t)$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable for the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $E^2$.
assumptions: $E$ is separable and $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a process such that $X_t$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable for all $t \in T$, then for all $s, t \in T$, the pair $(X_s, X_t)$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable for the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $E^2$.
$X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a process such that $X_t$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable for all $t \in T$
conclusions: for all $s, t \in T$, the pair $(X_s, X_t)$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable for the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $E^2$
nodes.label: lem:aemeasurable_pair_of_aemeasurable

nodes.name: A.e. measurability of the distance between values
nodes.statement: If $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition, then for all $s,t \in T$ the function $\omega \mapsto d_E(X_s(\omega), X_t(\omega))$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable.
assumptions: $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition
conclusions: for all $s,t \in T$ the function $\omega \mapsto d_E(X_s(\omega), X_t(\omega))$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable
nodes.label: lem:IsKolmogorovProcess.aemeasurable_edist

nodes.name: Expected supremum over a finite set of close pairs
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $C \subseteq T^2$ be a finite set such that for all $(s, t) \in C$, $d_T(s, t) \le \varepsilon$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{(s,t) \in C} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le \vert C \vert M \varepsilon^q \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $C \subseteq T^2$ be a finite set such that for all $(s, t) \in C$, $d_T(s, t) \le \varepsilon$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{(s,t) \in C} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le \vert C \vert M \varepsilon^q \: . \end{align*}
Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $C \subseteq T^2$ be a finite set such that for all $(s, t) \in C$, $d_T(s, t) \le \varepsilon$.
conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{(s,t) \in C} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le \vert C \vert M \varepsilon^q \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_card_mul_rpow

nodes.name: Proof of Expected supremum over a finite set of close pairs
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{(s,t) \in C} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{(s,t) \in C} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \\ &\le M \sum_{(s,t) \in C} d_T(s, t)^q \\ &\le \vert C \vert M \varepsilon^q \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the supremum by the sum, then apply the Kolmogorov condition termwise.

nodes.name: Expected supremum over pairs at bounded distance in a finite set
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $J \subseteq T$ be finite, $a, c \in \mathbb R_+$ with $a \ge 1$ and $n \in \{1, 2, ...\}$ such that $|J| \le a^n$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^p a |J| M (cn)^q \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $J \subseteq T$ be finite, $a, c \in \mathbb R_+$ with $a \ge 1$ and $n \in \{1, 2, ...\}$ such that $|J| \le a^n$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^p a |J| M (cn)^q \: . \end{align*}
Let $J \subseteq T$ be finite, $a, c \in \mathbb R_+$ with $a \ge 1$ and $n \in \{1, 2, ...\}$ such that $|J| \le a^n$.
conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^p a |J| M (cn)^q \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_of_dist_le

nodes.name: Proof of Expected supremum over pairs at bounded distance in a finite set
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:pair_reduction}, there exists $K \subseteq J^2$ such that \begin{align*} |K| & \le a |J| \:, \\ \forall (s,t) \in K, & \ d_T(s,t) \le c n \:, \\ \sup_{s,t\in J, d_T(s,t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t) & \le 2 \sup_{(s,t) \in K} d_E(X_s, X_t) \: . \end{align*} Hence for such a set $K$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^p \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{(s, t) \in K} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \: . \end{align*} Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_card_mul_rpow}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{(s, t) \in K} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le |K| M (cn)^q \le a |J| M (cn)^q \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Pair reduction to a set K of at most a|J| pairs, then the finite-set moment bound.

nodes.name: Pair reduction
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:pair_reduction}, there exists $K \subseteq J^2$ such that \begin{align*} |K| & \le a |J| \:, \\ \forall (s,t) \in K, & \ d_T(s,t) \le c n \:, \\ \sup_{s,t\in J, d_T(s,t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t) & \le 2 \sup_{(s,t) \in K} d_E(X_s, X_t) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Obtain a set K of at most a|J| pairs at distance <= cn controlling the supremum

nodes.name: Reduce to supremum over K
nodes.statement: Hence for such a set $K$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^p \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{(s, t) \in K} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the expectation by 2^p times the supremum over K

nodes.name: Apply finite-set moment bound
nodes.statement: Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_card_mul_rpow}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{(s, t) \in K} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le |K| M (cn)^q \le a |J| M (cn)^q \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the supremum over K by |K| M (cn)^q <= a|J| M (cn)^q

nodes.name: Strategy of the chaining bound
nodes.statement: We consider covers of $T$ at different scales. $C_n$ is a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $\varepsilon_n = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n}$. $T$ is equal to $C_k$ for some $k$ large enough, so the supremum over $T$ is a supremum at that scale $k$. We will change scale to some $m \le k$ that depends on the distance bound $\delta$ ($m$ is of order $\log_2 \delta$) and consider the supremum over $C_m$ (plus a term due to the scale change). Then for the supremum over a set in $C_m$, we use the reduction in the number of pairs of Lemma~\ref{lem:pair_reduction}.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: use dyadic covers C_n, change scale from the finest k to m ~ log2(delta), and apply pair reduction at scale m.
nodes.section: 5.3.2 Bound for a set of points that are close together

nodes.name: Scale change
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to E$. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $J \subseteq T$ with $C_n \subseteq J$. For $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t) &\le \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m}) + 2 \sup_{s \in C_k} d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_m}) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5.3.2 Bound for a set of points that are close together
nodes.statement_short: Triangle-inequality bound relating distances at scale k to distances between scale-m projections plus twice the projection error.
assumptions: Let $X : T \to E$. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $J \subseteq T$ with $C_n \subseteq J$. For $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t) &\le \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m}) + 2 \sup_{s \in C_k} d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_m}) \: . \end{align*}
Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $J \subseteq T$ with $C_n \subseteq J$.

For $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t) &\le \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m}) + 2 \sup_{s \in C_k} d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_m}) \: . \end{align*}
conclusions: \begin{align*} \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t) &\le \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m}) + 2 \sup_{s \in C_k} d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_m}) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:scale_change

nodes.name: Proof of Scale change
nodes.statement: By the triangle inequality, \begin{align*} d_E(X_s, X_t) &\le d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_m}) + d(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m}) + d_E(X_{\bar{t}_m}, X_t) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5.3.2 Bound for a set of points that are close together
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality through the scale-m projections.

nodes.name: Scale change, p-th power version
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to E$. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $J \subseteq T$ with $C_n \subseteq J$. For $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p &\le 2^p \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p + 4^p \sup_{s \in C_k} d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_m})^p \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5.3.2 Bound for a set of points that are close together
assumptions: Let $X : T \to E$. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $J \subseteq T$ with $C_n \subseteq J$. For $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p &\le 2^p \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p + 4^p \sup_{s \in C_k} d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_m})^p \: . \end{align*}
Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers, $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $J \subseteq T$ with $C_n \subseteq J$.

For $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p &\le 2^p \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p + 4^p \sup_{s \in C_k} d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_m})^p \: . \end{align*}
conclusions: \begin{align*} \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p &\le 2^p \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p + 4^p \sup_{s \in C_k} d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_m})^p \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:scale_change_rpow

nodes.name: Proof of Scale change, p-th power version
nodes.statement: This is Lemma~\ref{lem:scale_change}, together with the fact that for $a, b \ge 0$, \begin{align*} (a + b)^p \le (2\max(a,b))^p = 2^p \max(a^p,b^p) \le 2^p (a^p + b^p) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5.3.2 Bound for a set of points that are close together
nodes.statement_short: Scale change lemma plus the elementary inequality (a+b)^p <= 2^p(a^p+b^p).

nodes.name: First term bound on a minimal cover
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $C$ be a finite $\varepsilon$-cover of $J \subseteq T$ with $C \subseteq J$, with minimal cardinal. Then for $c \ge 0$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C; d_T(s, t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} M \left(2 c \log_2 N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \right)^q N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \: . \end{align*} Note the logarithm has base $2$.
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $C$ be a finite $\varepsilon$-cover of $J \subseteq T$ with $C \subseteq J$, with minimal cardinal. Then for $c \ge 0$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C; d_T(s, t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} M \left(2 c \log_2 N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \right)^q N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \: . \end{align*} Note the logarithm has base $2$.
Let $C$ be a finite $\varepsilon$-cover of $J \subseteq T$ with $C \subseteq J$, with minimal cardinal.
$c \ge 0$
conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C; d_T(s, t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} M \left(2 c \log_2 N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \right)^q N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_cover_of_dist_le

nodes.name: Proof of First term bound on a minimal cover
nodes.statement: Let $\bar{r} = 1 + \log_2 N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J)$. Then \begin{align*} \vert C \vert = N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \le 2^{\bar{r}} \: . \end{align*} By Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_of_dist_le} with $J = C$, $a = 2$, $c = c$, $n = \bar{r}$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C; d_T(s, t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} |C| M (c \bar{r})^q = 2^{p+1} M (c \bar{r})^q N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \: . \end{align*} Suppose $N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \ge 2$ (if it equals one the result is trivial). Then $\bar{r} \le 2 \log_2 N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J)$. \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C; d_T(s, t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} M \left(2 c \log_2 N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \right)^q N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the bounded-distance lemma with a=2 and n = 1 + log2 N, then bound that n by 2 log2 N.

nodes.name: Define r-bar
nodes.statement: Let $\bar{r} = 1 + \log_2 N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J)$. Then \begin{align*} \vert C \vert = N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \le 2^{\bar{r}} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Set r-bar = 1 + log2 N and note |C| <= 2^{r-bar}

nodes.name: Apply bounded-distance lemma
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_of_dist_le} with $J = C$, $a = 2$, $c = c$, $n = \bar{r}$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C; d_T(s, t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} |C| M (c \bar{r})^q = 2^{p+1} M (c \bar{r})^q N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the bounded-distance lemma with a = 2, n = r-bar

nodes.name: Bound r-bar by 2 log2 N
nodes.statement: Suppose $N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \ge 2$ (if it equals one the result is trivial). Then $\bar{r} \le 2 \log_2 N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J)$. \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C; d_T(s, t) \le c} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} M \left(2 c \log_2 N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \right)^q N^{int}_{\varepsilon}(J) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: For N >= 2, r-bar <= 2 log2 N gives the claim

nodes.name: First term bound after rescaling
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $J \subseteq T$ with $C_n \subseteq J$ for $\varepsilon_n = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n}$, with minimal cardinal. Suppose $\varepsilon_0 < \infty$, let $\delta \in (0, 4 \varepsilon_0]$ and let $m$ be a natural number such that $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \le \delta$ and $\delta \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+2}$. Then for $k \ge m$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} M \left(16 \delta \log_2 N^{int}_{\delta/4}(J) \right)^q N^{int}_{\delta/4}(J) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $J \subseteq T$ with $C_n \subseteq J$ for $\varepsilon_n = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n}$, with minimal cardinal. Suppose $\varepsilon_0 < \infty$, let $\delta \in (0, 4 \varepsilon_0]$ and let $m$ be a natural number such that $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \le \delta$ and $\delta \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+2}$. Then for $k \ge m$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} M \left(16 \delta \log_2 N^{int}_{\delta/4}(J) \right)^q N^{int}_{\delta/4}(J) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof of First term bound after rescaling
nodes.statement: By definition of $m$, $\delta \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+2}$. For $s, t \in C_k$ with $d_T(s, t) \le \delta$, $d_T(\bar{s}_m, \bar{t}_m) \le \delta + \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+2} \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+3}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:dist_chainingSequence_pow_two_le}). It thus suffices to get a bound on $\mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_m; d_T(s, t) \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+3}} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right]$. We can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_cover_of_dist_le} with $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_m$, $c = \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+3}$. We obtain \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_m; d_T(s, t) \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+3}} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} M \left(16 \varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \log_2 N^{int}_{\varepsilon_m}(J) \right)^q N^{int}_{\varepsilon_m}(J) \: . \end{align*} By definition of $m$, $\varepsilon_m = \varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \ge \delta/4$, hence $N^{int}_{\varepsilon_m}(J) \le N^{int}_{\delta / 4}(J)$. Finally, by definition of $m$ we have $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \le \delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound distances of scale-m projections, reduce to a supremum over C_m and apply the first-term cover bound with eps = eps_m.

nodes.name: Distance of projections
nodes.statement: By definition of $m$, $\delta \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+2}$. For $s, t \in C_k$ with $d_T(s, t) \le \delta$, $d_T(\bar{s}_m, \bar{t}_m) \le \delta + \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+2} \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+3}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:dist_chainingSequence_pow_two_le}).
nodes.statement_short: Projections of close points are within eps_0 2^{-m+3}

nodes.name: Reduction to C_m
nodes.statement: It thus suffices to get a bound on $\mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_m; d_T(s, t) \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+3}} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right]$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to bounding the supremum over C_m at distance eps_0 2^{-m+3}

nodes.name: Apply first-term cover bound
nodes.statement: We can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_cover_of_dist_le} with $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_m$, $c = \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+3}$. We obtain \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_m; d_T(s, t) \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+3}} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} M \left(16 \varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \log_2 N^{int}_{\varepsilon_m}(J) \right)^q N^{int}_{\varepsilon_m}(J) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the cover bound with eps = eps_m

nodes.name: Compare covering numbers
nodes.statement: By definition of $m$, $\varepsilon_m = \varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \ge \delta/4$, hence $N^{int}_{\varepsilon_m}(J) \le N^{int}_{\delta / 4}(J)$.
nodes.statement_short: eps_m >= delta/4 so N_{eps_m} <= N_{delta/4}

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Finally, by definition of $m$ we have $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \le \delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Use eps_0 2^{-m} <= delta to finish

nodes.name: Expected supremum of consecutive chaining increments
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers and $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $C_n \subseteq T$. Then for $j < k$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_j}, X_{\bar{t}_{j+1}})^p \right] &\le \vert C_{j+1} \vert M \varepsilon_j^q \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers and $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $C_n \subseteq T$. Then for $j < k$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_j}, X_{\bar{t}_{j+1}})^p \right] &\le \vert C_{j+1} \vert M \varepsilon_j^q \: . \end{align*}

$j < k$
conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_j}, X_{\bar{t}_{j+1}})^p \right] &\le \vert C_{j+1} \vert M \varepsilon_j^q \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_succ

nodes.name: Proof of Expected supremum of consecutive chaining increments
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_j}, X_{\bar{t}_{j+1}})^p \right] &\le \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{u \in C_{j+1}} d_E(X_{\bar{u}_j}, X_{u})^p \right] \: . \end{align*} We then apply Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_card_mul_rpow} to the set $C = \{(\bar{u}_j, u) \mid u \in C_{j+1}\}$, which satisfies the condition $d_T(\bar{u}_j, u) \le \varepsilon_j$ and has cardinal $\vert C_{j+1} \vert$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to pairs (u_j, u) for u in C_{j+1} and apply the finite-set moment bound.

nodes.name: Chaining bound via Minkowski (p >= 1)
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a stochastic process. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers and $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $C_n \subseteq T$. For $p \ge 1$ and $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le \left(\sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \left( \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}})^p\right] \right)^{1/p}\right)^p \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a stochastic process. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers and $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $C_n \subseteq T$. For $p \ge 1$ and $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le \left(\sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \left( \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}})^p\right] \right)^{1/p}\right)^p \: . \end{align*}

$p \ge 1$ and $m \le k$

nodes.label: lem:integral_sup_dist_le_sum_rpow

nodes.name: Proof of Chaining bound via Minkowski (p >= 1)
nodes.statement: By the triangle inequality, \begin{align*} \sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p &\le \sup_{t \in C_k} \left( \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}}) \right)^p \\ &\le \left( \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}}) \right)^p \: . \end{align*} We thus have \begin{align*} \left(\mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right]\right)^{1/p} &\le \left(\mathbb{E} \left[\left( \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}}) \right)^p\right]\right)^{1/p} \: . \end{align*} And then, by Minkowski's inequality, since $p \ge 1$, \begin{align*} \left(\mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right]\right)^{1/p} &\le \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \left( \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}})^p \right] \right)^{1/p} \: . \end{align*} Finally, we raise to the $p$-th power to obtain the result.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality along the chain, then Minkowski's inequality in L^p.

nodes.name: Triangle inequality along the chain
nodes.statement: By the triangle inequality, \begin{align*} \sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p &\le \sup_{t \in C_k} \left( \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}}) \right)^p \\ &\le \left( \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}}) \right)^p \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the distance to the scale-m projection by the chain sum

nodes.name: Take L^p norms
nodes.statement: We thus have \begin{align*} \left(\mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right]\right)^{1/p} &\le \left(\mathbb{E} \left[\left( \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}}) \right)^p\right]\right)^{1/p} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Take p-th moments and p-th roots

nodes.name: Minkowski's inequality
nodes.statement: And then, by Minkowski's inequality, since $p \ge 1$, \begin{align*} \left(\mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right]\right)^{1/p} &\le \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \left( \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}})^p \right] \right)^{1/p} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Minkowski to the sum

nodes.name: Raise to the p-th power
nodes.statement: Finally, we raise to the $p$-th power to obtain the result.
nodes.statement_short: Raise to the p-th power

nodes.name: Second term bound for minimal covers (p >= 1)
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers in $(0, \mathrm{diam}(T))$ and $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $C_n \subseteq T$, and with minimal cardinality. Suppose that $T$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$. Then for $p \ge 1$ and $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le M c_1 \left( \sum_{j=m}^{k-1} \varepsilon_{j+1}^{-d/p} \varepsilon_j^{q/p} \right)^p \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers in $(0, \mathrm{diam}(T))$ and $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $C_n \subseteq T$, and with minimal cardinality. Suppose that $T$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$. Then for $p \ge 1$ and $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le M c_1 \left( \sum_{j=m}^{k-1} \varepsilon_{j+1}^{-d/p} \varepsilon_j^{q/p} \right)^p \: . \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof of Second term bound for minimal covers (p >= 1)
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_sum}, we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le M \left( \sum_{j=m}^{k-1} \vert C_{j+1} \vert^{1/p} \varepsilon_j^{q/p} \right)^p \: . \end{align*} Then by the minimality of the cardinality of $C_n$ and the bounded internal covering number hypothesis, we have \begin{align*} \vert C_{j+1} \vert &\le N^{int}_{\varepsilon_{j+1}}(T) \le c_1 \varepsilon_{j+1}^{-d} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Previous bound plus |C_{j+1}| <= N^int <= c_1 eps^{-d} from minimality and the covering hypothesis.

nodes.name: Second term bound for dyadic scales (p >= 1)
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_of_minimal_cover}, for $\varepsilon_n = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n}$, then for $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m + 1})^{q - d} \frac{1}{\left( 2^{(q -d)/p} - 1\right)^p} \: . \end{align*}

conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m + 1})^{q - d} \frac{1}{\left( 2^{(q -d)/p} - 1\right)^p} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_of_minimal_cover_two

nodes.name: Proof of Second term bound for dyadic scales (p >= 1)
nodes.statement: Applying first Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_of_minimal_cover}, we get \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^d M c_1 \varepsilon_0^{q - d} \left( \sum_{j=m}^{k-1} 2^{- j(q - d)/p} \right)^p \\ &= 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m})^{q - d} \left( \sum_{j=0}^{k-m-1} 2^{- j(q - d)/p} \right)^p \\ &\le 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m})^{q - d} \left( \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} 2^{- j(q - d)/p} \right)^p \\ &= 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m})^{q - d} \frac{1}{(1 - 2^{-(q-d)/p})^p} \\ &= 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m+1})^{q - d} \frac{1}{(2^{(q-d)/p} - 1)^p} \: . \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof of Chaining bound via subadditivity (p <= 1)
nodes.statement: For $0 < p \le 1$, the power function is sub-additive, i.e. for $a, b \ge 0$, \begin{align*} (a + b)^p \le a^p + b^p \: . \end{align*} We can thus apply the triangle inequality to obtain \begin{align*} \sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p &\le \sup_{t \in C_k} \left(\sum_{i=m}^{k-1} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}})\right)^p \\ &\le \sup_{t \in C_k} \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}})^p \\ &\le \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_{\bar{t}_i}, X_{\bar{t}_{i+1}})^p \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Subadditivity of x -> x^p for p <= 1 combined with the triangle inequality along the chain.

nodes.name: Second term bound for minimal covers (p <= 1)
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers in $(0, \mathrm{diam}(T)]$ and $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $C_n \subseteq T$, and with minimal cardinality. Suppose that $T$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$. Then for $p \le 1$ and $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le M c_1 \sum_{j=m}^{k-1} \varepsilon_{j+1}^{-d} \varepsilon_j^{q} \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of positive numbers in $(0, \mathrm{diam}(T)]$ and $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $C_n \subseteq T$, and with minimal cardinality. Suppose that $T$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$. Then for $p \le 1$ and $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le M c_1 \sum_{j=m}^{k-1} \varepsilon_{j+1}^{-d} \varepsilon_j^{q} \: . \end{align*}
