nodes.label: lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_of_minimal_cover_of_le_one

nodes.name: Proof of Second term bound for minimal covers (p <= 1)
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_sum_of_le_one}, we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le M \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \vert C_{j+1} \vert \varepsilon_j^{q} \: . \end{align*} Then by the minimality of the cardinality of $C_n$ and the bounded internal covering number hypothesis, we have \begin{align*} \vert C_{j+1} \vert &= N^{int}_{\varepsilon_{j+1}}(T) \le c_1 \varepsilon_{j+1}^{-d} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Previous bound plus |C_{j+1}| = N^int <= c_1 eps^{-d}.

nodes.name: Second term bound for dyadic scales (p <= 1)
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_of_minimal_cover_of_le_one}, for $\varepsilon_n = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n}$, then for $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m + 1})^{q - d} \frac{1}{\left( 2^{(q -d)} - 1\right)} \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Under the assumptions of Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_of_minimal_cover_of_le_one}, for $\varepsilon_n = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n}$
conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m + 1})^{q - d} \frac{1}{\left( 2^{(q -d)} - 1\right)} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_of_minimal_cover_two_of_le_one

nodes.name: Proof of Second term bound for dyadic scales (p <= 1)
nodes.statement: Applying first Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_le_of_minimal_cover_of_le_one}, we get \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m})^{q-d}\sum_{j=0}^{k-m-1} 2^{- j (q - d)} \\ &\le 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m})^{q-d}\sum_{j=0}^{+\infty} 2^{- j (q - d)} \\ &= 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m})^{q-d} \frac{1}{1 - 2^{-(q - d)}} \\ &= 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m+1})^{q-d} \frac{1}{2^{(q - d)} - 1} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Specialize to dyadic scales and sum the geometric series.

nodes.name: Constant C_p
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} C_p = \max\left\{\frac{1}{\left( 2^{(q -d)/p} - 1\right)^p}, \frac{1}{\left( 2^{(q -d)} - 1\right)} \right\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: C_p is the larger of the two geometric-series constants from the cases p >= 1 and p <= 1.
nodes.label: def:Cp

nodes.name: Second term bound for any p > 0
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$. Let $C_n$ a finite $(\varepsilon_0 2^{-n})$-cover of $T$ for $\varepsilon_0 \le \mathrm{diam}(T)$ with $C_n \subseteq T$, and with minimal cardinality. Suppose that $T$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$. Then for $m \le k$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m + 1})^{q - d} C_p \: . \end{align*}

Suppose that $T$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$. Suppose that $T$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$.

nodes.label: lem:second_term_bound

nodes.name: Proof of Second term bound for any p > 0
nodes.statement: This is the max of the two bounds obtained $p \ge 1$ and $p \le 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the maximum of the bounds for p >= 1 and p <= 1.

nodes.name: Supremum over a fine cover equals supremum over the set
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$ and let $J$ be a finite subset of $T$. Let $C$ be an $\varepsilon$-cover of $J$ with $C \subseteq J$. If $\varepsilon < \inf_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t)>0} d_T(s, t)$ then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$ and let $J$ be a finite subset of $T$. Let $C$ be an $\varepsilon$-cover of $J$ with $C \subseteq J$. If $\varepsilon < \inf_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t)>0} d_T(s, t)$ then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \end{align*}
let $J$ be a finite subset of $T$
Let $C$ be an $\varepsilon$-cover of $J$ with $C \subseteq J$.
$\varepsilon < \inf_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t)>0} d_T(s, t)$
conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:lintegral_sup_cover_eq_of_lt_iInf_dist

nodes.name: Proof of Supremum over a fine cover equals supremum over the set
nodes.statement: First, remark that $C$ is actually a $0$-cover of $J$. For $s, t \in J$, let $s', t' \in C$ be such that $d_T(s, s') = 0$ and $d_T(t, t') = 0$. Then by the triangle inequality, \begin{align*} d_E(X_s, X_t) &\le d_E(X_s, X_{s'}) + d_E(X_{s'}, X_{t'}) + d_E(X_t, X_{t'}) \end{align*} and by Lemma~\ref{lem:IsKolmogorovProcess.edist_eq_zero}, we have $d_E(X_s, X_{s'}) = 0$ and $d_E(X_t, X_{t'}) = 0$ almost surely, hence $d_E(X_s, X_t) \le d_E(X_{s'}, X_{t'})$. Since $J$ is finite, almost surely we have that inequality for all pairs $(s, t) \in J$ and their corresponding $(s', t') \in C$. Note that $d_T(s', t') = d_T(s, t)$, hence $d_T(s, t) \le \delta$ is equivalent to $d_T(s', t') \le \delta$. We obtain \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{s'}, X_{t'})^p \right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s', t') \le \delta} d_E(X_{s'}, X_{t'})^p \right] \\ &\le \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \: . \end{align*} The reverse inequality holds because $C$ is a subset of $J$.
nodes.statement_short: C is a 0-cover; replace points by cover points at distance 0, which a.s. carry equal values, and compare suprema both ways.

nodes.name: C is a 0-cover
nodes.statement: First, remark that $C$ is actually a $0$-cover of $J$.
nodes.statement_short: Observe C is a 0-cover of J

nodes.name: Choose representatives
nodes.statement: For $s, t \in J$, let $s', t' \in C$ be such that $d_T(s, s') = 0$ and $d_T(t, t') = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick s', t' in C at distance 0

nodes.name: Compare distances
nodes.statement: Then by the triangle inequality, \begin{align*} d_E(X_s, X_t) &\le d_E(X_s, X_{s'}) + d_E(X_{s'}, X_{t'}) + d_E(X_t, X_{t'}) \end{align*} and by Lemma~\ref{lem:IsKolmogorovProcess.edist_eq_zero}, we have $d_E(X_s, X_{s'}) = 0$ and $d_E(X_t, X_{t'}) = 0$ almost surely, hence $d_E(X_s, X_t) \le d_E(X_{s'}, X_{t'})$.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality and a.s. equality at distance 0 give d(X_s,X_t) <= d(X_s',X_t')

nodes.name: Simultaneous a.s. bound
nodes.statement: Since $J$ is finite, almost surely we have that inequality for all pairs $(s, t) \in J$ and their corresponding $(s', t') \in C$.
nodes.statement_short: Finiteness gives the inequality for all pairs simultaneously a.s.

nodes.name: Distances preserved
nodes.statement: Note that $d_T(s', t') = d_T(s, t)$, hence $d_T(s, t) \le \delta$ is equivalent to $d_T(s', t') \le \delta$.
nodes.statement_short: The distance constraint transfers to the representatives

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: We obtain \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{s'}, X_{t'})^p \right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J; d_T(s', t') \le \delta} d_E(X_{s'}, X_{t'})^p \right] \\ &\le \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Supremum over J is at most supremum over C

nodes.name: Reverse inequality
nodes.statement: The reverse inequality holds because $C$ is a subset of $J$.
nodes.statement_short: Reverse inequality since C is a subset of J

nodes.name: Finite set bound for large distance threshold
nodes.statement: Suppose that $T$ is a finite set with bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$. Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$, with $q > d$ and $p > 0$. For all $\delta \ge 4\mathrm{diam}(T)$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in T; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \le 4^p 2^q M c_1 \delta^{q - d} C_p \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Suppose that $T$ is a finite set with bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$.
Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$, with $q > d$ and $p > 0$.
For all $\delta \ge 4\mathrm{diam}(T)$
conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in T; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \le 4^p 2^q M c_1 \delta^{q - d} C_p \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: thm:finite_set_bound_of_dist_le_of_diam_le

nodes.name: Proof of Finite set bound for large distance threshold
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon_0 = \mathrm{diam}(T)$. For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $C_n \subseteq T$ for $\varepsilon_n = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n}$, with minimal cardinal. Let $k$ be a natural number such that $\varepsilon_0 2^{-k} < \inf_{s, t \in T; d_T(s,t)>0} d_T(s, t)$, which exists since $T$ is finite. By Lemma~\ref{lem:lintegral_sup_cover_eq_of_lt_iInf_dist}, the supremum over $T$ can be replaced by a supremum over $C_k$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:scale_change_rpow}, \begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \\ &\le 2^p \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_0}, X_{\bar{t}_0})^p \right] + 4^p \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s \in C_k} d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_0})^p \right] \: . \end{align*} Since $\varepsilon_0 = \mathrm{diam}(T)$, $C_0$ is a singleton and $d_E(X_{\bar{s}_0}, X_{\bar{t}_0}) = 0$ for all $s, t$. We thus have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_0}, X_{\bar{t}_0})^p \right] &= 0 \: . \end{align*} By Lemma~\ref{lem:second_term_bound}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_0})^p \right] &\le 2^q M c_1 \varepsilon_0^{q - d} C_p \le 2^q M c_1 \delta^{q - d} C_p \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Chaining with eps_0 = diam(T): scale change to scale 0 where C_0 is a singleton, then the second-term bound.

nodes.name: Dyadic covers
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon_0 = \mathrm{diam}(T)$. For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $C_n \subseteq T$ for $\varepsilon_n = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n}$, with minimal cardinal.
nodes.statement_short: Set eps_0 = diam(T) and take minimal dyadic covers

nodes.name: Reduce to finest cover
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be a natural number such that $\varepsilon_0 2^{-k} < \inf_{s, t \in T; d_T(s,t)>0} d_T(s, t)$, which exists since $T$ is finite. By Lemma~\ref{lem:lintegral_sup_cover_eq_of_lt_iInf_dist}, the supremum over $T$ can be replaced by a supremum over $C_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose k finer than all positive distances and replace T by C_k

nodes.name: Scale change to scale 0
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{cor:scale_change_rpow}, \begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \\ &\le 2^p \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_0}, X_{\bar{t}_0})^p \right] + 4^p \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s \in C_k} d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_0})^p \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the scale change bound with m = 0

nodes.name: First term vanishes
nodes.statement: Since $\varepsilon_0 = \mathrm{diam}(T)$, $C_0$ is a singleton and $d_E(X_{\bar{s}_0}, X_{\bar{t}_0}) = 0$ for all $s, t$. We thus have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_0}, X_{\bar{t}_0})^p \right] &= 0 \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: C_0 is a singleton so the first term is 0

nodes.name: Second term bound
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:second_term_bound}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_0})^p \right] &\le 2^q M c_1 \varepsilon_0^{q - d} C_p \le 2^q M c_1 \delta^{q - d} C_p \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the second term with the second-term lemma

nodes.name: Finite set bound for small distance threshold
nodes.statement: Suppose that $T$ is a finite set with bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$. Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$, with $q > d$ and $p > 0$. For all $\delta \in (0, 4\mathrm{diam}(T)]$, \begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in T; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \\ &\le 2^{2p+4q+1} M \delta^{q-d} \left(\delta^d \left(\log_2 N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \right)^q N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) + c_1 C_p\right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Chaining bound on E[sup over pairs at distance <= delta of d(X_s,X_t)^p] for a finite T, delta <= 4 diam(T).
assumptions: Suppose that $T$ is a finite set with bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$.
Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$, with $q > d$ and $p > 0$.
For all $\delta \in (0, 4\mathrm{diam}(T)]$
conclusions: \begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in T; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \\ &\le 2^{2p+4q+1} M \delta^{q-d} \left(\delta^d \left(\log_2 N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \right)^q N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) + c_1 C_p\right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: thm:finite_set_bound_of_dist_le_of_le_diam

nodes.name: Proof of Finite set bound for small distance threshold
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon_0 = \mathrm{diam}(T)$. For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $C_n \subseteq T$ for $\varepsilon_n = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n}$, with minimal cardinal. Let $k$ be a natural number such that $\varepsilon_0 2^{-k} < \inf_{s, t \in T; d_T(s,t)>0} d_T(s, t)$, which exists since $T$ is finite. If $\delta \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-k}$, then $\{(s, t) \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta\} = \{(s, t) \mid s,t \in C_k, d_T(s,t) = 0\}$ and the inequality holds trivially (by Lemma~\ref{lem:IsKolmogorovProcess.lintegral_sup_rpow_edist_eq_zero}). We can thus assume $\delta > \varepsilon_0 2^{-k}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:lintegral_sup_cover_eq_of_lt_iInf_dist}, the supremum over $T$ can be replaced by a supremum over $C_k$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:scale_change_rpow}, for any $m \le k$, \begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \\ &\le 2^p \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] + 4^p \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s \in C_k} d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_m})^p \right] \: . \end{align*} \emph{First term} We have $\delta \le 4\varepsilon_0$ by assumption. Let $n_2 = \lfloor \log_2(4\varepsilon_0/\delta) \rfloor$ and $m = \min\{n_2, k\}$. If $m = n_2$ then $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n_2} < \delta/2$. Otherwise, $m = k$ and $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} = \varepsilon_0 2^{-k} < \delta$ as argued at the start of the proof. We thus get $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \le \delta$. We can also verify that $\delta \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-n_2+2} \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+2}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_cover_rescale}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} M \left(16 \delta \log_2 N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \right)^q N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \: . \end{align*} \emph{Second term} By Lemma~\ref{lem:second_term_bound} and then the inequality $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \le \delta$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m+1})^{q - d} C_p \\ &\le 2^q M c_1 \delta^{q - d} C_p \: . \end{align*} Putting the two terms together, we obtain \begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \\ &\le 4^p M \left(4\left(16 \delta \log_2 N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \right)^q N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) + 2^q c_1 \delta^{q - d} C_p\right) \\ &\le 2^{2p+4q+1} M \delta^{q-d} \left(\delta^d \left(\log_2 N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \right)^q N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) + c_1 C_p\right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Chaining argument: reduce to a fine cover C_k, split by scale change at a scale m ~ log2(1/delta) into a first term (pair reduction) and a second term (chaining sum).

nodes.name: Dyadic covers
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon_0 = \mathrm{diam}(T)$. For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $C_n$ a finite $\varepsilon_n$-cover of $T$ with $C_n \subseteq T$ for $\varepsilon_n = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n}$, with minimal cardinal.
nodes.statement_short: Set eps_0 = diam(T) and take minimal dyadic covers

nodes.name: Trivial case of small delta
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be a natural number such that $\varepsilon_0 2^{-k} < \inf_{s, t \in T; d_T(s,t)>0} d_T(s, t)$, which exists since $T$ is finite. If $\delta \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-k}$, then $\{(s, t) \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta\} = \{(s, t) \mid s,t \in C_k, d_T(s,t) = 0\}$ and the inequality holds trivially (by Lemma~\ref{lem:IsKolmogorovProcess.lintegral_sup_rpow_edist_eq_zero}). We can thus assume $\delta > \varepsilon_0 2^{-k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose k; if delta <= eps_0 2^{-k} the bound is trivial, so assume otherwise

nodes.name: Reduce to finest cover
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:lintegral_sup_cover_eq_of_lt_iInf_dist}, the supremum over $T$ can be replaced by a supremum over $C_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace the supremum over T by one over C_k

nodes.name: Scale change
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{cor:scale_change_rpow}, for any $m \le k$, \begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \\ &\le 2^p \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] + 4^p \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s \in C_k} d_E(X_s, X_{\bar{s}_m})^p \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Split into a first term at scale m and a second term

nodes.name: First term
nodes.statement: \emph{First term} We have $\delta \le 4\varepsilon_0$ by assumption. Let $n_2 = \lfloor \log_2(4\varepsilon_0/\delta) \rfloor$ and $m = \min\{n_2, k\}$. If $m = n_2$ then $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n_2} < \delta/2$. Otherwise, $m = k$ and $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} = \varepsilon_0 2^{-k} < \delta$ as argued at the start of the proof. We thus get $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \le \delta$. We can also verify that $\delta \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-n_2+2} \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+2}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_cover_rescale}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} M \left(16 \delta \log_2 N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \right)^q N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Choose m ~ log2(4 eps_0/delta) and bound the first term

nodes.name: Choose the scale m
nodes.statement: We have $\delta \le 4\varepsilon_0$ by assumption. Let $n_2 = \lfloor \log_2(4\varepsilon_0/\delta) \rfloor$ and $m = \min\{n_2, k\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define n_2 and m = min(n_2, k)

nodes.name: Case m = n_2
nodes.statement: If $m = n_2$ then $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} = \varepsilon_0 2^{-n_2} < \delta/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Case m = n_2

nodes.name: Case m = k
nodes.statement: Otherwise, $m = k$ and $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} = \varepsilon_0 2^{-k} < \delta$ as argued at the start of the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Case m = k

nodes.name: Scale inequalities
nodes.statement: We thus get $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \le \delta$. We can also verify that $\delta \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-n_2+2} \le \varepsilon_0 2^{-m+2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Get eps_0 2^{-m} <= delta <= eps_0 2^{-m+2}

nodes.name: Apply rescaled cover bound
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_sup_rpow_dist_cover_rescale}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_{\bar{s}_m}, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^{p+1} M \left(16 \delta \log_2 N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \right)^q N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the rescaled first-term bound

nodes.name: Second term
nodes.statement: \emph{Second term} By Lemma~\ref{lem:second_term_bound} and then the inequality $\varepsilon_0 2^{-m} \le \delta$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{t \in C_k} d_E(X_t, X_{\bar{t}_m})^p \right] &\le 2^d M c_1 (\varepsilon_0 2^{-m+1})^{q - d} C_p \\ &\le 2^q M c_1 \delta^{q - d} C_p \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the second term via the second-term lemma and eps_0 2^{-m} <= delta

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: Putting the two terms together, we obtain \begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in C_k; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \\ &\le 4^p M \left(4\left(16 \delta \log_2 N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \right)^q N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) + 2^q c_1 \delta^{q - d} C_p\right) \\ &\le 2^{2p+4q+1} M \delta^{q-d} \left(\delta^d \left(\log_2 N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \right)^q N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) + c_1 C_p\right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Add the two bounds and simplify constants

nodes.name: Finite set bound in terms of the covering constant
nodes.statement: With the same assumptions and notations as in Theorem~\ref{thm:finite_set_bound_of_dist_le_of_le_diam}, for all $\delta \in (0, 4\mathrm{diam}(T)]$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in T; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{2p+4q+1} M c_1 \delta^{q-d} \left(4^d \left(\log_2 \left(c_1 \delta^{-d} 4^d \right) \right)^q + C_p\right) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: With the same assumptions and notations as in Theorem~\ref{thm:finite_set_bound_of_dist_le_of_le_diam}, for all $\delta \in (0, 4\mathrm{diam}(T)]$
conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in T; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{2p+4q+1} M c_1 \delta^{q-d} \left(4^d \left(\log_2 \left(c_1 \delta^{-d} 4^d \right) \right)^q + C_p\right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:finite_set_bound_of_dist_le_of_le_diam_bis

nodes.name: Proof of Finite set bound in terms of the covering constant
nodes.statement: We apply Theorem~\ref{thm:finite_set_bound_of_dist_le_of_le_diam} and then remark that for $\delta \le 4\mathrm{diam}(T)$, we can use the bounded internal covering number hypothesis to bound $N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T)$~: \begin{align*} N^{int}_{\delta/4}(T) \le c_1 \left(\frac{\delta}{4}\right)^{-d} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the small-threshold theorem and bound N^int_{delta/4}(T) by the covering hypothesis.

nodes.name: Finite set bound for all distance thresholds
nodes.statement: Suppose that $T$ is a finite set with bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$. Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$, with $q > d$ and $p > 0$. For all $\delta > 0$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in T; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{2p+4q+1} M c_1 \delta^{q-d} \left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2 \left(c_1 \delta^{-d} 4^d\right) \right\} \right)^q + C_p\right) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Suppose that $T$ is a finite set with bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$.
Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$, with $q > d$ and $p > 0$.
$\delta > 0$
conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in T; d_T(s, t) \le \delta} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] &\le 2^{2p+4q+1} M c_1 \delta^{q-d} \left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2 \left(c_1 \delta^{-d} 4^d\right) \right\} \right)^q + C_p\right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:finite_set_bound_of_dist_le

nodes.name: Proof of Finite set bound for all distance thresholds
nodes.statement: We combine Corollary~\ref{cor:finite_set_bound_of_dist_le_of_le_diam_bis} and Theorem~\ref{thm:finite_set_bound_of_dist_le_of_diam_le}.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on delta versus 4 diam(T), combining the two previous bounds.

nodes.name: Hölder ratio bound by dyadic distance shells
nodes.statement: Let $J \subseteq T$ be a finite set and suppose that $T$ has finite diameter. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\eta_k = 2^{-k}(\mathrm{diam}(T) + 1)$. For $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ a stochastic process and $\beta \in(0, (q - d)/p)$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s \ne t} \frac{d_E(X_s, X_t)^p}{d_T(s, t)^{\beta p}} \right] &\le \sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{k \beta p} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s \ne t, \: d_T(s, t) \le 2 \eta_k} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5.4.1 Sets with bounded internal covering number
assumptions: Let $J \subseteq T$ be a finite set and suppose that $T$ has finite diameter.
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\eta_k = 2^{-k}(\mathrm{diam}(T) + 1)$.
For $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ a stochastic process and $\beta \in(0, (q - d)/p)$

nodes.label: lem:integral_div_dist_le_sum_integral_dist_le

We introduce for each $k \in \mathbb{N}$ the set of pairs $(s, t)$ such that $\eta_k < d_T(s, t) \le 2 \eta_k$. Note that $\eta_k \ge 2^{-k}$.  egin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s

e t, \: \eta_k < d_T(s, t) \le 2 \eta_k}  rac{d_E(X_s, X_t)^p}{d_T(s, t)^{ eta p}} ight] \ &\le \sum_{k=0}^\infty \eta_k^{- eta p} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s 
e t, \: d_T(s, t) \le 2 \eta_k} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p ight] \ &\le \sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{k  eta p} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s 
e t, \: d_T(s, t) \le 2 \eta_k} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p ight] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5.4.1 Sets with bounded internal covering number
nodes.statement_short: Decompose pairs into dyadic distance shells eta_k < d <= 2 eta_k and bound the denominator on each shell.

nodes.name: Constant L(c_1, d, p, q, beta)
nodes.statement: We introduce the constant \begin{align*} L(c_1, d, p, q, \beta) &= 2^{2p+5q+1} c_1 (c_1^{1/d}+1)^{q-d} \\&\quad \times \sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{k (\beta p - (q-d))}\left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2(c_1) + (k + 2)d \right\}\right)^q + C_p\right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5.4.1 Sets with bounded internal covering number
nodes.statement_short: The constant L is a series over k of dyadic chaining bounds weighted by 2^{k(beta p - (q-d))}.
nodes.label: def:L

nodes.name: Finiteness of the constant L
nodes.statement: For $c_1 < \infty$, $p> 0$, $q > d > 0$ and $\beta \in (0, (q-d)/p)$, the constant $L(c_1, d, p, q, \beta)$ is finite.
nodes.section: 5.4.1 Sets with bounded internal covering number
assumptions: $c_1 < \infty$, $p> 0$, $q > d > 0$ and $\beta \in (0, (q-d)/p)$
conclusions: the constant $L(c_1, d, p, q, \beta)$ is finite
nodes.label: lem:L_lt_top

nodes.name: Proof of Finiteness of the constant L
nodes.statement: Let $a_k = 2^{2p+5q+1} M c_1 (c_1^{1/d}+1)^{q-d} 2^{k (\beta p - (q-d))} \left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2(c_1) + (k + 2)d \right\}\right)^q + C_p\right)$. Then $L(c_1, d, p, q, \beta) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty a_k$. To show that the sum is finite, we can use the ratio test. \begin{align*} \frac{\vert a_{k+1} \vert}{\vert a_k \vert} &= 2^{\beta p - (q - d)} \frac{\left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2(c_1) + (k + 3)d \right\}\right)^q + C_p\right)} {\left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2(c_1) + (k + 2)d \right\}\right)^q + C_p\right)} \end{align*} The limit at infinity of that ratio is $2^{\beta p - (q - d)} < 1$, hence the series $\sum_{k=0}^\infty a_k$ converges.
nodes.section: 5.4.1 Sets with bounded internal covering number
nodes.statement_short: Ratio test: the ratio of consecutive terms tends to 2^{beta p - (q-d)} < 1.

nodes.name: Series terms
nodes.statement: Let $a_k = 2^{2p+5q+1} M c_1 (c_1^{1/d}+1)^{q-d} 2^{k (\beta p - (q-d))} \left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2(c_1) + (k + 2)d \right\}\right)^q + C_p\right)$. Then $L(c_1, d, p, q, \beta) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty a_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Write L as a series of terms a_k

nodes.name: Ratio test

nodes.statement_short: Compute the ratio of consecutive terms
nodes.section: 5.4.1 Sets with bounded internal covering number

nodes.name: Convergence
nodes.statement: The limit at infinity of that ratio is $2^{\beta p - (q - d)} < 1$, hence the series $\sum_{k=0}^\infty a_k$ converges.
nodes.statement_short: The ratio tends to a limit < 1, so the series converges

nodes.name: Hölder ratio moment bound on finite sets
nodes.statement: Suppose that $J \subseteq T$ is a finite set and that $T$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $c_1>0$ and exponent $d > 0$. Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$, with $q > d$ and $p > 0$. Let $\beta \in(0, (q - d)/p)$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s \ne t} \frac{d_E(X_s, X_t)^p}{d_T(s, t)^{\beta p}} \right] \le M L(c_1, d, p, q, \beta) \: . \end{align*}

Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition for exponents $(p,q)$ with constant $M$, with $q > d$ and $p > 0$.
Let $\beta \in(0, (q - d)/p)$.
conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s \ne t} \frac{d_E(X_s, X_t)^p}{d_T(s, t)^{\beta p}} \right] \le M L(c_1, d, p, q, \beta) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.statement:
Since $J \subseteq T$, $J$ has bounded internal covering number with constant $2^d c_1$ and exponent $d$ (Lemma~ef{lem:hasBoundedInternalCoveringNumber_subset}). Let $\eta_k = 2^{-k}(\mathrm{diam}(T) + 1)$ for $k \in \mathbb{N}$. By Lemma~ef{lem:integral_div_dist_le_sum_integral_dist_le}, we have  egin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s 
e t}  rac{d_E(X_s, X_t)^p}{d_T(s, t)^{ eta p}} ight] &\le \sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{k  eta p} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s 
e t, \: d_T(s, t) \le 2 \eta_k} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p ight] \: . \end{align*} We apply Corollary~ef{cor:finite_set_bound_of_dist_le} to bound each expectation in the sum.  egin{align*} &\mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s 
e t, \: d_T(s, t) \le 2 \eta_k} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p ight] \ &\le 2^{2p+4q+1} M 2^d c_1 (2 \eta_k)^{q-d} \left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2 \left(2^d c_1 (2 \eta_k)^{-d} 4^d ight) ight\} ight)^q + C_pight) \ &\le 2^{2p+5q+1} M c_1 (\mathrm{diam}(T)+1)^{q-d} 2^{-k(q-d)} \left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2 \left(c_1 2^{(k + 2)d} ight) ight\} ight)^q + C_pight) \ &= 2^{2p+5q+1} M c_1 (\mathrm{diam}(T)+1)^{q-d} 2^{-k(q-d)} \left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2(c_1) + (k + 2)d ight\} ight)^q + C_pight) \ &\le 2^{2p+5q+1} M c_1 (c_1^{1/d}+1)^{q-d} 2^{-k(q-d)} \left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2(c_1) + (k + 2)d ight\} ight)^q + C_pight) \: , \end{align*} where the last inequality uses $\mathrm{diam}(T) \le c_1^{1/d}$ (Lemma~ef{lem:hasBoundedInternalCoveringNumber_diam_le}). nodes.name: Dyadic shell decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $\eta_k = 2^{-k}(\mathrm{diam}(T) + 1)$ for $k \in \mathbb{N}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_div_dist_le_sum_integral_dist_le}, we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s \ne t} \frac{d_E(X_s, X_t)^p}{d_T(s, t)^{\beta p}} \right] &\le \sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{k \beta p} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s \ne t, \: d_T(s, t) \le 2 \eta_k} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \: . \end{align*}

nodes.name: Bound each shell
nodes.statement: We apply Corollary~\ref{cor:finite_set_bound_of_dist_le} to bound each expectation in the sum. \begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{s, t \in J;\: s \ne t, \: d_T(s, t) \le 2 \eta_k} d_E(X_s, X_t)^p \right] \\ &\le 2^{2p+4q+1} M 2^d c_1 (2 \eta_k)^{q-d} \left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2 \left(2^d c_1 (2 \eta_k)^{-d} 4^d \right) \right\} \right)^q + C_p\right) \\ &\le 2^{2p+5q+1} M c_1 (\mathrm{diam}(T)+1)^{q-d} 2^{-k(q-d)} \left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2 \left(c_1 2^{(k + 2)d} \right) \right\} \right)^q + C_p\right) \\ &= 2^{2p+5q+1} M c_1 (\mathrm{diam}(T)+1)^{q-d} 2^{-k(q-d)} \left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2(c_1) + (k + 2)d \right\} \right)^q + C_p\right) \\ &\le 2^{2p+5q+1} M c_1 (c_1^{1/d}+1)^{q-d} 2^{-k(q-d)} \left(4^d \left(\max\left\{0, \log_2(c_1) + (k + 2)d \right\} \right)^q + C_p\right) \: , \end{align*} where the last inequality uses $\mathrm{diam}(T) \le c_1^{1/d}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:hasBoundedInternalCoveringNumber_diam_le}).
nodes.statement_short: Bound each expectation with the finite set bound and diam(T) <= c_1^{1/d}

nodes.name: Moment bound on the modulus of continuity over countable sets

nodes.name: Proof of Hölder modification of a fixed order
nodes.statement: Let $T'$ be a countable dense subset of $T$. Let $A$ be the event \begin{align*} \left\{\sup_{s, t \in T';\: s \ne t} \frac{d_E(X_s, X_t)^p}{d_T(s, t)^{\beta p}} < \infty \right\} \: . \end{align*} As a consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm:countable_set_bound}, we have $\mathbb{P}(A) = 1$. On the event $A$, $(X_t)_{t \in T'}$ has Hölder continuous paths of order $\beta$. Let $x_0 \in E$ be arbitrary and let $Y: T \to \Omega \to E$ be the process defined by \begin{align*} Y_t(\omega) &= \begin{cases} \lim_{s \to t, s \in T'} X_s(\omega) & \text{if } \omega \in A \\ x_0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \: . \end{align*} Then $Y$ has Hölder continuous paths of order $\beta$ almost surely. We can show that $(Y_s, Y_t)$ is $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. measurable for all $s, t \in T$. It remains to show that $Y$ is a modification of $X$. Let then $t \in T$ and let $(t_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $T'$ that converges to $t$. We want to show that $\mathbb{P}(Y_t \ne X_t) = 0$. It suffices to show that $\mathbb{P}(d_E(Y_t, X_t) > 0) = 0$, which itself would follow from $\mathbb{P}(d_E(Y_t, X_t) > \varepsilon) = 0$ for all $\varepsilon > 0$. \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}(d_E(Y_t, X_t) > \varepsilon) &\le \mathbb{P}(d_E(Y_t, X_{t_n}) + d_E(X_{t_n}, X_t) > \varepsilon) \\ &\le \mathbb{P}(d_E(Y_t, X_{t_n}) > \varepsilon/2) + \mathbb{P}(d_E(X_{t_n}, X_t) > \varepsilon/2) \: . \end{align*} TODO

nodes.statement_short: A process satisfying the Kolmogorov condition on a space with bounded internal covering number has a modification with Hölder paths of all orders below (q-d)/p.

nodes.name: Proof of Kolmogorov-Chentsov theorem
nodes.statement: Let $(\beta_n)$ be an increasing sequence of numbers in $(0, (q - d)/p)$ such that $\beta_n \to (q - d)/p$. For each $n$, let $Y^n$ be the modification of $X$ given by Lemma~\ref{lem:holder_modification_single} for $\beta = \beta_n$. Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:indistinguishable_of_modification_of_continuous}, the processes $Y^0$ and $Y^n$ are indistinguishable for all $n$. That is, there exists an event $A_n$ such that $\mathbb{P}(A_n) = 1$ and such that for all $\omega \in A_n$, $Y^0_t(\omega) = Y^n_t(\omega)$ for all $t \in T$. Let $A = \bigcap_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n$ and let $x_0 \in E$ be arbitrary. Then $\mathbb{P}(A) = 1$ and the process $Y(\omega) = Y^0(\omega)$ for $\omega \in A$ and $Y(\omega) = x_0$ for $\omega \notin A$ has paths that are Hölder continuous of all orders $\gamma \in (0, (q - d)/p)$.

nodes.name: Cover with bounded covering numbers

nodes.name: Localized Kolmogorov-Chentsov theorem
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a metric space with a cover $(T_n)$ with bounded covering numbers with constants $c_n$ and the same exponent $d$. Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition with exponents $(p, q)$ with $q > d$. Then $X$ has a modification $Y$ such that almost surely the paths of $Y$ are locally Hölder continuous of all orders $\gamma \in (0, (q - d)/p)$.
assumptions: Let $T$ be a metric space with a cover $(T_n)$ with bounded covering numbers with constants $c_n$ and the same exponent $d$.
Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process that satisfies the Kolmogorov condition with exponents $(p, q)$ with $q > d$.

nodes.name: Proof of Localized Kolmogorov-Chentsov theorem
nodes.statement: For each $n$, by Theorem~\ref{thm:holder_modification} there is a modification $Y_n$ of $X$ seen as a process on $T_n$ such that the paths of $Y_n$ are Hölder continuous of all orders $\gamma \in (0, (q - d)/p)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:indistinguishable_of_modification_of_continuous}, $Y_n$ and $Y_{n+1}$ are indistinguishable on $T_n$. That is, almost surely $Y_n = Y_{n+1}$ on $T_n$. Since there are countably many such almost sure equalities, we get that almost surely there is equality for all $n$. Let $A$ be the event that this happens, let $x_0 \in E$ be arbitrary and define a process $Y : T \to \Omega \to E$ by \begin{align*} Y(t, \omega) &= \begin{cases} Y_n(t, \omega) & \text{if } \omega \in A \: , \: t \in T_n \setminus T_{n-1} \: , \\ x_0 & \text{if } \omega \notin A \: . \end{cases} \end{align*} Then $Y$ is a modification of $X$ and has paths that are locally Hölder continuous of all orders $\gamma \in (0, (q - d)/p)$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Kolmogorov-Chentsov theorem on each T_n; consecutive modifications are indistinguishable, so glue them on a full-measure event.

nodes.name: Local modifications
nodes.statement: For each $n$, by Theorem~\ref{thm:holder_modification} there is a modification $Y_n$ of $X$ seen as a process on $T_n$ such that the paths of $Y_n$ are Hölder continuous of all orders $\gamma \in (0, (q - d)/p)$.

nodes.name: Countable intersection

nodes.statement_short: All equalities hold simultaneously a.s.

nodes.name: Glue the modifications

nodes.statement_short: Define Y piecewise on A and constant off A

Then $X$ has a modification $Y$ such that almost surely the paths of $Y$ are locally Hölder continuous of all orders $\gamma \in (0, \sup_n (q_n - d)/p_n)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Localized Kolmogorov-Chentsov theorem for a sequence of exponents
nodes.statement: For each $n$, by Theorem~\ref{thm:localized_holder_modification} there is a modification $Y_n$ of $X$ such that the paths of $Y_n$ are locally Hölder continuous of all orders $\gamma \in (0, (q_n - d)/p_n)$. nodes.name: pre-Brownian process
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega = \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}_+}$ and consider the probability space $(\Omega, P_B)$ (where $P_B$ is the measure defined in Definition~\ref{def:gaussianLimit}). The identity on that space is a function $\Omega \to \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}$. We reorder the arguments to define a stochastic process $X : \mathbb{R}_+ \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$, which we call the pre-Brownian process.
nodes.statement_short: The coordinate process on R^{R_+} under the Gaussian projective limit measure P_B.

nodes.name: The pre-Brownian process is Gaussian

nodes.name: Proof of The pre-Brownian process is Gaussian
nodes.statement: For any $t_1, \ldots, t_n \in \mathbb{R}_+$, the distribution of $(X_{t_1}, \ldots, X_{t_n})$ is given by a finite-dimensional distribution of $P_B$, and therefore is Gaussian.

nodes.name: Law of pre-Brownian increments
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be the pre-Brownian process of Definition~\ref{def:preBrownian}. Then, for all $s, t \in \mathbb{R}_+$, the random variable $X_t - X_s$ is a Gaussian random variable with mean $0$ and variance $|t - s|$.

nodes.name: Proof of Law of pre-Brownian increments
nodes.statement: The map \begin{align*} L : \mathbb{R}^2 &\to \mathbb{R} \\ (x_1, x_2) &\mapsto x_2 - x_1 \end{align*} is a continuous linear map, and $(X_s, X_t)$ is Gaussian by Lemma~\ref{lem:isGaussianProcess_preBrownian}, therefore $X_t - X_s$ is Gaussian by Lemma~\ref{lem:isGaussian_map}. By definition of $P_B$, we have $$\mathbb{E}[X_t - X_s] = \mathbb{E}[X_t] - \mathbb{E}[X_s] = 0 - 0 = 0,$$ and $$\mathrm{Var}(X_t - X_s) = \mathrm{Var}(X_t) - 2\mathrm{Cov}(X_t, X_s) + \mathrm{Var}(X_s) = t - 2(t \land s) + s = t \lor s - t \land s = |t - s|.$$ Therefore $X_t - X_s$ is Gaussian with mean $0$ and variance $|t - s|$.
nodes.statement_short: X_t - X_s is a linear image of a Gaussian vector; compute its mean and variance from the covariance s ∧ t.

nodes.name: Increment is Gaussian

nodes.name: Mean and variance

nodes.statement_short: Compute mean 0 and variance |t-s|

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore $X_t - X_s$ is Gaussian with mean $0$ and variance $|t - s|$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the law of the increment

That is, for all $s, t \in \mathbb{R}_+$, we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ |X_t - X_s|^{2n} \right] \le (2n - 1)!! |t - s|^n \: . \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof of Brownian motion is a Gaussian process
nodes.statement: The pre-Brownian process is a Gaussian process by Lemma~\ref{lem:isGaussianProcess_preBrownian}. The Brownian motion is a modification of the pre-Brownian process by Definition~\ref{def:brownian}. Thus, the Brownian motion is a Gaussian process as well by Lemma~\ref{lem:isGaussianProcess_of_modification}.
nodes.statement_short: Modification of a Gaussian process (the pre-Brownian process) is Gaussian.

nodes.name: Pre-Brownian is Gaussian
nodes.statement: The pre-Brownian process is a Gaussian process by Lemma~\ref{lem:isGaussianProcess_preBrownian}.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the pre-Brownian process is Gaussian

nodes.name: Modification
nodes.statement: The Brownian motion is a modification of the pre-Brownian process by Definition~\ref{def:brownian}.
nodes.statement_short: B is a modification of the pre-Brownian process

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus, the Brownian motion is a Gaussian process as well by Lemma~\ref{lem:isGaussianProcess_of_modification}.
nodes.statement_short: Modifications of Gaussian processes are Gaussian

nodes.name: Local Hölder continuity of Brownian paths
nodes.statement: The paths of the Brownian motion are locally Hölder continuous of all orders $\gamma \in (0, 1/2)$.
conclusions: The paths of the Brownian motion are locally Hölder continuous of all orders $\gamma \in (0, 1/2)$.
nodes.label: lem:isHolderWith_brownian

nodes.name: Proof of Local Hölder continuity of Brownian paths
nodes.statement: Consider the cover of $\mathbb{R}_+$ given by $T_n := [0, n + 1)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:hasBoundedCoveringNumberCover_nnreal}, this cover has bounded covering numbers with exponent $1$. Moreover, by Lemma~\ref{lem:isKolmogorovProcess_preBrownian}, the pre-Brownian process satisfies the Kolmogorov condition with exponents $(2n + 4, n + 2)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. In particular, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $2n + 4 > 1$. Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:localized_holder_modification_sup} we deduce that the modification used in Definition~\ref{def:brownian} has locally Hölder continuous paths for all orders $\gamma \in (0, \sup_n (n + 1) / (2n + 4))$. Clearly for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ we have $(n + 1) / (2n + 4) \leqslant 2$, and this quantity tends to $2$ as $n$ goes to infinity. Therefore the Brownian motion has Hölder continuous paths of order $\gamma$ for all $\gamma \in (0, 1 / 2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the localized Kolmogorov-Chentsov theorem with the cover [0, n+1) and exponents (2n+4, n+2), and take the supremum of the orders.

nodes.name: Cover of R_+
nodes.statement: Consider the cover of $\mathbb{R}_+$ given by $T_n := [0, n + 1)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:hasBoundedCoveringNumberCover_nnreal}, this cover has bounded covering numbers with exponent $1$.
nodes.statement_short: The cover [0, n+1) has bounded covering numbers with exponent 1

nodes.name: Kolmogorov condition
nodes.statement: Moreover, by Lemma~\ref{lem:isKolmogorovProcess_preBrownian}, the pre-Brownian process satisfies the Kolmogorov condition with exponents $(2n + 4, n + 2)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: The pre-Brownian process satisfies the Kolmogorov condition with exponents (2n+4, n+2)

nodes.name: Apply localized Kolmogorov-Chentsov
nodes.statement: In particular, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $2n + 4 > 1$. Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:localized_holder_modification_sup} we deduce that the modification used in Definition~\ref{def:brownian} has locally Hölder continuous paths for all orders $\gamma \in (0, \sup_n (n + 1) / (2n + 4))$. Clearly for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ we have $(n + 1) / (2n + 4) \leqslant 2$, and this quantity tends to $2$ as $n$ goes to infinity.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the localized theorem for the exponent sequence

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore the Brownian motion has Hölder continuous paths of order $\gamma$ for all $\gamma \in (0, 1 / 2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Supremum of orders is 1/2

nodes.name: Continuity of Brownian paths
nodes.statement: The paths of the Brownian motion are continuous.
conclusions: The paths of the Brownian motion are continuous.
nodes.label: lem:continuous_brownian

nodes.name: Proof of Continuity of Brownian paths
nodes.statement: The paths are $1/4$-Hölder continuous by Lemma~\ref{lem:isHolderWith_brownian} because $0 < 1/4 < 1/2$, therefore they are continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Hölder continuity of order 1/4 implies continuity.

nodes.name: Law of Brownian motion at a fixed time
nodes.statement: For $t \in \mathbb{R}_+$, the law of $B_t$ (the Brownian motion at time $t$) is the real Gaussian measure $\mathcal{N}(0,t)$.
assumptions: $t \in \mathbb{R}_+$
conclusions: the law of $B_t$ (the Brownian motion at time $t$) is the real Gaussian measure $\mathcal{N}(0,t)$
nodes.label: lem:hasLaw_brownian_eval

nodes.name: Proof of Law of Brownian motion at a fixed time
nodes.statement: The Brownian motion $B$ is a modification of the pre-Brownian process, and therefore has same finite dimensional distributions. By Definition~\ref{def:gaussianLimit}, $B_t$ has law $\mathcal{N}(0,t)$.
nodes.statement_short: A modification has the same finite-dimensional distributions as the pre-Brownian process.

nodes.name: Law of Brownian increments
nodes.statement: For $s, t \in \mathbb{R}_+$, the law of $B_t - B_s$ is the real Gaussian measure $\mathcal{N}(0,\vert t - s \vert)$.
assumptions: $s, t \in \mathbb{R}_+$
conclusions: the law of $B_t - B_s$ is the real Gaussian measure $\mathcal{N}(0,\vert t - s \vert)$
nodes.label: lem:hasLaw_brownian_sub

nodes.name: Proof of Law of Brownian increments
nodes.statement: The Brownian motion $B$ is a modification of the pre-Brownian process, and therefore has same finite dimensional distributions. By Lemma~\ref{lem:hasLaw_preBrownian_sub}, $B_t - B_s$ has law $\mathcal{N}(0,\vert t - s \vert)$.
nodes.statement_short: Same finite-dimensional distributions as the pre-Brownian process, whose increments have the stated law.

nodes.name: Independent increments
nodes.statement: We say that a stochastic process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ has independent increments if for all $t_1, \ldots, t_n \in T$ with $t_1 \le t_2 \le \cdots \le t_n$, the random variables $X_{t_2} - X_{t_1}, X_{t_3} - X_{t_2}, \ldots, X_{t_n} - X_{t_{n-1}}$ are independent.
differentia: for all $t_1, \ldots, t_n \in T$ with $t_1 \le t_2 \le \cdots \le t_n$, the random variables $X_{t_2} - X_{t_1}, X_{t_3} - X_{t_2}, \ldots, X_{t_n} - X_{t_{n-1}}$ are independent
nodes.label: def:HasIndepIncrements

nodes.name: Brownian motion has independent increments
nodes.statement: The Brownian motion has independent increments.
conclusions: The Brownian motion has independent increments.
nodes.label: lem:hasIndepIncrements_brownian

nodes.name: Proof of Brownian motion has independent increments
nodes.statement: Let $t_1 \le t_2 \le \ldots \le t_n$ be $n$ times in $\mathbb{R}_+$. Then $(B_{t_2} - B_{t_1}, B_{t_3} - B_{t_2}, \ldots, B_{t_n} - B_{t_{n-1}})$ is a linear transformation of $(B_{t_1}, \ldots, B_{t_n})$, hence it is Gaussian. We can compute its mean (which is $0$) and its covariance matrix. The covariance matrix is diagonal, which means the the random variables are uncorrelated. Because they are jointly Gaussian, this implies that they are independent.
nodes.statement_short: The increment vector is a linear image of a Gaussian vector with diagonal covariance, and uncorrelated jointly Gaussian variables are independent.

nodes.name: Increments are jointly Gaussian
nodes.statement: Let $t_1 \le t_2 \le \ldots \le t_n$ be $n$ times in $\mathbb{R}_+$. Then $(B_{t_2} - B_{t_1}, B_{t_3} - B_{t_2}, \ldots, B_{t_n} - B_{t_{n-1}})$ is a linear transformation of $(B_{t_1}, \ldots, B_{t_n})$, hence it is Gaussian.
nodes.statement_short: Increment vector is a linear transformation of a Gaussian vector

nodes.name: Covariance is diagonal
nodes.statement: We can compute its mean (which is $0$) and its covariance matrix. The covariance matrix is diagonal, which means the the random variables are uncorrelated.
nodes.statement_short: Compute mean and diagonal covariance

nodes.name: Conclude independence
nodes.statement: Because they are jointly Gaussian, this implies that they are independent.
nodes.statement_short: Uncorrelated jointly Gaussian variables are independent

nodes.name: Auxiliary Wiener measure
nodes.statement: The pushforward of the measure $P_B$ of Definition~\ref{def:gaussianLimit} by the Brownian motion $B$ is a measure on the continuous functions on $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}_+}$, with the sigma-algebra induced by the product sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}_+}$.
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions
nodes.statement_short: Pushforward of P_B by the Brownian motion, a measure on continuous functions inside R^{R_+} with the product sigma-algebra.
nodes.label: def:wienerMeasureAux

nodes.name: Lean remark on the auxiliary Wiener measure
nodes.statement: \textbf{Lean remark}: the auxiliary Wiener measure is a measure on the subtype \texttt{\{f // Continuous f\}}. This is not the same type as $C(\mathbb{R}_+, \mathbb{R})$.
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Borel sigma-algebra of C(R_+, R) is generated by evaluations
nodes.statement: The Borel sigma-algebra on $C(\mathbb{R}_+, \mathbb{R})$ coming from the compact-open topology is equal to the smallest sigma-algebra for which the evaluation maps $f \mapsto f(t)$ are measurable for every $t \in \mathbb{R}_+$.
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions
nodes.statement_short: On C(R_+, R) the compact-open Borel sigma-algebra equals the sigma-algebra generated by evaluation maps.
conclusions: The Borel sigma-algebra on $C(\mathbb{R}_+, \mathbb{R})$ coming from the compact-open topology is equal to the smallest sigma-algebra for which the evaluation maps $f \mapsto f(t)$ are measurable for every $t \in \mathbb{R}_+$.
nodes.label: thm:ContinuousMap.borel_eq_iSup_comap_eval

nodes.name: Proof of Borel sigma-algebra of C(R_+, R) is generated by evaluations
nodes.statement: We prove that this holds for $C(X, Y)$ as long as $X$ and $Y$ are second-countable topological spaces endowed with their Borel sigma-algebra, $X$ is locally compact (i.e.\ each point of $X$ has a basis of compact neighbourhoods), and $Y$ is regular (i.e.\ for any $C \subseteq Y$ closed and $y \notin C$, there exist disjoint open subsets $U, V \subseteq Y$ such that $C \subseteq U$ and $y \in V$). The proof is taken from \href{https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4789531/when-does-the-borel-sigma-algebra-of-compact-convergence-coincide-with-the-pr}{this stackexchange question}. We denote by $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ the two sigma-algebras. First of all, the evaluation maps are continuous for the compact-open topology, and therefore measurable for $\mathcal{T}_1$. We deduce that $\mathcal{T}_2 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_1$. Let us turn to the converse direction. For any $A \subseteq X$ and $B \subseteq Y$, denote $$M(A, B) := \{f \in C(X, Y), f(A) \subset B\}.$$ The compact-open topology is generated by the sets of the form $M(K, U)$, for $K$ compact and $U$ open. Because $X$ and $Y$ are second-countable and $X$ is locally compact, $C(X, Y)$ is second-countable. Therefore it is enough to show that for any $K$ compact and $U$ open, $M(K, U) \in \mathcal{T}_2$. We now fix $K$ and $U$. Consider $(V_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ a countable family of subsets of $Y$ which generates the topology (it exists by second-countability assumption). Clearly we have that $$\bigcup_{\overline{V_n} \subseteq U} V_n \subseteq U.$$ Conversely, consider $y \in U$. Because $Y$ is regular, the set of $\overline{V_n}$ such that $y \in V_n$ is a basis of neighbourhoods of $y$. Indeed, consider $A$ an open neighbourhood of $y$. Then $A^c$ is a closed set which does not contain $y$. Therefore there exist disjoint open sets $B$ and $C$ such that $y \in B$ and $A^c \subseteq C$. There exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x \in V_n \subseteq B$. Therefore $V_n \subseteq C^c$, so $\overline{V_n} \subseteq C^c \subseteq A$, and we are done. This proves that we have in fact $$U = \bigcup_{\overline{V_n} \subseteq U} V_n = \bigcup_{\overline{V_n} \subseteq U} \overline{V_n}.$$ Consider now $f \in M(K, U)$. We then have $$f(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{\overline{V_n} \subseteq U} V_n.$$ Because $K$ is compact and $f$ is continuous, $f(K)$ is compact. But each $V_n$ is open, so there exists a finite set $\hat{f}$ of natural integers such that for any $n \in \hat{f}$, $\overline{V_n} \subseteq U$, and $$f(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{n \in \hat{f}} V_n \subseteq \bigcup_{n \in \hat{f}} \overline{V_n}.$$ Conversely, if there exists a finite set $\hat{f}$ such that for any $n \in \hat{f}$, $\overline{V_n} \subseteq U$, and $$f(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{n \in \hat{f}} \overline{V_n},$$ then $f(K) \subseteq U$. We can therefore write that $$M(K, U) = \bigcup_{\substack{I \subseteq \mathbb{N} \\ I \text{ finite} \\ \forall n \in I, \overline{V_n} \subseteq U}} M\left(K, \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}\right).$$ This is a countable union, so we just have to prove that each term is measurable. We now fix a finite set $I$ as in the union above. Because $X$ is second countable, there exists $Q$ a countable dense subset of $K$. For any $f$ continuous, because $Q$ is dense and $\bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}$ is closed, we have $$f(K) \subset \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i} \Longleftrightarrow f(Q) \subset \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}.$$ In other words, $M\left(K, \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}\right) = M\left(Q, \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}\right)$. We can write $$M\left(Q, \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}\right) = \bigcap_{q \in Q} (f \mapsto f(q))^{-1} \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i},$$ and it is enough to show that each term in the intersection is measurable. Because $\bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}$ is closed, it is measurable. It therefore remains to prove that $f \mapsto f(q)$ is measurable for all $q \in Q$, but this is obvious from the definition of $\mathcal{T}_2$. This concludes the proof.
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions
nodes.statement_short: Prove it for C(X,Y) with X second-countable locally compact and Y second-countable regular: evaluations are continuous for one inclusion; for the other, write M(K,U) as a countable union of sets M(Q, finite union of closed basis sets) with Q countable dense in K.

nodes.name: Generalize to C(X, Y)
nodes.statement: We prove that this holds for $C(X, Y)$ as long as $X$ and $Y$ are second-countable topological spaces endowed with their Borel sigma-algebra, $X$ is locally compact (i.e.\ each point of $X$ has a basis of compact neighbourhoods), and $Y$ is regular (i.e.\ for any $C \subseteq Y$ closed and $y \notin C$, there exist disjoint open subsets $U, V \subseteq Y$ such that $C \subseteq U$ and $y \in V$). The proof is taken from \href{https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4789531/when-does-the-borel-sigma-algebra-of-compact-convergence-coincide-with-the-pr}{this stackexchange question}.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the general statement for C(X,Y) under countability, local compactness and regularity
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Easy inclusion
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ the two sigma-algebras. First of all, the evaluation maps are continuous for the compact-open topology, and therefore measurable for $\mathcal{T}_1$. We deduce that $\mathcal{T}_2 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluations are continuous, so T_2 ⊆ T_1
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Converse inclusion
nodes.statement: Let us turn to the converse direction. For any $A \subseteq X$ and $B \subseteq Y$, denote $$M(A, B) := \{f \in C(X, Y), f(A) \subset B\}.$$ The compact-open topology is generated by the sets of the form $M(K, U)$, for $K$ compact and $U$ open. Because $X$ and $Y$ are second-countable and $X$ is locally compact, $C(X, Y)$ is second-countable. Therefore it is enough to show that for any $K$ compact and $U$ open, $M(K, U) \in \mathcal{T}_2$. We now fix $K$ and $U$. Consider $(V_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ a countable family of subsets of $Y$ which generates the topology (it exists by second-countability assumption). Clearly we have that $$\bigcup_{\overline{V_n} \subseteq U} V_n \subseteq U.$$ Conversely, consider $y \in U$. Because $Y$ is regular, the set of $\overline{V_n}$ such that $y \in V_n$ is a basis of neighbourhoods of $y$. Indeed, consider $A$ an open neighbourhood of $y$. Then $A^c$ is a closed set which does not contain $y$. Therefore there exist disjoint open sets $B$ and $C$ such that $y \in B$ and $A^c \subseteq C$. There exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x \in V_n \subseteq B$. Therefore $V_n \subseteq C^c$, so $\overline{V_n} \subseteq C^c \subseteq A$, and we are done. This proves that we have in fact $$U = \bigcup_{\overline{V_n} \subseteq U} V_n = \bigcup_{\overline{V_n} \subseteq U} \overline{V_n}.$$ Consider now $f \in M(K, U)$. We then have $$f(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{\overline{V_n} \subseteq U} V_n.$$ Because $K$ is compact and $f$ is continuous, $f(K)$ is compact. But each $V_n$ is open, so there exists a finite set $\hat{f}$ of natural integers such that for any $n \in \hat{f}$, $\overline{V_n} \subseteq U$, and $$f(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{n \in \hat{f}} V_n \subseteq \bigcup_{n \in \hat{f}} \overline{V_n}.$$ Conversely, if there exists a finite set $\hat{f}$ such that for any $n \in \hat{f}$, $\overline{V_n} \subseteq U$, and $$f(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{n \in \hat{f}} \overline{V_n},$$ then $f(K) \subseteq U$. We can therefore write that $$M(K, U) = \bigcup_{\substack{I \subseteq \mathbb{N} \\ I \text{ finite} \\ \forall n \in I, \overline{V_n} \subseteq U}} M\left(K, \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}\right).$$ This is a countable union, so we just have to prove that each term is measurable. We now fix a finite set $I$ as in the union above. Because $X$ is second countable, there exists $Q$ a countable dense subset of $K$. For any $f$ continuous, because $Q$ is dense and $\bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}$ is closed, we have $$f(K) \subset \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i} \Longleftrightarrow f(Q) \subset \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}.$$ In other words, $M\left(K, \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}\right) = M\left(Q, \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}\right)$. We can write $$M\left(Q, \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}\right) = \bigcap_{q \in Q} (f \mapsto f(q))^{-1} \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i},$$ and it is enough to show that each term in the intersection is measurable. Because $\bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}$ is closed, it is measurable. It therefore remains to prove that $f \mapsto f(q)$ is measurable for all $q \in Q$, but this is obvious from the definition of $\mathcal{T}_2$. This concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Show T_1 ⊆ T_2
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Sets M(A, B)
nodes.statement: For any $A \subseteq X$ and $B \subseteq Y$, denote $$M(A, B) := \{f \in C(X, Y), f(A) \subset B\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Denote M(A,B) = {f : f(A) ⊂ B}
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Reduction to subbasic sets
nodes.statement: The compact-open topology is generated by the sets of the form $M(K, U)$, for $K$ compact and $U$ open. Because $X$ and $Y$ are second-countable and $X$ is locally compact, $C(X, Y)$ is second-countable. Therefore it is enough to show that for any $K$ compact and $U$ open, $M(K, U) \in \mathcal{T}_2$. We now fix $K$ and $U$.
nodes.statement_short: By second countability it suffices to show M(K,U) ∈ T_2
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Countable basis
nodes.statement: Consider $(V_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ a countable family of subsets of $Y$ which generates the topology (it exists by second-countability assumption). Clearly we have that $$\bigcup_{\overline{V_n} \subseteq U} V_n \subseteq U.$$
nodes.statement_short: Take a countable basis (V_n); the union of V_n with closure in U is inside U
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Regularity argument
nodes.statement: Conversely, consider $y \in U$. Because $Y$ is regular, the set of $\overline{V_n}$ such that $y \in V_n$ is a basis of neighbourhoods of $y$. Indeed, consider $A$ an open neighbourhood of $y$. Then $A^c$ is a closed set which does not contain $y$. Therefore there exist disjoint open sets $B$ and $C$ such that $y \in B$ and $A^c \subseteq C$. There exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x \in V_n \subseteq B$. Therefore $V_n \subseteq C^c$, so $\overline{V_n} \subseteq C^c \subseteq A$, and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: By regularity, closures of basis sets form a neighbourhood basis
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: U as a union of closed basis sets
nodes.statement: This proves that we have in fact $$U = \bigcup_{\overline{V_n} \subseteq U} V_n = \bigcup_{\overline{V_n} \subseteq U} \overline{V_n}.$$
nodes.statement_short: U is the union of V_n (or their closures) with closure in U
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Compactness
nodes.statement: Consider now $f \in M(K, U)$. We then have $$f(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{\overline{V_n} \subseteq U} V_n.$$ Because $K$ is compact and $f$ is continuous, $f(K)$ is compact. But each $V_n$ is open, so there exists a finite set $\hat{f}$ of natural integers such that for any $n \in \hat{f}$, $\overline{V_n} \subseteq U$, and $$f(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{n \in \hat{f}} V_n \subseteq \bigcup_{n \in \hat{f}} \overline{V_n}.$$
nodes.statement_short: By compactness f(K) is covered by finitely many V_n
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Countable union representation
nodes.statement: Conversely, if there exists a finite set $\hat{f}$ such that for any $n \in \hat{f}$, $\overline{V_n} \subseteq U$, and $$f(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{n \in \hat{f}} \overline{V_n},$$ then $f(K) \subseteq U$. We can therefore write that $$M(K, U) = \bigcup_{\substack{I \subseteq \mathbb{N} \\ I \text{ finite} \\ \forall n \in I, \overline{V_n} \subseteq U}} M\left(K, \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: Write M(K,U) as a countable union over finite index sets
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Reduction to each term
nodes.statement: This is a countable union, so we just have to prove that each term is measurable.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to show each term is measurable
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Density reduction
nodes.statement: We now fix a finite set $I$ as in the union above. Because $X$ is second countable, there exists $Q$ a countable dense subset of $K$. For any $f$ continuous, because $Q$ is dense and $\bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}$ is closed, we have $$f(K) \subset \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i} \Longleftrightarrow f(Q) \subset \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}.$$ In other words, $M\left(K, \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}\right) = M\left(Q, \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace K by a countable dense subset Q
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Intersection of evaluation preimages
nodes.statement: We can write $$M\left(Q, \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}\right) = \bigcap_{q \in Q} (f \mapsto f(q))^{-1} \bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i},$$ and it is enough to show that each term in the intersection is measurable. Because $\bigcup_{i \in I} \overline{V_i}$ is closed, it is measurable. It therefore remains to prove that $f \mapsto f(q)$ is measurable for all $q \in Q$, but this is obvious from the definition of $\mathcal{T}_2$. This concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Each term is a countable intersection of preimages of a closed set under evaluations
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions

nodes.name: Measurable equivalence with C(R_+, R)
nodes.statement: The identity is a measurable equivalence between the continuous functions of $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}_+}$ with the subset sigma-algebra obtained from the product sigma-algebra, and $C(\mathbb{R}_+, \mathbb{R})$ with the Borel sigma-algebra coming from the compact-open topology. Mathematically this says nothing more than the equality of sigma-algebras of Theorem~\ref{thm:ContinuousMap.borel_eq_iSup_comap_eval} but in Lean we have two different types so we need an equivalence.
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions
nodes.statement_short: The identity map as a measurable equivalence between continuous functions in R^{R_+} (product sigma-algebra) and C(R_+, R) (Borel sigma-algebra).
nodes.label: def:MeasurableEquiv.continuousMap

nodes.name: Wiener measure
nodes.statement: The Wiener measure on $C(\mathbb{R}_+, \mathbb{R})$ with the Borel sigma-algebra is the map of the auxiliary Wiener measure by the measurable equivalence of definition~\ref{def:MeasurableEquiv.continuousMap}.
nodes.section: 6.2 Wiener measure on the continuous functions
nodes.statement_short: Image of the auxiliary Wiener measure under the measurable equivalence onto C(R_+, R).
nodes.label: def:wienerMeasure

nodes.name: Filtration
nodes.statement: A filtration on a measurable space $(\Omega, \mathcal{A})$ with measure $P$ indexed by a preordered set $T$ is a family of sigma-algebras $\mathcal{F} = (\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \in T}$ such that for all $i \le j$, $\mathcal{F}_i \subseteq \mathcal{F}_j$ and for all $t \in T$, $\mathcal{F}_t \subseteq \mathcal{A}$.
differentia: for all $i \le j$, $\mathcal{F}_i \subseteq \mathcal{F}_j$
for all $t \in T$, $\mathcal{F}_t \subseteq \mathcal{A}$
nodes.label: def:filtration

nodes.name: Adapted process
nodes.statement: A process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is said to be adapted with respect to a filtration $\mathcal{F}$ if for all $t \in T$, $X_t$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable.
differentia: for all $t \in T$, $X_t$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable
nodes.label: def:adapted

nodes.name: Progressively measurable
nodes.statement: A stochastic process $X$ is said to be progressively measurable with respect to a filtration $\mathcal{F}$ if at each point in time $i$, $X$ restricted to $(-\infty, i] \times \Omega$ is measurable with respect to the product $\sigma$-algebra where the $\sigma$-algebra used for $\Omega$ is $\mathcal{F}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: X restricted to (-inf, i] x Omega is B x F_i measurable for every time i.
nodes.label: def:IsStronglyProgressive

nodes.name: Right continuous function
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be equipped with a partial order and $f : T \to E$ be a function. Then $f$ is right continuous if for all $t \in T$, $\lim_{s \downarrow t} f(s) = f(t)$.
nodes.label: def:RightContinuous

nodes.name: Cadlag function
nodes.statement: A function $f : T \to E$ is cadlag if it is right continuous and the limit $\lim_{s \uparrow t} f(s)$ exists for all $t \in T$.
differentia: right continuous
the limit $\lim_{s \uparrow t} f(s)$ exists for all $t \in T$
nodes.label: def:IsCadlag

nodes.name: Right-continuous adapted processes are progressively measurable
nodes.statement: Suppose $T$ is a linearly ordered set equipped with the order topology. If $T$ is second countable and a stochastic process $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ is right continuous and adapted, then it is progressively measurable.
assumptions: $T$ is a linearly ordered set equipped with the order topology
$T$ is second countable
a stochastic process $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ is right continuous and adapted
conclusions: it is progressively measurable
nodes.label: lem:Adapted.isStronglyProgressive_of_rightContinuous

nodes.name: Proof of Right-continuous adapted processes are progressively measurable
nodes.statement: Fixing $t \in T$, let $S$ be a union of a dense set of $(-\infty,t]$ and the set of points isolated from right in $(-\infty,t]$. As $T$ is second countable, $S$ can be chosen so that it is countable, which means that there exists a surjective function $u: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow S$. We need to show that $X$ restricted to $(-\infty, t] \times \Omega$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal{B}((-\infty, t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_t$. To this end, we rearrange the image of the first $n$ numbers under the map $u$ in nondecreasing order, denoted by $v_0\le v_1\le \cdots\le v_n$, and define a left continuous discrete approximation of $X$ on $(-\infty, t]$ by $$X^n_s = \begin{cases} X_{v_0} & \text{if } s \le v_0 \\ X_{v_i} & \text{if } s \in (- v_{i-1}, v_i] \end{cases}$$ As $X$ is right continuous, it is easy to see that $X^n \to X$ pointwise as $n \to \infty$. Thus, as each $X^n$ is measurable, it follows that $X$ is also measurable (by using \verb|stronglyMeasurable_of_tendsto|).
nodes.statement_short: Discrete left-continuous approximations X^n built from a countable dense set converge pointwise to X by right continuity; the measurable limit gives progressive measurability.

nodes.name: Countable dense set
nodes.statement: Fixing $t \in T$, let $S$ be a union of a dense set of $(-\infty,t]$ and the set of points isolated from right in $(-\infty,t]$. As $T$ is second countable, $S$ can be chosen so that it is countable, which means that there exists a surjective function $u: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow S$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a countable set S enumerated by u

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We need to show that $X$ restricted to $(-\infty, t] \times \Omega$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal{B}((-\infty, t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to measurability on (-inf,t] x Omega

nodes.name: Discrete approximation
nodes.statement: To this end, we rearrange the image of the first $n$ numbers under the map $u$ in nondecreasing order, denoted by $v_0\le v_1\le \cdots\le v_n$, and define a left continuous discrete approximation of $X$ on $(-\infty, t]$ by $$X^n_s = \begin{cases} X_{v_0} & \text{if } s \le v_0 \\ X_{v_i} & \text{if } s \in (- v_{i-1}, v_i] \end{cases}$$ As $X$ is right continuous, it is easy to see that $X^n \to X$ pointwise as $n \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Define left-continuous approximations X^n converging pointwise to X

nodes.name: Measurable limit
nodes.statement: Thus, as each $X^n$ is measurable, it follows that $X$ is also measurable (by using \verb|stronglyMeasurable_of_tendsto|).
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise limit of measurable maps is measurable

nodes.name: Martingale
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a filtration on a measurable space $\Omega$ with measure $P$ indexed by $T$. A family of functions $M : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a martingale with respect to a filtration $\mathcal{F}$ if $M$ is adapted with respect to $\mathcal{F}$ and for all $i \le j$, $P[M_j \mid \mathcal{F}_i] = M_i$ almost surely.
differentia: $M$ is adapted with respect to $\mathcal{F}$
for all $i \le j$, $P[M_j \mid \mathcal{F}_i] = M_i$ almost surely
nodes.label: def:Martingale

nodes.name: Submartingale
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a filtration on a measurable space $\Omega$ with measure $P$ indexed by $T$. A family of functions $M : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a submartingale with respect to a filtration $\mathcal{F}$ if $M$ is adapted with respect to $\mathcal{F}$ and for all $i \le j$, $P[M_j \mid \mathcal{F}_i] \ge M_i$ almost surely.
differentia: $M$ is adapted with respect to $\mathcal{F}$
for all $i \le j$, $P[M_j \mid \mathcal{F}_i] \ge M_i$ almost surely
nodes.label: def:Submartingale

nodes.name: Nonnegative conditional increments of a submartingale
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a real-valued submartingale with respect to a filtration $\mathcal{F}$. Then for all $i \le j$, we have $0 \le P[M_j - M_i \mid \mathcal{F}_i]$ almost surely.
assumptions: $X$ be a real-valued submartingale with respect to a filtration $\mathcal{F}$
conclusions: for all $i \le j$, we have $0 \le P[M_j - M_i \mid \mathcal{F}_i]$ almost surely
nodes.label: lem:condExp_sub_nonneg

nodes.name: Integrability of submartingale stopped values
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a submartingale. Then for all bounded stopping times $\tau$, the stopped value $X_\tau$ is integrable.
assumptions: $X$ be a submartingale
conclusions: for all bounded stopping times $\tau$, the stopped value $X_\tau$ is integrable
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.integrable_stoppedValue

nodes.name: Adapted modification of a martingale is a martingale
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a martingale and $Y$ is an adapted modification of $X$, then $Y$ is a martingale.
assumptions: $X$ is a martingale
$Y$ is an adapted modification of $X$
conclusions: $Y$ is a martingale
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.congr

nodes.name: Proof of Adapted modification of a martingale is a martingale
nodes.statement: Let $i \le j$ in $T$. We want to show that $P[Y_j \mid \mathcal{F}_i] = Y_i$ almost surely. It suffices to show that $\int_A Y_j \: dP = \int_A Y_i \: dP$ for all $A \in \mathcal{F}_i$. Let then $A \in \mathcal{F}_i$. \begin{align*} \int_A Y_j \: dP &= \int_A X_j \: dP = \int_A X_i \: dP = \int_A Y_i \: dP \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to equality of integrals over A in F_i, then swap Y for X using the modification property and the martingale property of X.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Let $i \le j$ in $T$. We want to show that $P[Y_j \mid \mathcal{F}_i] = Y_i$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: State the conditional-expectation goal

nodes.name: Reduction to integrals
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that $\int_A Y_j \: dP = \int_A Y_i \: dP$ for all $A \in \mathcal{F}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to integrals over sets of F_i

nodes.name: Integral computation
nodes.statement: Let then $A \in \mathcal{F}_i$. \begin{align*} \int_A Y_j \: dP &= \int_A X_j \: dP = \int_A X_i \: dP = \int_A Y_i \: dP \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Swap Y and X in the integrals

nodes.name: Adapted modification of a submartingale is a submartingale
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a submartingale and $Y$ is an adapted modification of $X$, then $Y$ is a submartingale.
assumptions: $X$ is a submartingale
$Y$ is an adapted modification of $X$
conclusions: $Y$ is a submartingale
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.congr

nodes.name: Proof of Adapted modification of a submartingale is a submartingale
nodes.statement: Let $i \le j$ in $T$. We want to show that $P[Y_j \mid \mathcal{F}_i] \ge Y_i$ almost surely. It suffices to show that $\int_A Y_j \: dP \ge \int_A Y_i \: dP$ for all $A \in \mathcal{F}_i$. Let then $A \in \mathcal{F}_i$. \begin{align*} \int_A Y_j \: dP &= \int_A X_j \: dP \ge \int_A X_i \: dP = \int_A Y_i \: dP \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to inequality of integrals over A in F_i, then swap Y for X using the modification property and the submartingale property of X.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Let $i \le j$ in $T$. We want to show that $P[Y_j \mid \mathcal{F}_i] \ge Y_i$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: State the conditional-expectation goal

nodes.name: Reduction to integrals
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that $\int_A Y_j \: dP \ge \int_A Y_i \: dP$ for all $A \in \mathcal{F}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to integrals over sets of F_i

nodes.name: Integral computation
nodes.statement: Let then $A \in \mathcal{F}_i$. \begin{align*} \int_A Y_j \: dP &= \int_A X_j \: dP \ge \int_A X_i \: dP = \int_A Y_i \: dP \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Swap Y and X in the integrals

nodes.name: Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation
nodes.statement: Let $X : \Omega \to E$ be an integrable random variable with values in a normed space $E$ and let $\phi : E \to \mathbb{R}$ be a convex function such that $\phi \circ X$ is integrable. Then, for any sub-$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{G}$, we have \begin{align*} \phi\left( \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \right) &\le \mathbb{E}[\phi(X) \mid \mathcal{G}] \quad \text{a.s.} \end{align*}
assumptions: $X : \Omega \to E$ be an integrable random variable with values in a normed space $E$
$\phi : E \to \mathbb{R}$ be a convex function such that $\phi \circ X$ is integrable
conclusions: \phi\left( \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \right) &\le \mathbb{E}[\phi(X) \mid \mathcal{G}] \quad \text{a.s.}
nodes.label: lem:conditional_jensen

nodes.name: Proof of Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation
nodes.statement: Done in a Mathlib PR for finite measures: \href{https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/27953}{\#27953}.
nodes.statement_short: Pointer to the Mathlib proof (PR #27953, finite measures).

nodes.name: Norm of conditional expectation bound
nodes.statement: Let $X : \Omega \to E$ be an integrable random variable with values in a normed space $E$. Then, for any sub-$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{G}$, we have \begin{align*} \Vert \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \Vert &\le \mathbb{E}[\Vert X \Vert \mid \mathcal{G}] \quad \text{a.s.} \end{align*}
assumptions: $X : \Omega \to E$ be an integrable random variable with values in a normed space $E$
conclusions: \Vert \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \Vert &\le \mathbb{E}[\Vert X \Vert \mid \mathcal{G}] \quad \text{a.s.}
nodes.label: cor:norm_condExp_le

nodes.name: Convex function of a martingale is a submartingale
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \rightarrow \Omega\rightarrow E$ a martingale with values in a normed space $E$. Let $\phi : E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ convex and continuous such that $\phi(X_t)\in L^1(\Omega)$ for every $t\in T$. Then $\phi(X)$ is a sub-martingale.
assumptions: $X : T \rightarrow \Omega\rightarrow E$ a martingale with values in a normed space $E$
$\phi : E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ convex and continuous such that $\phi(X_t)\in L^1(\Omega)$ for every $t\in T$
conclusions: $\phi(X)$ is a sub-martingale
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.submartingale_convex_comp

nodes.name: Proof of Convex function of a martingale is a submartingale
nodes.statement: By the conditional Jensen inequality (Lemma~\ref{lem:conditional_jensen}), $\phi(X_t) = \phi\left( \mathbb{E}[X_T\ |\ \mathcal{F}_t] \right)\leq \mathbb{E}[\phi(X_T)\ |\ \mathcal{F}_t]$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply conditional Jensen to X_t = E[X_T | F_t].

nodes.name: Norm of a martingale is a submartingale
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \rightarrow \Omega \rightarrow E$ a martingale with values in a normed space $E$. Then $\Vert X \Vert$ is a sub-martingale.
assumptions: $X : T \rightarrow \Omega \rightarrow E$ a martingale with values in a normed space $E$
conclusions: $\Vert X \Vert$ is a sub-martingale
nodes.label: cor:Martingale.submartingale_norm

nodes.name: Proof of Norm of a martingale is a submartingale
