nodes.statement: Same proof as Lemma~\ref{lem:Martingale.submartingale_convex_comp}, specialized to $\phi = \Vert \cdot \Vert$, for which we can use Corollary~\ref{cor:norm_condExp_le}.
nodes.statement_short: Same as the convex-composition lemma with phi the norm, using the conditional norm bound.

nodes.name: Convex increasing function of a submartingale is a submartingale
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \rightarrow \Omega \rightarrow E$ a sub-martingale. Let $\phi:E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ convex, continuous, and increasing such that $\phi(X_t)\in L^1(\Omega)$ for every $t\in T$. Then $\phi(X)$ is a sub-martingale.
assumptions: $X : T \rightarrow \Omega \rightarrow E$ a sub-martingale
$\phi:E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ convex, continuous, and increasing such that $\phi(X_t)\in L^1(\Omega)$ for every $t\in T$
conclusions: $\phi(X)$ is a sub-martingale
nodes.label: lem:convex_of_submg_is_submg

nodes.name: Proof of Convex increasing function of a submartingale is a submartingale
nodes.statement: By Jensen and the fact that $\phi$ is increasing $\phi(X_t) \leq \phi\left( \mathbb{E}[X_T\ |\ \mathcal{F}_t] \right)\leq \mathbb{E}[\phi(X_T)\ |\ \mathcal{F}_t]$.
nodes.statement_short: Conditional Jensen plus monotonicity of phi.

nodes.name: Stopping time
nodes.statement: A stopping time with respect to some filtration $\mathcal{F}$ indexed by $T$ is a function $\tau : \Omega \to T \cup \{\infty\}$ such that for all $i$, the preimage of $\{j \mid j \le i\}$ along $\tau$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal{F}_i$.
differentia: for all $i$, the preimage of $\{j \mid j \le i\}$ along $\tau$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal{F}_i$
nodes.label: def:IsStoppingTime

nodes.name: $\sigma$-algebra generated by a stopping time
nodes.statement: Given a stopping time $\tau$ on a time index $T$, define $\mathcal{F}_\tau = \bigcap_{t \in T} \{A \in \mathcal{F} \mid A \cap \{\tau \le t\} \in \mathcal{F}_t\}.$
nodes.label: def:StoppingTimeGen

nodes.name: Monotonicity of stopping-time sigma-algebras
nodes.statement: Let $\tau, \sigma$ be stopping times such that $\tau \le \sigma$. Then, $\mathcal{F}_\tau \subseteq \mathcal{F}_\sigma$.
assumptions: $\tau, \sigma$ be stopping times such that $\tau \le \sigma$
conclusions: $\mathcal{F}_\tau \subseteq \mathcal{F}_\sigma$
nodes.label: lem:StoppingTimeGenMono

nodes.name: Stopped process
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a stochastic process and let $\tau : \Omega \to T$. The stopped process with respect to $\tau$ is defined by \begin{align*} (X^{\tau})_t = \begin{cases} X_t & \text{if } t \le \tau \\ X_{\tau} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:stoppedProcess

nodes.name: Stopped submartingale (discrete time)
nodes.statement: Let $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sub-martingale and $\tau$ a stopping time with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$. Then, the stopped process $X^{\tau}$ is a sub-martingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$.
assumptions: $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sub-martingale and $\tau$ a stopping time with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$
conclusions: the stopped process $X^{\tau}$ is a sub-martingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.stoppedProcess

nodes.name: Hitting time
nodes.statement: For $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ a stochastic process, $B$ a subset of $E$ and $t_0 \in T$, the hitting time of $X$ in $B$ after $t_0$ is the random variable $\Omega \to T\cup\{\infty\}$ defined by \begin{align*} \tau_{B, t_0}(\omega) = \inf\{t \in T \mid t \ge t_0, \: X_t(\omega) \in B\} \: , \end{align*} in which the infimum is infinite if the set is empty.
nodes.statement_short: First time after t_0 at which the process enters B (infinite if never).
nodes.label: def:hittingAfter

nodes.name: Hitting time between two times
nodes.statement: For $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ a stochastic process, $B$ a subset of $E$ and $t_0, t_1 \in T$, the hitting time of $X$ in $B$ between $t_0$ and $t_1$ is the random variable $\Omega \to T\cup\{\infty\}$ defined by \begin{align*} \tau_{B, t_0, t_1}(\omega) = \inf\{t \in T \mid t_0 \le t \le t_1, \: X_t(\omega) \in B\} \: , \end{align*} in which the infimum is infinite if the set is empty.
nodes.statement_short: First time in [t_0, t_1] at which the process enters B (infinite if never).
nodes.label: def:hittingBtwn

nodes.name: Hitting time is a stopping time
nodes.statement: The hitting time $\tau_{B, t_0, t_1}$ of a measurable set by an adapted process on a discrete time index is a stopping time.
nodes.label: lem:isStoppingTime_hittingBtwn

nodes.name: Left continuation
nodes.statement: Assume that $T$ is a partial order. For $\mathcal{F}$ a filtration indexed by $T$ and $t \in T$, we define the \emph{left continuation} as $$\mathcal{F}_{t-} = \begin{cases} \mathcal{F}_t, & \text{if $t$ is isolated on the left in the order topology}; \\ \bigsqcup_{s < t} \mathcal{F}_s, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$ Note that $\bigsqcup$ denotes the supremum in the lattice of sigma-algebras on $\Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: F_{t-} is F_t at left-isolated t, else the supremum of F_s over s < t.
nodes.label: def:leftLimitFiltration

nodes.name: Right continuation
nodes.statement: Assume that $T$ is a partial order. For $\mathcal{F}$ a filtration indexed by $T$ and $t \in T$, we define the \emph{right continuation} as $$\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \begin{cases} \mathcal{F}_t, & \text{if $t$ is isolated on the right in the order topology}; \\ \bigsqcap_{s > t} \mathcal{F}_s, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$ Note that $\bigsqcap$ denotes the infimum in the lattice of sigma-algebras on $\Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: F_{t+} is F_t at right-isolated t, else the infimum of F_s over s > t.
nodes.label: def:rightLimitFiltration

nodes.name: Right continuation is a filtration
nodes.statement: The right continuation of $\mathcal{F}$ is a filtration.
nodes.label: lem:filtrationRightCont

nodes.name: Proof of Right continuation is a filtration
nodes.statement: We endow $T$ with the order topology. Let us first prove that the right continuation is nondecreasing. Let $s, t \in T$ such that $s \le t$. \begin{itemize} \item Suppose $s$ is isolated on the right. Then $\mathcal{F}_{s+} = \mathcal{F}_s$. \begin{itemize} \item If $t$ is isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t$. Because $\mathcal{F}$ is a filtration, we have $\mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t$, and thus $\mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t+}$. \item If $t$ is not isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_{u}$. Let $u > t$. Then $s \le u$, thus $\mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u$. This proves that $\mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \bigsqcap_{u > t}, \mathcal{F}_u$, and thus $\mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t+}$. \end{itemize} \item Suppose now that $s$ is not isolated on the right, so that $\mathcal{F}_{s+} = \bigsqcup_{u > s} \mathcal{F}_u$. \begin{itemize} \item If $t$ is isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t$. As $s$ is not isolated on the right, we deduce that $s \ne t$, and thus $s < t$ because $T$ is a partial order. Therefore $\bigsqcap_{u > s} \mathcal{F}_u \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t$, and thus $\mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t+}$. \item If $t$ is not isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$. For any $u > t$, we have $u > s$ and thus $\bigsqcap_{v > s} \mathcal{F}_v \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u$, proving that $\bigsqcap_{u > s} \mathcal{F}_u \subseteq \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$, and thus $\mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t+}$. \end{itemize} \end{itemize} Turn now to the proof that for all $t \in T$, $\mathcal{F}_{t+} \subseteq \mathcal{A}$. Let $t \in T$. If $t$ is isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t \subseteq \mathcal{A}$ by definition of a filtration. Otherwise there exists $u > t$, and $\mathcal{F}_{t+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u \subseteq \mathcal{A}$, so we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on whether s and t are isolated on the right to show monotonicity, then show each F_{t+} lies in the ambient sigma-algebra.

nodes.name: Order topology
nodes.statement: We endow $T$ with the order topology.
nodes.statement_short: Endow T with the order topology

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: Let us first prove that the right continuation is nondecreasing. Let $s, t \in T$ such that $s \le t$. \begin{itemize} \item Suppose $s$ is isolated on the right. Then $\mathcal{F}_{s+} = \mathcal{F}_s$. \begin{itemize} \item If $t$ is isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t$. Because $\mathcal{F}$ is a filtration, we have $\mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t$, and thus $\mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t+}$. \item If $t$ is not isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_{u}$. Let $u > t$. Then $s \le u$, thus $\mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u$. This proves that $\mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \bigsqcap_{u > t}, \mathcal{F}_u$, and thus $\mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t+}$. \end{itemize} \item Suppose now that $s$ is not isolated on the right, so that $\mathcal{F}_{s+} = \bigsqcup_{u > s} \mathcal{F}_u$. \begin{itemize} \item If $t$ is isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t$. As $s$ is not isolated on the right, we deduce that $s \ne t$, and thus $s < t$ because $T$ is a partial order. Therefore $\bigsqcap_{u > s} \mathcal{F}_u \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t$, and thus $\mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t+}$. \item If $t$ is not isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$. For any $u > t$, we have $u > s$ and thus $\bigsqcap_{v > s} \mathcal{F}_v \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u$, proving that $\bigsqcap_{u > s} \mathcal{F}_u \subseteq \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$, and thus $\mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t+}$. \end{itemize} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Show the right continuation is nondecreasing

nodes.name: Fix s <= t
nodes.statement: Let $s, t \in T$ such that $s \le t$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix s <= t

nodes.name: s right-isolated
nodes.statement: Suppose $s$ is isolated on the right. Then $\mathcal{F}_{s+} = \mathcal{F}_s$. \begin{itemize} \item If $t$ is isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t$. Because $\mathcal{F}$ is a filtration, we have $\mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t$, and thus $\mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t+}$. \item If $t$ is not isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_{u}$. Let $u > t$. Then $s \le u$, thus $\mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u$. This proves that $\mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \bigsqcap_{u > t}, \mathcal{F}_u$, and thus $\mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t+}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Case s isolated on the right, subcases on t

nodes.name: s not right-isolated
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $s$ is not isolated on the right, so that $\mathcal{F}_{s+} = \bigsqcup_{u > s} \mathcal{F}_u$. \begin{itemize} \item If $t$ is isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t$. As $s$ is not isolated on the right, we deduce that $s \ne t$, and thus $s < t$ because $T$ is a partial order. Therefore $\bigsqcap_{u > s} \mathcal{F}_u \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t$, and thus $\mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t+}$. \item If $t$ is not isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$. For any $u > t$, we have $u > s$ and thus $\bigsqcap_{v > s} \mathcal{F}_v \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u$, proving that $\bigsqcap_{u > s} \mathcal{F}_u \subseteq \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$, and thus $\mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t+}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Case s not isolated on the right, subcases on t

nodes.name: Sub-sigma-algebra
nodes.statement: Turn now to the proof that for all $t \in T$, $\mathcal{F}_{t+} \subseteq \mathcal{A}$. Let $t \in T$. If $t$ is isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t \subseteq \mathcal{A}$ by definition of a filtration. Otherwise there exists $u > t$, and $\mathcal{F}_{t+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u \subseteq \mathcal{A}$, so we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Each F_{t+} is contained in A

nodes.name: Right continuation in the order topology
nodes.statement: Suppose $T$ is a topological space with the topology being the order topology. For $t \in T$, the right continuation of $\mathcal{F}$ at $t$ is given by $$\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \begin{cases} \mathcal{F}_t, & \text{if $t$ is isolated on the right}; \\ \bigsqcap_{s > t} \mathcal{F}_s, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$
assumptions: $T$ is a topological space with the topology being the order topology
conclusions: the right continuation of $\mathcal{F}$ at $t$ is given by $$\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \begin{cases} \mathcal{F}_t, & \text{if $t$ is isolated on the right}; \\ \bigsqcap_{s > t} \mathcal{F}_s, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$
nodes.label: lem:rightContDef

nodes.name: Proof of Right continuation in the order topology
nodes.statement: This follows from Definition~\ref{def:rightLimitFiltration} because the topology on $T$ agrees with the one used to define the right continuation.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition of the right continuation.

nodes.name: Right continuation at right-isolated points
nodes.statement: Suppose $T$ is a topological space with the topology being the order topology. Assume that $t \in T$ is isolated on the right, meaning that there exists a neighbourhood $\mathcal{V}$ of $t$ such that $\mathcal{V} \cap \{u \mid u > t\} = \emptyset$. Then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t$.
assumptions: $T$ is a topological space with the topology being the order topology
$t \in T$ is isolated on the right, meaning that there exists a neighbourhood $\mathcal{V}$ of $t$ such that $\mathcal{V} \cap \{u \mid u > t\} = \emptyset$
conclusions: $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t$
nodes.label: lem:rightContIsolated

nodes.name: Proof of Right continuation at right-isolated points
nodes.statement: This is a direct consequence of Lemma~\ref{lem:rightContDef}.
nodes.statement_short: Direct consequence of the order-topology description of the right continuation.

nodes.name: Right continuation for orders with successor
nodes.statement: Assume that $T$ is a linear order with successor. This means that for any $t$, there is an element $succ(t) \ge t$ such that for any $u > t$, $u \ge succ(t)$, and if $succ(t) \le t$, then $t$ is maximal. Then the right continuation of $\mathcal{F}$ is equal to $\mathcal{F}$.
assumptions: $T$ is a linear order with successor. This means that for any $t$, there is an element $succ(t) \ge t$ such that for any $u > t$, $u \ge succ(t)$, and if $succ(t) \le t$, then $t$ is maximal
conclusions: the right continuation of $\mathcal{F}$ is equal to $\mathcal{F}$
nodes.label: lem:rightContSuccOrder

nodes.name: Proof of Right continuation for orders with successor
nodes.statement: Endow $T$ with the order topology. In a linear order with successor equipped with the order topology, every point is isolated on the right, so we can conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:rightContIsolated}.
nodes.statement_short: Every point is right-isolated in a successor order; apply the right-isolated case.

nodes.name: Right continuation at maximal points
nodes.statement: If $t \in T$ is maximal, $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t$.
assumptions: $t \in T$ is maximal
conclusions: $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t$
nodes.label: lem:rightContIsMax

nodes.name: Proof of Right continuation at maximal points
nodes.statement: Endow $T$ with the order topology. As $t$ is maximal, it is isolated on the right for this topology, so we can conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:rightContIsolated}.
nodes.statement_short: A maximal point is right-isolated; apply the right-isolated case.

nodes.name: Right continuation with an immediate successor
nodes.statement: If $T$ is a linear order and there exists $u > t$ such that $(t, u) = \emptyset$, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t$.
assumptions: $T$ is a linear order
there exists $u > t$ such that $(t, u) = \emptyset$
conclusions: $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t$
nodes.label: lem:rightContExistsGt

nodes.name: Proof of Right continuation with an immediate successor
nodes.statement: Endow $T$ with the order topology. The hypothesis implies that $t$ is isolated on the right in this topology, so we can conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:rightContIsolated}.
nodes.statement_short: The empty gap makes t right-isolated; apply the right-isolated case.

nodes.name: Right continuation at non-isolated points
nodes.statement: Suppose $T$ is a topological space with the topology being the order topology. Assume that $t \in T$ is not isolated on the right, meaning that for all neighbourhood $\mathcal{V}$ of $t$, $\mathcal{V} \cap \{u | u > t\} \ne \emptyset$. Then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$.
assumptions: $T$ is a topological space with the topology being the order topology
$t \in T$ is not isolated on the right, meaning that for all neighbourhood $\mathcal{V}$ of $t$, $\mathcal{V} \cap \{u | u > t\} \ne \emptyset$
conclusions: $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$
nodes.label: lem:rightContNeBot

nodes.name: Proof of Right continuation at non-isolated points
nodes.statement: This is a direct consequence of Lemma~\ref{lem:rightContDef}.
nodes.statement_short: Direct consequence of the order-topology description of the right continuation.

nodes.name: Right continuation in dense orders
nodes.statement: Assume that $T$ is a densely ordered linear order, meaning that for all $s < t$, there exists $u$ such that $s < u < t$. If $t$ is not maximal, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$.
assumptions: $T$ is a densely ordered linear order, meaning that for all $s < t$, there exists $u$ such that $s < u < t$
$t$ is not maximal
conclusions: $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$
nodes.label: lem:rightContNotIsMax

nodes.name: Proof of Right continuation in dense orders
nodes.statement: Endow $T$ with the order topology. In a densely ordered linear order, a point which is not maximal is not isolated on the right, so we can conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:rightContNeBot}.
nodes.statement_short: In a dense order a non-maximal point is not right-isolated; apply the non-isolated case.

nodes.name: Right continuation in dense orders without maximum
nodes.statement: If $T$ is a densely ordered linear order with no maximal element, then forall $t \in T$ we have $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$.
assumptions: $T$ is a densely ordered linear order with no maximal element
conclusions: forall $t \in T$ we have $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$
nodes.label: lem:rightContEq

nodes.name: Proof of Right continuation in dense orders without maximum
nodes.statement: For all $t$, $t$ is not maximal, so we can conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:rightContNotIsMax}.
nodes.statement_short: No point is maximal; apply the dense-order lemma.

nodes.name: Filtration is contained in its right continuation
nodes.statement: The filtration $\mathcal{F}$ is contained in its right continuation.
nodes.label: lem:leRightCont

nodes.name: Proof of Filtration is contained in its right continuation
nodes.statement: Endow $T$ with the order topology, and consider $t \in T$. Using Lemma~\ref{lem:rightContDef}, we split into two cases. If $t$ is isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t \supseteq \mathcal{F}_t$ and we are done. Otherwise, for all $u > t$, $\mathcal{F}_t \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u$, therefore $\mathcal{F}_t \subseteq \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$, and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether t is right-isolated, using monotonicity of the filtration.

nodes.name: Case split setup
nodes.statement: Endow $T$ with the order topology, and consider $t \in T$. Using Lemma~\ref{lem:rightContDef}, we split into two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Split on right-isolation via the order-topology lemma

nodes.name: Right-isolated case
nodes.statement: If $t$ is isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t+} = \mathcal{F}_t \supseteq \mathcal{F}_t$ and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: F_{t+} = F_t

nodes.name: Non-isolated case
nodes.statement: Otherwise, for all $u > t$, $\mathcal{F}_t \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u$, therefore $\mathcal{F}_t \subseteq \bigsqcap_{u > t} \mathcal{F}_u$, and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: F_t lies in every F_u, u > t

nodes.name: Right continuation is idempotent
nodes.statement: The right continuation of the right continuation of $\mathcal{F}$ is equal to the right continuation of $\mathcal{F}$.
nodes.label: lem:rightContSelf

nodes.name: Proof of Right continuation is idempotent
nodes.statement: Let $t \in T$. From Lemma~\ref{lem:leRightCont}, we already now that $\mathcal{F}_{t+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t++}$. Endow $T$ with the order topology and split according to Lemma~\ref{lem:rightContDef}. If $t$ is isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t++} = \mathcal{F}_{t+}$ and we are done. Otherwise consider $u > t$. Then there exists $v \in T$ such that $t < v < u$. If $v$ is not isolated on the right then $$\mathcal{F}_{t++} = \bigsqcap_{s > t} \mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{v+} = \bigsqcap_{s > v} \mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u,$$ and otherwise $$\mathcal{F}_{t++} = \bigsqcap_{s > t} \mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{v+} = \mathcal{F}_v \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u,$$ thus $\mathcal{F}_{t++} \subseteq \bigsqcap_{s > t} \mathcal{F}_s = \mathcal{F}_{t+}$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: One inclusion from F <= F_+; for the other, case split on right-isolation and use an intermediate point v between t and u.

nodes.name: Easy inclusion
nodes.statement: Let $t \in T$. From Lemma~\ref{lem:leRightCont}, we already now that $\mathcal{F}_{t+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{t++}$.
nodes.statement_short: F_{t+} <= F_{t++} by the previous lemma

nodes.name: Case split setup
nodes.statement: Endow $T$ with the order topology and split according to Lemma~\ref{lem:rightContDef}.
nodes.statement_short: Split on right-isolation

nodes.name: Right-isolated case
nodes.statement: If $t$ is isolated on the right, then $\mathcal{F}_{t++} = \mathcal{F}_{t+}$ and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Equality is immediate

nodes.name: Non-isolated case
nodes.statement: Otherwise consider $u > t$. Then there exists $v \in T$ such that $t < v < u$. If $v$ is not isolated on the right then $$\mathcal{F}_{t++} = \bigsqcap_{s > t} \mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{v+} = \bigsqcap_{s > v} \mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u,$$ and otherwise $$\mathcal{F}_{t++} = \bigsqcap_{s > t} \mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{v+} = \mathcal{F}_v \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u,$$ thus $\mathcal{F}_{t++} \subseteq \bigsqcap_{s > t} \mathcal{F}_s = \mathcal{F}_{t+}$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Bound F_{t++} by every F_u via an intermediate v

nodes.name: Intermediate point
nodes.statement: Otherwise consider $u > t$. Then there exists $v \in T$ such that $t < v < u$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick v with t < v < u

nodes.name: Bound via v
nodes.statement: If $v$ is not isolated on the right then $$\mathcal{F}_{t++} = \bigsqcap_{s > t} \mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{v+} = \bigsqcap_{s > v} \mathcal{F}_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u,$$ and otherwise $$\mathcal{F}_{t++} = \bigsqcap_{s > t} \mathcal{F}_{s+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{v+} = \mathcal{F}_v \subseteq \mathcal{F}_u,$$ thus $\mathcal{F}_{t++} \subseteq \bigsqcap_{s > t} \mathcal{F}_s = \mathcal{F}_{t+}$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: F_{t++} <= F_{v+} <= F_u in both subcases, hence <= F_{t+}

nodes.name: Right-continuous filtration
nodes.statement: We say that the filtration is \emph{right-continuous} if for all $t \in T$, $\mathcal{F}_{t+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t$.
differentia: for all $t \in T$, $\mathcal{F}_{t+} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t$
nodes.label: def:rightContinuous

nodes.name: Right-continuous filtration equals its right continuation
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{F}$ is right-continuous, then for all $t \in T$, $\mathcal{F}_t = \mathcal{F}_{t+}$.
assumptions: $\mathcal{F}$ is right-continuous
conclusions: for all $t \in T$, $\mathcal{F}_t = \mathcal{F}_{t+}$
nodes.label: lem:eqRightCont

nodes.name: Proof of Right-continuous filtration equals its right continuation
nodes.statement: This is a direct consequence of Definition~\ref{def:rightContinuous} and Lemma~\ref{lem:leRightCont}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the definition of right-continuity with F <= F_+.

nodes.name: Right continuation is right-continuous
nodes.statement: The right continuation of $\mathcal{F}$ is right-continuous.
nodes.label: lem:rightContinuousRightCont

nodes.name: Proof of Right continuation is right-continuous
nodes.statement: This follows immediately from Lemma~\ref{lem:rightContSelf}.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from idempotence of the right continuation.

nodes.name: Measurable sets of a right-continuous filtration
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{F}$ is right-continuous, then for all $t \in T$, any set $A \subseteq \Omega$ which is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable is also $\mathcal{F}_{t+}$-measurable.
assumptions: $\mathcal{F}$ is right-continuous
conclusions: for all $t \in T$, any set $A \subseteq \Omega$ which is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable is also $\mathcal{F}_{t+}$-measurable
nodes.label: lem:rightContinuousMeasurableSet

nodes.name: Proof of Measurable sets of a right-continuous filtration
nodes.statement: This is a direct consequence of Definition~\ref{def:rightContinuous}.
nodes.statement_short: Direct consequence of the definition of right-continuity.

nodes.name: Usual conditions
nodes.statement: We say that a filtered probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ satisfies the usual conditions if the filtration is right-continuous and if $\mathcal{F}_t$ contains all the $P$-null sets for all $t \in T$.
differentia: the filtration is right-continuous
$\mathcal{F}_t$ contains all the $P$-null sets for all $t \in T$
nodes.label: def:hasUsualConditions

nodes.name: Predictable $\sigma$-algebra
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a filtration on a measurable space indexed $\Omega$ by a linearly ordered set $T$. Let $S = \{\{\bot\} \times A \mid A \in \mathcal{F}_\bot\}$ if $T$ has a bottom element and $S = \emptyset$ otherwise. The predictable sigma-algebra on $T \times \Omega$ is the sigma-algebra generated by the set of sets $\{(t, \infty] \times A \mid t \in T, \: A \in \mathcal{F}_t\} \cup S$.
nodes.statement_short: Sigma-algebra on T x Omega generated by the sets (t, inf] x A with A in F_t, plus {bot} x A for A in F_bot.
nodes.label: def:predictableMeasurableSpace

nodes.name: Predictable process
nodes.statement: A process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is said to be predictable with respect to a filtration $\mathcal{F}$ if it is measurable with respect to the predictable sigma-algebra on $T \times \Omega$.
differentia: it is measurable with respect to the predictable sigma-algebra on $T \times \Omega$
nodes.label: def:predictable

nodes.name: Predictable processes are progressively measurable
nodes.statement: A predictable process is progressively measurable.
nodes.label: lem:Predictable.progressive

nodes.name: Proof of Predictable processes are progressively measurable
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \times \Omega \to E$ be a predictable process, we will show that it is progressively measurable. Namely, fixing $t \in T$, denoting $$\iota_t : [0, t] \to T : s \mapsto s$$ we need to show that $\iota_t \circ X : [0, t] \times \Omega \to E$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal{B}([0, t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_t$. Denoting $\Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$ for the predictable $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\mathcal{F}$, as $u$ is predictable, we have that $X^{-1}(\mathcal{B}(E)) \le \Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$. Thus, to show that $\iota_t \circ X$ is $\mathcal{B}([0, t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_t$-measurable, it suffices to show that $\iota_t^{-1}(\Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}) \le \mathcal{B}([0, t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_t$. In particular, as $$\Sigma_{\mathcal{F}} = \sigma(\{(s, \infty) \times A \mid A \in \mathcal{F}_s\} \cup \{\{\perp\} \times A \mid A \in \mathcal{F}_\perp\})$$ is suffices to show that sets of the form $\iota_t^{-1}((s, \infty) \times A)$ for some $s \in T, A \in \mathcal{F}_s$ and $\iota_t^{-1}(\{\bot\} \times A)$ for some $A \in \mathcal{F}_\bot$ are $\mathcal{B}([0, t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_t$-measurable. Indeed, if $A \in \mathcal{F}_\bot$ $$\iota_t^{-1}(\{\bot\} \times A) = \{\bot\} \times A$$ while for any $s \in T$ and $A \in \mathcal{F}_s$, $$\iota_t^{-1}((s, \infty) \times A) = \begin{cases} \varnothing, & t < s\\ (s, t] \times A, & s \le t. \end{cases}$$ By the monotonicity of the filtration $\mathcal{F}$, all of these cases are $\mathcal{B}([0, t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_t$-measurable allowing us to conclude.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the generators of the predictable sigma-algebra and compute their preimages under the inclusion of [0,t]; monotonicity of the filtration concludes.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \times \Omega \to E$ be a predictable process, we will show that it is progressively measurable. Namely, fixing $t \in T$, denoting $$\iota_t : [0, t] \to T : s \mapsto s$$ we need to show that $\iota_t \circ X : [0, t] \times \Omega \to E$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal{B}([0, t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce progressive measurability to measurability of the restriction

nodes.name: Reduction to generators
nodes.statement: Denoting $\Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$ for the predictable $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\mathcal{F}$, as $u$ is predictable, we have that $X^{-1}(\mathcal{B}(E)) \le \Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$. Thus, to show that $\iota_t \circ X$ is $\mathcal{B}([0, t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_t$-measurable, it suffices to show that $\iota_t^{-1}(\Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}) \le \mathcal{B}([0, t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_t$. In particular, as $$\Sigma_{\mathcal{F}} = \sigma(\{(s, \infty) \times A \mid A \in \mathcal{F}_s\} \cup \{\{\perp\} \times A \mid A \in \mathcal{F}_\perp\})$$ is suffices to show that sets of the form $\iota_t^{-1}((s, \infty) \times A)$ for some $s \in T, A \in \mathcal{F}_s$ and $\iota_t^{-1}(\{\bot\} \times A)$ for some $A \in \mathcal{F}_\bot$ are $\mathcal{B}([0, t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_t$-measurable.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to check preimages of the generating sets

nodes.name: Preimages of generators
nodes.statement: Indeed, if $A \in \mathcal{F}_\bot$ $$\iota_t^{-1}(\{\bot\} \times A) = \{\bot\} \times A$$ while for any $s \in T$ and $A \in \mathcal{F}_s$, $$\iota_t^{-1}((s, \infty) \times A) = \begin{cases} \varnothing, & t < s\\ (s, t] \times A, & s \le t. \end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: Compute preimages of the generators

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: By the monotonicity of the filtration $\mathcal{F}$, all of these cases are $\mathcal{B}([0, t]) \otimes \mathcal{F}_t$-measurable allowing us to conclude.
nodes.statement_short: All preimages are measurable by monotonicity

nodes.name: Predictable rectangles are predictable-measurable
nodes.statement: Sets of the form $(s, t] \times A$ for any $A \in \mathcal{F}_s$ is measurable with respect to the predictable $\sigma$-algebra.
nodes.label: lem:predictable_Ioc_prod

nodes.name: Proof of Predictable rectangles are predictable-measurable
nodes.statement: For $t \le s$, the set in question is empty and thusly, trivially measurable. On the other hand, for $s < t$, measurability follows as $(s, t] \times A = (s, \infty) \times A \setminus (t, \infty) \times A$.
nodes.statement_short: Write (s,t] x A as a difference of two generating sets.

nodes.name: Predictability in discrete time
nodes.statement: Let $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to E$ be a stochastic process and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a filtration indexed by $\mathbb{N}$. Then $X$ is predictable if and only if $X_0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable and for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X_{n+1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable.
assumptions: $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to E$ be a stochastic process
$\mathcal{F}$ be a filtration indexed by $\mathbb{N}$
conclusions: $X$ is predictable if and only if $X_0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable and for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X_{n+1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable
equivalent_conditions: $X$ is predictable
$X_0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable and for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X_{n+1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable
nodes.label: lem:predictable_nat_iff

nodes.name: Proof of Predictability in discrete time
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $X$ is predictable. Straightaway, $X_0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable as predictable implies progressively measurable which in turn implies adapted. Fixing $n$, we observe that for any $S \in \mathcal{B}(E)$, $$X_{n + 1}^{-1}(S) = \{\omega \mid (n + 1, \omega) \in X^{-1}(S)\} = \pi^{-1}(\iota^{-1}(X^{-1}(S)))$$ where $$\pi : \Omega \to \{n + 1\} \times \Omega : \omega \mapsto (n + 1, \omega)$$ and $$\iota : \{n + 1\} \times \Omega \to T \times \Omega : (n + 1, \omega) \mapsto (n + 1, \omega).$$ As $X^{-1}(S) \in \Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$ -- the predictable $\sigma$-algebra, it suffices to show that $\pi^{-1}(\iota^{-1}(\Sigma_{\mathcal{F}})) \in \mathcal{F}_n$. To this end, we again only need to show these for the generating sets of $\Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$: \begin{itemize} \item For $A \in \mathcal{F}_0$, measurability is clear as $\iota^{-1}(\{0\} \times A) = \varnothing$. \item Similarly, for $m > n$ and $A \in \mathcal{F}_m$, $\iota^{-1}((m, \infty) \times A) = \varnothing$. \item For $m \le n$ and $A \in \mathcal{F}_m \le \mathcal{F}_n$ we have that $\pi^{-1}(\iota^{-1}((m, \infty) \times A)) = A$ which is $\mathcal{F}_n$ measurable by the monotonicity of the filtration. \end{itemize} Now, supposing $X_0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable and $X_{n + 1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable, we will show that $X$ is predictable. Indeed, fixing $S \in \mathcal{B}(E)$, we have $$X^{-1}(S) = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \{n\} \times X_n^{-1}(S) = {0} \times X_0^{-1}(S) \cup \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \{n + 1\} \times X_{n + 1}^{-1}(S).$$ Thus, as $\{0\} \times X_0^{-1}(S) \in \Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$ by construction and $\{n + 1\} \times X_{n + 1}^{-1}(S) = (n, n + 1] \times X_{n + 1}^{-1}(S) \in \Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_Ioc_prod} and the fact that $X_{n + 1}^{-1}(S) \in \mathcal{F}_n$, we have that $X^{-1}(S) \in \Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Forward direction: check the preimages of the generators of the predictable sigma-algebra; converse: decompose X^{-1}(S) into predictable rectangles (n, n+1] x X_{n+1}^{-1}(S).

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $X$ is predictable. Straightaway, $X_0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable as predictable implies progressively measurable which in turn implies adapted. Fixing $n$, we observe that for any $S \in \mathcal{B}(E)$, $$X_{n + 1}^{-1}(S) = \{\omega \mid (n + 1, \omega) \in X^{-1}(S)\} = \pi^{-1}(\iota^{-1}(X^{-1}(S)))$$ where $$\pi : \Omega \to \{n + 1\} \times \Omega : \omega \mapsto (n + 1, \omega)$$ and $$\iota : \{n + 1\} \times \Omega \to T \times \Omega : (n + 1, \omega) \mapsto (n + 1, \omega).$$ As $X^{-1}(S) \in \Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$ -- the predictable $\sigma$-algebra, it suffices to show that $\pi^{-1}(\iota^{-1}(\Sigma_{\mathcal{F}})) \in \mathcal{F}_n$. To this end, we again only need to show these for the generating sets of $\Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$: \begin{itemize} \item For $A \in \mathcal{F}_0$, measurability is clear as $\iota^{-1}(\{0\} \times A) = \varnothing$. \item Similarly, for $m > n$ and $A \in \mathcal{F}_m$, $\iota^{-1}((m, \infty) \times A) = \varnothing$. \item For $m \le n$ and $A \in \mathcal{F}_m \le \mathcal{F}_n$ we have that $\pi^{-1}(\iota^{-1}((m, \infty) \times A)) = A$ which is $\mathcal{F}_n$ measurable by the monotonicity of the filtration. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Predictable implies the measurability conditions

nodes.name: X_0 measurable
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $X$ is predictable. Straightaway, $X_0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable as predictable implies progressively measurable which in turn implies adapted.
nodes.statement_short: X_0 is F_0-measurable since predictable implies adapted

nodes.name: Reduction for X_{n+1}
nodes.statement: Fixing $n$, we observe that for any $S \in \mathcal{B}(E)$, $$X_{n + 1}^{-1}(S) = \{\omega \mid (n + 1, \omega) \in X^{-1}(S)\} = \pi^{-1}(\iota^{-1}(X^{-1}(S)))$$ where $$\pi : \Omega \to \{n + 1\} \times \Omega : \omega \mapsto (n + 1, \omega)$$ and $$\iota : \{n + 1\} \times \Omega \to T \times \Omega : (n + 1, \omega) \mapsto (n + 1, \omega).$$ As $X^{-1}(S) \in \Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$ -- the predictable $\sigma$-algebra, it suffices to show that $\pi^{-1}(\iota^{-1}(\Sigma_{\mathcal{F}})) \in \mathcal{F}_n$. To this end, we again only need to show these for the generating sets of $\Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$:
nodes.statement_short: Reduce F_n-measurability of X_{n+1} to the generators

nodes.name: Empty preimage cases
nodes.statement: For $A \in \mathcal{F}_0$, measurability is clear as $\iota^{-1}(\{0\} \times A) = \varnothing$. \item Similarly, for $m > n$ and $A \in \mathcal{F}_m$, $\iota^{-1}((m, \infty) \times A) = \varnothing$.
nodes.statement_short: Generators at 0 and m > n have empty preimage

nodes.name: Case m <= n
nodes.statement: For $m \le n$ and $A \in \mathcal{F}_m \le \mathcal{F}_n$ we have that $\pi^{-1}(\iota^{-1}((m, \infty) \times A)) = A$ which is $\mathcal{F}_n$ measurable by the monotonicity of the filtration.
nodes.statement_short: Preimage is A, F_n-measurable by monotonicity

nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement: Now, supposing $X_0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable and $X_{n + 1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable, we will show that $X$ is predictable. Indeed, fixing $S \in \mathcal{B}(E)$, we have $$X^{-1}(S) = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \{n\} \times X_n^{-1}(S) = {0} \times X_0^{-1}(S) \cup \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \{n + 1\} \times X_{n + 1}^{-1}(S).$$ Thus, as $\{0\} \times X_0^{-1}(S) \in \Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$ by construction and $\{n + 1\} \times X_{n + 1}^{-1}(S) = (n, n + 1] \times X_{n + 1}^{-1}(S) \in \Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_Ioc_prod} and the fact that $X_{n + 1}^{-1}(S) \in \mathcal{F}_n$, we have that $X^{-1}(S) \in \Sigma_{\mathcal{F}}$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose X^{-1}(S) into predictable rectangles

nodes.name: Left-continuous adapted processes are predictable
nodes.statement: An adapted process with left-continuous paths is predictable.
nodes.label: lem:Adapted.isPredictable_of_leftContinuous

nodes.name: Uniform integrability of conditional expectations
nodes.statement: If $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is a family of (probabilistically) uniformly integrable functions and $(\mathcal{F}_j)_{j \in \kappa}$ is a family of $\sigma$-algebras, then the family $(P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j])_{i \in \iota, j \in \kappa}$ is uniformly integrable.
assumptions: $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is a family of (probabilistically) uniformly integrable functions
$(\mathcal{F}_j)_{j \in \kappa}$ is a family of $\sigma$-algebras
conclusions: the family $(P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j])_{i \in \iota, j \in \kappa}$ is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:condExpUI

nodes.name: Proof of Uniform integrability of conditional expectations
nodes.statement: Since $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is uniformly integrable, it is uniformly bounded in $L^1$, thus so is $(P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j])_{i \in \iota, j \in \kappa}$. Moreover, for any \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists some \(\delta > 0\) such that for any measurable set \(A\) with \(P(A) < \delta\), we have that \(\sup_{i \in \iota} P[|X_i| \mathbb{I}_A] < \epsilon\). On the other hand, by Markov's inequality, for any $\lambda > 0$, $i \in \iota$ and $j \in \kappa$ we have that \[P(|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j]| \ge \lambda) \le \lambda^{-1}P[|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j]|] \le \lambda^{-1}P[|X_i|].\] Now set \(\lambda := \delta^{-1} \sup_{i \in \iota} P[|X_i|] + 1\). Then for any $i \in \iota$ and $j \in \kappa$ we have that \[P(|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j]| \ge \lambda) \le \frac{P[|X_i|]}{\delta^{-1} \sup_{k \in \iota} P[|X_k|] + 1} < \delta,\] and so, \begin{align*} P[|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j]| \mathbb{I}_{|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_i]| \ge \lambda}] & = P[|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j] \mathbb{I}_{|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_i]| \ge \lambda}|] \\ & = P[|P[X_i \mathbb{I}_{|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_i]| \ge \lambda} \mid \mathcal{F}_j]|] \\ & \le P[P[|X_i|\mathbb{I}_{|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j]| \ge \lambda} \mid \mathcal{F}_j]] \\ & = P[|X_i|\mathbb{I}_{|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j]| \ge \lambda}] < \epsilon, \end{align*} showing that \((P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j])_{i \in \iota, j \in \kappa}\) is uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: L^1 boundedness transfers to conditional expectations; Markov's inequality makes {|E[X_i|F_j]| >= lambda} small, and uniform integrability of X bounds the tail integrals.

nodes.name: L1 boundedness
nodes.statement: Since $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is uniformly integrable, it is uniformly bounded in $L^1$, thus so is $(P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j])_{i \in \iota, j \in \kappa}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conditional expectations are uniformly L^1-bounded

nodes.name: Uniform absolute continuity
nodes.statement: Moreover, for any \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists some \(\delta > 0\) such that for any measurable set \(A\) with \(P(A) < \delta\), we have that \(\sup_{i \in \iota} P[|X_i| \mathbb{I}_A] < \epsilon\).
nodes.statement_short: Choose delta for epsilon from uniform integrability of X

nodes.name: Markov bound
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by Markov's inequality, for any $\lambda > 0$, $i \in \iota$ and $j \in \kappa$ we have that \[P(|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j]| \ge \lambda) \le \lambda^{-1}P[|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j]|] \le \lambda^{-1}P[|X_i|].\]
nodes.statement_short: Markov's inequality bounds the tail probability

nodes.name: Tail bound
nodes.statement: Now set \(\lambda := \delta^{-1} \sup_{i \in \iota} P[|X_i|] + 1\). Then for any $i \in \iota$ and $j \in \kappa$ we have that \[P(|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j]| \ge \lambda) \le \frac{P[|X_i|]}{\delta^{-1} \sup_{k \in \iota} P[|X_k|] + 1} < \delta,\] and so, \begin{align*} P[|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j]| \mathbb{I}_{|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_i]| \ge \lambda}] & = P[|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j] \mathbb{I}_{|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_i]| \ge \lambda}|] \\ & = P[|P[X_i \mathbb{I}_{|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_i]| \ge \lambda} \mid \mathcal{F}_j]|] \\ & \le P[P[|X_i|\mathbb{I}_{|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j]| \ge \lambda} \mid \mathcal{F}_j]] \\ & = P[|X_i|\mathbb{I}_{|P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j]| \ge \lambda}] < \epsilon, \end{align*} showing that \((P[X_i \mid \mathcal{F}_j])_{i \in \iota, j \in \kappa}\) is uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Choose lambda so the tail set has probability < delta and bound the tail integral

nodes.name: Bounded in Lp implies uniformly integrable in Lq
nodes.statement: Let $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a family of random variables that is bounded in $\mathrm L^p$, for $p > q \ge 1$. Then $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is uniformly integrable in $\mathrm L^q$.
assumptions: $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a family of random variables that is bounded in $\mathrm L^p$, for $p > q \ge 1$
conclusions: $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is uniformly integrable in $\mathrm L^q$
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrable_of_bounded

nodes.name: Proof of Bounded in Lp implies uniformly integrable in Lq
nodes.statement: For any measurable set $s$ we have by Hölder inequality that $$\|X_t \mathbb{I}_s\|_q \le \|X_t\|_p P(s)^{1/q - 1/p},$$ which goes to $0$ as $P(s)$ goes to zero. Moreover, $$\|X_t\|_q \le P(\Omega)^{1/q - 1/p} \|X_t\|_p,$$ so $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is bounded in $\mathrm L^q$.
nodes.statement_short: Hölder's inequality bounds ||X 1_s||_q by ||X||_p P(s)^{1/q-1/p}, giving uniform integrability and L^q boundedness.

nodes.name: Uniform integrability of martingale stopped values
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a martingale on a discrete index set and let $(\tau_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of stopping times that are uniformly bounded by $n$. Then, the family of stopped values $\{X_{\tau_k}\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable.
assumptions: $X$ be a martingale on a discrete index set
$(\tau_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of stopping times that are uniformly bounded by $n$
conclusions: the family of stopped values $\{X_{\tau_k}\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_martingale

nodes.name: Proof of Uniform integrability of martingale stopped values
nodes.statement: By optional sampling (Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSampling_discrete}), we have that for each $k$, $X_{\tau_k} = P[X_n \mid \mathcal{F}_{\tau_k}]$. Thus, the result follows by Lemma~\ref{lem:condExpUI} as $\{X_n\}$ is uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Optional sampling writes each X_{tau_k} as E[X_n | F_{tau_k}]; conclude by uniform integrability of conditional expectations.

nodes.name: Uniform integrability of martingale stopped values with countable range
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a martingale and let $(\tau_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of stopping times that are uniformly bounded by $n$. Then, the family of stopped values $\{X_{\tau_k}\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable if for each $k$, $\tau_k$ takes value in a countable set.
assumptions: $X$ be a martingale
$(\tau_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of stopping times that are uniformly bounded by $n$
for each $k$, $\tau_k$ takes value in a countable set
conclusions: the family of stopped values $\{X_{\tau_k}\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_martingale_of_countable_range

nodes.name: Proof of Uniform integrability of martingale stopped values with countable range
nodes.statement: Same proof as in Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_martingale}.
nodes.statement_short: Same proof as the bounded discrete-index case.

nodes.name: Sum of uniformly integrable families
nodes.statement: Let $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ and $(Y_t)_{t \in T}$ be two families of uniformly integrable random variables. Then the family $(X_t + Y_t)_{t \in T}$ is uniformly integrable.
assumptions: $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ and $(Y_t)_{t \in T}$ be two families of uniformly integrable random variables
conclusions: the family $(X_t + Y_t)_{t \in T}$ is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrableAdd

nodes.name: Proof of Sum of uniformly integrable families
nodes.statement: The families $X$ and $Y$ are uniformly integrable in the measure-theoretic sense and almost-everywhere strongly measurable, so $X + Y$ is too (see \href{https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Function/UniformIntegrable.html#MeasureTheory.UnifIntegrable.add}{MeasureTheory.UnifIntegrable.add}). Moreover, $X$ and $Y$ are bounded in $L^p$, so $X + Y$ is too. So $X + Y$ is uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Mathlib's UnifIntegrable.add plus L^p boundedness of the sum.

nodes.name: Measure-theoretic UI
nodes.statement: The families $X$ and $Y$ are uniformly integrable in the measure-theoretic sense and almost-everywhere strongly measurable, so $X + Y$ is too (see \href{https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Function/UniformIntegrable.html#MeasureTheory.UnifIntegrable.add}{MeasureTheory.UnifIntegrable.add}).
nodes.statement_short: Sum is UI in the measure-theoretic sense (Mathlib)

nodes.name: L^p bound
nodes.statement: Moreover, $X$ and $Y$ are bounded in $L^p$, so $X + Y$ is too.
nodes.statement_short: Sum is bounded in L^p

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: So $X + Y$ is uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude uniform integrability

nodes.name: Domination preserves uniform integrability
nodes.statement: Let $(X_s)_{s \in S}$ be a family of random variables and $(Y_t)_{t \in T}$ be a family of uniformly integrable random variables. If for all $s$, there exists $t$ such that $\|X_s\| \le \|Y_t\|$ almost surely, then $X$ is uniformly integrable.
assumptions: $(X_s)_{s \in S}$ be a family of random variables
$(Y_t)_{t \in T}$ be a family of uniformly integrable random variables
for all $s$, there exists $t$ such that $\|X_s\| \le \|Y_t\|$ almost surely
conclusions: $X$ is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrableDominated

nodes.name: Proof of Domination preserves uniform integrability
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon > 0$. The family $Y$ is uniformly integrable, thus there exists $C \ge 0$ such that for $t \in T$, $P[\|Y_t\|^p \mathbb{I}_{\|Y_t\| \ge C}]^{1/p} \le \epsilon$. For all $s$, there exists $t$ such that $\|X_s\|^p \le \|Y_t\|^p$, so $P[\|X_s\|^p \mathbb{I}_{\|X_s\| \ge C}]^{1/p} \le \epsilon$. Thus $X$ is uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer the uniform tail bound of Y to X through the pointwise domination.

nodes.name: Tail bound for Y
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon > 0$. The family $Y$ is uniformly integrable, thus there exists $C \ge 0$ such that for $t \in T$, $P[\|Y_t\|^p \mathbb{I}_{\|Y_t\| \ge C}]^{1/p} \le \epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Get C with uniform tail bound for Y

nodes.name: Transfer to X
nodes.statement: For all $s$, there exists $t$ such that $\|X_s\|^p \le \|Y_t\|^p$, so $P[\|X_s\|^p \mathbb{I}_{\|X_s\| \ge C}]^{1/p} \le \epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Domination transfers the tail bound to X

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Thus $X$ is uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: X is uniformly integrable

nodes.name: Domination by a single Lp variable
nodes.statement: Let $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ be a family of random variables and $Y$ be a real random variable in $L^p$. If for all $t$, (possibly infinite) $\|X_t\| \le Y$ almost surely, then $X$ is uniformly integrable.
assumptions: $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ be a family of random variables
$Y$ be a real random variable in $L^p$
for all $t$, (possibly infinite) $\|X_t\| \le Y$ almost surely
conclusions: $X$ is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrableDominatedSingleton

nodes.name: Proof of Domination by a single Lp variable
nodes.statement: Because $Y$ is in $L^p$, we deduce that $\{Y\}$ is uniformly integrable. The conclusion then follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated}.
nodes.statement_short: A singleton {Y} in L^p is uniformly integrable; apply the domination lemma.

nodes.name: Norms of a uniformly integrable family
nodes.statement: If $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ is a family of uniformly integrable random variables, then so is $(\|X_t\|)_{t \in T}$.
assumptions: $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ is a family of uniformly integrable random variables
conclusions: so is $(\|X_t\|)_{t \in T}$
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrableNorm

nodes.name: Proof of Norms of a uniformly integrable family
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated} with $Y := X$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the domination lemma with Y := X.

nodes.name: Uniform integrability iff uniform integrability of norms
nodes.statement: Let $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ be a family of uniformly integrable random variables. It is uniformly integrable if and only if $(\|X_t\|)_{t \in T}$ is.
assumptions: $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ be a family of uniformly integrable random variables
conclusions: It is uniformly integrable if and only if $(\|X_t\|)_{t \in T}$ is
equivalent_conditions: It is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrableIffNorm

nodes.name: Proof of Uniform integrability iff uniform integrability of norms
nodes.statement: The forward direction is Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableNorm}. The converse direction follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated} with $Y := (\|X_t\|)_{t \in T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Forward direction by the norm lemma, converse by domination.

nodes.name: Reindexing preserves uniform integrability
nodes.statement: If $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ is uniformly integrable and $\phi : S \to T$, then $(X_{\phi(s)})_{s \in S}$ is uniformly integrable.
assumptions: $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ is uniformly integrable
$\phi : S \to T$
conclusions: $(X_{\phi(s)})_{s \in S}$ is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrableComp

nodes.name: Proof of Reindexing preserves uniform integrability
nodes.statement: This is immediate from the definition.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition.

nodes.name: Uniform integrability of submartingale stopped values
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a submartingale on a discrete index set and let $(\tau_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of stopping times that are uniformly bounded by $p$. Then, the family of stopped values $\{X_{\tau_k}\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable.
assumptions: $X$ be a submartingale on a discrete index set
$(\tau_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of stopping times that are uniformly bounded by $p$
conclusions: the family of stopped values $\{X_{\tau_k}\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_submartingale

nodes.name: Proof of Uniform integrability of submartingale stopped values
nodes.statement: Use Doob decomposition to write $X_n = M_n + A_n$, where $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:martingalePart}) is a martingale (Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_martingalePart}) and $A$ (Definition~\ref{def:predictablePart}) is a predictable process (Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_predictablePart}). We know from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_martingale} that $(M_{\tau_k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable. Combining Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableAdd} and Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominatedSingleton}, it suffices to show that $(A_{\tau_k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is dominated. It is dominated by $A_p$ thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_zero} and Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.monotone_predictablePart}.
nodes.statement_short: Doob decomposition X = M + A: the martingale part is UI by optional sampling, the predictable part is dominated by A_p since it is nondecreasing.

nodes.name: Doob decomposition
nodes.statement: Use Doob decomposition to write $X_n = M_n + A_n$, where $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:martingalePart}) is a martingale (Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_martingalePart}) and $A$ (Definition~\ref{def:predictablePart}) is a predictable process (Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_predictablePart}).
nodes.statement_short: Write X = M + A

nodes.name: Martingale part
nodes.statement: We know from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_martingale} that $(M_{\tau_k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Stopped martingale part is UI

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: Combining Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableAdd} and Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominatedSingleton}, it suffices to show that $(A_{\tau_k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is dominated.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to dominate the predictable part

nodes.name: Domination
nodes.statement: It is dominated by $A_p$ thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_zero} and Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.monotone_predictablePart}.
nodes.statement_short: A_{tau_k} <= A_p since A is nondecreasing from 0

nodes.name: Lp limit in probability of a uniformly integrable sequence
nodes.statement: Let $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of $p$-uniformly integrable stochastic processes and suppose $X_n \to X$ in probability as $n \to \infty$. Then, $X$ is $L^p$.
assumptions: $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of $p$-uniformly integrable stochastic processes
$X_n \to X$ in probability as $n \to \infty$
conclusions: $X$ is $L^p$
nodes.label: lem:memLp_of_tendstoInMeasure

nodes.name: Proof of Lp limit in probability of a uniformly integrable sequence
nodes.statement: Since $X_n \to X$ in probability, it has a subsequence $(X_{n_k}) \subseteq (X_n)$ which converges to $X$ almost surely. Thus, we have by Fatou's lemma that \[P[|X|^p] = P[\liminf_{k \to \infty} |X_{n_k}|^p] \le \liminf_{k \to \infty} P[|X_{n_k}|^p] < \infty\] where the last inequality follows as uniform integrability implies that $(X_n)$ is uniform bounded in $L^p$.
nodes.statement_short: Extract an a.s. convergent subsequence and apply Fatou's lemma with the L^p bound from uniform integrability.

nodes.name: Uniform integrability of almost-everywhere limits
nodes.statement: Let $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ be a family of $p$-uniformly integrable stochastic processes. Then the family of limits in almost everywhere convergence of sequences of $X$ is $p$-uniformly integrable.
assumptions: $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ be a family of $p$-uniformly integrable stochastic processes
conclusions: the family of limits in almost everywhere convergence of sequences of $X$ is $p$-uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrable_of_tendsto_ae

nodes.name: Proof of Uniform integrability of almost-everywhere limits
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon > 0$. There exists $\delta > 0$ such that for all $t\in T$ and all measurable set $S$ such that $P(S)<\delta$, \[P[\|X_t\|^p\mathbb{I}_S]^{1/p}\le \varepsilon.\] Let $(t_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $T$ such that $X_{t_n}$ converges almost everywhere to $Y$. We have by Fatou's lemma that \[P[\|Y\|^p \mathbb{I}_{S}]^{1/p} = P[\liminf_{n \to \infty} \|X_{t_{n}}\|^p \mathbb{I}_{S}]^{1/p} \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} P[\|X_{t_{n}}\|^p \mathbb{I}_{S}]^{1/p} \le \epsilon.\] This proves that the family of limits in a.e convergence of sequences of $X$ is $p$-uniformly integrable in the measure theory sense. One can prove uniform boundedness of this family by using Fatou's lemma in a similar way.
nodes.statement_short: Fatou's lemma transfers the uniform tail bound to a.e. limits.

nodes.name: Uniform bound
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon > 0$. There exists $\delta > 0$ such that for all $t\in T$ and all measurable set $S$ such that $P(S)<\delta$, \[P[\|X_t\|^p\mathbb{I}_S]^{1/p}\le \varepsilon.\]
nodes.statement_short: Choose delta from uniform integrability

nodes.name: Fatou
nodes.statement: Let $(t_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $T$ such that $X_{t_n}$ converges almost everywhere to $Y$. We have by Fatou's lemma that \[P[\|Y\|^p \mathbb{I}_{S}]^{1/p} = P[\liminf_{n \to \infty} \|X_{t_{n}}\|^p \mathbb{I}_{S}]^{1/p} \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} P[\|X_{t_{n}}\|^p \mathbb{I}_{S}]^{1/p} \le \epsilon.\]
nodes.statement_short: Fatou's lemma bounds the limit's tail integral

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: This proves that the family of limits in a.e convergence of sequences of $X$ is $p$-uniformly integrable in the measure theory sense. One can prove uniform boundedness of this family by using Fatou's lemma in a similar way.
nodes.statement_short: Limits are uniformly integrable; boundedness similarly

nodes.name: Uniform integrability of limits in probability
nodes.statement: Let $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ be a family of $p$-uniformly integrable stochastic processes. Then the family of limits in probability of sequences of $X$ is $p$-uniformly integrable.
assumptions: $(X_t)_{t \in T}$ be a family of $p$-uniformly integrable stochastic processes
conclusions: the family of limits in probability of sequences of $X$ is $p$-uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrable_of_tendstoInMeasure

nodes.name: Proof of Uniform integrability of limits in probability
nodes.statement: A subfamily of a $p$-uniformly integrable family is $p$-uniformly integrable. As convergence in probability implies the existence of a subsequence that converges almost everywhere, the family of limits in probability is a subfamily of the family of limits in almost everywhere convergence, which is $p$-uniformly integrable by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_of_tendsto_ae}.
nodes.statement_short: Limits in probability are a.e. limits of subsequences, so a subfamily of the a.e.-limit family.

nodes.name: Vitali convergence theorem
nodes.statement: A sequence of functions converges in $L^1$ if and only if it converges in probability and is uniformly integrable.
conclusions: A sequence of functions converges in $L^1$ if and only if it converges in probability and is uniformly integrable
equivalent_conditions: A sequence of functions converges in $L^1$
it converges in probability and is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:vitali

nodes.name: Ordered Monoid
nodes.statement: Let $(M, +)$ be a commutative monoid that is also a partial order. It is said to be an \emph{ordered monoid} if for all $a, b, c \in M$, we have the following implication: $$a \le b \implies a + c \le b + c.$$
nodes.label: def:isOrderedAddMonoid

nodes.name: Ordered Module
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha, \beta$ be preorders with $0$ elements and such that there is a scalar multiplication $(\_ \cdot \_) : \alpha \times \beta \to \beta$. Then $\beta$ is said to be an \emph{ordered $\alpha$-module} (or \emph{ordered module} if $\alpha$ is clear from the context) if the following hold: \begin{itemize} \item $\forall a \in \alpha, \forall b_1, b_2 \in \beta, 0 \le a \implies b_1 \le b_2 \implies a \cdot b_1 \le a \cdot b_2$; \item $\forall a_1, a_2 \in \alpha, \forall b \in \beta, 0 \le b \implies a_1 \le a_2 \implies a_1 \cdot b \le a_2 \cdot b$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Scalar multiplication by nonnegative scalars is monotone in each argument.
nodes.label: def:isOrderedModule

nodes.name: Order-closed topology
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a topological space that is also a preorder. The space $X$ is set to be \emph{order-closed}, or to have \emph{order-closed topology}, if the set $\{(x, y) \in X \times X \mid x \le y\}$ is closed.
differentia: the set $\{(x, y) \in X \times X \mid x \le y\}$ is closed
nodes.label: def:orderClosedTopology

nodes.name: Optional sampling (discrete time)
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a discrete time martingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$ and let $\tau, \sigma$ be stopping times. Then, if $\tau$ is bounded, we have that almost surely, $X_{\tau \wedge \sigma} = P[X_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$.
assumptions: $X$ be a discrete time martingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$
$\tau, \sigma$ be stopping times
$\tau$ is bounded
conclusions: almost surely, $X_{\tau \wedge \sigma} = P[X_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$
nodes.label: lem:optionalSampling_discrete

nodes.name: Optional sampling for discrete-time submartingales
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a discrete time submartingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$ taking values in a real Banach space $E$. Assume $E$ is an order-closed partial order, an ordered monoid and an ordered module. Let $\tau, \sigma$ be stopping times. Then, if $\tau$ is bounded, we have that almost surely, $X_{\tau \wedge \sigma} \le P[X_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$.
assumptions: $X$ be a discrete time submartingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$ taking values in a real Banach space $E$
$E$ is an order-closed partial order, an ordered monoid and an ordered module
$\tau, \sigma$ be stopping times
$\tau$ is bounded
conclusions: almost surely, $X_{\tau \wedge \sigma} \le P[X_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$
nodes.label: lem:optionalSampling_discrete_submartingale

nodes.name: Proof of Optional sampling for discrete-time submartingales
nodes.statement: Use Doob decomposition to write $X_n = M_n + A_n$, where $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:martingalePart}) is a martingale (Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_martingalePart}) and $A$ (Definition~\ref{def:predictablePart}) is a predictable process (Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_predictablePart}). By Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSampling_discrete}, we have that almost surely, $M_{\tau \wedge \sigma} = P[M_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$. Because $A$ is predictable and $\tau \wedge \sigma \le \sigma$, we deduce that almost surely, $A_{\tau \wedge \sigma} = P[A_{\tau \wedge \sigma} \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma]$. Moreover, by Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.monotone_predictablePart}, we know that almost surely, $A$ is nondecreasing. Therefore, using the fact $\tau \wedge \sigma \le \tau$, we get that $P[A_{\tau \wedge \sigma} \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma] \le P[A_\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma]$. We deduce that almost surely, $$X_{\tau \wedge \sigma} = M_{\tau \wedge \sigma} + A_{\tau \wedge \sigma} \le P[M_\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma] + P[A_\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma] = P[X_\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma],$$ concluding the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Doob decomposition: apply discrete optional sampling to the martingale part and use that the predictable part is nondecreasing.

nodes.name: Doob decomposition
nodes.statement: Use Doob decomposition to write $X_n = M_n + A_n$, where $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:martingalePart}) is a martingale (Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_martingalePart}) and $A$ (Definition~\ref{def:predictablePart}) is a predictable process (Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_predictablePart}).
nodes.statement_short: Write X = M + A

nodes.name: Martingale part
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSampling_discrete}, we have that almost surely, $M_{\tau \wedge \sigma} = P[M_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$.
nodes.statement_short: Optional sampling for M

nodes.name: Predictable part measurable
nodes.statement: Because $A$ is predictable and $\tau \wedge \sigma \le \sigma$, we deduce that almost surely, $A_{\tau \wedge \sigma} = P[A_{\tau \wedge \sigma} \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma]$.
nodes.statement_short: A_{tau and sigma} equals its conditional expectation

nodes.name: Monotone predictable part
nodes.statement: Moreover, by Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.monotone_predictablePart}, we know that almost surely, $A$ is nondecreasing.
nodes.statement_short: A is a.s. nondecreasing

nodes.name: Compare predictable parts
nodes.statement: Therefore, using the fact $\tau \wedge \sigma \le \tau$, we get that $P[A_{\tau \wedge \sigma} \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma] \le P[A_\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma]$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of conditional expectation

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: We deduce that almost surely, $$X_{\tau \wedge \sigma} = M_{\tau \wedge \sigma} + A_{\tau \wedge \sigma} \le P[M_\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma] + P[A_\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma] = P[X_\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma],$$ concluding the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Add the two parts

nodes.name: Optional sampling for discrete-time supermartingales
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a discrete time supermartingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$ taking values in a real Banach space $E$. Assume $E$ is an order-closed partial order, an ordered monoid and an ordered module. Let $\tau, \sigma$ be stopping times. Then, if $\tau$ is bounded, we have that almost surely, $X_{\tau \wedge \sigma} \ge P[X_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$.
assumptions: $X$ be a discrete time supermartingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$ taking values in a real Banach space $E$
$E$ is an order-closed partial order, an ordered monoid and an ordered module
$\tau, \sigma$ be stopping times
$\tau$ is bounded
conclusions: almost surely, $X_{\tau \wedge \sigma} \ge P[X_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$
nodes.label: lem:optionalSampling_discrete_supermartingale

nodes.name: Proof of Optional sampling for discrete-time supermartingales
nodes.statement: We know that $-X$ is a submartingale, so from Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSampling_discrete_submartingale} we obtain that almost surely, $-X_{\tau \wedge \sigma} \le P[-X_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$. Multiplying by $-1$ yields the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the submartingale case to -X.

nodes.name: Discrete approximation sequence
nodes.statement: Given a stopping time \(\tau : \Omega \to T \cup \{\infty\}\), a sequence of stopping times \((\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\) is called an discrete approximation of \(\tau\) if \(\tau_n(\Omega)\) is countable for each \(n\) and \(\tau_n \downarrow \tau\) a.s. as \(n \to \infty\).
differentia: \(\tau_n(\Omega)\) is countable for each \(n\)
\(\tau_n \downarrow \tau\) a.s. as \(n \to \infty\)
nodes.label: def:approxSeq

nodes.name: Approximable time index
nodes.statement: A time index set \(T\) is said to be approximable if for any stopping time \(\tau : \Omega \to T \cup \{\infty\}\), there exists a discrete approximation sequence \((\tau_n)\) of \(\tau\).
differentia: for any stopping time \(\tau : \Omega \to T \cup \{\infty\}\), there exists a discrete approximation sequence \((\tau_n)\) of \(\tau\)
nodes.label: def:approximableTimeIndex

nodes.name: Convergence of stopped values along discrete approximations
nodes.statement: Given a right continuous process \(X\) and a discrete approximation sequence \((\tau_n)\) of the stopping time \(\tau\), we have that \[\lim_{n \to \infty} X_{\tau_n} = X_\tau \text{ a.s.}\]
assumptions: a right continuous process \(X\)
a discrete approximation sequence \((\tau_n)\) of the stopping time \(\tau\)
conclusions: \[\lim_{n \to \infty} X_{\tau_n} = X_\tau \text{ a.s.}\]
nodes.label: lem:tendsto_stoppedValue_discreteApproxSequence

nodes.name: Proof of Convergence of stopped values along discrete approximations
nodes.statement: This follows directly as \(X\) is right continuous and \(\tau_n \downarrow \tau\) a.s.
nodes.statement_short: Right continuity of X with tau_n decreasing to tau.

nodes.name: Truncated discrete approximation sequence
nodes.statement: Let \(\tau\) be a stopping time bounded by \(t \in T\) and \((\tau_n)\) be a discrete approximation sequence of \(\tau\). Then, the sequence of stopping times \(\tau_n \wedge t\) is also a discrete approximation sequence of \(\tau\).
assumptions: \(\tau\) be a stopping time bounded by \(t \in T\)
\((\tau_n)\) be a discrete approximation sequence of \(\tau\)
conclusions: the sequence of stopping times \(\tau_n \wedge t\) is also a discrete approximation sequence of \(\tau\)
nodes.label: lem:discreteApproxSequence_of

nodes.name: Uniform integrability along discrete approximations
nodes.statement: Let \(\tau\) be a stopping time bounded by \(t \in T\) and \((\tau_n)\) be a discrete approximation sequence of \(\tau\). Then, for any martingale \(X\), the sequence of stopped values \((X_{\tau_n \wedge t})\) is uniformly integrable.
assumptions: \(\tau\) be a stopping time bounded by \(t \in T\)
\((\tau_n)\) be a discrete approximation sequence of \(\tau\)
any martingale \(X\)
conclusions: the sequence of stopped values \((X_{\tau_n \wedge t})\) is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_discreteApproxSequence

nodes.name: Proof of Uniform integrability along discrete approximations
nodes.statement: Follows directly by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_martingale_of_countable_range} and Lemma~\ref{lem:discreteApproxSequence_of}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the countable-range uniform integrability lemma with the truncated approximation lemma.

nodes.name: L1 convergence of stopped values along discrete approximations
nodes.statement: Let \(\tau\) be a stopping time bounded by \(t \in T\) and \((\tau_n)\) be a discrete approximation sequence of \(\tau\). Then, for any right continuous martingale \(X\), \(X_{\tau} \in L^1\) and \(X_{\tau_n \wedge t} \to X_{\tau}\) in \(L^1\) as \(n \to \infty\).
assumptions: \(\tau\) be a stopping time bounded by \(t \in T\)
\((\tau_n)\) be a discrete approximation sequence of \(\tau\)
any right continuous martingale \(X\)
conclusions: \(X_{\tau_n \wedge t} \to X_{\tau}\) in \(L^1\) as \(n \to \infty\)
nodes.label: lem:tendsto_eLpNorm_stoppedValue_discreteApproxSequence

nodes.name: Proof of L1 convergence of stopped values along discrete approximations
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:tendsto_stoppedValue_discreteApproxSequence}, as \(X\) is right continuous we have that \(X_{\tau_n \wedge t} \to X_{\tau}\) a.s. and so, also in probability. Moreover, by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_discreteApproxSequence}, the sequence \((X_{\tau_n \wedge t})\) is uniformly integrable. Thus, by Lemma~\ref{lem:memLp_of_tendstoInMeasure} and the Vitali convergence theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:vitali}), it follows that \(X_{\tau} \in L^1\) and \(X_{\tau_n \wedge t} \to X_{\tau}\) in \(L^1\) as \(n \to \infty\).
nodes.statement_short: A.s. convergence by right continuity plus uniform integrability gives L^1 convergence by Vitali.

nodes.name: A.s. convergence
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:tendsto_stoppedValue_discreteApproxSequence}, as \(X\) is right continuous we have that \(X_{\tau_n \wedge t} \to X_{\tau}\) a.s. and so, also in probability.
nodes.statement_short: Stopped values converge a.s., hence in probability

nodes.name: Uniform integrability
nodes.statement: Moreover, by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_discreteApproxSequence}, the sequence \((X_{\tau_n \wedge t})\) is uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Stopped values are UI

nodes.name: Vitali
nodes.statement: Thus, by Lemma~\ref{lem:memLp_of_tendstoInMeasure} and the Vitali convergence theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:vitali}), it follows that \(X_{\tau} \in L^1\) and \(X_{\tau_n \wedge t} \to X_{\tau}\) in \(L^1\) as \(n \to \infty\).
nodes.statement_short: Conclude L^1 convergence by Vitali

nodes.name: Dyadic approximation of stopping times on the nonnegative reals
nodes.statement: $T = \mathbb{R}_+$ is an approximable time index. In particular, for any stopping time $\tau$ on $\overline{\mathbb{R}_+}$, defining $\tau_n = 2^{-n} \lceil 2^n \tau \rceil$, we have that $(\tau_n)$ is a discrete approximation sequence of $\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: R_+ is approximable: the dyadic roundings tau_n = 2^{-n} ceil(2^n tau) approximate tau.
conclusions: $T = \mathbb{R}_+$ is an approximable time index
for any stopping time $\tau$ on $\overline{\mathbb{R}_+}$, defining $\tau_n = 2^{-n} \lceil 2^n \tau \rceil$, we have that $(\tau_n)$ is a discrete approximation sequence of $\tau$
nodes.label: lem:stoppingTime_approximation

nodes.name: Proof of Dyadic approximation of stopping times on the nonnegative reals
nodes.statement: Clearly $\tau_n \downarrow \tau$ as $n \to \infty$ and so it remains to show that each $\tau_n$ is a stopping time. Indeed, \[\{\tau_n \le t\} = \{\tau \le 2^{-n} \lfloor 2^n t\rfloor\} \in \mathcal{F}_{2^{-n} \lfloor 2^n t\rfloor} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t\] where the last inclusion follows as \(2^{-n} \lfloor 2^n t\rfloor \le t\).
nodes.statement_short: Check that each dyadic rounding tau_n is a stopping time via {tau_n <= t} = {tau <= 2^{-n} floor(2^n t)}.

nodes.name: Natural numbers are an approximable time index
nodes.statement: $T = \mathbb{N}$ is an approximable time index.
nodes.label: lem:stoppingTime_approximationNat

nodes.name: Proof of Natural numbers are an approximable time index
nodes.statement: Immediate as we can take \(\tau_n = \tau\) for all \(n\).
nodes.statement_short: Take the constant approximation tau_n = tau.

nodes.name: Optional sampling (continuous time)
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a right-continuous $\mathcal{F}$-martingale on an approximable time index. Then, for any stopping times $\sigma, \tau$ with $\tau$ bounded, we have that $X_{\sigma \wedge \tau} = P[X_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$ almost surely.
assumptions: $X$ be a right-continuous $\mathcal{F}$-martingale on an approximable time index
any stopping times $\sigma, \tau$ with $\tau$ bounded
conclusions: $X_{\sigma \wedge \tau} = P[X_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$ almost surely
nodes.label: lem:optionalSampling

nodes.name: Proof of Optional sampling (continuous time)
nodes.statement: Fixing $A \in \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}$, we need to show that $P[X_{\tau} \mathbb{I}_A] = P[X_{\sigma \wedge \tau} \mathbb{I}_A]$. Let $(\tau_n), (\sigma_n)$ be discrete approximation sequences of $\tau$ and $\sigma$ respectively. As $\tau_n, \sigma_n$ take values in a countable set, we have by the discrete time optional sampling theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSampling_discrete}) that $$X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} = P[X_{\tau_n} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma_n}]$$ and so, as \(\mathcal{F}_{\sigma} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{\sigma_n}\) by Lemma~\ref{lem:StoppingTimeGenMono}, we have that $P[X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_A] = P[X_{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_A]$. On the other hand, by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_martingale}, the families $\{X_{\tau_n}\}$ and $\{X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n}\}$ are uniformly integrable. Thus, as $X$ is right-continuous, $(X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n}, X_{\tau_n}) \to (X_{\sigma \wedge \tau}, X_{\tau})$ a.s. We have $P[X_{\tau} \mathbb{I}_A] = P[X_{\sigma \wedge \tau} \mathbb{I}_A]$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:tendsto_eLpNorm_stoppedValue_discreteApproxSequence} as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate sigma and tau by discrete stopping times, apply discrete optional sampling, and pass to the limit using uniform integrability and right continuity (L^1 convergence).

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Fixing $A \in \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}$, we need to show that $P[X_{\tau} \mathbb{I}_A] = P[X_{\sigma \wedge \tau} \mathbb{I}_A]$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to integrals over A in F_sigma

nodes.name: Discrete optional sampling
nodes.statement: Let $(\tau_n), (\sigma_n)$ be discrete approximation sequences of $\tau$ and $\sigma$ respectively. As $\tau_n, \sigma_n$ take values in a countable set, we have by the discrete time optional sampling theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSampling_discrete}) that $$X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} = P[X_{\tau_n} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma_n}]$$ and so, as \(\mathcal{F}_{\sigma} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{\sigma_n}\) by Lemma~\ref{lem:StoppingTimeGenMono}, we have that $P[X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_A] = P[X_{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_A]$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply discrete optional sampling to approximations

nodes.name: Uniform integrability
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_martingale}, the families $\{X_{\tau_n}\}$ and $\{X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n}\}$ are uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Approximating stopped values are UI

nodes.name: A.s. convergence
nodes.statement: Thus, as $X$ is right-continuous, $(X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n}, X_{\tau_n}) \to (X_{\sigma \wedge \tau}, X_{\tau})$ a.s.
nodes.statement_short: Right continuity gives a.s. convergence

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: We have $P[X_{\tau} \mathbb{I}_A] = P[X_{\sigma \wedge \tau} \mathbb{I}_A]$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:tendsto_eLpNorm_stoppedValue_discreteApproxSequence} as desired.
nodes.statement_short: L^1 convergence passes the identity to the limit

nodes.name: Optional sampling for submartingales (continuous time)
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a right-continuous $\mathcal{F}$-submartingale on an approximable time index. Then, for any stopping times $\sigma, \tau$ with $\tau$ bounded, we have that $X_{\sigma \wedge \tau} \le P[X_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$ almost surely.
assumptions: $X$ be a right-continuous $\mathcal{F}$-submartingale on an approximable time index
any stopping times $\sigma, \tau$ with $\tau$ bounded
conclusions: $X_{\sigma \wedge \tau} \le P[X_{\tau} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}]$ almost surely
nodes.label: lem:optionalSamplingSubmartingale

nodes.name: Proof of Optional sampling for submartingales (continuous time)
nodes.statement: Fixing $A \in \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}$, we need to show that $P[X_{\tau} \mathbb{I}_A] \le P[X_{\sigma \wedge \tau} \mathbb{I}_A]$. Let $(\tau_n), (\sigma_n)$ be discrete approximation sequences of $\tau$ and $\sigma$ respectively. As $\tau_n, \sigma_n$ take values in a countable set, we have by the discrete time optional sampling theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSampling_discrete_submartingale}) that $$X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \le P[X_{\tau_n} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma_n}]$$ and so, as \(\mathcal{F}_{\sigma} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{\sigma_n}\) by Lemma~\ref{lem:StoppingTimeGenMono}, we have that $P[X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_A] \le P[X_{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_A]$.
