On the other hand, by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_submartingale}, the families $\{X_{\tau_n}\}$ and $\{X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n}\}$ are uniformly integrable. Thus, as $X$ is right-continuous, $(X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n}, X_{\tau_n}) \to (X_{\sigma \wedge \tau}, X_{\tau})$ a.s. We have $P[X_{\tau} \mathbb{I}_A] \le P[X_{\sigma \wedge \tau} \mathbb{I}_A]$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:tendsto_eLpNorm_stoppedValue_discreteApproxSequence} as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate sigma and tau by discrete stopping times, apply discrete submartingale optional sampling, and pass to the limit using uniform integrability and right continuity.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Fixing $A \in \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}$, we need to show that $P[X_{\tau} \mathbb{I}_A] \le P[X_{\sigma \wedge \tau} \mathbb{I}_A]$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to integrals over A in F_sigma

nodes.name: Discrete optional sampling
nodes.statement: Let $(\tau_n), (\sigma_n)$ be discrete approximation sequences of $\tau$ and $\sigma$ respectively. As $\tau_n, \sigma_n$ take values in a countable set, we have by the discrete time optional sampling theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSampling_discrete_submartingale}) that $$X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \le P[X_{\tau_n} \mid \mathcal{F}_{\sigma_n}]$$ and so, as \(\mathcal{F}_{\sigma} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{\sigma_n}\) by Lemma~\ref{lem:StoppingTimeGenMono}, we have that $P[X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_A] \le P[X_{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_A]$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply discrete optional sampling to approximations

nodes.name: Uniform integrability
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue_submartingale}, the families $\{X_{\tau_n}\}$ and $\{X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n}\}$ are uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Approximating stopped values are UI

nodes.name: A.s. convergence
nodes.statement: Thus, as $X$ is right-continuous, $(X_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n}, X_{\tau_n}) \to (X_{\sigma \wedge \tau}, X_{\tau})$ a.s.
nodes.statement_short: Right continuity gives a.s. convergence

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: We have $P[X_{\tau} \mathbb{I}_A] \le P[X_{\sigma \wedge \tau} \mathbb{I}_A]$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:tendsto_eLpNorm_stoppedValue_discreteApproxSequence} as desired.
nodes.statement_short: L^1 convergence passes the identity to the limit

nodes.name: Limit process
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a stochastic process, let $\mathcal{F}$ be a filtration on $\Omega$ indexed by $T$ and let $P$ be a measure on $\Omega$. If there exists a function $Y : \Omega \to E$ which is measurable with respect to $\mathcal{F}_\infty$ such that for $P$-almost surely, $X_t$ converges to $Y$ as $t$ goes to infinity, then we say that $Y$ is the limit of $X$. We denote it by $X_\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: X_infinity is the F_infinity-measurable a.s. limit of X_t as t goes to infinity, when it exists.
nodes.label: def:limitProcess

nodes.name: Martingale convergence theorem for cadlag uniformly integrable martingales
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an uniformly integrable cadlag martingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$. Then there exists a limit process $X_\infty$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal{F}_\infty$ such that $X_t$ converges to $X_\infty$ almost surely as $t$ goes to infinity. Furthermore, $X_t = P[X_\infty \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ almost surely.
assumptions: $X$ be an uniformly integrable cadlag martingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}$
conclusions: there exists a limit process $X_\infty$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal{F}_\infty$ such that $X_t$ converges to $X_\infty$ almost surely as $t$ goes to infinity
$X_t = P[X_\infty \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ almost surely
nodes.label: thm:tendsto_limitProcess_of_cadlag

nodes.name: Characterization of the limit process
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process such that there exists $g : \Omega \to E$ that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and such that $X$ converges almost surely to $g$. Then $X_\infty$ and $g$ are a.e. equal.
assumptions: $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a process such that there exists $g : \Omega \to E$ that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and such that $X$ converges almost surely to $g$
conclusions: $X_\infty$ and $g$ are a.e. equal
nodes.label: lem:limitProcess_ae_eq

nodes.name: Proof of Characterization of the limit process
nodes.statement: Because there exist a function that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and towards which $X$ converges almost surely, $X_\infty$ is such a function by definition. Because $X$ converges almost surely towards $g$, $g$ and $X_\infty$ are equal on the set where $X$ converges to $X_\infty$ and $X$ converges to $g$ by uniqueness of the limit.
nodes.statement_short: By definition X_infinity is an admissible limit; uniqueness of a.s. limits identifies it with g.

nodes.name: Limit process of indistinguishable processes
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two indistinguishable processes. Then $X_\infty$ and $Y_\infty$ are a.e. equal.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ be two indistinguishable processes
conclusions: $X_\infty$ and $Y_\infty$ are a.e. equal
nodes.label: lem:limitProcess_congr

nodes.name: Proof of Limit process of indistinguishable processes
nodes.statement: If there exists $g : \Omega \to E$ that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and such that $X$ converges almost surely to $g$, then it is enough to show that $Y$ converges almost surely to $g$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_ae_eq}. This follows from indistinguishability. Otherwise, $X_\infty = 0$, and by indistinguishability there does not exist $g : \Omega \to E$ that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and such that $Y$ converges almost surely to $g$, so $Y_\infty = 0$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether X has an admissible a.s. limit; indistinguishability transfers convergence or its failure to Y.

nodes.name: Limit exists
nodes.statement: If there exists $g : \Omega \to E$ that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and such that $X$ converges almost surely to $g$, then it is enough to show that $Y$ converges almost surely to $g$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_ae_eq}. This follows from indistinguishability.
nodes.statement_short: Y converges to the same g

nodes.name: No limit
nodes.statement: Otherwise, $X_\infty = 0$, and by indistinguishability there does not exist $g : \Omega \to E$ that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and such that $Y$ converges almost surely to $g$, so $Y_\infty = 0$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Both limit processes are 0

nodes.name: Limit process of a constant process
nodes.statement: Let $c \in E$ and $X$ be the constant process equal to $c$. Then $X_\infty$ is a.e. equal to $c$.
assumptions: $c \in E$ and $X$ be the constant process equal to $c$
conclusions: $X_\infty$ is a.e. equal to $c$
nodes.label: lem:limitProcess_const

nodes.name: Proof of Limit process of a constant process
nodes.statement: This follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_ae_eq} as a constant function converges to a constant, and a constant function is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to any sigma-algebra.
nodes.statement_short: A constant converges to itself and is measurable for any sigma-algebra; apply the limit characterization.

nodes.name: Limit process of a scalar multiple
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a stochastic process and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, then $(c \cdot X)_\infty$ is a.e. equal to $c \cdot X_\infty$.
assumptions: $X$ is a stochastic process and $c \in \mathbb{R}$
conclusions: $(c \cdot X)_\infty$ is a.e. equal to $c \cdot X_\infty$
nodes.label: lem:limitProcess_smul

nodes.name: Proof of Limit process of a scalar multiple
nodes.statement: If $c = 0$ we can conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_const}. Otherwise, if there exists $g : \Omega \to E$ that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and such that $X$ converges almost surely to $g$, then $c \cdot X$ converges almost surely to $c \cdot g$ and we can conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_ae_eq}. Otherwise there does not exist $g : \Omega \to E$ that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and such that $c \cdot X$ converges almost surely to $g$, because if it did it would also be the case for $X$, so $X_\infty$ and $(c \cdot X)_\infty$ are both a.e. equal to $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on c = 0 and on whether X has an admissible limit, using the limit characterization.

nodes.name: c = 0
nodes.statement: If $c = 0$ we can conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_const}.
nodes.statement_short: Constant case

nodes.name: Limit exists
nodes.statement: Otherwise, if there exists $g : \Omega \to E$ that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and such that $X$ converges almost surely to $g$, then $c \cdot X$ converges almost surely to $c \cdot g$ and we can conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_ae_eq}.
nodes.statement_short: c X converges to c g

nodes.name: No limit
nodes.statement: Otherwise there does not exist $g : \Omega \to E$ that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and such that $c \cdot X$ converges almost surely to $g$, because if it did it would also be the case for $X$, so $X_\infty$ and $(c \cdot X)_\infty$ are both a.e. equal to $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Both limit processes are 0

nodes.name: Limit process of the negation
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a stochastic process, then $(-X)_\infty$ is a.e. equal to $-X_\infty$.
assumptions: $X$ is a stochastic process
conclusions: $(-X)_\infty$ is a.e. equal to $-X_\infty$
nodes.label: lem:limitProcess_neg

nodes.name: Proof of Limit process of the negation
nodes.statement: If there exists $g : \Omega \to E$ that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and such that $X$ converges almost surely to $g$, then $-X$ converges almost surely to $-g$ and we can conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_ae_eq}. Otherwise there does not exist $g : \Omega \to E$ that is a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup t, \mathcal{F}_t$ and such that $-X$ converges almost surely to $g$, because if it did it would also be the case for $X$, so $X_\infty$ and $(-X)_\infty$ are both a.e. equal to $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether X has an admissible limit, using the limit characterization.

nodes.name: Closure of a cadlag uniformly integrable martingale by its limit
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a càdlàg and uniformly integrable martingale, then for any $t$, almost surely, $$P[X_\infty | \mathcal{F}_t] = X_t.$$
assumptions: $X$ is a càdlàg and uniformly integrable martingale
for any $t$
conclusions: $$P[X_\infty | \mathcal{F}_t] = X_t.$$
nodes.label: thm:condExp_limitProcess

nodes.name: Closure of a cadlag uniformly integrable martingale at stopping times
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a càdlàg and uniformly integrable martingale, then for any stopping time $\tau$, almost surely, $$P[X_\infty | \mathcal{F}_\tau] = X_\tau.$$
assumptions: $X$ is a càdlàg and uniformly integrable martingale
any stopping time $\tau$
conclusions: $$P[X_\infty | \mathcal{F}_\tau] = X_\tau.$$
nodes.label: thm:condExp_limitProcess_stopped

nodes.name: Limit of a stopped uniformly integrable martingale
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a càdlàg uniformly integrable martingale and $\tau$ be a stopping time. Then almost surely, $X^\tau_\infty = X_\tau$.
assumptions: $M$ be a càdlàg uniformly integrable martingale and $\tau$ be a stopping time
conclusions: almost surely, $X^\tau_\infty = X_\tau$
nodes.label: lem:limitProcess_stoppedProcess

nodes.name: Proof of Limit of a stopped uniformly integrable martingale
nodes.statement: We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_ae_eq}. Because $M$ is right-continuous and adapted, it is progressively measurable by Lemma~\ref{lem:Adapted.isStronglyProgressive_of_rightContinuous}. Therefore $X_\tau$ is $\mathcal{F}_\tau$-measurable. Convergence is obvious.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the limit characterization; X_tau is F_tau-measurable by progressive measurability and convergence is clear.

nodes.name: Use limit characterization
nodes.statement: We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_ae_eq}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the limit characterization lemma

nodes.name: Measurability
nodes.statement: Because $M$ is right-continuous and adapted, it is progressively measurable by Lemma~\ref{lem:Adapted.isStronglyProgressive_of_rightContinuous}. Therefore $X_\tau$ is $\mathcal{F}_\tau$-measurable. Convergence is obvious.
nodes.statement_short: X_tau is F_tau-measurable via progressive measurability

nodes.name: Doob's maximal inequality for $\mathbb{N}$
nodes.statement: Let $X : \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a non-negative sub-martingale. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\lambda > 0$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{i \le n}X_i\geq\lambda \right) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X_n \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \le n}X_i \ge \lambda}\right]}{\lambda} \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[X_n]}{\lambda} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: For a nonnegative discrete submartingale, P(max_{i<=n} X_i >= lambda) <= E[X_n; max >= lambda]/lambda <= E[X_n]/lambda.
assumptions: $X : \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a non-negative sub-martingale
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\lambda > 0$
conclusions: \mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{i \le n}X_i\geq\lambda \right) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X_n \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \le n}X_i \ge \lambda}\right]}{\lambda} \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[X_n]}{\lambda}
nodes.label: lem:maximal_ineq

nodes.name: Doob's maximal Inequality for countable
nodes.statement: Let $X : I \rightarrow \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a non-negative sub-martingale with $I$ countable. Then for every $M \in I,\lambda > 0$ and $p>1$ we have \begin{align*} P\left( \sup_{i\in I, i\leq M}X_i\geq\lambda \right) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X_M \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \le M}X_i \ge \lambda}\right]}{\lambda} \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[X_M]}{\lambda} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Doob's maximal inequality for a nonnegative submartingale indexed by a countable set.
assumptions: $X : I \rightarrow \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a non-negative sub-martingale with $I$ countable
$M \in I,\lambda > 0$ and $p>1$
conclusions: P\left( \sup_{i\in I, i\leq M}X_i\geq\lambda \right) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X_M \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \le M}X_i \ge \lambda}\right]}{\lambda} \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[X_M]}{\lambda}
nodes.label: lem:doob_countable

nodes.name: Proof of Doob's maximal Inequality for countable
nodes.statement: For any finite subset $J \subset I$ with $M \in J$, we have by Lemma~\ref{lem:maximal_ineq} \begin{align*} P\left( \sup_{i\in J, i \le M}X_i\geq\lambda \right) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X_{M} \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \in J, i \le M}X_i \ge \lambda}\right]}{\lambda} \: . \end{align*} Then we build a countable increasing sequence of finite sets $J_n$ with $\bigcup_nJ_n=I$. Note for any $\lambda' < \lambda$, \begin{align*} \lambda' P\left( \sup_{i\in I, i\leq M}X_i>\lambda' \right) &= \lambda' P\left( \bigcup_{i\in I, i\leq M}\{X_i>\lambda'\} \right) \\ &= \lambda' \lim_{n\to\infty} P\left( \bigcup_{i\in J_n, i\leq M}\{X_i>\lambda'\} \right) \\ &\le \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\left[X_{M} \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \in J_n, i \le M}X_i \ge \lambda'}\right] \\ &\le \mathbb{E}\left[X_{M} \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \in I, i \le M}X_i \ge \lambda'}\right] \end{align*} Now take $\lambda'\uparrow\lambda$ and use monotone or dominated convergence to derive the desired inequality. In the above, we first interpret $\sup_{i\in I, i\leq M}X_i$ in extended reals for well-definedness, then observe by the (now proved) maximal inequality that $\sup_{i\in I, i\leq M}X_i < \infty$ a.s.\ by taking $\lambda\to\infty$, so the supremum is well-defined in $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the finite-index maximal inequality on an increasing exhaustion J_n of I and pass to the limit, then let lambda' increase to lambda. Well-definedness of the supremum follows from the inequality itself.

nodes.name: Finite case
nodes.statement: For any finite subset $J \subset I$ with $M \in J$, we have by Lemma~\ref{lem:maximal_ineq} \begin{align*} P\left( \sup_{i\in J, i \le M}X_i\geq\lambda \right) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[X_{M} \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \in J, i \le M}X_i \ge \lambda}\right]}{\lambda} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Maximal inequality on finite subsets

nodes.name: Exhaustion
nodes.statement: Then we build a countable increasing sequence of finite sets $J_n$ with $\bigcup_nJ_n=I$.
nodes.statement_short: Increasing finite sets J_n exhausting I

nodes.name: Limit over J_n
nodes.statement: Note for any $\lambda' < \lambda$, \begin{align*} \lambda' P\left( \sup_{i\in I, i\leq M}X_i>\lambda' \right) &= \lambda' P\left( \bigcup_{i\in I, i\leq M}\{X_i>\lambda'\} \right) \\ &= \lambda' \lim_{n\to\infty} P\left( \bigcup_{i\in J_n, i\leq M}\{X_i>\lambda'\} \right) \\ &\le \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\left[X_{M} \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \in J_n, i \le M}X_i \ge \lambda'}\right] \\ &\le \mathbb{E}\left[X_{M} \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \in I, i \le M}X_i \ge \lambda'}\right] \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of measure gives the bound at lambda' < lambda

nodes.name: Let lambda' -> lambda
nodes.statement: Now take $\lambda'\uparrow\lambda$ and use monotone or dominated convergence to derive the desired inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Monotone/dominated convergence gives the inequality

nodes.name: Well-definedness
nodes.statement: In the above, we first interpret $\sup_{i\in I, i\leq M}X_i$ in extended reals for well-definedness, then observe by the (now proved) maximal inequality that $\sup_{i\in I, i\leq M}X_i < \infty$ a.s.\ by taking $\lambda\to\infty$, so the supremum is well-defined in $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: The supremum is a.s. finite

nodes.name: Doob Lp Inequality for countable
nodes.statement: Let $X : I \rightarrow \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a non-negative sub-martingale. Let $I$ be countable. For every $M\in I,\lambda > 0$ and $p>1$ we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{i\in I, i \leq M}X_i^p \right] \leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p\mathbb{E}[X_M^p] \: . \end{align*} That is, for $\Vert \cdot \Vert_p$ the $L^p$ norm, $\left\Vert \sup_{i \le M} X_i \right\Vert_p \leq \frac{p}{p-1} \left\Vert X_M \right\Vert_p \: .$
nodes.statement_short: Doob's L^p inequality ||sup X||_p <= p/(p-1) ||X_M||_p for countably indexed nonnegative submartingales.
assumptions: $X : I \rightarrow \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a non-negative sub-martingale
$I$ be countable
$M\in I,\lambda > 0$ and $p>1$
conclusions: \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{i\in I, i \leq M}X_i^p \right] \leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p\mathbb{E}[X_M^p]
\left\Vert \sup_{i \le M} X_i \right\Vert_p \leq \frac{p}{p-1} \left\Vert X_M \right\Vert_p
nodes.label: lem:doob_Lp_countable

nodes.name: Proof of Doob Lp Inequality for countable
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{i \le M}X_i^p \right] = p \int_0^\infty \mathbb{P}\left( \sup_{i \le M}X_i \geq \lambda \right) \lambda^{p-1} d\lambda \end{align*} By Theorem~\ref{lem:doob_countable} and then Fubini's theorem, we have then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{i \le M}X_i^p \right] &\le p \int_0^\infty \mathbb{E}\left[X_M \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \le M}X_i \ge \lambda}\right] \lambda^{p-2} d\lambda \\ &= p \mathbb{E}\left[X_M \int_0^{\sup_{i \le M}X_i} \lambda^{p-2} d\lambda\right] \\ &= \frac{p}{p - 1} \mathbb{E}\left[X_M (\sup_{i \le M}X_i)^{p-1}\right] \: . \end{align*} Then by Hölder's inequality, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{i \le M}X_i^p \right] &\le \frac{p}{p - 1} \left(\mathbb{E}[X_M^p]\right)^{1/p} \left(\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{i \le M}X_i^p \right]\right)^{(p-1)/p} \: . \end{align*} We then divide the two sides by $\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{i \le M}X_i^p \right]\right)^{(p-1)/p}$ and raise to the power $p$ to conclude.
nodes.statement_short: Layer-cake formula, the countable maximal inequality with Fubini, then Hölder's inequality and division.

nodes.name: Layer cake
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{i \le M}X_i^p \right] = p \int_0^\infty \mathbb{P}\left( \sup_{i \le M}X_i \geq \lambda \right) \lambda^{p-1} d\lambda \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write E[sup^p] as an integral of tail probabilities

nodes.name: Maximal inequality and Fubini
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{lem:doob_countable} and then Fubini's theorem, we have then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{i \le M}X_i^p \right] &\le p \int_0^\infty \mathbb{E}\left[X_M \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \le M}X_i \ge \lambda}\right] \lambda^{p-2} d\lambda \\ &= p \mathbb{E}\left[X_M \int_0^{\sup_{i \le M}X_i} \lambda^{p-2} d\lambda\right] \\ &= \frac{p}{p - 1} \mathbb{E}\left[X_M (\sup_{i \le M}X_i)^{p-1}\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound by E[X_M sup^{p-1}] p/(p-1)

nodes.name: Hölder
nodes.statement: Then by Hölder's inequality, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{i \le M}X_i^p \right] &\le \frac{p}{p - 1} \left(\mathbb{E}[X_M^p]\right)^{1/p} \left(\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{i \le M}X_i^p \right]\right)^{(p-1)/p} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Hölder's inequality

nodes.name: Rearrange
nodes.statement: We then divide the two sides by $\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{i \le M}X_i^p \right]\right)^{(p-1)/p}$ and raise to the power $p$ to conclude.
nodes.statement_short: Divide and raise to the power p

nodes.name: Doob Inequality
nodes.statement: Let $X: \mathbb{R}_+ \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a right-continuous non-negative sub-martingale. For every $T \in \mathbb{R}_+$ and $\lambda>0$ we have \begin{align*} P\left( \sup_{t\in[0,T]}X_t \geq \lambda \right) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[X_T \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \le T}X_i \ge \lambda}]}{\lambda} \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[X_T]}{\lambda} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Doob's maximal inequality for right-continuous nonnegative submartingales on [0,T].
assumptions: $X: \mathbb{R}_+ \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a right-continuous non-negative sub-martingale
$T \in \mathbb{R}_+$ and $\lambda>0$
conclusions: P\left( \sup_{t\in[0,T]}X_t \geq \lambda \right) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[X_T \mathbb{I}_{\sup_{i \le T}X_i \ge \lambda}]}{\lambda} \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[X_T]}{\lambda}
nodes.label: thm:doob_ineq

nodes.name: Proof of Doob Inequality
nodes.statement: Since $X$ is right-continuous and $[0,T]$ is a compact interval, we have that \begin{align*} \sup_{t\in[0,T]}X_t = \sup_{t\in[0,T] \cap \mathbb{Q}}X_t \: . \end{align*} Then apply Lemma~\ref{lem:doob_countable} with $I = [0,T] \cap \mathbb{Q}$ and $M = T$.
nodes.statement_short: Right continuity reduces the supremum to rational times; apply the countable maximal inequality.

nodes.name: Doob Inequality for normed spaces
nodes.statement: Let $X:\mathbb{R}_+ \to \Omega \to E$ be a right-continuous martingale with values in a normed space $E$. For every $T$ and $\lambda>0$ we have $$ P\left( \sup_{t\in[0,T]} \lVert X_t \rVert \geq \lambda \right) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[\lVert X_T \rVert]}{\lambda}. $$
assumptions: $X:\mathbb{R}_+ \to \Omega \to E$ be a right-continuous martingale with values in a normed space $E$
$T$ and $\lambda>0$
conclusions: P\left( \sup_{t\in[0,T]} \lVert X_t \rVert \geq \lambda \right) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[\lVert X_T \rVert]}{\lambda}.
nodes.label: cor:doob_ineq_norm

nodes.name: Proof of Doob Inequality for normed spaces
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{cor:Martingale.submartingale_norm}, $\lVert X \rVert$ is a sub-martingale. Then apply Theorem~\ref{thm:doob_ineq}.
nodes.statement_short: The norm of a martingale is a submartingale; apply Doob's inequality.

nodes.name: Doob's Lp inequality in $\mathbb{R}$
nodes.statement: Let $X:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a right-continuous non-negative sub-martingale. For every $T, \lambda>0$ and $p>1$ we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{t\in[0,T]}X_t^p \right] \leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p\mathbb{E}[X_T^p] \: . \end{align*} That is, for $\Vert \cdot \Vert_p$ the $L^p$ norm, $\left\Vert \sup_{t\in[0,T]} X_t \right\Vert_p \leq \frac{p}{p-1} \left\Vert X_T \right\Vert_p \: .$
nodes.statement_short: Doob's L^p inequality ||sup_{[0,T]} X||_p <= p/(p-1) ||X_T||_p for right-continuous nonnegative submartingales.
assumptions: $X:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a right-continuous non-negative sub-martingale
$T, \lambda>0$ and $p>1$
conclusions: \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{t\in[0,T]}X_t^p \right] \leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p\mathbb{E}[X_T^p]
\left\Vert \sup_{t\in[0,T]} X_t \right\Vert_p \leq \frac{p}{p-1} \left\Vert X_T \right\Vert_p
nodes.label: thm:doob_lp

nodes.name: Proof of Doob's Lp inequality in $\mathbb{R}$
nodes.statement: Since $X$ is right-continuous and $[0,T]$ is a compact interval, we have that \begin{align*} \sup_{t\in[0,T]}X_t = \sup_{t\in[0,T] \cap \mathbb{Q}}X_t \: . \end{align*} Then apply Lemma~\ref{lem:doob_Lp_countable} with $I = [0,T] \cap \mathbb{Q}$ and $M = T$.
nodes.statement_short: Right continuity reduces the supremum to rational times; apply the countable L^p inequality.

nodes.name: Doob's Lp inequality for normed spaces
nodes.statement: Let $X : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \Omega\rightarrow E$ be a right-continuous martingale with values in a normed space $E$. For every $T$ and $p>1$ we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{t\in[0,T]} \lVert X_t \rVert ^ p \right] \leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p\mathbb{E}[\lVert X_T \rVert ^p] \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: $X : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \Omega\rightarrow E$ be a right-continuous martingale with values in a normed space $E$
$T$ and $p>1$
conclusions: \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{t\in[0,T]} \lVert X_t \rVert ^ p \right] \leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p\mathbb{E}[\lVert X_T \rVert ^p]
nodes.label: cor:doob_lp_norm

nodes.name: Proof of Doob's Lp inequality for normed spaces
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{cor:Martingale.submartingale_norm}, $\lVert X \rVert$ is a sub-martingale. Then apply Theorem~\ref{thm:doob_lp}.
nodes.statement_short: The norm of a martingale is a submartingale; apply Doob's L^p inequality.

nodes.name: Doob's Lp inequality over all times in normed spaces
nodes.statement: Let $X : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \Omega\rightarrow E$ be a right-continuous martingale with values in a normed space $E$. For every $T$ and $p>1$ we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_t \lVert X_t \rVert ^ p \right] \leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p \sup_t \mathbb{E}[\lVert X_t \rVert ^p] \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: $X : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \Omega\rightarrow E$ be a right-continuous martingale with values in a normed space $E$
$T$ and $p>1$
conclusions: \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_t \lVert X_t \rVert ^ p \right] \leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p \sup_t \mathbb{E}[\lVert X_t \rVert ^p]
nodes.label: cor:doob_lp_norm_top

nodes.name: Proof of Doob's Lp inequality over all times in normed spaces
nodes.statement: Take limits on both sides in Corollary~\ref{cor:doob_lp_norm}.
nodes.statement_short: Take limits in the normed-space Doob L^p inequality.

nodes.name: Stopped Submartingale
nodes.statement: Let $X:\mathbb{R}_+ \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a cadlag submartingale and $\tau$ a stopping time. Then the stopped process $X^\tau$ is a submartingale.
assumptions: $X:\mathbb{R}_+ \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a cadlag submartingale and $\tau$ a stopping time
conclusions: the stopped process $X^\tau$ is a submartingale
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.stoppedProcess_of_cadlag

nodes.name: Doob Inequality for stopping times
nodes.statement: Let $X:\mathbb{R}\times\Omega\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a right-continuous non-negative sub-martingale. For every $\lambda>0$ and $p>1$ and $\tau$ stopping time a.s. bounded by $T>0$, we have $$ P\left( \sup_{t\in[0,\tau]}X_t\geq\lambda \right)\leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[X_\tau]}{\lambda}. $$
assumptions: $X:\mathbb{R}\times\Omega\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a right-continuous non-negative sub-martingale
$\lambda>0$ and $p>1$ and $\tau$ stopping time a.s. bounded by $T>0$
conclusions: P\left( \sup_{t\in[0,\tau]}X_t\geq\lambda \right)\leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[X_\tau]}{\lambda}.

nodes.name: Doob Inequality for stopping times in normed spaces
nodes.statement: Let $X:\mathbb{R}\times\Omega\rightarrow E$ be a right-continuous martingale with values in a normed space $E$. For every $\lambda>0$ and $p>1$ and $\tau$ stopping time a.s. bounded by $T>0$, we have $$ P\left( \sup_{t\in[0,\tau]}\lVert X_t \rVert \geq\lambda \right)\leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[\lVert X_\tau \rVert]}{\lambda}. $$
assumptions: $X:\mathbb{R}\times\Omega\rightarrow E$ be a right-continuous martingale with values in a normed space $E$
$\lambda>0$ and $p>1$ and $\tau$ stopping time a.s. bounded by $T>0$
conclusions: P\left( \sup_{t\in[0,\tau]}\lVert X_t \rVert \geq\lambda \right)\leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[\lVert X_\tau \rVert]}{\lambda}.

nodes.name: Proof of Doob Inequality for stopping times in normed spaces
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{cor:Martingale.submartingale_norm}, $\lVert X \rVert$ is a sub-martingale. Then apply Theorem~\ref{lem:doob_ineq_stop}.
nodes.statement_short: The norm of a martingale is a submartingale; apply the stopping-time Doob inequality.

nodes.name: Doob's Lp Inequality for stopping times
nodes.statement: Let $X:\mathbb{R}\times\Omega\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a right-continuous non-negative sub-martingale. For every $\lambda>0$ and $p>1$ and $\tau$ stopping time a.s. bounded by $T>0$, we have $$ \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{t\in[0,\tau]}X_t^p \right]\leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p\mathbb{E}[X_\tau^p]. $$
assumptions: $X:\mathbb{R}\times\Omega\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a right-continuous non-negative sub-martingale
$\lambda>0$ and $p>1$ and $\tau$ stopping time a.s. bounded by $T>0$
conclusions: \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{t\in[0,\tau]}X_t^p \right]\leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p\mathbb{E}[X_\tau^p].
nodes.label: lem:doob_ineq_stop_exp_val

nodes.name: Proof of Doob's Lp Inequality for stopping times
nodes.statement: 8.1.3 Pascucci.
nodes.statement_short: Reference to Pascucci, 8.1.3.

nodes.name: Doob's Lp Inequality for stopping times in normed spaces
nodes.statement: Let $X:\mathbb{R}\times\Omega\rightarrow E$ be a right-continuous martingale with values in a normed space $E$. For every $\lambda>0$ and $p>1$ and $\tau$ stopping time a.s. bounded by $T>0$, we have $$ \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{t\in[0,\tau]}\lVert X_t \rVert^p \right]\leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p\mathbb{E}[\lVert X_\tau \rVert^p]. $$
assumptions: $X:\mathbb{R}\times\Omega\rightarrow E$ be a right-continuous martingale with values in a normed space $E$
$\lambda>0$ and $p>1$ and $\tau$ stopping time a.s. bounded by $T>0$
conclusions: \mathbb{E}\left[ \sup_{t\in[0,\tau]}\lVert X_t \rVert^p \right]\leq \left(\frac{p}{p-1}\right)^p\mathbb{E}[\lVert X_\tau \rVert^p].
nodes.label: cor:doob_ineq_stop_exp_val

nodes.name: Proof of Doob's Lp Inequality for stopping times in normed spaces
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{cor:Martingale.submartingale_norm}, $\lVert X \rVert$ is a sub-martingale. Then apply Theorem~\ref{lem:doob_ineq_stop_exp_val}.
nodes.statement_short: The norm of a martingale is a submartingale; apply the stopping-time Doob L^p inequality.

nodes.name: Paving
nodes.statement: A paving is simply a set of sets.

nodes.name: Product of pavings
nodes.statement: The product of two pavings $S$ and $T$ is the set of sets of the form $s \times t$ where $s \in S$ and $t \in T$. We denote that product by $S \times T$.
differentia: of the form $s \times t$ where $s \in S$ and $t \in T$
nodes.label: def:image2_prod

nodes.name: Finite union closure
nodes.statement: For a paving $S$, we denote by $S^{\cup f}$ the set of finite unions of sets in $S$.
nodes.label: def:supClosure

nodes.name: Finite intersection closure
nodes.statement: For a paving $S$, we denote by $S^{\cap f}$ the set of finite intersections of sets in $S$.
nodes.label: def:infClosure

nodes.name: Countable union closure
nodes.statement: We denote by $S_\sigma$ the set of countable unions of sets in $S$.
nodes.label: def:countableSupClosure

nodes.name: Countable intersection closure
nodes.statement: We denote by $S_\delta$ the set of countable intersections of sets in $S$.
nodes.label: def:countableInfClosure

nodes.name: Monotone characterization of S_delta
nodes.statement: If a paving $S$ is closed under pairwise intersection, then a set $s$ is in $S_\delta$ if and only if there exists a monotone decreasing family of sets $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in $S$ such that $s = \bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} A_n$.
assumptions: a paving $S$ is closed under pairwise intersection
conclusions: a set $s$ is in $S_\delta$ if and only if there exists a monotone decreasing family of sets $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in $S$ such that $s = \bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} A_n$
equivalent_conditions: a set $s$ is in $S_\delta$
there exists a monotone decreasing family of sets $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in $S$ such that $s = \bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} A_n$
nodes.label: lem:InfClosed.mem_countableInfClosure_iff

nodes.name: Proof of Monotone characterization of S_delta
nodes.statement: The ``monotone decreasing'' condition is the only non-trivial part of the statement: without it it would just be the definition of $S_\delta$. If $s \in S_\delta$ there exists a family $(B_n)$ that satisfies the condition but may not be monotone. We can then define $A_n = \bigcap_{k \le n} B_k$, and the family $(A_n)$ is monotone decreasing and satisfies $\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} A_n = \bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} B_n = s$.
nodes.statement_short: Make an arbitrary countable family monotone by taking partial intersections $A_n = \bigcap_{k\le n} B_k$.

nodes.name: Reduction to monotonicity
nodes.statement: The ``monotone decreasing'' condition is the only non-trivial part of the statement: without it it would just be the definition of $S_\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Only monotonicity needs proof

nodes.name: Take a representing family
nodes.statement: If $s \in S_\delta$ there exists a family $(B_n)$ that satisfies the condition but may not be monotone.
nodes.statement_short: Take a possibly non-monotone family $(B_n)$

nodes.name: Partial intersections
nodes.statement: We can then define $A_n = \bigcap_{k \le n} B_k$, and the family $(A_n)$ is monotone decreasing and satisfies $\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} A_n = \bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} B_n = s$.
nodes.statement_short: Partial intersections give a decreasing family with the same intersection

nodes.name: Monotone characterization of S_sigma
nodes.statement: If a paving $S$ is closed under pairwise union, then a set $s$ is in $S_\sigma$ if and only if there exists a monotone increasing family of sets $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in $S$ such that $s = \bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} A_n$.
assumptions: a paving $S$ is closed under pairwise union
conclusions: a set $s$ is in $S_\sigma$ if and only if there exists a monotone increasing family of sets $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in $S$ such that $s = \bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} A_n$
equivalent_conditions: a set $s$ is in $S_\sigma$
there exists a monotone increasing family of sets $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in $S$ such that $s = \bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} A_n$
nodes.label: lem:SupClosed.mem_countableSupClosure_iff

nodes.name: Proof of Monotone characterization of S_sigma
nodes.statement: Similar to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:InfClosed.mem_countableInfClosure_iff}.
nodes.statement_short: Dual of the intersection case: take partial unions.

nodes.name: Compact system
nodes.statement: A set of sets $K$ is a compact system if for every countable family $(C_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of sets in $K$ such that $\bigcap_{n \in\mathbb{N}} C_n = \emptyset$, there exists a finite subset $S$ of $\mathbb{N}$ such that $\bigcap_{n \in S} C_n = \emptyset$.
differentia: for every countable family $(C_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of sets in $K$ such that $\bigcap_{n \in\mathbb{N}} C_n = \emptyset$, there exists a finite subset $S$ of $\mathbb{N}$ such that $\bigcap_{n \in S} C_n = \emptyset$
nodes.label: def:IsCompactSystem

nodes.name: Compact closed sets form a compact system
nodes.statement: The family of compact closed sets of a topological space is a compact system.
conclusions: The family of compact closed sets of a topological space is a compact system.
nodes.label: lem:isCompactSystem_isCompact_isClosed

nodes.name: Compact sets of a T2 space form a compact system
nodes.statement: The family of compact sets of a T2 topological space is a compact system.
assumptions: a T2 topological space
conclusions: The family of compact sets of a T2 topological space is a compact system.
nodes.label: lem:isCompactSystem_isCompact

nodes.name: Proof of Compact sets of a T2 space form a compact system
nodes.statement: The T2 assumption ensures that compact sets are closed, so the family of compact sets is the family of compact closed sets, which is a compact system by Lemma~\ref{lem:isCompactSystem_isCompact_isClosed}.
nodes.statement_short: In a T2 space compact sets are closed, so reduce to compact closed sets.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of compact systems
nodes.statement: If $S \subseteq T$ and $T$ is a compact system, then $S$ is a compact system.
assumptions: $S \subseteq T$
$T$ is a compact system
conclusions: $S$ is a compact system
nodes.label: lem:IsCompactSystem.mono

nodes.name: Proof of Monotonicity of compact systems
nodes.statement: Any sequence of sets in $S$ is a sequence of sets in $T$, so if the intersection of the sequence is empty, then there is a finite subset of the sequence whose intersection is empty by the compact system property of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: A sequence in $S$ is a sequence in $T$; apply the compact system property of $T$.

nodes.name: Closed compact intervals form a compact system
nodes.statement: The family of closed compact intervals of $\mathbb{R}$ is a compact system.
conclusions: The family of closed compact intervals of $\mathbb{R}$ is a compact system.
nodes.label: lem:isCompactSystem_Icc

nodes.name: Proof of Closed compact intervals form a compact system
nodes.statement: The family of closed compact intervals of $\mathbb{R}$ is a family of compact sets, so it is a compact system by Lemma~\ref{lem:isCompactSystem_isCompact} and~\ref{lem:IsCompactSystem.mono}.
nodes.statement_short: Closed compact intervals are compact sets; combine the T2 and monotonicity lemmas.

nodes.name: Countable product of compact systems
nodes.statement: The product of a countable family of compact systems is a compact system.
conclusions: The product of a countable family of compact systems is a compact system.
nodes.label: lem:IsCompactSystem.pi

nodes.name: Countable sum of compact systems
nodes.statement: The sum of a countable family of compact systems is a compact system.
conclusions: The sum of a countable family of compact systems is a compact system.
nodes.label: lem:IsCompactSystem.sigma

nodes.name: Product of two compact systems
nodes.statement: The product of two compact systems $S \times T$ is a compact system.
conclusions: The product of two compact systems $S \times T$ is a compact system.
nodes.label: lem:IsCompactSystem.image2_prod

nodes.name: Finite-union closure of a compact system
nodes.statement: If $S$ is a compact system, then $S^{\cup f}$ is a compact system.
assumptions: $S$ is a compact system
conclusions: $S^{\cup f}$ is a compact system
nodes.label: lem:IsCompactSystem.supClosure

nodes.name: Countable-intersection closure of a compact system
nodes.statement: If $S$ is a compact system, then $S_\delta$ is a compact system.
assumptions: $S$ is a compact system
conclusions: $S_\delta$ is a compact system
nodes.label: lem:IsCompactSystem.countableInfClosure

nodes.name: Finite-intersection closure of a compact system
nodes.statement: If $S$ is a compact system, then $S^{\cap f}$ is a compact system.
assumptions: $S$ is a compact system
conclusions: $S^{\cap f}$ is a compact system
nodes.label: lem:IsCompactSystem.infClosure

nodes.name: Proof of Finite-intersection closure of a compact system
nodes.statement: $S_\delta$ is a compact system by Lemma~\ref{lem:IsCompactSystem.countableInfClosure}, and $S^{\cap f} \subseteq S_\delta$, so we can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:IsCompactSystem.mono}.
nodes.statement_short: $S^{\cap f}\subseteq S_\delta$, which is a compact system; apply monotonicity.

nodes.name: Projection commutes with decreasing intersections
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a paving of $\mathcal{X}$ and $T$ be a compact system of $\mathcal{K}$. Let $(B_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a monotone decreasing sequence of sets in $(S \times T)^{\cup f}$. Let $\pi_{\mathcal{X}} : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{K} \to \mathcal{X}$ be the projection on $\mathcal{X}$. Then \begin{align*} \pi_{\mathcal{X}}\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} B_n\right) = \bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \pi_{\mathcal{X}}(B_n). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: For a decreasing sequence in $(S\times T)^{\cup f}$ with $T$ a compact system, projection onto $\mathcal{X}$ commutes with the intersection.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a paving of $\mathcal{X}$ and $T$ be a compact system of $\mathcal{K}$.
Let $(B_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a monotone decreasing sequence of sets in $(S \times T)^{\cup f}$.
Let $\pi_{\mathcal{X}} : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{K} \to \mathcal{X}$ be the projection on $\mathcal{X}$.
conclusions: \pi_{\mathcal{X}}\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} B_n\right) = \bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \pi_{\mathcal{X}}(B_n).
nodes.label: thm:fst_iInter_of_supClosure_image2_prod_of_antitone

nodes.name: Analytic set
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a paving of a type $\mathcal{X}$. A set $s$ of $\mathcal{X}$ is said to be $F$-analytic if there exists a nonempty type $\mathcal{K}$ and a compact system $K$ of $\mathcal{K}$ with $\emptyset \in K$ such that $s$ is the projection on $\mathcal{X}$ of a set in $(F \times K)_{\sigma \delta}$. We denote the set of $F$-analytic sets by $\mathcal{A}(F)$.
nodes.statement_short: $s$ is $F$-analytic if it is the projection of a set in $(F\times K)_{\sigma\delta}$ for some compact system $K$ containing $\emptyset$.
nodes.label: def:IsPavingAnalytic

nodes.name: Sets of F are F-analytic
nodes.statement: Every set in $F$ is $F$-analytic: $F \subseteq \mathcal{A}(F)$.
conclusions: Every set in $F$ is $F$-analytic: $F \subseteq \mathcal{A}(F)$.
nodes.label: lem:isPavingAnalytic_of_prop

nodes.name: Monotonicity of analytic sets in the paving
nodes.statement: If $F \subseteq G$ and $s$ is $F$-analytic, then $s$ is $G$-analytic: $\mathcal{A}(F) \subseteq \mathcal{A}(G)$.
assumptions: $F \subseteq G$
$s$ is $F$-analytic
conclusions: $s$ is $G$-analytic: $\mathcal{A}(F) \subseteq \mathcal{A}(G)$
nodes.label: lem:IsPavingAnalytic.mono

nodes.name: Analytic set is covered by an F_sigma set
nodes.statement: If $s$ is $F$-analytic, then there exists a set $t$ in $F_\sigma$ such that $s \subseteq t$.
assumptions: $s$ is $F$-analytic
conclusions: there exists a set $t$ in $F_\sigma$ such that $s \subseteq t$
nodes.label: lem:IsPavingAnalytic.exists_mem_countableSupClosure_superset

nodes.name: Countable union of analytic sets
nodes.statement: A countable union of $F$-analytic sets is $F$-analytic.
conclusions: A countable union of $F$-analytic sets is $F$-analytic.
nodes.label: lem:IsPavingAnalytic.iUnion

nodes.name: Countable intersection of analytic sets
nodes.statement: A countable intersection of $F$-analytic sets is $F$-analytic.
conclusions: A countable intersection of $F$-analytic sets is $F$-analytic.
nodes.label: lem:IsPavingAnalytic.iInter

nodes.name: Projection of an analytic set is analytic
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a set of sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and $K$ be a compact system of $\mathcal{K}$, with $\emptyset \in K$. If a set $s$ of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{K}$ is $F \times K$-analytic, then its projection on $\mathcal{X}$ is $F$-analytic.
assumptions: Let $F$ be a set of sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and $K$ be a compact system of $\mathcal{K}$, with $\emptyset \in K$.
a set $s$ of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{K}$ is $F \times K$-analytic
conclusions: its projection on $\mathcal{X}$ is $F$-analytic
nodes.label: lem:IsPavingAnalytic.fst

nodes.name: Left product with an analytic set
nodes.statement: If $t \in T$ and $s$ is $F$-analytic, then $t \times s$ is $(T \times F)$-analytic: $T \times \mathcal{A}(F) \subseteq \mathcal{A}(T \times F)$.
assumptions: $t \in T$
$s$ is $F$-analytic
conclusions: $t \times s$ is $(T \times F)$-analytic: $T \times \mathcal{A}(F) \subseteq \mathcal{A}(T \times F)$
nodes.label: lem:IsPavingAnalytic.prod_left

nodes.name: Product of analytic sets
nodes.statement: If $s$ is $F$-analytic and $t$ is $G$-analytic, then $s \times t$ is $(F \times G)$-analytic: $\mathcal{A}(F) \times \mathcal{A}(G) \subseteq \mathcal{A}(F \times G)$.
assumptions: $s$ is $F$-analytic
$t$ is $G$-analytic
conclusions: $s \times t$ is $(F \times G)$-analytic: $\mathcal{A}(F) \times \mathcal{A}(G) \subseteq \mathcal{A}(F \times G)$
nodes.label: lem:IsPavingAnalytic.prod

nodes.name: Idempotence of analytic sets
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{A}(F)) = \mathcal{A}(F)$.
conclusions: $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{A}(F)) = \mathcal{A}(F)$.
nodes.label: lem:isPavingAnalytic_isPavingAnalytic

nodes.name: Pavings K_R and I_R
nodes.statement: We denote by $K_{\mathbb{R}}$ the paving of compact sets of $\mathbb{R}$ and let $I_{\mathbb{R}}$ be the paving of closed compact intervals of $\mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Paving M_X of measurable sets
nodes.statement: For a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$, we denote by $M_{\mathcal{X}}$ the paving of measurable sets of $\mathcal{X}$.

nodes.name: Generated sigma-algebra sets are analytic
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a paving with $\emptyset \in F$ and let $\sigma(F)$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $F$. Suppose that for every $t \in F$, $t^c$ is $F$-analytic. Then every set in $\sigma(F)$ is $F$-analytic: $\sigma(F) \subseteq \mathcal{A}(F)$.
assumptions: Let $F$ be a paving with $\emptyset \in F$ and let $\sigma(F)$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $F$.
Suppose that for every $t \in F$, $t^c$ is $F$-analytic.
conclusions: Then every set in $\sigma(F)$ is $F$-analytic: $\sigma(F) \subseteq \mathcal{A}(F)$.
nodes.label: lem:isPavingAnalytic_of_measurableSet_generateFrom

nodes.name: Measurable sets of R are interval-analytic
nodes.statement: A measurable set of $\mathbb{R}$ is $I_{\mathbb{R}}$-analytic. That is, $M_{\mathbb{R}} \subseteq \mathcal{A}(I_{\mathbb{R}})$.
conclusions: A measurable set of $\mathbb{R}$ is $I_{\mathbb{R}}$-analytic.
nodes.label: lem:MeasurableSet.isPavingAnalytic_Icc_real

nodes.name: M_R-analytic iff I_R-analytic
nodes.statement: A set of $\mathbb{R}$ is $M_{\mathbb{R}}$-analytic if and only if it is $I_{\mathbb{R}}$-analytic.
conclusions: A set of $\mathbb{R}$ is $M_{\mathbb{R}}$-analytic if and only if it is $I_{\mathbb{R}}$-analytic.
equivalent_conditions: A set of $\mathbb{R}$ is $M_{\mathbb{R}}$-analytic
it is $I_{\mathbb{R}}$-analytic
nodes.label: lem:IsPavingAnalytic_measurableSet_iff_isPavingAnalytic_Icc

nodes.name: Measurable sets of X x R are analytic
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a measurable space and $s$ be a measurable set of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathbb{R}$. Then $s$ is $(M_{\mathcal{X}} \times I_{\mathbb{R}})$-analytic.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a measurable space and $s$ be a measurable set of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathbb{R}$.
conclusions: Then $s$ is $(M_{\mathcal{X}} \times I_{\mathbb{R}})$-analytic.
nodes.label: lem:MeasurableSet.isPavingAnalytic_image2_prod

nodes.name: Projection of an (M_X x I_R)-analytic set
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a measurable space and $s$ be a set of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathbb{R}$ which is $(M_{\mathcal{X}} \times I_{\mathbb{R}})$-analytic. Then the projection $\pi_{\mathcal{X}}(s)$ is $M_{\mathcal{X}}$-analytic.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a measurable space and $s$ be a set of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathbb{R}$ which is $(M_{\mathcal{X}} \times I_{\mathbb{R}})$-analytic.
conclusions: Then the projection $\pi_{\mathcal{X}}(s)$ is $M_{\mathcal{X}}$-analytic.
