nodes.name: Projection of a measurable set is M_X-analytic
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a measurable space and $s$ be a measurable set of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathbb{R}$. Then the projection of $s$ on $\mathcal{X}$ is $M_{\mathcal{X}}$-analytic.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a measurable space and $s$ be a measurable set of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathbb{R}$.
conclusions: Then the projection of $s$ on $\mathcal{X}$ is $M_{\mathcal{X}}$-analytic.
nodes.label: lem:MeasurableSet.isPavingAnalytic_fst

nodes.name: Measurably analytic set
nodes.statement: We say that a set $s$ of a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$ is measurably analytic for a measurable space $\mathcal{K}$ if it is the projection of a measurable set of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{K}$. We say that $s$ is measurably analytic if it is measurably analytic for $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.genus: a set $s$ of a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$
differentia: it is the projection of a measurable set of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{K}$
nodes.label: def:IsMeasurableAnalytic

nodes.name: Measurably analytic for a standard Borel space
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{K}$ be a standard Borel space. If a set $s$ of $\mathcal{X}$ is measurably analytic for $\mathcal{K}$, then it is measurably analytic.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{K}$ be a standard Borel space.
a set $s$ of $\mathcal{X}$ is measurably analytic for $\mathcal{K}$
conclusions: it is measurably analytic
nodes.label: lem:IsMeasurableAnalyticFor.isMeasurableAnalytic

nodes.name: Proof of Measurably analytic for a standard Borel space
nodes.statement: There is a measurable embedding of $\mathcal{K}$ into $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Embed the standard Borel space $\mathcal{K}$ measurably into $\mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Measurably analytic implies M_X-analytic
nodes.statement: If a set $s$ of $\mathcal{X}$ is measurably analytic, then it is $M_{\mathcal{X}}$-analytic.
assumptions: a set $s$ of $\mathcal{X}$ is measurably analytic
conclusions: it is $M_{\mathcal{X}}$-analytic
nodes.label: lem:IsMeasurableAnalytic.isPavingAnalytic

nodes.name: Capacity
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a set of sets of a type $\mathcal{X}$. An $F$-capacity is a function $I$ from the sets of $\mathcal{X}$ to $\mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $I$ is monotone for set inclusion: for $s \subseteq t$, $I(s) \le I(t)$, \item if $(s_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is an increasing sequence of sets of $\mathcal{X}$, then $I(s_n)$ tends to $I(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} s_n)$ at infinity, \item if $(s_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a decreasing sequence of sets in $F$, then $I(s_n)$ tends to $I(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} s_n)$ at infinity. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: An $F$-capacity is a monotone set function continuous along increasing sequences and along decreasing sequences in $F$.
nodes.genus: a function $I$ from the sets of $\mathcal{X}$ to $\mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$
differentia: $I$ is monotone for set inclusion: for $s \subseteq t$, $I(s) \le I(t)$
if $(s_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is an increasing sequence of sets of $\mathcal{X}$, then $I(s_n)$ tends to $I(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} s_n)$ at infinity
if $(s_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a decreasing sequence of sets in $F$, then $I(s_n)$ tends to $I(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} s_n)$ at infinity
nodes.label: def:Capacity

nodes.name: Capacity composed with projection
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a set of sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity. Suppose that $\emptyset \in F$ and $F$ is closed under pairwise unions. Let $K$ be a compact system of $\mathcal{K}$. Let $\pi_{\mathcal{X}} : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{K} \to \mathcal{X}$ be the projection on the first coordinate. Then the function $I_{\mathcal{X}}(u) = I(\pi_{\mathcal{X}}(u))$ is a capacity for $(F \times K)^{\cup f}$.
assumptions: Let $F$ be a set of sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity.
Suppose that $\emptyset \in F$ and $F$ is closed under pairwise unions.
Let $K$ be a compact system of $\mathcal{K}$.
conclusions: Then the function $I_{\mathcal{X}}(u) = I(\pi_{\mathcal{X}}(u))$ is a capacity for $(F \times K)^{\cup f}$.
nodes.label: lem:Capacity.comp_fst_aux

nodes.name: Projected capacity
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a set of sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity. Suppose that $\emptyset \in F$ and $F$ is closed under pairwise unions. Let $K$ be a compact system of $\mathcal{K}$. Let $\pi_{\mathcal{X}} : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{K} \to \mathcal{X}$ be the projection on the first coordinate. Then we define a capacity for $(F \times K)^{\cup f}$ by $I_{\mathcal{X}}(u) = I(\pi_{\mathcal{X}}(u))$ (it is indeed a capacity by Lemma~\ref{lem:Capacity.comp_fst_aux}).
nodes.statement_short: Defines the capacity $I_{\mathcal{X}}(u) = I(\pi_{\mathcal{X}}(u))$ on $(F\times K)^{\cup f}$.
nodes.label: def:Capacity.comp_fst

nodes.name: Capacitable set
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a set of sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity. A set $s$ of $\mathcal{X}$ is said to be $I$-capacitable if for all $a < I(s)$, there exists a set $t \in F_\delta$ such that $t \subseteq s$ and $a \le I(t)$.
differentia: for all $a < I(s)$, there exists a set $t \in F_\delta$ such that $t \subseteq s$ and $a \le I(t)$
nodes.label: def:IsCapacitable

nodes.name: Sets of F are capacitable
nodes.statement: For $I$ an $F$-capacity, every set in $F$ is $I$-capacitable.
assumptions: $I$ an $F$-capacity
conclusions: every set in $F$ is $I$-capacitable
nodes.label: lem:isCapacitable_of_prop

nodes.name: F_sigma-delta sets are capacitable
nodes.statement: Suppose that $F$ contains the empty set and is closed under pairwise intersections and unions, and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity. Then every set of $F_{\sigma \delta}$ is $I$-capacitable.
assumptions: Suppose that $F$ contains the empty set and is closed under pairwise intersections and unions, and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity.
conclusions: Then every set of $F_{\sigma \delta}$ is $I$-capacitable.
nodes.label: lem:isCapacitable_mem_countableInfClosure_countableSupClosure

nodes.name: Projection of a ((F x K)^{cup f})_delta set lies in F_delta
nodes.statement: Suppose that $F$ contains the empty set and is closed under pairwise intersections and unions, and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity. Let $K$ be a compact system which is also closed under pairwise intersections. Let $s \in ((F \times K)^{\cup f})_\delta$. Then $\pi_{\mathcal{X}}(s) \in F_\delta$.
assumptions: Suppose that $F$ contains the empty set and is closed under pairwise intersections and unions, and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity.
Let $K$ be a compact system which is also closed under pairwise intersections.
Let $s \in ((F \times K)^{\cup f})_\delta$.
conclusions: Then $\pi_{\mathcal{X}}(s) \in F_\delta$.
nodes.label: lem:mem_countableInfClosure_fst

nodes.name: Projection of a capacitable set is capacitable
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a set of sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity. Suppose that $F$ contains the empty set and is closed under pairwise intersections and unions. Let $K$ be a compact system of $\mathcal{K}$ which is also closed under pairwise intersections. If a set $s$ of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{K}$ is capacitable with respect to the capacity $I_{\mathcal{X}}$ of Definition~\ref{def:Capacity.comp_fst}, then its projection on $\mathcal{X}$ is capacitable with respect to $I$.
assumptions: Let $F$ be a set of sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity.
Suppose that $F$ contains the empty set and is closed under pairwise intersections and unions.
Let $K$ be a compact system of $\mathcal{K}$ which is also closed under pairwise intersections.
a set $s$ of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{K}$ is capacitable with respect to the capacity $I_{\mathcal{X}}$ of Definition~\ref{def:Capacity.comp_fst}
conclusions: its projection on $\mathcal{X}$ is capacitable with respect to $I$
nodes.label: lem:IsCapacitable.fst

nodes.name: Choquet's capacitability theorem
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a set of sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity. Suppose that $F$ contains the empty set and is closed under pairwise intersections and unions. Then every $F$-analytic set is $I$-capacitable.
assumptions: Let $F$ be a set of sets of $\mathcal{X}$ and let $I$ be an $F$-capacity.
Suppose that $F$ contains the empty set and is closed under pairwise intersections and unions.
conclusions: Then every $F$-analytic set is $I$-capacitable.
nodes.label: thm:IsPavingAnalytic.isCapacitable

nodes.name: Capacity of a finite measure
nodes.statement: Every finite measure defines a capacity by $I(s) = \mu(s)$ (where $\mu(s)$ is the value of the outer measure defined by $\mu$, but in Lean that's how $\mu(s)$ is defined already).
nodes.definiendum: capacity defined by a finite measure
nodes.label: def:Measure.capacity

nodes.name: Capacitable iff null-measurable
nodes.statement: A set is capacitable with respect to the capacity defined by a finite measure if and only if it is null-measurable for this measure.
conclusions: A set is capacitable with respect to the capacity defined by a finite measure if and only if it is null-measurable for this measure.
equivalent_conditions: A set is capacitable with respect to the capacity defined by a finite measure
it is null-measurable for this measure
nodes.label: lem:isCapacitable_measure_iff

nodes.name: Analytic sets are universally measurable
nodes.statement: An $M_{\mathcal{X}}$-analytic set of a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$ is universally measurable: it is null-measurable for every finite measure on $\mathcal{X}$.
assumptions: An $M_{\mathcal{X}}$-analytic set of a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$
conclusions: is universally measurable: it is null-measurable for every finite measure on $\mathcal{X}$
nodes.label: lem:IsPavingAnalytic.nullMeasurableSet

nodes.name: Measurably analytic sets are universally measurable
nodes.statement: A measurably analytic set of a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$ is universally measurable: it is null-measurable for every finite measure on $\mathcal{X}$.
assumptions: A measurably analytic set of a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$
conclusions: is universally measurable: it is null-measurable for every finite measure on $\mathcal{X}$
nodes.label: lem:IsMeasurableAnalytic.nullMeasurableSet

nodes.name: Measurable projection
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ be measurable spaces, with $\mathcal{Y}$ standard Borel. Then the projection of a measurable set of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ on $\mathcal{X}$ is universally measurable.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ be measurable spaces, with $\mathcal{Y}$ standard Borel.
conclusions: Then the projection of a measurable set of $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ on $\mathcal{X}$ is universally measurable.
nodes.label: thm:MeasurableSet.nullMeasurableSet_fst

nodes.name: Monotone class
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a collection of subsets of a set $X$. We say that $\mathcal{M}$ is a monotone class if it is closed under countable monotone unions and countable monotone intersections, i.e.: \begin{enumerate} \item if \( A_1, A_2, \ldots \in M \) and \( A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq \cdots \), then \( \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i \in M \), \item if \( B_1, B_2, \ldots \in M \) and \( B_1 \supseteq B_2 \supseteq \cdots \), then \( \bigcap_{i=1}^\infty B_i \in M \). \end{enumerate} Given a collection $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $X$, we call the smallest monotone class containing $\mathcal{F}$ the monotone class generated by $\mathcal{F}$.
nodes.genus: a collection of subsets of a set $X$
differentia: closed under countable monotone unions and countable monotone intersections
nodes.label: def:monotone_class

nodes.name: Monotone class theorem
nodes.statement: Let \(G\) be an algebra of subsets of a set \(X\). Then the monotone class generated by \(G\) coincides with the $\sigma$-algebra generated by \(G\).
assumptions: Let \(G\) be an algebra of subsets of a set \(X\).
conclusions: Then the monotone class generated by \(G\) coincides with the $\sigma$-algebra generated by \(G\).
nodes.label: thm:monotone_class

nodes.name: Progressively measurable set
nodes.statement: A subset of $[0, \infty) \times \Omega$ is progressively measurable if its indicator is a progressively measurable process.
differentia: its indicator is a progressively measurable process
nodes.label: def:progr_meas_set

nodes.name: Debut of a set
nodes.statement: Let $E \subseteq{} [0, \infty) \times \Omega $, define $D_E = \inf\left\lbrace t \geq 0\ :\ (t, \omega) \in E\right\rbrace$, the debut of $E$.
nodes.label: def:debut_set

nodes.name: Debut theorem
nodes.statement: If $E$ is a progressively measurable set and the filtration satisfies the usual conditions, then $D_E$ is a stopping time.
assumptions: $E$ is a progressively measurable set
the filtration satisfies the usual conditions
conclusions: $D_E$ is a stopping time
nodes.label: thm:debut_of_progr_meas_is_stop_time

nodes.name: Hitting times are stopping times
nodes.statement: If $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a progressively measurable process with respect to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions and $B$ is a Borel-measurable subset of $E$, then the hitting time of $X$ in $B$ is a stopping time.
assumptions: $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is a progressively measurable process with respect to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions
$B$ is a Borel-measurable subset of $E$
conclusions: the hitting time of $X$ in $B$ is a stopping time
nodes.label: thm:hitting_is_stopping_time

nodes.name: Proof of Hitting times are stopping times
nodes.statement: Since $B$ is a Borel subset of $\mathcal{S}$ and $X$ is progressively measurable, then $\mathbf{1}_B(X_t)$ is also progressively measurable. The hitting time is then the debut of the set $E = \{(s,\omega) : \mathbf{1}_B(X_s(\omega)) = 1\}$, and therefore is a stopping time by Theorem~\ref{thm:debut_of_progr_meas_is_stop_time}.
nodes.statement_short: Write the hitting time as the debut of the progressively measurable set $\{\mathbf{1}_B(X_s)=1\}$ and apply the debut theorem.

nodes.name: Hitting time of [a, infinity)
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a conditionally complete linear order with a bottom element and let $R$ be a preorder. For a process $X : T \to Ω \to R$ and $a \in R$, define the random time \begin{align*} \tau_{X \ge a} = \inf\{t \in T \mid X_t \ge a\} \: , \end{align*} in which the infimum is infinite if the set is empty.
nodes.label: def:leastGE

nodes.name: Hitting time of [a, infinity) is a stopping time
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a conditionally complete linear order with a bottom element, which is a Polish space for its order topology, on which we put the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Let $R$ be a preorder with a metrizable topology for which sets of the form $\{x \in R \mid x \ge a\}$ are closed, with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. If $X : T \to Ω \to R$ is a progressively measurable process with respect to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions, then for any $a \in R$, the random time $\tau_{X \ge a}$ is a stopping time.
assumptions: Let $T$ be a conditionally complete linear order with a bottom element, which is a Polish space for its order topology, on which we put the Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
Let $R$ be a preorder with a metrizable topology for which sets of the form $\{x \in R \mid x \ge a\}$ are closed, with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
$X : T \to Ω \to R$ is a progressively measurable process with respect to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions
conclusions: for any $a \in R$, the random time $\tau_{X \ge a}$ is a stopping time
nodes.label: lem:isStoppingTime_leastGE

nodes.name: Proof of Hitting time of [a, infinity) is a stopping time
nodes.statement: This is a direct application of Theorem~\ref{thm:hitting_is_stopping_time} with the set $B = [a, +\infty)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the hitting time theorem with $B=[a,+\infty)$.

nodes.name: Hitting time of a right-continuous adapted process is a stopping time
nodes.statement: If $X : ι \to Ω \to ℝ$ is a right-continuous and adapted process with respect to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions, then for any $a \in \mathbb{R}$, the random time $\tau_{X \ge a}$ is a stopping time.
assumptions: $X : ι \to Ω \to ℝ$ is a right-continuous and adapted process with respect to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions
conclusions: for any $a \in \mathbb{R}$, the random time $\tau_{X \ge a}$ is a stopping time
nodes.label: cor:isStoppingTime_leastGE_of_rightContinuous

nodes.name: Proof of Hitting time of a right-continuous adapted process is a stopping time
nodes.statement: This follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:isStoppingTime_leastGE} since $X$ is progressively measurable by Lemma~\ref{lem:Adapted.isStronglyProgressive_of_rightContinuous}.
nodes.statement_short: Right-continuous adapted processes are progressively measurable; apply the $\tau_{X\ge a}$ lemma.

nodes.name: Hitting time of (a, infinity)
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a conditionally complete linear order with a bottom element and let $R$ be a preorder. For a process $X : T \to Ω \to R$ and $a \in R$, define the random time \begin{align*} \tau_{X > a} = \inf\{t \in T \mid X_t > a\} \: , \end{align*} in which the infimum is infinite if the set is empty.
nodes.label: def:leastGT

nodes.name: Hitting time of (a, infinity) is a stopping time
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a conditionally complete linear order with a bottom element, which is a Polish space for its order topology, on which we put the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Let $R$ be a preorder with a metrizable topology for which sets of the form $\{x \in R \mid x \ge a\}$ are closed, with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. If $X : T \to Ω \to R$ is a progressively measurable process with respect to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions, then for any $a \in R$, the random time $\tau_{X > a}$ is a stopping time.
assumptions: Let $T$ be a conditionally complete linear order with a bottom element, which is a Polish space for its order topology, on which we put the Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
Let $R$ be a preorder with a metrizable topology for which sets of the form $\{x \in R \mid x \ge a\}$ are closed, with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
$X : T \to Ω \to R$ is a progressively measurable process with respect to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions
conclusions: for any $a \in R$, the random time $\tau_{X > a}$ is a stopping time
nodes.label: lem:isStoppingTime_leastGT

nodes.name: Proof of Hitting time of (a, infinity) is a stopping time
nodes.statement: This is a direct application of Theorem~\ref{thm:hitting_is_stopping_time} with the set $B = (a, +\infty)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the hitting time theorem with $B=(a,+\infty)$.

nodes.name: Characterization of tau_{X>a} < t
nodes.statement: For $t \in T$, $\tau_{X > a} < t$ if and only if there exists $s < t$ such that $X_s > a$.
assumptions: For $t \in T$
conclusions: $\tau_{X > a} < t$ if and only if there exists $s < t$ such that $X_s > a$
equivalent_conditions: $\tau_{X > a} < t$
there exists $s < t$ such that $X_s > a$
nodes.label: lem:leastGT_lt_iff

nodes.name: Pre-localizing sequence
nodes.statement: A pre-localizing sequence is a sequence of stopping times $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that $\tau_n \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ (a.s.).
differentia: $\tau_n \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ (a.s.)
nodes.label: def:preLocalizingSequence

nodes.name: Localizing sequence
nodes.statement: A localizing sequence is a sequence of stopping times $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that $\tau_n$ is non-decreasing and $\tau_n \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ (a.s.). That is, it is a pre-localizing sequence that is also almost surely non-decreasing.
differentia: $\tau_n$ is non-decreasing
$\tau_n \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ (a.s.)
nodes.label: def:localizingSequence

nodes.name: Constant infinite localizing sequence
nodes.statement: The constant sequence $\tau_n = \infty$ is a localizing sequence.
conclusions: The constant sequence $\tau_n = \infty$ is a localizing sequence.
nodes.label: lem:localizingSequence_const_top

nodes.name: Minimum of localizing sequences
nodes.statement: Let $(\sigma_n), (\tau_n)$ be localizing sequences. Then $(\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n)$ is a localizing sequence.
assumptions: Let $(\sigma_n), (\tau_n)$ be localizing sequences.
conclusions: Then $(\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n)$ is a localizing sequence.
nodes.label: lem:localizingSequence_min

nodes.name: Localizing sequence from a pre-localizing sequence
nodes.statement: If $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a pre-localizing sequence, then the sequence defined by $\tau'_n = \inf_{m \ge n} \tau_m$ is a localizing sequence.
assumptions: $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a pre-localizing sequence
conclusions: the sequence defined by $\tau'_n = \inf_{m \ge n} \tau_m$ is a localizing sequence
nodes.label: lem:isLocalizingSequence_of_isPreLocalizingSequence

nodes.name: Diagonal pre-localizing sequence
nodes.statement: Let $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a localizing sequence and let $(\sigma_{n,k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a localizing sequence for each $n$. Then, there exists a strictly increasing sequence $(k_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that the sequence defined by $\tau'_n = \tau_n \wedge \sigma_{n,k_n}$ is a pre-localizing sequence.
assumptions: Let $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a localizing sequence and let $(\sigma_{n,k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a localizing sequence for each $n$.
conclusions: Then, there exists a strictly increasing sequence $(k_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that the sequence defined by $\tau'_n = \tau_n \wedge \sigma_{n,k_n}$ is a pre-localizing sequence.
nodes.label: lem:isPreLocalizingSequence_of_isLocalizingSequence

nodes.name: Proof of Diagonal pre-localizing sequence
nodes.statement: For each $n$, since $\sigma_{n,k} \to \infty$ a.s. as $k \to \infty$, we may choose $k_n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $P(\sigma_{n,k_n} < \tau_n \wedge n) \le 2^{-n}$. Then, defining $\tau'_n = \tau_n \wedge \sigma_{n,k_n}$, we have $\tau_n' \to \infty$ by the Borel-Cantelli lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $k_n$ with $P(\sigma_{n,k_n} < \tau_n\wedge n)\le 2^{-n}$ and conclude by the Borel-Cantelli lemma.

nodes.name: Localizing sequence for an a.s. path property
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a predicate on paths and suppose $X$ is a stochastic process satisfying $P$ a.s. Then, defining $$\tau_n(\omega) = \begin{cases} \infty & \text{if } X(\omega) \text{ satisfies } P \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a localizing sequence.
assumptions: Let $P$ be a predicate on paths and suppose $X$ is a stochastic process satisfying $P$ a.s.
conclusions: the sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a localizing sequence
nodes.label: lem:isLocalizingSequence_ae

nodes.name: Local property
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a class of stochastic processes (or equivalently a predicate on stochastic processes). We say that a stochastic process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is locally in $P$ (or satisfies $P$ locally) if there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the process $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is in $P$ (in which $X^{\tau_n}$ denotes the stopped process). We denote the class of processes that are locally in $P$ by $P_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.statement_short: $X$ is locally in $P$ if some localizing sequence makes every stopped process $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n>0}$ belong to $P$.
nodes.label: def:locally

nodes.name: P is contained in P_loc
nodes.statement: For any class of processes $P$, we have $P \subseteq P_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
conclusions: For any class of processes $P$, we have $P \subseteq P_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.label: lem:implies_locally

nodes.name: Proof of P is contained in P_loc
nodes.statement: Take $\tau_n = \infty$ for all $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the constant localizing sequence $\tau_n=\infty$.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of localization
nodes.statement: If $P \subseteq Q$ then $P_{\mathrm{loc}} \subseteq Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
assumptions: $P \subseteq Q$
conclusions: $P_{\mathrm{loc}} \subseteq Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$
nodes.label: lem:locally_mono

nodes.name: Proof of Monotonicity of localization
nodes.statement: Let $X \in P_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Then there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0} \in P$. Since $P \subseteq Q$, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0} \in Q$. Thus $X \in Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.statement_short: The same localizing sequence works, since $P\subseteq Q$.

nodes.name: Localizing sequence for P
nodes.statement: Let $X \in P_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Then there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0} \in P$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a localizing sequence witnessing $X\in P_{loc}$

nodes.name: Transfer to Q
nodes.statement: Since $P \subseteq Q$, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0} \in Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Stopped processes lie in $Q$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus $X \in Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $X\in Q_{loc}$

nodes.name: Stable class of processes
nodes.statement: A class of stochastic processes $P$ is stable if whenever $X$ is in $P$, then for any stopping time $\tau$, the process $X^{\tau}\mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ is also in $P$.
differentia: whenever $X$ is in $P$, then for any stopping time $\tau$, the process $X^{\tau}\mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ is also in $P$
nodes.label: def:stable

nodes.name: Localization preserves stability
nodes.statement: If $P$ is a stable class of processes, then $P_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is also stable.
assumptions: $P$ is a stable class of processes
conclusions: $P_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is also stable
nodes.label: lem:isStable_locally

nodes.name: Localization commutes with intersection
nodes.statement: If $P, Q$ are stable classes of processes then $(P\cap Q)_{\mathrm{loc}} = P_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
assumptions: $P, Q$ are stable classes of processes
conclusions: $(P\cap Q)_{\mathrm{loc}} = P_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$
nodes.label: lem:locally_inter

nodes.name: Proof of Localization commutes with intersection
nodes.statement: The forward direction is trivial so we only provide proof for the reverse. Suppose that $X \in P_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Then, there exists localizing sequences $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ and $(\sigma_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that $X^{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}\in P$ and $X^{\sigma_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n > 0} \in Q$. Consequently, by the stability of $P$, \[X^{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n > 0} = (X^{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n > 0} \in P.\] Similarly, by the stability of $Q$, $X^{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n > 0} \in Q$. Thus, as $\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n$ is a localizing sequence by Lemma~\ref{lem:localizingSequence_min} and $X^{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n > 0} \in P \cap Q$ for all $n$, it follows that $X \in (P \cap Q)_{\mathrm{loc}}$
nodes.statement_short: For the reverse inclusion, combine the two localizing sequences by their minimum and use stability of $P$ and $Q$.

nodes.name: Two localizing sequences
nodes.statement: The forward direction is trivial so we only provide proof for the reverse. Suppose that $X \in P_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Then, there exists localizing sequences $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ and $(\sigma_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that $X^{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}\in P$ and $X^{\sigma_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n > 0} \in Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the reverse inclusion; take localizing sequences for $P$ and $Q$

nodes.name: Stability on the minimum
nodes.statement: Consequently, by the stability of $P$, \[X^{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n > 0} = (X^{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n > 0} \in P.\] Similarly, by the stability of $Q$, $X^{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n > 0} \in Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Stopping at the minimum stays in $P$ and in $Q$ by stability

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus, as $\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n$ is a localizing sequence by Lemma~\ref{lem:localizingSequence_min} and $X^{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\sigma_n \wedge \tau_n > 0} \in P \cap Q$ for all $n$, it follows that $X \in (P \cap Q)_{\mathrm{loc}}$
nodes.statement_short: The minimum is localizing, so $X\in(P\cap Q)_{loc}$

nodes.name: Local property from a pre-localizing sequence
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a stable class of processes and let $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a pre-localizing sequence such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is in $P$. If the filtration is right-continuous, then $X$ is locally in $P$.
assumptions: Let $P$ be a stable class of processes and let $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a pre-localizing sequence such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is in $P$.
the filtration is right-continuous
conclusions: $X$ is locally in $P$
nodes.label: lem:locally_of_isPreLocalizingSequence

nodes.name: Proof of Local property from a pre-localizing sequence
nodes.statement: Using the localizing sequence defined by Lemma~\ref{lem:isLocalizingSequence_of_isPreLocalizingSequence} suffices.
nodes.statement_short: Replace the pre-localizing sequence by the localizing sequence $\inf_{m\ge n}\tau_m$.

nodes.name: Localization is idempotent
nodes.statement: Suppose that the filtration is right-continuous. For any stable class of processes $P$, we have $(P_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}} = P_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
assumptions: Suppose that the filtration is right-continuous.
For any stable class of processes $P$
conclusions: we have $(P_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}} = P_{\mathrm{loc}}$
nodes.label: lem:locally_locally

nodes.name: Proof of Localization is idempotent
nodes.statement: $(P_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}} \supseteq P_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_locally} so we only prove the reverse inclusion. Let $X$ be a process in $(P_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}}$. By definition there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is in $P_{\mathrm{loc}}$. By definition of $P_{\mathrm{loc}}$, for each $n$ there exists a localizing sequence $(\sigma_{n,k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $(X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^{\sigma_{n,k}}\mathbb{I}_{\sigma_{n,k} > 0}$ is in $P$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_of_isPreLocalizingSequence}, it suffices to show that there exists a pre-localizing sequence $(\tau'_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau'_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau'_n > 0}$ is in $P$. Thus, using the localizing sequences $\tau'_n = \tau_n \wedge \sigma_{n, k_n}$ defined by Lemma~\ref{lem:isPreLocalizingSequence_of_isLocalizingSequence}, it remains to argue that by stability of $P$, $X^{\tau'_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau'_n > 0}$ is in $P$ for all $n$. Indeed, this follows as $X^{\tau'_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau'_n > 0} = ((X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^{\sigma_{n,k_n}}\mathbb{I}_{\sigma_{n,k_n} > 0})^{\tau'_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau'_n > 0}$ where $(X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^{\sigma_{n,k_n}}\mathbb{I}_{\sigma_{n,k_n} > 0}$ is in $P$ by construction and $P$ is stable.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal argument: build a pre-localizing sequence $\tau_n\wedge\sigma_{n,k_n}$ from the nested localizing sequences and use stability. The key step is the diagonal choice of $k_n$.

nodes.name: Easy inclusion
nodes.statement: $(P_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}} \supseteq P_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_locally} so we only prove the reverse inclusion.
nodes.statement_short: One inclusion is immediate; prove the reverse

nodes.name: Outer localizing sequence
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a process in $(P_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}}$. By definition there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is in $P_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $\tau_n$ with stopped processes in $P_{loc}$

nodes.name: Inner localizing sequences
nodes.statement: By definition of $P_{\mathrm{loc}}$, for each $n$ there exists a localizing sequence $(\sigma_{n,k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $(X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^{\sigma_{n,k}}\mathbb{I}_{\sigma_{n,k} > 0}$ is in $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $\sigma_{n,k}$ for each stopped process

nodes.name: Reduce to a pre-localizing sequence
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_of_isPreLocalizingSequence}, it suffices to show that there exists a pre-localizing sequence $(\tau'_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X^{\tau'_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau'_n > 0}$ is in $P$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to find a pre-localizing sequence

nodes.name: Diagonal sequence
nodes.statement: Thus, using the localizing sequences $\tau'_n = \tau_n \wedge \sigma_{n, k_n}$ defined by Lemma~\ref{lem:isPreLocalizingSequence_of_isLocalizingSequence}, it remains to argue that by stability of $P$, $X^{\tau'_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau'_n > 0}$ is in $P$ for all $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the diagonal sequence $\tau_n\wedge\sigma_{n,k_n}$

nodes.name: Conclude by stability
nodes.statement: Indeed, this follows as $X^{\tau'_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau'_n > 0} = ((X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^{\sigma_{n,k_n}}\mathbb{I}_{\sigma_{n,k_n} > 0})^{\tau'_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau'_n > 0}$ where $(X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^{\sigma_{n,k_n}}\mathbb{I}_{\sigma_{n,k_n} > 0}$ is in $P$ by construction and $P$ is stable.
nodes.statement_short: Stability of $P$ gives the stopped process in $P$

nodes.name: Local implication from global implication
nodes.statement: Suppose that the filtration is right-continuous. Let $P, Q$ be two classes of stochastic processes such that $P \subseteq Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and $Q$ is stable. Let $X$ be a stochastic process that satisfies $P$ locally. Then $X$ satisfies $Q$ locally. In short, if $P$ implies $Q$ locally, then $P$ locally implies $Q$ locally.
assumptions: Suppose that the filtration is right-continuous.
Let $P, Q$ be two classes of stochastic processes such that $P \subseteq Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and $Q$ is stable.
Let $X$ be a stochastic process that satisfies $P$ locally.
conclusions: Then $X$ satisfies $Q$ locally.
nodes.label: lem:local_induction

nodes.name: Proof of Local implication from global implication
nodes.statement: Since $X \in P_{\mathrm{loc}}$, then $X \in (Q_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by assumption and Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_mono}. By Lemma \ref{lem:locally_locally}, $(Q_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}} = Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Thus $X \in Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of localization then idempotence $(Q_{loc})_{loc}=Q_{loc}$.

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: Since $X \in P_{\mathrm{loc}}$, then $X \in (Q_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by assumption and Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_mono}.
nodes.statement_short: $X\in(Q_{loc})_{loc}$ by monotonicity

nodes.name: Idempotence
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:locally_locally}, $(Q_{\mathrm{loc}})_{\mathrm{loc}} = Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Localization is idempotent

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus $X \in Q_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude

nodes.name: Usual conditions in Section 9.2
nodes.statement: We in this section assume $\mathcal{F}$ satisfies the usual conditions (i.e. complete and right-continuous).

nodes.name: A.s. path property holds locally
nodes.statement: If $P$ be a predicate on paths such that the constant path $0$ satisfies $P$ and $X$ is a stochastic process satisfying $P$ a.s. then, $X$ satisfies $P$ locally.
assumptions: $P$ be a predicate on paths such that the constant path $0$ satisfies $P$
$X$ is a stochastic process satisfying $P$ a.s.
conclusions: $X$ satisfies $P$ locally
nodes.label: lem:locally_of_ae

nodes.name: Proof of A.s. path property holds locally
nodes.statement: Follows directly by using the localizing sequence defined in Lemma~\ref{lem:isLocalizingSequence_ae}.
nodes.statement_short: Use the localizing sequence equal to $\infty$ where the path satisfies $P$ and $0$ elsewhere.

nodes.name: Locally right continuous iff a.s. right continuous
nodes.statement: A stochastic process $X$ is locally right continuous if and only if it is right continuous almost surely.
conclusions: A stochastic process $X$ is locally right continuous if and only if it is right continuous almost surely.
equivalent_conditions: A stochastic process $X$ is locally right continuous
it is right continuous almost surely
nodes.label: lem:locally_rightContinuous

nodes.name: Proof of Locally right continuous iff a.s. right continuous
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a.s. right continuous, then it is locally right continuous by Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_of_ae}. On the other hand, assuming $X$ is locally right continuous, there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\omega \in \Omega$, $(X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})(\omega)$ is right continuous. Thus, for almost surely every $\omega$ and any $t \in T$ there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\tau_N(\omega) > t + 1$ (not that the ordering of a.s. and for all is important). Hence, as $X_s(\omega) = (X^{\tau_N}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_N > 0})_s(\omega)$ on a neighborhood of $t$, we have that $X(\omega)$ is right continuous at $t$. Consequently, as $t$ was arbitrary, $X$ is a.s. right continuous.
nodes.statement_short: One direction from the a.s.-property lemma; for the other, at each $t$ pick $N$ with $\tau_N > t+1$ so $X$ agrees with a right-continuous stopped process near $t$.

nodes.name: A.s. implies locally
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a.s. right continuous, then it is locally right continuous by Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_of_ae}.
nodes.statement_short: Reverse direction from the a.s.-property lemma

nodes.name: Locally implies a.s.
nodes.statement: On the other hand, assuming $X$ is locally right continuous, there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\omega \in \Omega$, $(X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})(\omega)$ is right continuous. Thus, for almost surely every $\omega$ and any $t \in T$ there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\tau_N(\omega) > t + 1$ (not that the ordering of a.s. and for all is important). Hence, as $X_s(\omega) = (X^{\tau_N}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_N > 0})_s(\omega)$ on a neighborhood of $t$, we have that $X(\omega)$ is right continuous at $t$. Consequently, as $t$ was arbitrary, $X$ is a.s. right continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Forward direction via a large stopping index

nodes.name: Localizing sequence
nodes.statement: On the other hand, assuming $X$ is locally right continuous, there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\omega \in \Omega$, $(X^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})(\omega)$ is right continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Take a localizing sequence with right-continuous stopped paths

nodes.name: Choose N
nodes.statement: Thus, for almost surely every $\omega$ and any $t \in T$ there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\tau_N(\omega) > t + 1$ (not that the ordering of a.s. and for all is important).
nodes.statement_short: Pick $N$ with $\tau_N(\omega)>t+1$

nodes.name: Local agreement
nodes.statement: Hence, as $X_s(\omega) = (X^{\tau_N}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_N > 0})_s(\omega)$ on a neighborhood of $t$, we have that $X(\omega)$ is right continuous at $t$.
nodes.statement_short: $X$ agrees with a right-continuous path near $t$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Consequently, as $t$ was arbitrary, $X$ is a.s. right continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude a.s. right continuity

nodes.name: Locally left limits iff a.s. left limits
nodes.statement: A stochastic process $X$ has left limits locally if and only if it has left limits almost surely.
conclusions: A stochastic process $X$ has left limits locally if and only if it has left limits almost surely.
equivalent_conditions: A stochastic process $X$ has left limits locally
it has left limits almost surely
nodes.label: lem:locally_leftLimit

nodes.name: Proof of Locally left limits iff a.s. left limits
nodes.statement: Same proof as in Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_rightContinuous}.
nodes.statement_short: Same argument as for right continuity.

nodes.name: Locally cadlag iff a.s. cadlag
nodes.statement: A stochastic process $X$ is locally cadlag if and only if it is cadlag almost surely.
conclusions: A stochastic process $X$ is locally cadlag if and only if it is cadlag almost surely.
equivalent_conditions: A stochastic process $X$ is locally cadlag
it is cadlag almost surely
nodes.label: lem:locally_isCadlag

nodes.name: Proof of Locally cadlag iff a.s. cadlag
nodes.statement: The forward direction follows from Lemmas~\ref{lem:locally_rightContinuous} and \ref{lem:locally_leftLimit} while the reverse direction follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_of_ae}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the right-continuity and left-limit lemmas, and the a.s.-property lemma for the converse.

nodes.name: Right continuous processes are stable
nodes.statement: The class of right continuous processes is stable.
conclusions: The class of right continuous processes is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_rightContinuous

nodes.name: Proof of Right continuous processes are stable
nodes.statement: Trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial.

nodes.name: Processes with left limits are stable
nodes.statement: The class of processes with left limits is stable.
conclusions: The class of processes with left limits is stable.

nodes.name: Proof of Processes with left limits are stable
nodes.statement: Trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial.

nodes.name: Cadlag processes are stable
nodes.statement: The class of cadlag processes is stable.
conclusions: The class of cadlag processes is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_isCadlag

nodes.name: Proof of Cadlag processes are stable
nodes.statement: Follows from Lemmas~\ref{lem:isStable_rightContinuous} and \ref{lem:isStable_left_limit}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine stability of right continuity and of left limits.

nodes.name: Progressively measurable processes are stable
nodes.statement: The class of progressively measurable processes is stable.
conclusions: The class of progressively measurable processes is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_isStronglyProgressive

nodes.name: Local martingale
nodes.statement: We say a stochastic process $(M_t)_{t \in T}$ is a local martingale if it is locally a cadlag martingale in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:locally}. That is, there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the process $M^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is a cadlag martingale.
differentia: it is locally a cadlag martingale
nodes.label: def:IsLocalMartingale

nodes.name: Local submartingale
nodes.statement: A stochastic process is a local submartingale if it is locally a cadlag submartingale in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:locally}. That is, there exists a localizing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the process $M^{\tau_n}\mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is a cadlag submartingale.
differentia: it is locally a cadlag submartingale
nodes.label: def:IsLocalSubmartingale

nodes.name: Cadlag martingales are local martingales
nodes.statement: Every cadlag martingale is a local martingale.
conclusions: Every cadlag martingale is a local martingale.
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.IsLocalMartingale

nodes.name: Proof of Cadlag martingales are local martingales
nodes.statement: This follows from Lemma \ref{lem:implies_locally}.
nodes.statement_short: Instance of $P\subseteq P_{loc}$.

nodes.name: Cadlag martingales are stable
nodes.statement: The class of cadlag martingales is stable. That is, if $M$ is a cadlag martingale and $\tau$ is a stopping time, then the stopped process cadlag $M^{\tau}\mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ is also a martingale.
assumptions: $M$ is a cadlag martingale
$\tau$ is a stopping time
conclusions: The class of cadlag martingales is stable.
the stopped process cadlag $M^{\tau}\mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ is also a martingale
nodes.label: lem:stable_IsMartingale

nodes.name: Proof of Cadlag martingales are stable
nodes.statement: Clearly, the stopped process $M^{\tau}\mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ is cadlag and it remains to show that it is a martingale. Fixing $s \le t \in T$, as $\{\tau > 0\} \in \mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{F}_s$, we have $$P[M^{\tau}_t \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0} \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}P[M_{\tau \wedge t} \mid \mathcal{F}_{s}].$$ Thus, as $\tau \wedge t$ is a bounded stopping time, we have by the optional stopping theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSampling}) that $P[M_{\tau \wedge t} \mid \mathcal{F}_{s}] = M_{(\tau \wedge t) \wedge s} = M_{\tau \wedge s}$ and so, $P[M^{\tau}_t \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0} \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = M^{\tau}_s \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Pull $\mathbb{I}_{\tau>0}$ out of the conditional expectation and apply the optional stopping theorem to the bounded time $\tau\wedge t$.

nodes.name: Pull out the indicator
nodes.statement: Clearly, the stopped process $M^{\tau}\mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ is cadlag and it remains to show that it is a martingale. Fixing $s \le t \in T$, as $\{\tau > 0\} \in \mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{F}_s$, we have $$P[M^{\tau}_t \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0} \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}P[M_{\tau \wedge t} \mid \mathcal{F}_{s}].$$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the martingale property; pull $\mathbb{I}_{\tau>0}$ out of the conditional expectation

nodes.name: Optional stopping
nodes.statement: Thus, as $\tau \wedge t$ is a bounded stopping time, we have by the optional stopping theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSampling}) that $P[M_{\tau \wedge t} \mid \mathcal{F}_{s}] = M_{(\tau \wedge t) \wedge s} = M_{\tau \wedge s}$ and so, $P[M^{\tau}_t \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0} \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = M^{\tau}_s \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Apply optional stopping at the bounded time $\tau\wedge t$

nodes.name: Cadlag submartingales are stable
nodes.statement: The class of cadlag submartingales is stable. That is, if $M$ is a cadlag submartingale and $\tau$ is a stopping time, then the stopped process $M^{\tau}\mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ is also a cadlag submartingale.
assumptions: $M$ is a cadlag submartingale
$\tau$ is a stopping time
conclusions: The class of cadlag submartingales is stable.
the stopped process $M^{\tau}\mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0}$ is also a cadlag submartingale
nodes.label: lem:stable_IsSubmartingale

nodes.name: Continuous finite-variation local martingale is zero
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a continuous local martingale with $M_0 = 0$. If $M$ is also a finite variation process, then $M_t = 0$ for all $t$.
assumptions: Let $M$ be a continuous local martingale with $M_0 = 0$.
$M$ is also a finite variation process
conclusions: $M_t = 0$ for all $t$
nodes.label: thm:IsLocalMartingale.eq_zero_of_finiteVariation

nodes.name: Integrable supremum
nodes.statement: We say that a stochastic process is integrable if the map $(t,\omega) \mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is strongly measurable and for all $t$, $X_t$ is integrable. A process has an integrable supremum if $(\sup_{s \le t} \Vert X_s \Vert)_t$ is integrable.
nodes.statement_short: A process has integrable supremum if $\sup_{s\le t}\Vert X_s\Vert$ is an integrable process.
nodes.label: def:HasIntegrableSup

nodes.name: Locally integrable supremum
nodes.statement: A process has locally integrable supremum if it is locally a process with integrable supremum.
nodes.label: def:locallyIntegrableSup

nodes.name: Doob-Meyer class, class D
nodes.statement: A stochastic process $(X_t)$ is of class D (or in the Doob-Meyer class) if it is progressively measurable and the set $\{X_\tau \mid \tau \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$ is uniformly integrable.
differentia: it is progressively measurable
the set $\{X_\tau \mid \tau \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$ is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: def:classD

nodes.name: Class DL
nodes.statement: A stochastic process $(X_t)$ is of class DL if it is progressively measurable and for all $t \ge 0$, the set $\{X_\tau \mid \tau \text{ is a stopping time with } \tau \le t\}$ is uniformly integrable.
differentia: it is progressively measurable
for all $t \ge 0$, the set $\{X_\tau \mid \tau \text{ is a stopping time with } \tau \le t\}$ is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: def:classDL

nodes.name: Class D implies class DL
nodes.statement: A stochastic process of class D is of class DL.
conclusions: A stochastic process of class D is of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:classDLOfClassD

nodes.name: Proof of Class D implies class DL
nodes.statement: This follows from the definitions and Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableComp}.
nodes.statement_short: Bounded stopping times are finite; apply the uniform integrability subset lemma.

nodes.name: Class D processes are uniformly integrable
nodes.statement: A stochastic process of class D is uniformly integrable.
conclusions: A stochastic process of class D is uniformly integrable.
nodes.label: lem:ClassD.uniformIntegrable

nodes.name: Proof of Class D processes are uniformly integrable
nodes.statement: Use the Class D property with the constant stopping times $\tau_n = n$ for all $n$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableComp}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply class D to the constant stopping times $\tau_n=n$.

nodes.name: Class DL iff norm is class DL
nodes.statement: A progressively measurable process is of class DL iff its norm is of class DL.
conclusions: A progressively measurable process is of class DL iff its norm is of class DL.
equivalent_conditions: A progressively measurable process is of class DL
its norm is of class DL
nodes.label: lem:classDL_iff_norm

nodes.name: Class D from bounded stopping times
nodes.statement: If a stochastic process is progressively measurable and the set \begin{align*} \{X_\tau \mid \tau \text{ is a stopping time and } \exists t, \forall \omega, \tau(\omega) \le t\} \end{align*} is uniformly integrable, then the process is of class D.
assumptions: a stochastic process is progressively measurable
the set \begin{align*} \{X_\tau \mid \tau \text{ is a stopping time and } \exists t, \forall \omega, \tau(\omega) \le t\} \end{align*} is uniformly integrable
conclusions: the process is of class D
nodes.label: lem:classD_of_uniformIntegrable_bounded_stoppingTime

nodes.name: Class D iff norm is class D
nodes.statement: A progressively measurable process is of class D iff its norm is of class D.
conclusions: A progressively measurable process is of class D iff its norm is of class D.
equivalent_conditions: A progressively measurable process is of class D
its norm is of class D
nodes.label: lem:classD_iff_norm

nodes.name: Nonnegative submartingales are class DL
nodes.statement: Every nonnegative right-continuous submartingale is of class DL.
conclusions: Every nonnegative right-continuous submartingale is of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.classDL

nodes.name: Proof of Nonnegative submartingales are class DL
nodes.statement: Let $t \in T$ and $\tau \le t$ be a stopping time. By Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSamplingSubmartingale} and nonnegativity we get that $0 \le X_\tau \le P[X_t \mid X_\tau]$. As $X$ is a submartingale, $X_t$ is integrable, thus $\{X_t\}$ is uniformly integrable, and we can conclude from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated} and Lemma~\ref{lem:condExpUI}.
nodes.statement_short: Optional sampling bounds $0\le X_\tau\le E[X_t\mid X_\tau]$; conclude by domination and uniform integrability of conditional expectations.

nodes.name: Optional sampling bound
nodes.statement: Let $t \in T$ and $\tau \le t$ be a stopping time. By Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSamplingSubmartingale} and nonnegativity we get that $0 \le X_\tau \le P[X_t \mid X_\tau]$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $X_\tau$ by a conditional expectation of $X_t$

nodes.name: Conclude by domination
nodes.statement: As $X$ is a submartingale, $X_t$ is integrable, thus $\{X_t\}$ is uniformly integrable, and we can conclude from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated} and Lemma~\ref{lem:condExpUI}.
nodes.statement_short: Conditional expectations of an integrable variable are UI; dominate

nodes.name: Nonnegative submartingale is class D iff UI
nodes.statement: A nonnegative right-continuous submartingale is of class D if and only if it is uniformly integrable.
conclusions: A nonnegative right-continuous submartingale is of class D if and only if it is uniformly integrable.
equivalent_conditions: A nonnegative right-continuous submartingale is of class D
it is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.classD_iff_uniformIntegrable

nodes.name: Proof of Nonnegative submartingale is class D iff UI
nodes.statement: Assume that $X$ is uniformly integrable. Just like what we did in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.classDL}, we use Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSamplingSubmartingale} and Lemma~\ref{lem:condExpUI} to deduce that $\{X_\tau|\exists t\in T, \tau\le t\}$ is uniformly integrable. Moreover, for any finite stopping time $\tau$, We have that $X_\tau = \lim_{n \to +\infty} X_{\tau \land n}$. Thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_of_tendsto_ae}, we deduce that $X$ is of class D. Conversely, if $X$ is of class D, then it is uniformly integrable by Lemma~\ref{lem:ClassD.uniformIntegrable}.
nodes.statement_short: If uniformly integrable, optional sampling gives class DL and an a.e. limit along $\tau\wedge n$ gives class D; the converse is the class D UI lemma.

nodes.name: UI implies class D
nodes.statement: Assume that $X$ is uniformly integrable. Just like what we did in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.classDL}, we use Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSamplingSubmartingale} and Lemma~\ref{lem:condExpUI} to deduce that $\{X_\tau|\exists t\in T, \tau\le t\}$ is uniformly integrable. Moreover, for any finite stopping time $\tau$, We have that $X_\tau = \lim_{n \to +\infty} X_{\tau \land n}$. Thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_of_tendsto_ae}, we deduce that $X$ is of class D.
nodes.statement_short: Case: $X$ uniformly integrable

nodes.name: Bounded stopping times
nodes.statement: Just like what we did in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.classDL}, we use Lemma~\ref{lem:optionalSamplingSubmartingale} and Lemma~\ref{lem:condExpUI} to deduce that $\{X_\tau|\exists t\in T, \tau\le t\}$ is uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Values at bounded stopping times are UI

nodes.name: Approximate finite times
nodes.statement: Moreover, for any finite stopping time $\tau$, We have that $X_\tau = \lim_{n \to +\infty} X_{\tau \land n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $X_\tau$ by $X_{\tau\wedge n}$

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: Thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_of_tendsto_ae}, we deduce that $X$ is of class D.
nodes.statement_short: UI is preserved under a.e. limits

nodes.name: Class D implies UI
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $X$ is of class D, then it is uniformly integrable by Lemma~\ref{lem:ClassD.uniformIntegrable}.
nodes.statement_short: Case: class D gives UI

nodes.name: Cadlag martingales are class DL
nodes.statement: Every càdlàg martingale is of class DL.
conclusions: Every càdlàg martingale is of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.classDL

nodes.name: Proof of Cadlag martingales are class DL
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be càdlàg martingale. By Lemma~\ref{lem:Martingale.submartingale_convex_comp}, $(|X_t|)_{t \in T}$ is a nonnegative càdlàg submartingale, and the result follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.classDL} along with Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableIffNorm}.
nodes.statement_short: $|X|$ is a nonnegative càdlàg submartingale; apply the submartingale class DL lemma and the norm UI lemma.

nodes.name: Martingale is class D iff UI
nodes.statement: A right-continuous martingale is of class D if and only if it is uniformly integrable.
conclusions: A right-continuous martingale is of class D if and only if it is uniformly integrable.
equivalent_conditions: A right-continuous martingale is of class D
it is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.classD_iff_uniformIntegrable

nodes.name: Proof of Martingale is class D iff UI
nodes.statement: Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:classD_iff_norm} and Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableIffNorm}, it suffices to show the result for the norm of the martingale. That norm is a nonnegative right-continuous submartingale by Lemma~\ref{cor:Martingale.submartingale_norm} so this follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.classD_iff_uniformIntegrable}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the norm, a nonnegative right-continuous submartingale, and apply the submartingale version.

nodes.name: Joint strong measurability is stable
nodes.statement: The class of processes for which the induced map $(t,\omega)\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is strongly measurable is stable.
conclusions: The class of processes for which the induced map $(t,\omega)\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is strongly measurable is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_stronglyMeasurable_uncurry

nodes.name: Proof of Joint strong measurability is stable
nodes.statement: The stopped process at $\tau$ is obtained by precomposition with $(t, \omega) \mapsto (\min (\tau(\omega), t), \omega)$. Precomposing a strongly measurable function with a measurable function gives a strongly measurable function. On a second-countable space, the minimum of two functions is measurable, and by assumption $\tau$ is measurable. The result follows from this.
nodes.statement_short: Stopping is precomposition with the measurable map $(t,\omega)\mapsto(\min(\tau(\omega),t),\omega)$.

nodes.name: Stopping as precomposition
nodes.statement: The stopped process at $\tau$ is obtained by precomposition with $(t, \omega) \mapsto (\min (\tau(\omega), t), \omega)$.
nodes.statement_short: Write stopping as a precomposition

nodes.name: Precomposition preserves measurability
nodes.statement: Precomposing a strongly measurable function with a measurable function gives a strongly measurable function.
nodes.statement_short: Strong measurability is preserved

nodes.name: Measurability of the minimum
nodes.statement: On a second-countable space, the minimum of two functions is measurable, and by assumption $\tau$ is measurable.
nodes.statement_short: The time change is measurable

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The result follows from this.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude

nodes.name: Integrable supremum is stable
nodes.statement: The class of process with integrable supremum is stable.
conclusions: The class of process with integrable supremum is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_hasIntegrableSup

nodes.name: Proof of Integrable supremum is stable
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a process with integrable supremum and $\tau$ be a stopping time. Let $t \in T$. Then $(X^\tau)^*_t = \sup_{s \le t} \|X_{\tau \land s}\| \le \sup_{s \le t} \|X_s\| = X^*_t$, and as $X^*_t$ is integrable, so is $(X^\tau)^*_t$. Thus $(X^\tau \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0})^*_t$ is integrable, concluding the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the stopped running supremum by the original one, which is integrable.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a process with integrable supremum and $\tau$ be a stopping time. Let $t \in T$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $X$, $\tau$ and $t$

nodes.name: Bound stopped supremum
nodes.statement: Then $(X^\tau)^*_t = \sup_{s \le t} \|X_{\tau \land s}\| \le \sup_{s \le t} \|X_s\| = X^*_t$, and as $X^*_t$ is integrable, so is $(X^\tau)^*_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Stopped supremum is dominated by $X^*_t$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus $(X^\tau \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0})^*_t$ is integrable, concluding the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplying by the indicator keeps integrability

nodes.name: Locally integrable supremum is stable

conclusions: The class of process with locally integrable supremum is stable.

nodes.name: Proof of Locally integrable supremum is stable
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_hasIntegrableSup} and Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_locally}.
nodes.statement_short: Stability of integrable supremum plus stability of localization.

nodes.name: Class D is stable
nodes.statement: The class D is stable.
conclusions: The class D is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_classD

nodes.name: Proof of Class D is stable
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a process of class D and $\tau$ be a stopping time. For any finite stopping time $\sigma$, we have that $X_\sigma^\tau = X_{\sigma \land \tau}$. Because $\sigma \land \tau$ is finite and $X$ is of class D, we deduce from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableComp} that $\{X_{\sigma \land \tau} \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$ is uniformly integrable, and thus that $\{X^\tau_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$ is uniformly integrable. Using Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated}, we obtain that $\{X^\tau_\sigma \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0} \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$ is uniformly integrable, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: $X^\tau_\sigma = X_{\sigma\wedge\tau}$ with $\sigma\wedge\tau$ finite; use subset and domination lemmas for uniform integrability.

nodes.name: Stopped values
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a process of class D and $\tau$ be a stopping time. For any finite stopping time $\sigma$, we have that $X_\sigma^\tau = X_{\sigma \land \tau}$.
nodes.statement_short: Express stopped values as $X_{\sigma\wedge\tau}$

nodes.name: Subset of UI family
nodes.statement: Because $\sigma \land \tau$ is finite and $X$ is of class D, we deduce from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableComp} that $\{X_{\sigma \land \tau} \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$ is uniformly integrable, and thus that $\{X^\tau_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$ is uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Subfamily of a UI family is UI

nodes.name: Domination
nodes.statement: Using Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated}, we obtain that $\{X^\tau_\sigma \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0} \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$ is uniformly integrable, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Indicator multiplication preserves UI by domination

nodes.name: Class DL is stable
nodes.statement: The class DL is stable.
conclusions: The class DL is stable.
nodes.label: lem:isStable_classDL

nodes.name: Proof of Class DL is stable
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a process of class DL, $\tau$ be a stopping time. Let $t \in T$. For any stopping time $\sigma \le t$, we have that $X_\sigma^\tau = X_{\sigma \land \tau}$. Because $\sigma \land \tau$ is bounded by $t$ and $X$ is of class DL, we deduce from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableComp} that $\{X_{\sigma \land \tau} \mid \sigma \text{ is a stopping time with } \sigma \le t\}$ is uniformly integrable, and thus that $\{X^\tau_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a stopping time with } \sigma \le t\}$ is uniformly integrable. Using Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated}, we obtain that $\{X^\tau_\sigma \mathbb{I}_{\tau > 0} \mid \sigma \text{ is a stopping time with } \sigma \le t\}$ is uniformly integrable, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: $X^\tau_\sigma = X_{\sigma\wedge\tau}$ with $\sigma\wedge\tau\le t$; use subset and domination lemmas for uniform integrability.

nodes.name: Integrable supremum implies class DL
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a progressively measurable stochastic process with integrable supremum (Definition~\ref{def:HasIntegrableSup}). Then $X$ is of class DL.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a progressively measurable stochastic process with integrable supremum (Definition~\ref{def:HasIntegrableSup}).
conclusions: Then $X$ is of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:Integrable.classDL

nodes.name: Proof of Integrable supremum implies class DL
nodes.statement: Let $t \in T$. For every stopping time $\tau$ with $\tau \le t$, we have $\|X_\tau\| \le X^*_t$. Measurability of $X_\tau$ follows from progressive measurability of $X$. Because by hypothesis $X^*_t$ is integrable, we deduce from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominatedSingleton} that $\{X_\tau \mid \tau \text{ is a stopping time with } \tau \le t\}$ is uniformly integrable. This proves that $X$ is of class DL.
nodes.statement_short: Dominate $\|X_\tau\|$ by the integrable $X^*_t$ and apply the dominated uniform integrability lemma.

nodes.name: Domination by the supremum
nodes.statement: Let $t \in T$. For every stopping time $\tau$ with $\tau \le t$, we have $\|X_\tau\| \le X^*_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\|X_\tau\|$ by $X^*_t$

nodes.name: Measurability
nodes.statement: Measurability of $X_\tau$ follows from progressive measurability of $X$.
nodes.statement_short: $X_\tau$ is measurable

nodes.name: Conclude by domination
nodes.statement: Because by hypothesis $X^*_t$ is integrable, we deduce from Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominatedSingleton} that $\{X_\tau \mid \tau \text{ is a stopping time with } \tau \le t\}$ is uniformly integrable. This proves that $X$ is of class DL.
nodes.statement_short: Dominated family is UI, so class DL

nodes.name: Progressive process has measurable supremum
