assumptions: the filtration satisfies the usual conditions
conclusions: a progressively measurable process has a supremum that is jointly strongly measurable
nodes.label: lem:IsStronglyProgressive.hasStronglyMeasurableSup

nodes.name: Locally integrable supremum implies locally class DL
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a progressively measurable stochastic process with locally integrable supremum. Then $X$ is locally of class DL.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a progressively measurable stochastic process with locally integrable supremum.
conclusions: Then $X$ is locally of class DL.
nodes.label: lem:HasLocallyIntegrableSup.locally_classDL

nodes.name: Proof of Locally integrable supremum implies locally class DL
nodes.statement: Combine Lemma~\ref{lem:Integrable.classDL} and Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_mono}. Use Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_isStronglyProgressive} to get progressive measurability of the stopped processes.
nodes.statement_short: Localize the integrable-supremum-implies-DL lemma, using stability of progressive measurability.

nodes.name: Class DL implies locally class D
nodes.statement: If $X$ is of class DL then it is locally of class D.
assumptions: $X$ is of class DL
conclusions: it is locally of class D
nodes.label: lem:ClassDL.locally_classD

nodes.name: Proof of Class DL implies locally class D
nodes.statement: Take $\tau_n := n$. Then \begin{align*} \{X^{\tau_n}_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\} & = \{X_{\sigma \land n} \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\} \\ & \subseteq \{X_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a stopping time with } \sigma \le n\}. \end{align*} Because $X$ is of class DL, that last set is uniformly integrable, thus $$\{X^{\tau_n}_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$$ is uniformly integrable thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableComp}. Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated} allows to conclude that $$\{X^{\tau_n}_\sigma \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0} \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$$ is uniformly integrable, thus $X^{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is of class D. Obviously $\tau_n \rightarrow +\infty$ as $n$ goes to infinity, so $X$ is locally of class D.
nodes.statement_short: Localize with $\tau_n=n$: the stopped values lie in the class DL family at time $n$, hence are uniformly integrable.

nodes.name: Deterministic localization
nodes.statement: Take $\tau_n := n$. Then \begin{align*} \{X^{\tau_n}_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\} & = \{X_{\sigma \land n} \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\} \\ & \subseteq \{X_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a stopping time with } \sigma \le n\}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Take $\tau_n=n$; stopped values lie in the class DL family at time $n$

nodes.name: UI of stopped values
nodes.statement: Because $X$ is of class DL, that last set is uniformly integrable, thus $$\{X^{\tau_n}_\sigma \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$$ is uniformly integrable thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableComp}.
nodes.statement_short: Class DL gives UI of the stopped values

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrableDominated} allows to conclude that $$\{X^{\tau_n}_\sigma \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0} \mid \sigma \text{ is a finite stopping time}\}$$ is uniformly integrable, thus $X^{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0}$ is of class D. Obviously $\tau_n \rightarrow +\infty$ as $n$ goes to infinity, so $X$ is locally of class D.
nodes.statement_short: Stopped processes are class D and $\tau_n\to\infty$

nodes.name: Locally class DL implies locally class D
nodes.statement: If the filtration is right-continuous and $X$ is locally of class DL then it is locally of class D.
assumptions: the filtration is right-continuous
$X$ is locally of class DL
conclusions: it is locally of class D
nodes.label: lem:locally_classD_of_locally_classDL

nodes.name: Proof of Locally class DL implies locally class D
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:local_induction} using Lemma~\ref{lem:ClassDL.locally_classD} and Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_classD}.
nodes.statement_short: Local induction from class DL implies locally class D and stability of class D.

nodes.name: Cadlag paths are bounded on compact sets
nodes.statement: Assume $T$ is a linear order endowed with a topology making it first countable and $E$ is a pseudo-metric space. If $X$ is a càdlàg process then it maps compact sets of $T$ to bounded sets.
assumptions: Assume $T$ is a linear order endowed with a topology making it first countable and $E$ is a pseudo-metric space.
$X$ is a càdlàg process
conclusions: it maps compact sets of $T$ to bounded sets
nodes.label: lem:isBounded_image_of_isCadlag_of_isCompact

nodes.name: Proof of Cadlag paths are bounded on compact sets
nodes.statement: Let $K \subseteq T$ be a compact set and $\omega \in \Omega$. Assume that $X(\omega)(K)$ is not bounded. Then there exists a sequence $(t_n)$ in $K$ such that for all $n \in N$, $d(X_{t_n}(\omega), x) \ge n$, for some arbitrary $x \in E$. Because $K$ is compact, there is a subsequence $(t_{\phi(n)})$ that converges. Then one can extract a subsequence $(t_{\phi(\psi(n))})$ which either converges from below or from above. In both cases the sequence $(X_{t_{\phi(\psi(n))}})$ will converge, contradicting the hypotheses.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: an unbounded sequence in a compact set has a monotone convergent subsequence, along which càdlàg paths converge.

nodes.name: Assume unbounded
nodes.statement: Let $K \subseteq T$ be a compact set and $\omega \in \Omega$. Assume that $X(\omega)(K)$ is not bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose the image of a compact set is unbounded

nodes.name: Escaping sequence
nodes.statement: Then there exists a sequence $(t_n)$ in $K$ such that for all $n \in N$, $d(X_{t_n}(\omega), x) \ge n$, for some arbitrary $x \in E$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $t_n$ with $X_{t_n}$ escaping to infinity

nodes.name: Compactness
nodes.statement: Because $K$ is compact, there is a subsequence $(t_{\phi(n)})$ that converges.
nodes.statement_short: Extract a convergent subsequence

nodes.name: Monotone subsequence
nodes.statement: Then one can extract a subsequence $(t_{\phi(\psi(n))})$ which either converges from below or from above.
nodes.statement_short: Refine to a one-sided convergent subsequence

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: In both cases the sequence $(X_{t_{\phi(\psi(n))}})$ will converge, contradicting the hypotheses.
nodes.statement_short: Càdlàg paths converge along it, a contradiction

nodes.name: Level hitting times form a localizing sequence
nodes.statement: Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous. If $X$ is a real-valued càdlàg and adapted process, then the sequence $\tau_n := \inf \{t | X_t \ge n\}$ is a localizing sequence.
assumptions: Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous.
$X$ is a real-valued càdlàg and adapted process
conclusions: the sequence $\tau_n := \inf \{t | X_t \ge n\}$ is a localizing sequence
nodes.label: lem:isLocalizingSequence_leastGE

nodes.name: Proof of Level hitting times form a localizing sequence
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{cor:isStoppingTime_leastGE_of_rightContinuous}, each $\tau_n$ is a stopping time. Moreover, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X_t \ge n+1 \implies X_t \ge n$, thus $\tau_n \le \tau_{n+1}$. Finally, for every $\omega \in \Omega$ and $t_0 \in T$ there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $s \le t_0$, $X_s \le N$ thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:isBounded_image_of_isCadlag_of_isCompact}. Thus for all $n \ge N$, $\tau_n(\omega) \ge t_0$, proving that $\tau_n$ tends to infinity as n goes to infinity.
nodes.statement_short: Each $\tau_n$ is a stopping time, the sequence is monotone, and boundedness on compacts forces $\tau_n\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Stopping times
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{cor:isStoppingTime_leastGE_of_rightContinuous}, each $\tau_n$ is a stopping time.
nodes.statement_short: Each $\tau_n$ is a stopping time

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: Moreover, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X_t \ge n+1 \implies X_t \ge n$, thus $\tau_n \le \tau_{n+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: The sequence is non-decreasing

nodes.name: Bounded on compacts
nodes.statement: Finally, for every $\omega \in \Omega$ and $t_0 \in T$ there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $s \le t_0$, $X_s \le N$ thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:isBounded_image_of_isCadlag_of_isCompact}.
nodes.statement_short: Paths are bounded on $[\bot,t_0]$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus for all $n \ge N$, $\tau_n(\omega) \ge t_0$, proving that $\tau_n$ tends to infinity as n goes to infinity.
nodes.statement_short: $\tau_n\to\infty$

nodes.name: Bound on the supremum of a stopped process
nodes.statement: For $Y$ a stochastic process, let $Y^*_t = \sup_{s \le t} \Vert Y_s \Vert$. Let $X$ be a stochastic process and let $\tau = \inf \{t \mid \Vert X_t \Vert \ge n\}$ for some $n \in \mathbb{R}$. Then \begin{align*} (X^{\tau})^*_t \le n + \mathbb{1}_{\tau \le t} \Vert X_{\tau} \Vert \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For $Y$ a stochastic process, let $Y^*_t = \sup_{s \le t} \Vert Y_s \Vert$.
Let $X$ be a stochastic process and let $\tau = \inf \{t \mid \Vert X_t \Vert \ge n\}$ for some $n \in \mathbb{R}$.
conclusions: (X^{\tau})^*_t \le n + \mathbb{1}_{\tau \le t} \Vert X_{\tau} \Vert
nodes.label: lem:sup_stoppedProcess_le

nodes.name: Proof of Bound on the supremum of a stopped process
nodes.statement: If $\tau > t$, then for all $s \le t$, $\|X_s\| \le n$, and thus $(X^\tau)^*_t = \sup_{s \le t} \|X_{\tau \land s}\| \le n = n + \mathbb{1}_{\tau \le t} \|X_{\tau}\|$. Otherwise $(X^\tau)^*_t = \sup_{s \le \tau} \|X_s\|$. For $s < \tau$, $\|X_s\| \le n$, and $\|X_\tau\| \le \|X_\tau\|$ so $\sup_{s \le \tau} \|X_s\| \le n \lor \|X_\tau\| \le n + \|X_\tau\| = n + \mathbb{I}_{\tau \le t} \|X_\tau\|$.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on $\tau>t$ versus $\tau\le t$.

nodes.name: Case tau > t
nodes.statement: If $\tau > t$, then for all $s \le t$, $\|X_s\| \le n$, and thus $(X^\tau)^*_t = \sup_{s \le t} \|X_{\tau \land s}\| \le n = n + \mathbb{1}_{\tau \le t} \|X_{\tau}\|$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $\tau>t$: supremum bounded by $n$

nodes.name: Case tau <= t
nodes.statement: Otherwise $(X^\tau)^*_t = \sup_{s \le \tau} \|X_s\|$. For $s < \tau$, $\|X_s\| \le n$, and $\|X_\tau\| \le \|X_\tau\|$ so $\sup_{s \le \tau} \|X_s\| \le n \lor \|X_\tau\| \le n + \|X_\tau\| = n + \mathbb{I}_{\tau \le t} \|X_\tau\|$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $\tau\le t$: bound by $n\vee\|X_\tau\|$

nodes.name: Class DL implies locally integrable supremum
nodes.statement: Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous. If $X$ is a càdlàg process of class DL, then it has locally integrable supremum.
assumptions: Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous.
$X$ is a càdlàg process of class DL
conclusions: it has locally integrable supremum
nodes.label: lem:ClassDL.hasLocallyIntegrableSup

nodes.name: Proof of Class DL implies locally integrable supremum
nodes.statement: Set $\tau_n := \inf \{t | X_t \ge n\}$. This is a localizing sequence by Lemma~\ref{lem:isLocalizingSequence_leastGE}. For every $t \in T$, we have by Lemma~\ref{lem:sup_stoppedProcess_le} that $(X^{\tau_n})^*_t \le n + \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n \le t} \|X_{\tau_n}\| = n + \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n \le t} \|X_{\tau_n \land t}\|$. Because X is of class DL, $X_{\tau_n \land t}$ is integrable, so $(X^{\tau_n})^*_t$ is integrable too, so $(X^{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^*_t$ is integrable. Thus $X$ has locally integrable supremum.
nodes.statement_short: Localize by the level hitting times $\tau_n$ and bound the stopped supremum by $n+\|X_{\tau_n\wedge t}\|$, integrable by class DL.

nodes.name: Level hitting times
nodes.statement: Set $\tau_n := \inf \{t | X_t \ge n\}$. This is a localizing sequence by Lemma~\ref{lem:isLocalizingSequence_leastGE}.
nodes.statement_short: Localize by level hitting times

nodes.name: Bound stopped supremum
nodes.statement: For every $t \in T$, we have by Lemma~\ref{lem:sup_stoppedProcess_le} that $(X^{\tau_n})^*_t \le n + \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n \le t} \|X_{\tau_n}\| = n + \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n \le t} \|X_{\tau_n \land t}\|$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the stopped supremum

nodes.name: Integrability
nodes.statement: Because X is of class DL, $X_{\tau_n \land t}$ is integrable, so $(X^{\tau_n})^*_t$ is integrable too, so $(X^{\tau_n} \mathbb{I}_{\tau_n > 0})^*_t$ is integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Class DL makes the bound integrable

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus $X$ has locally integrable supremum.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude

nodes.name: Locally class DL implies locally integrable supremum
nodes.statement: Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact. Assume that the filtration is right-continuous. If a process is càdlàg and locally of class DL, then it has locally integrable supremum.
assumptions: Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact.
Assume that the filtration is right-continuous.
a process is càdlàg and locally of class DL
conclusions: it has locally integrable supremum
nodes.label: lem:hasLocallyIntegrableSup_of_locally_classDL

nodes.name: Proof of Locally class DL implies locally integrable supremum
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:local_induction} using Lemma~\ref{lem:ClassDL.hasLocallyIntegrableSup} and Lemma~\ref{lem:isStable_hasIntegrableSup}.
nodes.statement_short: Local induction from the class DL lemma and stability of integrable supremum.

nodes.name: Locally class DL iff locally integrable supremum
nodes.statement: Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous. If $X$ is a càdlàg process, then it is locally of class DL if and only if it has locally integrable supremum.
assumptions: Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous.
$X$ is a càdlàg process
conclusions: it is locally of class DL if and only if it has locally integrable supremum
equivalent_conditions: it is locally of class DL
it has locally integrable supremum
nodes.label: lem:locally_classDL_iff_locallyIntegrableSup

nodes.name: Proof of Locally class DL iff locally integrable supremum
nodes.statement: The two directions are proved in Lemmas~\ref{lem:hasLocallyIntegrableSup_of_locally_classDL} and \ref{lem:HasLocallyIntegrableSup.locally_classDL}.
nodes.statement_short: Each direction is a previous lemma.

nodes.name: Locally class D iff locally class DL
nodes.statement: Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous. A càdlàg process is locally of class D if and only if it is locally of class DL.
assumptions: Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous.
conclusions: A càdlàg process is locally of class D if and only if it is locally of class DL.
equivalent_conditions: A càdlàg process is locally of class D
it is locally of class DL

nodes.name: Proof of Locally class D iff locally class DL
nodes.statement: The forward direction follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:classDLOfClassD} along with Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_mono}. The reverse direction is Lemma~\ref{lem:locally_classD_of_locally_classDL}.
nodes.statement_short: Forward by class D implies DL and monotonicity of localization; reverse is a previous lemma.

nodes.name: Locally class D iff locally integrable supremum
nodes.statement: Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous. A càdlàg process is locally of class D if and only if it has locally integrable supremum.
assumptions: Assume $T$ has a bottom element and that its closed intervals are compact, and that the filtration is right-continuous.
conclusions: A càdlàg process is locally of class D if and only if it has locally integrable supremum.
equivalent_conditions: A càdlàg process is locally of class D
it has locally integrable supremum
nodes.label: lem:locally_classD_iff_locallyIntegrableSup

nodes.name: Proof of Locally class D iff locally integrable supremum
nodes.statement: This follows from Lemmas~\ref{lem:locally_classD_iff_locally_classDL} and \ref{lem:locally_classDL_iff_locallyIntegrableSup}.
nodes.statement_short: Chain the two previous equivalences.

nodes.name: Submartingales have locally integrable supremum
nodes.statement: Every cadlag submartingale for a right-continuous filtration has locally integrable supremum.
conclusions: Every cadlag submartingale for a right-continuous filtration has locally integrable supremum.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.locallyIntegrableSup

nodes.name: Proof of Submartingales have locally integrable supremum
nodes.statement: Define the stopping times $\sigma_n = \inf\{t \mid \Vert X_t \Vert \ge n\}$ and set $\tau_n = \sigma_n \wedge n$. $\sigma_n$ is a stopping time by Lemma~\ref{cor:isStoppingTime_leastGE_of_rightContinuous} and so $\tau_n$ is also a stopping time. The times $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ form a localizing sequence. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sup_stoppedProcess_le}, we have that \begin{align*} (X^{\tau_n})^*_t & \le n + \mathbb{1}_{\tau_n \le t} \Vert X_{\tau_n} \Vert \\ & \le n + \Vert X_{\tau_n} \Vert \: . \end{align*} It remains to show that $X_{\tau_n}$ is integrable for each $n$. This follows by Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.integrable_stoppedValue} as $\tau_n$ is a bounded stopping time.
nodes.statement_short: Localize by $\tau_n=\sigma_n\wedge n$ with $\sigma_n$ level hitting times; bound the stopped supremum by $n+\|X_{\tau_n}\|$, integrable at bounded stopping times.

nodes.name: Define localizing times
nodes.statement: Define the stopping times $\sigma_n = \inf\{t \mid \Vert X_t \Vert \ge n\}$ and set $\tau_n = \sigma_n \wedge n$. $\sigma_n$ is a stopping time by Lemma~\ref{cor:isStoppingTime_leastGE_of_rightContinuous} and so $\tau_n$ is also a stopping time.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\tau_n=\sigma_n\wedge n$ from level hitting times

nodes.name: Localizing sequence
nodes.statement: The times $(\tau_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ form a localizing sequence.
nodes.statement_short: They form a localizing sequence

nodes.name: Bound stopped supremum
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:sup_stoppedProcess_le}, we have that \begin{align*} (X^{\tau_n})^*_t & \le n + \mathbb{1}_{\tau_n \le t} \Vert X_{\tau_n} \Vert \\ & \le n + \Vert X_{\tau_n} \Vert \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the stopped supremum by $n+\|X_{\tau_n}\|$

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It remains to show that $X_{\tau_n}$ is integrable for each $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to integrability of $X_{\tau_n}$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This follows by Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.integrable_stoppedValue} as $\tau_n$ is a bounded stopping time.
nodes.statement_short: Submartingale values at bounded stopping times are integrable

nodes.name: Semi-ring of sets
nodes.statement: A \emph{semi-ring of sets} $C$ is a family of sets containing $\emptyset$, stable by intersection and such that for all $s, t \in C$, $s \setminus t$ is equal to a disjoint union of finitely many sets in $C$~.

nodes.name: Predictable rectangles
nodes.statement: The class of \emph{predictable rectangles} on $T \times \Omega$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal{R}_T := \big\{(s, t] \times F : s, t \in T,\ s < t,\ F \in \mathcal{F}_s\big\} \cup \big\{\{0\} \times F : F \in \mathcal{F}_0\big\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets
nodes.label: def:predictableRectangles

nodes.name: Predictable rectangles form a semi-ring
nodes.statement: The class $\mathcal{R}_T$ of predictable rectangles is a semi-ring of sets.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets
assumptions: The class $\mathcal{R}_T$ of predictable rectangles
conclusions: is a semi-ring of sets
nodes.label: lem:predictableRectangles_isSetSemiring

nodes.name: Proof of Predictable rectangles form a semi-ring
nodes.statement: Take two elements $A, B \in \mathcal{R}_T$~. If only one of $A, B$ is of the form $\{0\} \times F$, they are disjoint, so both the intersection and the difference are trivially in $\mathcal{R}_T$~. If both are of this form, then $A\cap B$, $A\setminus B\in\mathcal{R}_T$ follows from the fact that $\mathcal{F}_0$ is a $\sigma$-algebra. Let then $A=(s, t] \times F$ and $B=(s', t'] \times F'$~. We shall understand $(s,t]$ as the empty set if $s \ge t$~. Both $F \cap F'$ and $F \setminus F'$ are in $\mathcal{F}_{s \vee s'}$~. It is now clear that $A\cap B$ is a predictable rectangle, since \[ A \cap B = (s \vee s', t \wedge t'] \times (F \cap F'). \] Finally, let $I=(s,t]$ and $J=(s',t']$. Then \[ (I\times F)\setminus(J\times F') = ((I\setminus J)\times F) \cup ((I\cap J)\times(F\setminus F')). \] The union is disjoint, and \[ I\setminus J = (s,t\wedge s']\cup(s\vee t',t]. \] Hence $A\setminus B$ is a disjoint union of at most three predictable rectangles. Indeed, $F\in\mathcal{F}_{s\vee t'}$ by monotonicity of the filtration, and $F\setminus F'\in\mathcal{F}_{s\vee s'}$ as noted earlier.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on the form of the rectangles; intersections and differences of intervals computed explicitly.

nodes.name: Mixed case
nodes.statement: Take two elements $A, B \in \mathcal{R}_T$~. If only one of $A, B$ is of the form $\{0\} \times F$, they are disjoint, so both the intersection and the difference are trivially in $\mathcal{R}_T$~.
nodes.statement_short: Take $A,B$; if exactly one is a time-0 rectangle they are disjoint.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets

nodes.name: Both time-0 rectangles
nodes.statement: If both are of this form, then $A\cap B$, $A\setminus B\in\mathcal{R}_T$ follows from the fact that $\mathcal{F}_0$ is a $\sigma$-algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Both time-0: closure since $\mathcal{F}_0$ is a $\sigma$-algebra.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets

nodes.name: Interval rectangles
nodes.statement: Let then $A=(s, t] \times F$ and $B=(s', t'] \times F'$~. We shall understand $(s,t]$ as the empty set if $s \ge t$~. Both $F \cap F'$ and $F \setminus F'$ are in $\mathcal{F}_{s \vee s'}$~.
nodes.statement_short: Set up two interval rectangles; $F\cap F'$, $F\setminus F'$ are $\mathcal{F}_{s\vee s'}$-measurable.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets

nodes.name: Intersection
nodes.statement: It is now clear that $A\cap B$ is a predictable rectangle, since \[ A \cap B = (s \vee s', t \wedge t'] \times (F \cap F'). \]
nodes.statement_short: Compute the intersection as a rectangle.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets

nodes.name: Difference decomposition
nodes.statement: Finally, let $I=(s,t]$ and $J=(s',t']$. Then \[ (I\times F)\setminus(J\times F') = ((I\setminus J)\times F) \cup ((I\cap J)\times(F\setminus F')). \] The union is disjoint, and \[ I\setminus J = (s,t\wedge s']\cup(s\vee t',t]. \]
nodes.statement_short: Decompose the difference into disjoint pieces.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $A\setminus B$ is a disjoint union of at most three predictable rectangles. Indeed, $F\in\mathcal{F}_{s\vee t'}$ by monotonicity of the filtration, and $F\setminus F'\in\mathcal{F}_{s\vee s'}$ as noted earlier.
nodes.statement_short: The difference is a disjoint union of at most three rectangles.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets

nodes.name: Elementary predictable set
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq T \times \Omega$ is an \emph{elementary predictable set} if it is a finite union of sets of the form ${0} \times B$ for $B \in \mathcal{F}_0$ or of the form $(s, t] \times B$ with $0 \le s < t$ in $T$ and $B \in \mathcal{F}_s$~.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets
differentia: it is a finite union of sets of the form ${0} \times B$ for $B \in \mathcal{F}_0$ or of the form $(s, t] \times B$ with $0 \le s < t$ in $T$ and $B \in \mathcal{F}_s$
nodes.label: def:elementaryPredictableSet

nodes.name: Elementary predictable sets are finite unions of rectangles
nodes.statement: Every elementary predictable set (Definition~\ref{def:elementaryPredictableSet}) is a finite union of predictable rectangles.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets
assumptions: Every elementary predictable set
conclusions: is a finite union of predictable rectangles

nodes.name: Proof of Elementary predictable sets are finite unions of rectangles
nodes.statement: This follows immediately from the definitions.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definitions.

nodes.name: Elementary predictable sets form a ring
nodes.statement: The family of elementary predictable sets (Definition~\ref{def:elementaryPredictableSet}) is a ring of sets, the one generated by the semi-ring of predictable rectangles.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets
conclusions: is a ring of sets, the one generated by the semi-ring of predictable rectangles

nodes.statement: Since elementary predictable sets are finite unions of predictable rectangles (Lemma~\ref{lem:predictableRectangles_generate_elementaryPredictableSets}), the claim follows by Lemma~\ref{lem:setRing_of_finiteUnions}.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets
nodes.statement_short: Finite unions of predictable rectangles plus the ring generated by a semi-ring.

nodes.name: Elementary predictable sets as disjoint unions
nodes.statement: Any elementary predictable set (Definition~\ref{def:elementaryPredictableSet}) is a disjoint union of predictable rectangles.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets
conclusions: is a disjoint union of predictable rectangles
nodes.label: lem:elementaryPredictableSets_asDisjointUnions

nodes.name: Proof of Elementary predictable sets as disjoint unions
nodes.statement: Since elementary predictable sets are finite unions of predictable rectangles (Lemma~\ref{lem:predictableRectangles_generate_elementaryPredictableSets}), which form a semi-ring of sets (Lemma~\ref{lem:predictableRectangles_isSetSemiring}), the claim follows by Lemma~\ref{lem:semiRingOfSets_disjoint_of_union}.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets
nodes.statement_short: Rectangles form a semi-ring, so finite unions become disjoint unions.

nodes.name: Elementary predictable sets are predictable
nodes.statement: An elementary predictable set is measurable with respect to the predictable $\sigma$-algebra.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets
conclusions: is measurable with respect to the predictable $\sigma$-algebra
