nodes.name: Proof of Elementary predictable sets are predictable
nodes.statement: It is a union of sets of the form ${0} \times B$ with $B \in \mathcal{F}_0$ or of the form $(s, t] \times B$ with $B \in \mathcal{F}_s$, which are measurable by Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_Ioc_prod}.
nodes.section: 10.2.1 Predictable rectangles and elementary predictable sets
nodes.statement_short: Union of predictable rectangles, each measurable by an earlier lemma.

nodes.name: Simple process
nodes.statement: Let $(s_k < t_k)_{k \in \{1, ..., n\}}$ be points in a linear order $T$ with a bottom element 0. Let $(\eta_k)_{0 \le k \le n}$ be bounded random variables with values in a normed real vector space $E$ such that $\eta_0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable and $\eta_k$ is $\mathcal{F}_{s_k}$-measurable for $k \ge 1$~. Then the simple process for that sequence is the process $V : T \to \Omega \to E$ defined by \begin{align*} V_t = \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{(s_k, t_k]}(t) \: . \end{align*} Let $\mathcal{E}_{T, E}$ be the set of simple processes indexed by $T$ with value in $E$.
nodes.statement_short: Process $V_t=\eta_0 1_{\{0\}}(t)+\sum_k \eta_k 1_{(s_k,t_k]}(t)$ with bounded adapted-at-left-endpoint coefficients; $\mathcal{E}_{T,E}$ their set.
nodes.label: def:simpleProcess

nodes.name: Simple processes with disjoint intervals
nodes.statement: The definition of simple process does not change if we require the intervals $(s_k, t_k]$ to be disjoint.
conclusions: The definition of simple process does not change if we require the intervals $(s_k, t_k]$ to be disjoint.
nodes.label: lem:simpleProcess_admitsDisjointIntervals

nodes.name: Proof of Simple processes with disjoint intervals
nodes.statement: Fix a simple process $V$. The union of its time intervals is $A=\bigcup_{k=1}^n A_k$ with $A_k = (s_k, t_k]$~. Intervals of this type form a semi-ring of sets (Lemma~\ref{lem:semiRingOfSets_of_intervals}), so we may use the Lemma~\ref{lem:semiRingOfSets_disjoint_of_union_finer} to write $A$ as a disjoint union of intervals $B_j=(u_j, v_j]$, where for each $j$ and $k$, \[ B_j \cap A_k \in \{\emptyset, B_j\}. \] For each $j$, we then construct the random variable $\xi_j$ by summing the $\eta_k$'s for which $B_j \subseteq A_k$; as $s_k\le u_j$ in that case, $\xi_j$ is $\mathcal{F}_{u_j}$-measurable. Each $B_j$ is either disjoint from an $A_k$ or contained in it, which justifies \begin{align*} V_t &= \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{A_k}(t) = \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{j=1}^{m} \xi_j \mathbb{1}_{B_j}(t) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Refine the intervals into a disjoint family via the semi-ring refinement lemma and sum the coefficients on each piece.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Fix a simple process $V$. The union of its time intervals is $A=\bigcup_{k=1}^n A_k$ with $A_k = (s_k, t_k]$~.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $V$ and the union of its intervals.

nodes.name: Refine intervals
nodes.statement: Intervals of this type form a semi-ring of sets (Lemma~\ref{lem:semiRingOfSets_of_intervals}), so we may use the Lemma~\ref{lem:semiRingOfSets_disjoint_of_union_finer} to write $A$ as a disjoint union of intervals $B_j=(u_j, v_j]$, where for each $j$ and $k$, \[ B_j \cap A_k \in \{\emptyset, B_j\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply the semi-ring refinement lemma to get disjoint refining intervals.

nodes.name: New coefficients
nodes.statement: For each $j$, we then construct the random variable $\xi_j$ by summing the $\eta_k$'s for which $B_j \subseteq A_k$; as $s_k\le u_j$ in that case, $\xi_j$ is $\mathcal{F}_{u_j}$-measurable.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\xi_j$ as sums of the $\eta_k$; measurability check.

nodes.name: Rewrite V
nodes.statement: Each $B_j$ is either disjoint from an $A_k$ or contained in it, which justifies \begin{align*} V_t &= \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{A_k}(t) = \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{j=1}^{m} \xi_j \mathbb{1}_{B_j}(t) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $V$ over the disjoint intervals.

nodes.name: Simple processes are predictable
nodes.statement: A simple process is predictable.
conclusions: A simple process is predictable.
nodes.label: lem:predictable_simpleProcess

nodes.name: Simple processes generate the predictable sigma-algebra
nodes.statement: Real simple processes generate the predictable $\sigma$-algebra, i.e., the predictable $\sigma$-algebra is the supremum of the comaps by simple processes (seen as maps from $T \times \Omega$ to $\mathbb{R}$) of the Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
conclusions: the predictable $\sigma$-algebra is the supremum of the comaps by simple processes (seen as maps from $T \times \Omega$ to $\mathbb{R}$) of the Borel $\sigma$-algebra
nodes.label: lem:iSup_comap_simpleProcess

nodes.name: Elementary predictable sets iff indicator is simple
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq T \times \Omega$ is an elementary predictable set if and only if the indicator function $\mathbb{1}_A$ is a simple process.
assumptions: A set $A \subseteq T \times \Omega$
conclusions: is an elementary predictable set if and only if the indicator function $\mathbb{1}_A$ is a simple process
equivalent_conditions: is an elementary predictable set
the indicator function $\mathbb{1}_A$ is a simple process
nodes.label: lem:elementaryPredictableSet_iff_indicator

nodes.name: Proof of Elementary predictable sets iff indicator is simple
nodes.statement: Suppose that $A$ is an elementary predictable set; by Lemma~\ref{lem:elementaryPredictableSets_asDisjointUnions}, $A$ is a disjoint union of predictable rectangles. In other words, $\mathbb{1}_A$ is a sum of indicator functions of predictable rectangles, and thus a simple process. In the other direction, suppose $\mathbb{1}_A$ is a simple process, \[ \mathbb{1}_A(t,\cdot) = \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{(s_k, t_k]}(t). \] By Lemma~\ref{lem:simpleProcess_admitsDisjointIntervals}, we can assume that $(s_k, t_k]$ are pairwise disjoint; then each of $\eta_1$, \dots, $\eta_n$ must be an indicator function, \[ \eta_k = \mathbb{1}_{F_k}, \quad\text{with } F_k \in \mathcal{F}_{s_k}, \] and $\eta_0 = \mathbb{1}_{F_0}$ for some $F_0 \in \mathcal{F}_0$~. This shows that $A$ is a finite union of predictable rectangles, and thus an elementary predictable set.
nodes.statement_short: Both directions: disjoint rectangle decomposition gives a sum of indicators; conversely disjoint intervals force indicator coefficients.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: Suppose that $A$ is an elementary predictable set; by Lemma~\ref{lem:elementaryPredictableSets_asDisjointUnions}, $A$ is a disjoint union of predictable rectangles. In other words, $\mathbb{1}_A$ is a sum of indicator functions of predictable rectangles, and thus a simple process.
nodes.statement_short: Disjoint rectangle decomposition makes $1_A$ a simple process.

nodes.name: Converse direction
nodes.statement: In the other direction, suppose $\mathbb{1}_A$ is a simple process, \[ \mathbb{1}_A(t,\cdot) = \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{(s_k, t_k]}(t). \] By Lemma~\ref{lem:simpleProcess_admitsDisjointIntervals}, we can assume that $(s_k, t_k]$ are pairwise disjoint; then each of $\eta_1$, \dots, $\eta_n$ must be an indicator function, \[ \eta_k = \mathbb{1}_{F_k}, \quad\text{with } F_k \in \mathcal{F}_{s_k}, \] and $\eta_0 = \mathbb{1}_{F_0}$ for some $F_0 \in \mathcal{F}_0$~. This shows that $A$ is a finite union of predictable rectangles, and thus an elementary predictable set.
nodes.statement_short: With disjoint intervals the coefficients are indicators, so $A$ is a finite union of rectangles.

nodes.name: Simple processes form an additive group
nodes.statement: The simple processes $\mathcal{E}_{T, F}$ form an additive commutative group.
conclusions: form an additive commutative group
nodes.label: lem:addCommGroup_simpleProcess

nodes.name: Simple processes form a real module
nodes.statement: The simple processes $\mathcal{E}_{T, F}$ form a module over the scalars $\mathbb{R}$.
conclusions: form a module over the scalars $\mathbb{R}$
nodes.label: lem:module_simpleProcess

nodes.name: Elementary stochastic integral
nodes.statement: Let $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, E}$ be a simple process and let $X$ be a stochastic process with values in a normed space $F$. Let $B$ be a continuous bilinear map from $E \times F$ to another normed space $G$. The \emph{general elementary stochastic integral} process $V \bullet_B X : T \to \Omega \to G$ is defined by \begin{align*} (V \bullet_B X)_t &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, X^t_{t_k} - X^t_{s_k}) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: For simple $V$, process $X$ and bilinear $B$: $(V\bullet_B X)_t=\sum_k B(\eta_k, X^t_{t_k}-X^t_{s_k})$.
nodes.label: def:elemStochIntegralBilin

nodes.name: Bilinear combination of simple processes is simple
nodes.statement: For $V, W$ two simple processes with values in $E$ and $F$ respectively, the process defined by $B(V, W)_t(\omega) = B(V_t(\omega), W_t(\omega))$ is a simple process. Note: in Lean, the above is not a lemma but a definition of a simple process with a lemma that its coercion to a function is given by above.
assumptions: $V, W$ two simple processes with values in $E$ and $F$ respectively
conclusions: the process defined by $B(V, W)_t(\omega) = B(V_t(\omega), W_t(\omega))$ is a simple process
nodes.label: lem:simpleProcess_map2

nodes.name: Proof of Bilinear combination of simple processes is simple
nodes.statement: It has values $B(\eta_i, \xi_j)$ on the intervals $(s_i, t_i] \cap (u_j, v_j]$ if $V$ and $W$ are defined by the sequences $(s_i, t_i, \eta_i)$ and $(u_j, v_j, \xi_j)$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit description of the values on intersections of intervals.

nodes.name: Linear elementary stochastic integral
nodes.statement: Let $E$ and $F$ be normed real vector spaces. We call \emph{linear elementary stochastic integral} the general elementary stochastic integral of Definition~\ref{def:elemStochIntegralBilin} with $V$ being valued in $L(E, F)$-valued and $B(L, x) = L(x)$ the evaluation map. We denote it by $V \bullet_L X$, or just $V \bullet X$ when $L$ is clear from the context.
differentia: with $V$ being valued in $L(E, F)$-valued and $B(L, x) = L(x)$ the evaluation map
nodes.label: def:elemStochIntegralLinear

nodes.name: Scalar elementary stochastic integral
nodes.statement: We call \emph{scalar elementary stochastic integral} the general elementary stochastic integral of Definition~\ref{def:elemStochIntegralBilin} with $V$ being $\mathbb{R}$-valued and $B(r, x) = r \cdot x$ the scalar multiplication. We denote it by $V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X$.
differentia: with $V$ being $\mathbb{R}$-valued and $B(r, x) = r \cdot x$ the scalar multiplication
nodes.label: def:elemStochIntegral

nodes.name: Linearity of elementary stochastic integrals
nodes.statement: The elementary stochastic integrals $\bullet_B$, $\bullet_L$ and $\bullet_{\mathbb{R}}$ are linear in both arguments.
conclusions: are linear in both arguments
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegral_linear

nodes.name: Proof of Linearity of elementary stochastic integrals
nodes.statement: (In Lean, this is split into several lemmas about each argument and add/sub/smul.) Immediate from the definition.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition (split into several Lean lemmas).

nodes.name: Elementary stochastic integral vanishes at 0
nodes.statement: $(V \bullet_B X)_0 = 0$ for every simple process $V$ and stochastic process $X$.
assumptions: for every simple process $V$ and stochastic process $X$
conclusions: $(V \bullet_B X)_0 = 0$
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_zero

nodes.name: Proof of Elementary stochastic integral vanishes at 0
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} (V \bullet_B X)_0 &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, X^0_{t_k} - X^0_{s_k}) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, X_{0} - X_{0}) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, 0) \\ &= 0 \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation: stopped increments at time 0 vanish.

nodes.name: Integral against a constant process vanishes
nodes.statement: Let $X_c$ be a constant process (equal to the same random variable for all times). Then for every simple process $V$, \begin{align*} V \bullet_B X_c = 0 \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X_c$ be a constant process (equal to the same random variable for all times).
conclusions: for every simple process $V$, \begin{align*} V \bullet_B X_c = 0 \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_const

nodes.name: Associativity of the general elementary stochastic integral
nodes.statement: Let $E, F, G, H, I, J$ be normed real vector spaces. Let $B_1 : E \times H \to I$, $B_2 : F \times G \to H$, $B_3 : E \times F \to J$ and $B_4 : J \times G \to I$ be continuous bilinear maps such that for all $x \in E$, $y \in F$ and $z \in G$, $B_1(x, B_2(y, z)) = B_4(B_3(x, y), z)$. Then for every simple process $V$ with values in $E$, simple process $W$ with values in $F$, and stochastic process $X$ with values in $G$, we have \begin{align*} V \bullet_{B_1} (W \bullet_{B_2} X) &= B_3(V, W) \bullet_{B_4} X \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Iterated elementary integrals collapse to one integral against the bilinear product of integrands, given compatible bilinear maps.
assumptions: Let $E, F, G, H, I, J$ be normed real vector spaces.

Let $B_1 : E \times H \to I$, $B_2 : F \times G \to H$, $B_3 : E \times F \to J$ and $B_4 : J \times G \to I$ be continuous bilinear maps such that for all $x \in E$, $y \in F$ and $z \in G$, $B_1(x, B_2(y, z)) = B_4(B_3(x, y), z)$.
for every simple process $V$ with values in $E$, simple process $W$ with values in $F$, and stochastic process $X$ with values in $G$
conclusions: \begin{align*} V \bullet_{B_1} (W \bullet_{B_2} X) &= B_3(V, W) \bullet_{B_4} X \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_assoc

nodes.name: Proof of Associativity of the general elementary stochastic integral
nodes.statement: Unfold definitions, use linearity.
nodes.statement_short: Unfold definitions and use linearity.

nodes.name: Associativity with a real-valued outer integrand
nodes.statement: Let $E, F, G$ be normed real vector spaces. Let $B : E \times F \to G$ be a continuous bilinear map. Then for every simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}$, simple process $W$ with values in $E$, and stochastic process $X$ with values in $F$, we have \begin{align*} V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (W \bullet_{B} X) &= (V \cdot W) \bullet_{B} X \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $E, F, G$ be normed real vector spaces.
Let $B : E \times F \to G$ be a continuous bilinear map.
for every simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}$, simple process $W$ with values in $E$, and stochastic process $X$ with values in $F$
conclusions: \begin{align*} V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (W \bullet_{B} X) &= (V \cdot W) \bullet_{B} X \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:elemStochIntegral_assoc_real_bilin

nodes.name: Proof of Associativity with a real-valued outer integrand
nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_assoc}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the general associativity lemma.

nodes.name: Associativity of the scalar elementary integral
nodes.statement: $V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X) = (V \times W) \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X$ for real-valued simple processes $V, W$ and stochastic process $X$.
assumptions: for real-valued simple processes $V, W$ and stochastic process $X$
conclusions: $V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X) = (V \times W) \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X$
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegral_assoc

nodes.name: Proof of Associativity of the scalar elementary integral
nodes.statement: Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:elemStochIntegral_assoc_real_bilin} with $B$ the scalar multiplication.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the real-bilinear associativity corollary with scalar multiplication.

nodes.name: Associativity of the linear elementary integral
nodes.statement: For simple process $W$ with values in $L(E, F)$, simple process $V$ with values in $L(F, G)$, and stochastic process $X$ with values in $E$, we have \begin{align*} V \bullet_L (W \bullet_L X) &= (V \circ W) \bullet_L X \: , \end{align*} in which $V \circ W$ is the simple process defined by $(V \circ W)_t = V_t \circ W_t$.
assumptions: For simple process $W$ with values in $L(E, F)$, simple process $V$ with values in $L(F, G)$, and stochastic process $X$ with values in $E$
conclusions: \begin{align*} V \bullet_L (W \bullet_L X) &= (V \circ W) \bullet_L X \: , \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegralLinear_assoc

nodes.name: Proof of Associativity of the linear elementary integral
nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_assoc} with $B_1, B_2, B_4$ equal to the evaluation maps and $B_3$ the composition of continuous linear maps.
nodes.statement_short: General associativity lemma with evaluation maps and composition.

nodes.name: Elementary integral of a cadlag process is cadlag
nodes.statement: For $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, F}$, $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ a càdlàg process and a continuous bilinear map $B: E \times F \to G$, the elementary stochastic integral $V \bullet_B X$ is càdlàg.
assumptions: $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, F}$
$X : T \to \Omega \to E$ a càdlàg process
a continuous bilinear map $B: E \times F \to G$
conclusions: the elementary stochastic integral $V \bullet_B X$ is càdlàg
nodes.label: lem:cadlag_elemStochIntegralBilin

nodes.name: Stopping the elementary integral stops the integrator
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a stochastic process, $V$ a simple process and $τ$ a stopping time. Then \begin{align*} (V \bullet_B X)^τ = V \bullet_B (X^τ) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X$ be a stochastic process, $V$ a simple process and $τ$ a stopping time.
conclusions: \begin{align*} (V \bullet_B X)^τ = V \bullet_B (X^τ) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegral_stoppedProcess

nodes.name: Proof of Stopping the elementary integral stops the integrator
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} (V \bullet_B X)^\tau_t &= (V \bullet_B X)_{t \wedge \tau} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, X^{t \wedge \tau}_{t_k} - X^{t \wedge \tau}_{s_k}) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, (X^{\tau})^t_{t_k} - (X^{\tau})^t_{s_k}) \\ &= (V \bullet_B (X^{\tau}))_t \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation with stopped increments.

nodes.name: Stopped process as an elementary integral
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a stochastic process and $τ$ be a stopping time taking finitely many values. Then $\mathbb{1}_{[0, τ]}$ is a simple process and \begin{align*} X^τ = X_0 + \mathbb{1}_{[0, τ]} \bullet X \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X$ be a stochastic process and $τ$ be a stopping time taking finitely many values.
conclusions: $\mathbb{1}_{[0, τ]}$ is a simple process
\begin{align*} X^τ = X_0 + \mathbb{1}_{[0, τ]} \bullet X \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:stoppedProcess_eq_elemStochIntegral

nodes.name: Stopped elementary integral as integral of stopped integrand
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a stochastic process, $V$ a real-valued simple process, and $τ$ a stopping time taking finitely many values. Then \begin{align*} (V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)^τ = (\mathbb{1}_{[0,τ]}V) \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X$ be a stochastic process, $V$ a real-valued simple process, and $τ$ a stopping time taking finitely many values.
conclusions: \begin{align*} (V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)^τ = (\mathbb{1}_{[0,τ]}V) \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:elemStochIntegral_stoppedIntegrator

nodes.name: Proof of Stopped elementary integral as integral of stopped integrand
nodes.statement: Replace, in the formula (Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegral_stoppedProcess}): \[ (V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)^τ = V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (X^τ), \] the $X^\tau$ by $X_0 + \mathbb{1}_{[0, τ]} \bullet X$ using Lemma~\ref{lem:stoppedProcess_eq_elemStochIntegral}. Now, $X_0$ may be dropped in the resulting integral, by linearity (Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegral_linear}) and Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_const}, that is, \[ (V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)^τ = V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (\mathbb{1}_{[0, τ]} \bullet X). \] Application of Corollary~\ref{cor:elemStochIntegral_assoc_real_bilin} gives the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the stopped process as an elementary integral, drop $X_0$ by linearity, then apply associativity.

nodes.name: Substitute stopped process
nodes.statement: Replace, in the formula (Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegral_stoppedProcess}): \[ (V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)^τ = V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (X^τ), \] the $X^\tau$ by $X_0 + \mathbb{1}_{[0, τ]} \bullet X$ using Lemma~\ref{lem:stoppedProcess_eq_elemStochIntegral}.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the stopped process as an elementary integral.

nodes.name: Drop constant
nodes.statement: Now, $X_0$ may be dropped in the resulting integral, by linearity (Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegral_linear}) and Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegralBilin_const}, that is, \[ (V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)^τ = V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (\mathbb{1}_{[0, τ]} \bullet X). \]
nodes.statement_short: Drop $X_0$ by linearity and the constant-process lemma.

nodes.name: Associativity
nodes.statement: Application of Corollary~\ref{cor:elemStochIntegral_assoc_real_bilin} gives the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by associativity.

nodes.name: Elementary integral converges to its limit process
nodes.statement: For $V$ a simple process and $X$ a stochastic process, $(V \bullet_B X)_t$ tends to its limit process $(V \bullet_B X)_\infty$ as $t$ goes to infinity.
assumptions: For $V$ a simple process and $X$ a stochastic process
conclusions: $(V \bullet_B X)_t$ tends to its limit process $(V \bullet_B X)_\infty$ as $t$ goes to infinity
nodes.label: lem:tendsto_elemStochIntegral_limitProcess

nodes.name: Proof of Elementary integral converges to its limit process
nodes.statement: That process is eventually constant.
nodes.statement_short: The process is eventually constant.

nodes.name: Limit process of the elementary integral
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} (V \bullet_B X)_\infty &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, X_{t_k} - X_{s_k}) \: . \end{align*}
conclusions: \begin{align*} (V \bullet_B X)_\infty &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} B (\eta_k, X_{t_k} - X_{s_k}) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:limitProcess_elemStochIntegral

nodes.name: Proof of Limit process of the elementary integral
nodes.statement: Immediate from the definition.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition.

nodes.name: Submartingale characterization by elementary integrals
nodes.statement: An adapted integrable process $X$ is a submartingale if and only if for every bounded simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}_+$, $\mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] \ge 0$. Note that in Lean $V$ comes with the data of a sum representation: by ``values in $\mathbb{R}_+$'' we mean that the random variables in that particular sum representing $V$ are nonnegative.
assumptions: An adapted integrable process $X$
conclusions: is a submartingale if and only if for every bounded simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}_+$, $\mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] \ge 0$
equivalent_conditions: is a submartingale
for every bounded simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}_+$, $\mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] \ge 0$
nodes.label: lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg

nodes.name: Proof of Submartingale characterization by elementary integrals
nodes.statement: First suppose that $X$ is a submartingale. The simple process $V$ can be written as $V_t = \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{(s_k, t_k]}(t)$ for nonnegative $\eta_k$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k (X_{t_k} - X_{s_k})\right] \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}[\eta_k (X_{t_k} - X_{s_k})] \: . \end{align*} It suffices to show that each term of the sum is nonnegative. Since $\eta_k$ is $\mathcal{F}_{s_k}$-measurable and nonnegative, by the submartingale property we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\eta_k (X_{t_k} - X_{s_k})] &= \mathbb{E}[\eta_k \mathbb{E}[X_{t_k} - X_{s_k} \mid \mathcal{F}_{s_k}]] \ge 0 \: . \end{align*} This concludes the proof in one direction. Suppose now that for every bounded simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}_+$, $\mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] \ge 0$. To show that $X$ is a submartingale, let $s < t$ in $T$ and let $A = \{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] < X_s\} \in \mathcal{F}_s$. Define the simple process $V$ by $V_r = \mathbb{1}_A \mathbb{1}_{(s, t]}(r)$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_A (X_t - X_s)] &= \mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] \ge 0 \: . \end{align*} But we also have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_A (X_t - X_s)] &= \mathbb{E}[\min\{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] - X_s, 0\}] \le 0 \: . \end{align*} Combining both inequalities, we get $\mathbb{E}[\min\{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] - X_s, 0\}] = 0$. Since $\min\{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] - X_s, 0\}$ is nonpositive and has expectation zero, it is almost surely zero. Thus $\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] \ge X_s$ almost surely, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Two directions: expand the integral and use the submartingale property termwise; conversely test with $V=1_A 1_{(s,t]}$ for $A=\{E[X_t|F_s]<X_s\}$. A nonpositive variable with zero expectation vanishes a.s.

nodes.name: Submartingale implies nonnegativity
nodes.statement: First suppose that $X$ is a submartingale. The simple process $V$ can be written as $V_t = \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{(s_k, t_k]}(t)$ for nonnegative $\eta_k$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k (X_{t_k} - X_{s_k})\right] \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}[\eta_k (X_{t_k} - X_{s_k})] \: . \end{align*} It suffices to show that each term of the sum is nonnegative. Since $\eta_k$ is $\mathcal{F}_{s_k}$-measurable and nonnegative, by the submartingale property we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\eta_k (X_{t_k} - X_{s_k})] &= \mathbb{E}[\eta_k \mathbb{E}[X_{t_k} - X_{s_k} \mid \mathcal{F}_{s_k}]] \ge 0 \: . \end{align*} This concludes the proof in one direction.
nodes.statement_short: If $X$ is a submartingale, each term of the integral has nonnegative expectation.

nodes.name: Expand the integral
nodes.statement: The simple process $V$ can be written as $V_t = \eta_0 \mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{(s_k, t_k]}(t)$ for nonnegative $\eta_k$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{n} \eta_k (X_{t_k} - X_{s_k})\right] \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}[\eta_k (X_{t_k} - X_{s_k})] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $V$ and expand the expected integral as a sum.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that each term of the sum is nonnegative.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to each term.

nodes.name: Termwise bound
nodes.statement: Since $\eta_k$ is $\mathcal{F}_{s_k}$-measurable and nonnegative, by the submartingale property we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\eta_k (X_{t_k} - X_{s_k})] &= \mathbb{E}[\eta_k \mathbb{E}[X_{t_k} - X_{s_k} \mid \mathcal{F}_{s_k}]] \ge 0 \: . \end{align*} This concludes the proof in one direction.
nodes.statement_short: Condition on $\mathcal{F}_{s_k}$ and use the submartingale property.

nodes.name: Nonnegativity implies submartingale
nodes.statement: Suppose now that for every bounded simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}_+$, $\mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] \ge 0$. To show that $X$ is a submartingale, let $s < t$ in $T$ and let $A = \{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] < X_s\} \in \mathcal{F}_s$. Define the simple process $V$ by $V_r = \mathbb{1}_A \mathbb{1}_{(s, t]}(r)$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_A (X_t - X_s)] &= \mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] \ge 0 \: . \end{align*} But we also have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_A (X_t - X_s)] &= \mathbb{E}[\min\{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] - X_s, 0\}] \le 0 \: . \end{align*} Combining both inequalities, we get $\mathbb{E}[\min\{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] - X_s, 0\}] = 0$. Since $\min\{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] - X_s, 0\}$ is nonpositive and has expectation zero, it is almost surely zero. Thus $\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] \ge X_s$ almost surely, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Conversely, test with $V=1_A1_{(s,t]}$ on the bad event to force the submartingale inequality.

nodes.name: Test process
nodes.statement: To show that $X$ is a submartingale, let $s < t$ in $T$ and let $A = \{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] < X_s\} \in \mathcal{F}_s$. Define the simple process $V$ by $V_r = \mathbb{1}_A \mathbb{1}_{(s, t]}(r)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the bad event $A$ and test process $V$.

nodes.name: Two-sided bound
nodes.statement: Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_A (X_t - X_s)] &= \mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] \ge 0 \: . \end{align*} But we also have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_A (X_t - X_s)] &= \mathbb{E}[\min\{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] - X_s, 0\}] \le 0 \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Expectation is both $\ge0$ and $\le0$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Combining both inequalities, we get $\mathbb{E}[\min\{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] - X_s, 0\}] = 0$. Since $\min\{\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] - X_s, 0\}$ is nonpositive and has expectation zero, it is almost surely zero. Thus $\mathbb{E}[X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s] \ge X_s$ almost surely, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: A nonpositive variable with zero mean vanishes a.s.; conclude.

nodes.name: Martingale characterization by elementary integrals
nodes.statement: An adapted integrable process $X$ is a martingale if and only if for every bounded simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] = 0$.
assumptions: An adapted integrable process $X$
conclusions: is a martingale if and only if for every bounded simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] = 0$
equivalent_conditions: is a martingale
for every bounded simple process $V$ with values in $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{E}[(V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty] = 0$
nodes.label: lem:martingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_eq_zero

nodes.name: Proof of Martingale characterization by elementary integrals
nodes.statement: There might not be an order on the type $E$ of values of $X$, so we cannot just say that $X$ is a martingale if and only if both $X$ and $-X$ are submartingales and conclude with Lemma~\ref{lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg}. But we can use almost the same proof as in Lemma~\ref{lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg}, replacing inequalities by equalities?
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: adapt the submartingale characterization proof with equalities instead of inequalities.

nodes.name: Expected elementary integral of a submartingale bounded by increment
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a submartingale and $A$ be an elementary predictable set. Then for all $t \in T$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_t] \le \mathbb{E}[X_t - X_0] \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X$ be a submartingale and $A$ be an elementary predictable set.
for all $t \in T$
conclusions: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_t] \le \mathbb{E}[X_t - X_0] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:Submartingale.integral_elemStochIntegral_le

nodes.name: Proof of Expected elementary integral of a submartingale bounded by increment
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be an elementary predictable set and let $t \in T$. \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_t] &= \mathbb{E}[X_t - X_0] - \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_{A^c} \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_t] \le \mathbb{E}[X_t - X_0] \: . \end{align*} The inequality follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg} applied to the nonnegative bounded simple process $\mathbb{1}_{A^c}$.
nodes.statement_short: Split the integral over $A$ and its complement and use nonnegativity for the complement.

nodes.name: Elementary integral of a submartingale is a submartingale
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a submartingale and $V$ be a nonnegative bounded simple process. Then the elementary stochastic integral $V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X$ is a submartingale.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a submartingale and $V$ be a nonnegative bounded simple process.
conclusions: the elementary stochastic integral $V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X$ is a submartingale
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.elemStochIntegral

nodes.name: Proof of Elementary integral of a submartingale is a submartingale
nodes.statement: We use Lemma~\ref{lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg} and have to show that for every nonnegative bounded simple process $W$, $\mathbb{E}[(W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X))_\infty] \ge 0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegral_assoc}, this is $\mathbb{E}[((W \times V) \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty]$. Since $W \times V$ is a nonnegative bounded simple process, this is nonnegative by Lemma~\ref{lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg} applied to $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Characterization by elementary integrals plus associativity of the scalar elementary integral.

nodes.name: Reduce via characterization
nodes.statement: We use Lemma~\ref{lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg} and have to show that for every nonnegative bounded simple process $W$, $\mathbb{E}[(W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X))_\infty] \ge 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to nonnegativity of expected iterated integrals.

nodes.name: Associativity
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegral_assoc}, this is $\mathbb{E}[((W \times V) \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} X)_\infty]$.
nodes.statement_short: Collapse the iterated integral by associativity.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $W \times V$ is a nonnegative bounded simple process, this is nonnegative by Lemma~\ref{lem:submartingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_nonneg} applied to $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the characterization to $X$.

nodes.name: Elementary integral of a martingale is a martingale
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a martingale and $V$ be a bounded simple process. Then the elementary stochastic integral $V \bullet_B X$ is a martingale.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a martingale and $V$ be a bounded simple process.
conclusions: the elementary stochastic integral $V \bullet_B X$ is a martingale
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.elemStochIntegral

nodes.name: Proof of Elementary integral of a martingale is a martingale
nodes.statement: We use Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_eq_zero} and have to show that for every bounded simple process $W$, $\mathbb{E}[(W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (V \bullet_B X))_\infty] = 0$. By Lemma~\ref{cor:elemStochIntegral_assoc_real_bilin}, this is $\mathbb{E}[((W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} V) \bullet_B X)_\infty]$. Since $W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} V$ is a bounded simple process, this is zero by Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_eq_zero} applied to $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Martingale characterization by elementary integrals plus associativity.

nodes.name: Reduce via characterization
nodes.statement: We use Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_eq_zero} and have to show that for every bounded simple process $W$, $\mathbb{E}[(W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} (V \bullet_B X))_\infty] = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to vanishing of expected iterated integrals.

nodes.name: Associativity
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{cor:elemStochIntegral_assoc_real_bilin}, this is $\mathbb{E}[((W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} V) \bullet_B X)_\infty]$.
nodes.statement_short: Collapse the iterated integral by associativity.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $W \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} V$ is a bounded simple process, this is zero by Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_eq_zero} applied to $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the characterization to $X$.

nodes.name: Stochastic intervals
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a time domain and let $\sigma, \tau$ be functions $\Omega \to T \cup \{\infty\}$. We define \begin{align*} [\![\sigma, \tau]\!] &= \{(t, \omega) \in T \times \Omega \mid \sigma(\omega) \le t \le \tau(\omega)\} \:, \\ [\![\sigma, \tau[\![ &= \{(t, \omega) \in T \times \Omega \mid \sigma(\omega) \le t < \tau(\omega)\} \:, \\ ]\!]\sigma, \tau]\!] &= \{(t, \omega) \in T \times \Omega \mid \sigma(\omega) < t \le \tau(\omega)\} \:, \\ ]\!]\sigma, \tau[\![ &= \{(t, \omega) \in T \times \Omega \mid \sigma(\omega) < t < \tau(\omega)\} \:, \\ [\![\sigma]\!] &= \{(t, \omega) \in T \times \Omega \mid \sigma(\omega) = t\} = [\![\sigma, \sigma]\!] \:. \end{align*} We call those stochastic intervals. Note that these are subsets of $T \times \Omega$, not of $ (T \cup \{\infty\}) \times \Omega$. $[\![\sigma]\!]$ is called the graph of $\sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Defines the stochastic intervals $[\![\sigma,\tau]\!]$ etc. as subsets of $T\times\Omega$ and the graph $[\![\sigma]\!]$.
nodes.label: def:stochasticInterval

nodes.name: Stochastic intervals of stopping times are predictable
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are stopping times, then the stochastic interval $]\!]\sigma, \tau]\!]$ is a predictable set.
assumptions: $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are stopping times
conclusions: the stochastic interval $]\!]\sigma, \tau]\!]$ is a predictable set
nodes.label: lem:predictable_stochasticInterval

nodes.name: Bounded discrete stochastic intervals are elementary predictable
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are stopping times on $\mathbb{N}$, with $\tau$ bounded, then the stochastic interval $]\!]\sigma, \tau]\!]$ is an elementary predictable set.
assumptions: $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are stopping times on $\mathbb{N}$, with $\tau$ bounded
conclusions: the stochastic interval $]\!]\sigma, \tau]\!]$ is an elementary predictable set
nodes.label: lem:elementaryPredictableSet_stochasticInterval

nodes.name: Proof of Bounded discrete stochastic intervals are elementary predictable
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be an upper bound for $\tau$. To see that the stochastic interval is an elementary predictable set, note that it can be written as a finite disjoint union of sets \begin{align*} \{\sigma(\omega) < t \le \tau(\omega)\} &= \bigcup_{k=1}^{n} \{k\} \times \{\sigma < k \le \tau\} \\ &= \bigcup_{k=1}^{n} (k-1, k] \times \{\sigma \le k-1 < \tau\} \end{align*} where $\{\sigma \le k-1 < \tau\} \in \mathcal{F}_{k-1}$. Therefore this is an elementary predictable set.
nodes.statement_short: Write the interval as a finite disjoint union of predictable rectangles $(k-1,k]\times\{\sigma\le k-1<\tau\}$.

nodes.name: Decompose interval
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be an upper bound for $\tau$. To see that the stochastic interval is an elementary predictable set, note that it can be written as a finite disjoint union of sets \begin{align*} \{\sigma(\omega) < t \le \tau(\omega)\} &= \bigcup_{k=1}^{n} \{k\} \times \{\sigma < k \le \tau\} \\ &= \bigcup_{k=1}^{n} (k-1, k] \times \{\sigma \le k-1 < \tau\} \end{align*} where $\{\sigma \le k-1 < \tau\} \in \mathcal{F}_{k-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the interval as a finite union of predictable rectangles.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore this is an elementary predictable set.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude it is elementary predictable.

nodes.name: Auxiliary lower crossing time
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a stochastic process, $t \in T$, and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The auxiliary lower crossing time $\sigma'_{a, s, t}$ is the hitting time of the set $(-\infty, a]$ by the process $X$ between times $s$ and $t$.
nodes.label: def:lowerCrossingTimeAux

nodes.name: Upper crossing time
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a stochastic process, $t \in T$, and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The $n$-th upper crossing time $\tau^n_{a, b, t}$ of the interval $[a, b]$ by $X$ before time $t$ is the hitting time of the set $[b, \infty)$ by $X$ after hitting the set $(-\infty, a]$ for the $n-1$-th time. That is, $\tau^0_{a, b, t} = 0$, and for all $n$, $\tau^{n+1}_{a, b, t}$ is the hitting time of $[b, \infty)$ by $X$ between $\sigma'_{a, \tau^{n}_{a, b, t}, t}$ and $t$.
nodes.label: def:upperCrossingTime

nodes.name: Lower crossing time
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a stochastic process, $t \in T$, and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The $n$-th lower crossing time $\sigma^n_{a, b, t}$ of the interval $[a, b]$ by $X$ before time $t$ is the hitting time of the set $(-\infty, a]$ by $X$ after hitting the set $[b, \infty)$ for the $n$-th time. That is, it is the hitting time of $(-\infty, a]$ by $X$ between $\tau^n_{a, b, t}$ and $t$.
nodes.label: def:lowerCrossingTime

nodes.name: Upcrossings before time $t$
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a stochastic process, $t \in T$, and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The number of upcrossings $U_t[a, b]$ of the interval $[a, b]$ by $X$ before time $t$ is the largest $n$ such that $\tau^n_{a, b, t} < t$, or $\infty$ if there is no such largest $n$.
nodes.label: def:upcrossingsBefore

nodes.name: Upcrossings
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a stochastic process and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The number of upcrossings $U[a, b]$ of the interval $[a, b]$ by $X$ is the supremum over $t \in T$ of the number of upcrossings $U_t[a, b]$ of $[a, b]$ by $X$ before time $t$.
nodes.label: def:upcrossings

nodes.name: Finite upcrossings imply convergence
nodes.statement: Let $u : \beta \to \alpha$, for $\alpha$ a densely ordered, conditionally complete linear order equipped with the order topology. Let $S$ be a dense subset of $\alpha$ and $f$ a filter of $\beta$. If for all $a < b$ in $S$, the number of upcrossings of the interval $[a, b]$ by $u$ along $f$ is finite, then $u$ tends to a limit along $f$.
assumptions: Let $u : \beta \to \alpha$, for $\alpha$ a densely ordered, conditionally complete linear order equipped with the order topology.
Let $S$ be a dense subset of $\alpha$ and $f$ a filter of $\beta$.
for all $a < b$ in $S$, the number of upcrossings of the interval $[a, b]$ by $u$ along $f$ is finite
conclusions: $u$ tends to a limit along $f$
nodes.label: lem:tendsto_of_no_upcrossings

nodes.name: Upper crossing times are stopping times
nodes.statement: For an adapted process $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by the natural numbers, the upper crossing time $\tau^n_{a, b, t}$ is a stopping time.
assumptions: For an adapted process $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by the natural numbers
conclusions: the upper crossing time $\tau^n_{a, b, t}$ is a stopping time
nodes.label: lem:isStoppingTime_upperCrossingTime

nodes.name: Lower crossing times are stopping times
nodes.statement: For an adapted process $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by the natural numbers, the lower crossing time $\sigma^n_{a, b, t}$ is a stopping time.
assumptions: For an adapted process $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by the natural numbers
conclusions: the lower crossing time $\sigma^n_{a, b, t}$ is a stopping time
nodes.label: lem:isStoppingTime_lowerCrossingTime

nodes.name: Upcrossing predictable set
nodes.statement: Let $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted process on the natural numbers. The upcrossing predictable set of $X$ before time $N$ is the predictable set defined by \begin{align*} A_N = \bigcup_{k=0}^{N-1} ]\!]\sigma^k_{a, b, N}, \tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}]\!] \:. \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:upcrossingPredictableSet

nodes.name: Upcrossing set is predictable
nodes.statement: The upcrossing predictable set $A_N$ of $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ before time $N$ is a predictable set.
conclusions: is a predictable set
nodes.label: lem:predictable_upcrossingPredictableSet

nodes.name: Proof of Upcrossing set is predictable
nodes.statement: By Lemmas \ref{lem:isStoppingTime_lowerCrossingTime} and \ref{lem:isStoppingTime_upperCrossingTime}, $\sigma^k_{a, b, N}$ and $\tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}$ are stopping times. Hence by Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_stochasticInterval}, the stochastic interval $]\!]\sigma^k_{a, b, N}, \tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}]\!]$ is a predictable set for each $k$. Since a finite union of predictable sets is predictable, $A_N$ is predictable.
nodes.statement_short: Crossing times are stopping times, so each stochastic interval is predictable; take the finite union.

nodes.name: Crossing times are stopping times
nodes.statement: By Lemmas \ref{lem:isStoppingTime_lowerCrossingTime} and \ref{lem:isStoppingTime_upperCrossingTime}, $\sigma^k_{a, b, N}$ and $\tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}$ are stopping times.
nodes.statement_short: The crossing times are stopping times.

nodes.name: Intervals predictable
nodes.statement: Hence by Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_stochasticInterval}, the stochastic interval $]\!]\sigma^k_{a, b, N}, \tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}]\!]$ is a predictable set for each $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Each stochastic interval is predictable.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since a finite union of predictable sets is predictable, $A_N$ is predictable.
nodes.statement_short: Finite union.

nodes.name: Upcrossing set is elementary predictable
nodes.statement: The upcrossing predictable set $A_N$ of $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ before time $N$ is an elementary predictable set.
conclusions: is an elementary predictable set
nodes.label: lem:elementaryPredictableSet_upcrossingPredictableSet

nodes.name: Proof of Upcrossing set is elementary predictable
nodes.statement: By Lemmas \ref{lem:isStoppingTime_lowerCrossingTime} and \ref{lem:isStoppingTime_upperCrossingTime}, $\sigma^k_{a, b, N}$ and $\tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}$ are stopping times, and are bounded by $N$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:elementaryPredictableSet_stochasticInterval}, the stochastic intervals $]\!]\sigma^k_{a, b, N}, \tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}]\!]$ are elementary predictable sets for each $k$. Since a finite union of elementary predictable sets is elementary predictable, $A_N$ is elementary predictable.
nodes.statement_short: Bounded crossing stopping times give elementary predictable stochastic intervals; take the finite union.

nodes.name: Bounded stopping times
nodes.statement: By Lemmas \ref{lem:isStoppingTime_lowerCrossingTime} and \ref{lem:isStoppingTime_upperCrossingTime}, $\sigma^k_{a, b, N}$ and $\tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}$ are stopping times, and are bounded by $N$.
nodes.statement_short: The crossing times are stopping times bounded by $N$.

nodes.name: Intervals elementary predictable
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:elementaryPredictableSet_stochasticInterval}, the stochastic intervals $]\!]\sigma^k_{a, b, N}, \tau^{k+1}_{a, b, N}]\!]$ are elementary predictable sets for each $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Each stochastic interval is elementary predictable.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since a finite union of elementary predictable sets is elementary predictable, $A_N$ is elementary predictable.
nodes.statement_short: Finite union.

nodes.name: Discrete upcrossing inequality
nodes.statement: Let $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted process on the natural numbers. Then for all $a < b$ in $\mathbb{R}$ and $t \in \mathbb{N}$, for $A_t$ the upcrossing predictable set of $X$ before time $t$, the number of upcrossings $U_t[a, b]$ of the interval $[a, b]$ before time $t$ satisfies \begin{align*} (b - a) U_t[a, b] \le (\mathbb{1}_{A_t} \bullet X)_t + \max\{a - X_t, 0\} \:. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Upcrossing count times $(b-a)$ is bounded by the elementary integral over the upcrossing set plus $(a-X_t)^+$.
assumptions: Let $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted process on the natural numbers.
for all $a < b$ in $\mathbb{R}$ and $t \in \mathbb{N}$, for $A_t$ the upcrossing predictable set of $X$ before time $t$
conclusions: \begin{align*} (b - a) U_t[a, b] \le (\mathbb{1}_{A_t} \bullet X)_t + \max\{a - X_t, 0\} \:. \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:upcrossing_simpleProcess_le_nat

nodes.name: Proof of Discrete upcrossing inequality
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} (\mathbb{1}_{A_t} \bullet X)_t &= \sum_{k=0}^t (X_{\tau^{k+1}_{a, b, t} \wedge t} - X_{\sigma^k_{a, b, t} \wedge t}) \\ &= \sum_{k=0}^{U_t[a, b]-1} (X_{\tau^{k+1}_{a, b, t} \wedge t} - X_{\sigma^k_{a, b, t} \wedge t}) + (X_t - X_{\sigma^{U_t[a, b]}_{a, b, t} \wedge t}) \\ &\ge (b - a) U_t[a, b] + \min\{X_t - a, 0\} \\ &= (b - a) U_t[a, b] - \max\{a - X_t, 0\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the elementary integral as a sum of crossing increments, each completed upcrossing contributing at least $b-a$.

nodes.name: Upcrossing inequality on a finite time domain
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted process on a finite time domain $T$. Then for all $a < b$ in $\mathbb{R}$ and $t \in T$, there exists an elementary predictable set $A$ such that the number of upcrossings $U_t[a, b]$ of the interval $[a, b]$ before time $t$ satisfies \begin{align*} (b - a) U_t[a, b] \le (\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t + \max\{a - X_t, 0\} \:. \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted process on a finite time domain $T$.
for all $a < b$ in $\mathbb{R}$ and $t \in T$
conclusions: there exists an elementary predictable set $A$ such that the number of upcrossings $U_t[a, b]$ of the interval $[a, b]$ before time $t$ satisfies \begin{align*} (b - a) U_t[a, b] \le (\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t + \max\{a - X_t, 0\} \:. \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:upcrossing_simpleProcess_le

nodes.name: Proof of Upcrossing inequality on a finite time domain
nodes.statement: Go from $T$ to a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ and use Lemma~\ref{lem:upcrossing_simpleProcess_le_nat}?
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: transfer to a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ and use the discrete upcrossing inequality.

nodes.name: Regularization of processes with bounded elementary integrals
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a separable time domain, and let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted stochastic process such that $X$ is integrable and for every $t \in T$ the set $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \mid A \text{ elementary predictable}\}$ is bounded. Then $X$ has a modification $Y$ which has left and right limits everywhere and such that there is a countable set $S \subseteq T$ for which $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$.
nodes.statement_short: An integrable adapted process with bounded expected elementary integrals has a modification with left/right limits, right-continuous off a countable set.
assumptions: Let $T$ be a separable time domain, and let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted stochastic process such that $X$ is integrable and for every $t \in T$ the set $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \mid A \text{ elementary predictable}\}$ is bounded.
conclusions: $X$ has a modification $Y$ which has left and right limits everywhere and such that there is a countable set $S \subseteq T$ for which $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$
nodes.label: thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral

nodes.name: Proof of Regularization of processes with bounded elementary integrals
nodes.statement:
Let $D$ be a countable dense subset of $T$ (e.g.\ the rationals in $T$) and let $t \in T$ and let $S$ be a finite subset of $D \cap [0, t]$. By Lemma~ef{lem:upcrossing_simpleProcess_le}, for all $a < b$ in $\mathbb{R}$, the number of upcrossings $U_S[a, b]$ of the interval $[a, b]$ along $S$ satisfies  egin{align*} (b - a) U_S[a, b] \le (\mathbb{1}_A  ullet X)_t + \max\{a - X_t, 0\} \end{align*} for some elementary predictable set $A$. Taking expectations and using the boundedness hypothesis, we obtain  egin{align*} (b - a) \mathbb{E}[U_S[a, b]] \le L + \mathbb{E}[\max\{a - X_t, 0\}] \le L + |a| + \mathbb{E}[|X_t|] \end{align*} where $L$ is a bound for $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A  ullet X)_t] \mid A 	ext{ elementary predictable}\}$. Now, let $S_1 \subseteq S_2 \subseteq \cdots$ be an increasing sequence of finite subsets of $D \cap [0, t]$ with $ igcup_n S_n = D \cap [0, t]$. The number of upcrossings $U_{S_n}[a, b]$ is increasing in $n$. By monotone convergence,  egin{align*} (b - a) \mathbb{E}[U_{D \cap [0, t]}[a, b]] = \lim_{n 	o \infty} (b - a) \mathbb{E}[U_{S_n}[a, b]] \le L + |a| + \mathbb{E}[|X_t|] < \infty. \end{align*} In particular, $U_{D \cap [0, t]}[a, b] < \infty$ a.s. for each pair $a < b$. Since $\mathbb{Q}^2$ is countable, we conclude that almost surely, for all rational $a < b$, the number of upcrossings of $[a, b]$ by $X$ along $D \cap [0, t]$ is finite. By Lemma~ef{lem:tendsto_of_no_upcrossings}, finite upcrossings of all rational intervals implies that the left and right limits of $s \mapsto X_s(\omega)$ along $D$ exist at every $t \in T$, for almost every $\omega$. Define $$	ilde{Y}_t(\omega) = \lim_{\substack{s \downarrow t \ s \in D}} X_s(\omega)$$ whenever this limit exists, and $	ilde{Y}_t(\omega) = 0$ otherwise. Then $	ilde{Y}$ has left and right limits everywhere (along $T$) almost surely, and is right-continuous at every point of $D$. We claim that the set  egin{align*} S = \{t \in T \mid 	ilde{Y}_t 
e X_t 	ext{ with positive probability}\} \end{align*} is countable. For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, consider the set  egin{align*} S_n = \{t \in T \cap [0, n] \mid \mathbb{P}(|	ilde{Y}_t - X_t| > 1/n) > 1/n\} \:. \end{align*} We have $S =  igcup_n S_n$, so it suffices to show each $S_n$ is finite. If $S_n$ were infinite, it would contain a monotone sequence $t_k$ converging to some limit $t^* \in [0, n]$. Adding $\{t_k\}$ to $D$ and repeating the upcrossing argument, we would obtain that $X_{t_k}$ converges along $D \cup \{t_k\}$ almost surely. But $	ilde{Y}_{t_k}$ also converges (since $	ilde{Y}$ has left/right limits), giving $	ilde{Y}_{t_k} - X_{t_k} 	o 0$ in probability, contradicting the definition of $S_n$. Therefore each $S_n$ is finite and $S$ is countable. Define  egin{align*} Y_t =  egin{cases} X_t & 	ext{if } t \in S \:, \ 	ilde{Y}_t & 	ext{if } t 
otin S \:. \end{cases} \end{align*} Then $Y_t = X_t$ almost surely for all $t$: for $t \in S$ this is by definition, and for $t 
otin S$ this follows from $	ilde{Y}_t = X_t$ a.s. Thus $Y$ is a modification of $X$. Since $	ilde{Y}$ has left and right limits everywhere almost surely, and $Y$ differs from $	ilde{Y}$ only on the countable set $S$, $Y$ also has left and right limits everywhere almost surely. Furthermore, $Y$ agrees with $	ilde{Y}$ on $T \setminus S$, so $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$.
nodes.statement_short: Upcrossing argument: bound expected upcrossings along a dense countable set, take right limits along it, and correct on a countable exceptional set. The key step shows that exceptional set is countable.

nodes.name: Upcrossing inequality on finite sets
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a countable dense subset of $T$ (e.g.\ the rationals in $T$) and let $t \in T$ and let $S$ be a finite subset of $D \cap [0, t]$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:upcrossing_simpleProcess_le}, for all $a < b$ in $\mathbb{R}$, the number of upcrossings $U_S[a, b]$ of the interval $[a, b]$ along $S$ satisfies \begin{align*} (b - a) U_S[a, b] \le (\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t + \max\{a - X_t, 0\} \end{align*} for some elementary predictable set $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix dense countable $D$ and finite $S$; apply the upcrossing inequality.

nodes.name: Expected upcrossing bound
nodes.statement: Taking expectations and using the boundedness hypothesis, we obtain \begin{align*} (b - a) \mathbb{E}[U_S[a, b]] \le L + \mathbb{E}[\max\{a - X_t, 0\}] \le L + |a| + \mathbb{E}[|X_t|] \end{align*} where $L$ is a bound for $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \mid A \text{ elementary predictable}\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound expected upcrossings uniformly in $S$.

nodes.name: Monotone convergence
nodes.statement: Now, let $S_1 \subseteq S_2 \subseteq \cdots$ be an increasing sequence of finite subsets of $D \cap [0, t]$ with $\bigcup_n S_n = D \cap [0, t]$. The number of upcrossings $U_{S_n}[a, b]$ is increasing in $n$. By monotone convergence, \begin{align*} (b - a) \mathbb{E}[U_{D \cap [0, t]}[a, b]] = \lim_{n \to \infty} (b - a) \mathbb{E}[U_{S_n}[a, b]] \le L + |a| + \mathbb{E}[|X_t|] < \infty. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Pass to $D\cap[0,t]$ by monotone convergence.

nodes.name: Finite upcrossings a.s.
nodes.statement: In particular, $U_{D \cap [0, t]}[a, b] < \infty$ a.s. for each pair $a < b$. Since $\mathbb{Q}^2$ is countable, we conclude that almost surely, for all rational $a < b$, the number of upcrossings of $[a, b]$ by $X$ along $D \cap [0, t]$ is finite.
nodes.statement_short: Almost surely finitely many upcrossings of all rational intervals.

nodes.name: Limits along D
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:tendsto_of_no_upcrossings}, finite upcrossings of all rational intervals implies that the left and right limits of $s \mapsto X_s(\omega)$ along $D$ exist at every $t \in T$, for almost every $\omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Finite upcrossings give left and right limits along $D$.

nodes.name: Right-limit process
nodes.statement: Define $$\tilde{Y}_t(\omega) = \lim_{\substack{s \downarrow t \\ s \in D}} X_s(\omega)$$ whenever this limit exists, and $\tilde{Y}_t(\omega) = 0$ otherwise. Then $\tilde{Y}$ has left and right limits everywhere (along $T$) almost surely, and is right-continuous at every point of $D$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\tilde Y$ as right limits along $D$.

nodes.name: Exceptional set countable
nodes.statement: We claim that the set \begin{align*} S = \{t \in T \mid \tilde{Y}_t \ne X_t \text{ with positive probability}\} \end{align*} is countable. For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, consider the set \begin{align*} S_n = \{t \in T \cap [0, n] \mid \mathbb{P}(|\tilde{Y}_t - X_t| > 1/n) > 1/n\} \:. \end{align*} We have $S = \bigcup_n S_n$, so it suffices to show each $S_n$ is finite. If $S_n$ were infinite, it would contain a monotone sequence $t_k$ converging to some limit $t^* \in [0, n]$. Adding $\{t_k\}$ to $D$ and repeating the upcrossing argument, we would obtain that $X_{t_k}$ converges along $D \cup \{t_k\}$ almost surely. But $\tilde{Y}_{t_k}$ also converges (since $\tilde{Y}$ has left/right limits), giving $\tilde{Y}_{t_k} - X_{t_k} \to 0$ in probability, contradicting the definition of $S_n$. Therefore each $S_n$ is finite and $S$ is countable.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: the set where $\tilde Y\ne X$ with positive probability is countable.

nodes.name: Level sets
nodes.statement: For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, consider the set \begin{align*} S_n = \{t \in T \cap [0, n] \mid \mathbb{P}(|\tilde{Y}_t - X_t| > 1/n) > 1/n\} \:. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the sets $S_n$.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: We have $S = \bigcup_n S_n$, so it suffices to show each $S_n$ is finite.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to finiteness of each $S_n$.

nodes.name: Suppose infinite
nodes.statement: If $S_n$ were infinite, it would contain a monotone sequence $t_k$ converging to some limit $t^* \in [0, n]$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $S_n$ infinite: extract a monotone convergent sequence.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Adding $\{t_k\}$ to $D$ and repeating the upcrossing argument, we would obtain that $X_{t_k}$ converges along $D \cup \{t_k\}$ almost surely. But $\tilde{Y}_{t_k}$ also converges (since $\tilde{Y}$ has left/right limits), giving $\tilde{Y}_{t_k} - X_{t_k} \to 0$ in probability, contradicting the definition of $S_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the upcrossing argument to force $\tilde Y_{t_k}-X_{t_k}\to0$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Claim concluded
nodes.statement: Therefore each $S_n$ is finite and $S$ is countable.
nodes.statement_short: Each $S_n$ finite, so $S$ countable.

nodes.name: Define modification
nodes.statement: Define \begin{align*} Y_t = \begin{cases} X_t & \text{if } t \in S \:, \\ \tilde{Y}_t & \text{if } t \notin S \:. \end{cases} \end{align*} Then $Y_t = X_t$ almost surely for all $t$: for $t \in S$ this is by definition, and for $t \notin S$ this follows from $\tilde{Y}_t = X_t$ a.s. Thus $Y$ is a modification of $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $Y$ (equal to $X$ on $S$) and check it is a modification.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $\tilde{Y}$ has left and right limits everywhere almost surely, and $Y$ differs from $\tilde{Y}$ only on the countable set $S$, $Y$ also has left and right limits everywhere almost surely. Furthermore, $Y$ agrees with $\tilde{Y}$ on $T \setminus S$, so $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$.
nodes.statement_short: $Y$ inherits limits and right-continuity off $S$.

nodes.name: Right-continuous in probability
nodes.statement: In the following, we say that a stochastic process $X$ is \emph{right-continuous in probability} if for all $t \in T$, $\lim_{s \downarrow t} X_s = X_t$ in which the limit is taken in probability.
differentia: for all $t \in T$, $\lim_{s \downarrow t} X_s = X_t$ in which the limit is taken in probability

nodes.name: Cadlag modification under right-continuity in probability
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a separable time domain, and let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted stochastic process which is right-continuous in probability and such that the boundedness condition of Theorem~\ref{thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral} holds. Then $X$ has a cadlag modification.
assumptions: Let $T$ be a separable time domain, and let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be an adapted stochastic process which is right-continuous in probability and such that the boundedness condition of Theorem~\ref{thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral} holds.
conclusions: $X$ has a cadlag modification
nodes.label: cor:exists_caldag_modification

nodes.name: Proof of Cadlag modification under right-continuity in probability
nodes.statement: Let $Y$ be the modification of $X$ given by Theorem~\ref{thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral}. $Y$ has left and right limits everywhere and there is a countable set $S$ such that $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$. It remains to show that $Y$ is right-continuous at the points of $S$. Let $Y_{t+}$ denote the right limit of $Y$ at $t$. Since $X$ is right-continuous in probability, for all $t \in S$, $Y_t = Y_{t+}$ almost surely. Therefore, since $S$ is countable, we have that almost surely $Y_t = Y_{t+}$ for all $t \in S$ (and hence for all $t \in T$). $Y$ is therefore almost surely cadlag. We can modify $Y$ on the null set to obtain a cadlag modification of $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the modification of the regularization theorem and use right-continuity in probability on the countable exceptional set.

nodes.name: Take modification
nodes.statement: Let $Y$ be the modification of $X$ given by Theorem~\ref{thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral}. $Y$ has left and right limits everywhere and there is a countable set $S$ such that $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the modification from the regularization theorem.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It remains to show that $Y$ is right-continuous at the points of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to right-continuity on $S$.

nodes.name: Right-continuity at S
nodes.statement: Let $Y_{t+}$ denote the right limit of $Y$ at $t$. Since $X$ is right-continuous in probability, for all $t \in S$, $Y_t = Y_{t+}$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: Right-continuity in probability gives $Y_t=Y_{t+}$ a.s. on $S$.

nodes.name: Countable union
nodes.statement: Therefore, since $S$ is countable, we have that almost surely $Y_t = Y_{t+}$ for all $t \in S$ (and hence for all $t \in T$). $Y$ is therefore almost surely cadlag.
nodes.statement_short: Countability gives a.s. cadlag paths.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: We can modify $Y$ on the null set to obtain a cadlag modification of $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Modify on a null set.

nodes.name: Submartingales have bounded expected elementary integrals
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale. Then for every $t \in T$, the set $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \mid A \text{ elementary predictable}\}$ is bounded.
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale.
for every $t \in T$
conclusions: the set $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \mid A \text{ elementary predictable}\}$ is bounded
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.integral_elemStochIntegral_bounded

nodes.name: Proof of Submartingales have bounded expected elementary integrals
nodes.statement: Since $X$ is a submartingale, for any elementary predictable set $A$, we have (Corollary~\ref{cor:Submartingale.integral_elemStochIntegral_le}) \begin{align*} 0 \le \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \le \mathbb{E}[X_t - X_0] \:. \end{align*} As $X_t$ and $X_0$ are integrable, the set $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \mid A \text{ elementary predictable}\}$ is bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich $0\le E[(1_A\bullet X)_t]\le E[X_t-X_0]$ and integrability.

nodes.name: Cadlag modification of a submartingale right-continuous in probability
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale which is right-continuous in probability. Then $X$ has a cadlag modification.
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale which is right-continuous in probability.
conclusions: $X$ has a cadlag modification
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.exists_cadlag_modification_of_rightContinuous

nodes.name: Proof of Cadlag modification of a submartingale right-continuous in probability
nodes.statement: We apply Corollary~\ref{cor:exists_caldag_modification}, in which the boundedness condition of Theorem~\ref{thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral} holds by Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.integral_elemStochIntegral_bounded}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the cadlag-modification corollary, the boundedness holding for submartingales.

nodes.name: Submartingale modification with limits
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale. Then $X$ has a modification $Y$ such that for all $t \in T$, $Y$ has left and right limits at $t$ and such that there is a countable set $S \subseteq T$ for which $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$.
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale.
conclusions: $X$ has a modification $Y$ such that for all $t \in T$, $Y$ has left and right limits at $t$ and such that there is a countable set $S \subseteq T$ for which $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.exists_modifications_limits

nodes.name: Proof of Submartingale modification with limits
nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral}, in which the boundedness condition holds by Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.integral_elemStochIntegral_bounded}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the regularization theorem, boundedness holding for submartingales.

nodes.name: Submartingale along a decreasing sequence is uniformly integrable
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale and let $t_n$ be a decreasing sequence in $T$ which is bounded below. Then the family $\{X_{t_n}\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable.
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale and let $t_n$ be a decreasing sequence in $T$ which is bounded below.
conclusions: the family $\{X_{t_n}\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.uniformIntegrable_of_antitone_of_ge

nodes.name: Submartingale bounded by conditional expectation of right limit
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale and $t \in T$. Let $t_n$ be a decreasing sequence in $T$ converging to $t$, and such that $X_{t_n}$ tends to a limit $X_{t+}$ almost surely. Then $X_t \le P[X_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ almost surely.
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale and $t \in T$.
Let $t_n$ be a decreasing sequence in $T$ converging to $t$, and such that $X_{t_n}$ tends to a limit $X_{t+}$ almost surely.
conclusions: $X_t \le P[X_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ almost surely
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.le_condExp_of_tendsto

nodes.name: Proof of Submartingale bounded by conditional expectation of right limit
nodes.statement: By the submartingale property, for all $n$ we have that $X_t \le P[X_{t_n} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ almost surely. By Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.uniformIntegrable_of_antitone_of_ge}, the family $\{X_{t_n}\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable. TODO: conclude that $P[X_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ is the limit of $P[X_{t_n} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$.
nodes.statement_short: Submartingale property at each $t_n$ plus uniform integrability; passage to the limit left as TODO.

nodes.name: Submartingale property
nodes.statement: By the submartingale property, for all $n$ we have that $X_t \le P[X_{t_n} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $X_t$ by conditional expectations at $t_n$.

nodes.name: Uniform integrability
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.uniformIntegrable_of_antitone_of_ge}, the family $\{X_{t_n}\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable.
nodes.statement_short: Apply uniform integrability.

nodes.name: Pass to the limit (TODO)
nodes.statement: TODO: conclude that $P[X_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ is the limit of $P[X_{t_n} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$.

nodes.name: Cadlag modification of submartingales
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale with respect to a right-continuous filtration. Then $X$ has a cadlag modification if and only if $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[X_t]$ is right-continuous.
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a submartingale with respect to a right-continuous filtration.
conclusions: $X$ has a cadlag modification if and only if $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[X_t]$ is right-continuous
equivalent_conditions: $X$ has a cadlag modification
$t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[X_t]$ is right-continuous
nodes.label: thm:Submartingale.exists_cadlag_modification_iff_rightContinuous

nodes.name: Proof of Cadlag modification of submartingales
nodes.statement: Let $Y$ be the modification of $X$ given by Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.exists_modifications_limits}. $Y$ has left and right limits everywhere and there is a countable set $S$ such that $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$. It remains to show that for each $t \in S$, $Y$ is right-continuous at $t$ almost surely. We will then be able to modify $Y$ on a null set to obtain a cadlag modification of $X$. Let $t \in S$ and let $Y_{t+}$ denote the right limit of $Y$ at $t$. We show that $Y_t = P[Y_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ almost surely, and that $P[Y_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = Y_{t+}$ almost surely, which will conclude the proof. For the second equality it suffices to show that $Y_{t+}$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable, which follows from the right-continuity of the filtration. For the first equality, it suffices to show that $P[Y_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t] - Y_t$ is an almost surely nonnegative random variable with zero expectation. Nonnegative follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.le_condExp_of_tendsto}. The expectation is $P[Y_{t+}] - P[Y_t]$. Let $t_n$ be a decreasing sequence in $T$ converging to $t$. By right-continuity of $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[Y_t]$, we have that \begin{align*} P[Y_t] = \lim_{n \to \infty} P[Y_{t_n}] \: . \end{align*} By uniform integrability (Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.uniformIntegrable_of_antitone_of_ge}), we have that \begin{align*} P[Y_{t+}] = \lim_{n \to \infty} P[Y_{t_n}] \: . \end{align*} Therefore $P[Y_{t+}] = P[Y_t]$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Take the modification with limits; at each exceptional point show $Y_t=E[Y_{t+}|F_t]=Y_{t+}$ a.s. via right-continuity of the filtration, the conditional-expectation bound and uniform integrability.

nodes.name: Take modification
nodes.statement: Let $Y$ be the modification of $X$ given by Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.exists_modifications_limits}. $Y$ has left and right limits everywhere and there is a countable set $S$ such that $Y$ is right-continuous on $T \setminus S$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the submartingale modification with limits.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It remains to show that for each $t \in S$, $Y$ is right-continuous at $t$ almost surely. We will then be able to modify $Y$ on a null set to obtain a cadlag modification of $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a.s. right-continuity at points of $S$.

nodes.name: Second equality
nodes.statement: Let $t \in S$ and let $Y_{t+}$ denote the right limit of $Y$ at $t$. We show that $Y_t = P[Y_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ almost surely, and that $P[Y_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = Y_{t+}$ almost surely, which will conclude the proof. For the second equality it suffices to show that $Y_{t+}$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable, which follows from the right-continuity of the filtration.
nodes.statement_short: Split into two equalities; the second follows from right-continuity of the filtration.

nodes.name: First equality
nodes.statement: For the first equality, it suffices to show that $P[Y_{t+} \mid \mathcal{F}_t] - Y_t$ is an almost surely nonnegative random variable with zero expectation. Nonnegative follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.le_condExp_of_tendsto}. The expectation is $P[Y_{t+}] - P[Y_t]$. Let $t_n$ be a decreasing sequence in $T$ converging to $t$. By right-continuity of $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[Y_t]$, we have that \begin{align*} P[Y_t] = \lim_{n \to \infty} P[Y_{t_n}] \: . \end{align*} By uniform integrability (Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.uniformIntegrable_of_antitone_of_ge}), we have that \begin{align*} P[Y_{t+}] = \lim_{n \to \infty} P[Y_{t_n}] \: . \end{align*} Therefore $P[Y_{t+}] = P[Y_t]$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Show the difference is nonnegative with zero mean.

nodes.name: Nonnegativity
nodes.statement: Nonnegative follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.le_condExp_of_tendsto}.
nodes.statement_short: Nonnegativity from the conditional-expectation bound.

nodes.name: Setup sequence
nodes.statement: The expectation is $P[Y_{t+}] - P[Y_t]$. Let $t_n$ be a decreasing sequence in $T$ converging to $t$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce a decreasing sequence $t_n\downarrow t$.

nodes.name: Right-continuity of mean
nodes.statement: By right-continuity of $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[Y_t]$, we have that \begin{align*} P[Y_t] = \lim_{n \to \infty} P[Y_{t_n}] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Expectations at $t_n$ converge to $P[Y_t]$.

nodes.name: Uniform integrability
nodes.statement: By uniform integrability (Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.uniformIntegrable_of_antitone_of_ge}), we have that \begin{align*} P[Y_{t+}] = \lim_{n \to \infty} P[Y_{t_n}] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Uniform integrability gives convergence to $P[Y_{t+}]$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore $P[Y_{t+}] = P[Y_t]$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Means agree; conclude.

nodes.name: Cadlag modification of martingales
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a martingale with respect to a right-continuous filtration. Then $X$ has a cadlag modification.
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a martingale with respect to a right-continuous filtration.
conclusions: $X$ has a cadlag modification
nodes.label: thm:Martingale.exists_cadlag_modification

nodes.name: Proof of Cadlag modification of martingales
nodes.statement: $X$ is in particular a submartingale, and for all $t \in T$, we have that $\mathbb{E}[X_t] = \mathbb{E}[X_0]$ by the martingale property. Therefore $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[X_t]$ is right-continuous, and we can apply Theorem~\ref{thm:Submartingale.exists_cadlag_modification_iff_rightContinuous}.
nodes.statement_short: A martingale has constant expectation, so apply the submartingale criterion.

nodes.name: Cadlag modification of nonnegative submartingales
nodes.statement: Let the filtered probability space satisfy the usual conditions. Then every nonnegative submartingale $X$ admits a modification that is still a nonnegative submartingale with cadlag trajectories.
assumptions: Let the filtered probability space satisfy the usual conditions.
conclusions: every nonnegative submartingale $X$ admits a modification that is still a nonnegative submartingale with cadlag trajectories
nodes.label: lem:exists_cadlag_mod_of_nonneg_submg

nodes.name: Proof of Cadlag modification of nonnegative submartingales
nodes.statement: See 8.2.3 of Pascucci.
nodes.statement_short: Reference to Pascucci, Section 8.2.3.

nodes.name: Cadlag modification of local martingales
nodes.statement: Let the filtered probability space satisfy the usual conditions. Then every local martingale $X$ admits a modification that is still a local martingale with cadlag trajectories.
assumptions: Let the filtered probability space satisfy the usual conditions.
conclusions: every local martingale $X$ admits a modification that is still a local martingale with cadlag trajectories
nodes.label: lem:exists_cadlag_mod_of_local_mg

nodes.name: Komlòs lemma for a bounded functional
nodes.statement: Let $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in a vector space $E$ and $\phi : E \to \mathbb{R}_+$ be a function such that $\phi(f_n)$ is a bounded sequence. For $\delta > 0$, let $S_\delta = \{(f, g) \mid \phi(f)/2 + \phi(g)/2 - \phi((f+g)/2) \ge \delta\}$. Then there exist $g_n\in convex(f_n,f_{n+1},\cdots)$ such that for all $\delta > 0$, for $N$ large enough and $n, m \ge N$, $(g_n, g_m) \notin S_\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Forward convex combinations of a sequence with bounded $\phi$ eventually avoid every midpoint-convexity gap set $S_\delta$.
assumptions: $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in a vector space $E$
$\phi : E \to \mathbb{R}_+$ be a function such that $\phi(f_n)$ is a bounded sequence
For $\delta > 0$, let $S_\delta = \{(f, g) \mid \phi(f)/2 + \phi(g)/2 - \phi((f+g)/2) \ge \delta\}$.
conclusions: there exist $g_n\in convex(f_n,f_{n+1},\cdots)$ such that for all $\delta > 0$, for $N$ large enough and $n, m \ge N$, $(g_n, g_m) \notin S_\delta$
nodes.label: lem:komlos_convex

nodes.name: Proof of Komlòs lemma for a bounded functional
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be the bound of $(\phi(f_n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$. Then for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $g\in convex(f_n,f_{n+1},\cdots)$ we have $\phi(g)\le B$ by convexity of $\phi$. Let $r_n = \inf(\phi(g) \mid g\in convex(f_n, f_{n+1},\ldots))$. By construction $(r_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is nondecreasing. Let $A = \sup_{n \ge 1} r_n$, which is finite (as $A \le B$) and for each $n$ we may pick some $g_n\in convex(f_n, f_{n+1},\ldots)$ such that $\phi(g_n) \le A+1/n$ by $\inf$ and $\sup$ definitions. Let $\varepsilon \in (0, \delta/4)$. By properties of $\sup$ there exists $\bar{n}$ such that $r_{\bar{n}} \ge A-\varepsilon$ and such that $\frac{1}{\bar{n}} \le \varepsilon$. Let $m \ge k \ge \bar{n}$. We have $(g_k+g_m)/2 \in convex(f_k,f_{k+1},\ldots)$ and it follows since $(r_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is nondecreasing that $\phi((g_k+g_m)/2) \ge A - \varepsilon$.
