Hence due to the ordering of $m,k,\bar{n}$, \begin{align*} \phi(g_k)/2 + \phi(g_m)/2 - \phi((g_k+g_m)/2) &\le 2(A + \frac{1}{\bar{n}}) - 2(A - \varepsilon) \\ &\le 4 \varepsilon \\ &< \delta \: . \end{align*} Thus, for $n, m \ge \bar{n}$, $(g_n, g_m) \notin S_\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick near-minimizers $g_n$ of $\phi$ over forward convex hulls; since the infima $r_n$ increase to $A$, midpoint convexity gaps are at most $4\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Uniform bound on forward convex hulls
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be the bound of $(\phi(f_n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$. Then for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $g\in convex(f_n,f_{n+1},\cdots)$ we have $\phi(g)\le B$ by convexity of $\phi$.
nodes.statement_short: Convexity of $\phi$ bounds $\phi$ by $B$ on every forward convex hull.

nodes.name: Infima r_n
nodes.statement: Let $r_n = \inf(\phi(g) \mid g\in convex(f_n, f_{n+1},\ldots))$. By construction $(r_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is nondecreasing.
nodes.statement_short: Define the infima $r_n$, which are nondecreasing.

nodes.name: Near-minimizers g_n and choice of n-bar
nodes.statement: Let $A = \sup_{n \ge 1} r_n$, which is finite (as $A \le B$) and for each $n$ we may pick some $g_n\in convex(f_n, f_{n+1},\ldots)$ such that $\phi(g_n) \le A+1/n$ by $\inf$ and $\sup$ definitions. Let $\varepsilon \in (0, \delta/4)$. By properties of $\sup$ there exists $\bar{n}$ such that $r_{\bar{n}} \ge A-\varepsilon$ and such that $\frac{1}{\bar{n}} \le \varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $A = \sup r_n$, pick $g_n$ with $\phi(g_n) \le A + 1/n$, and choose $\bar n$ with $r_{\bar n} \ge A-\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Lower bound at midpoints
nodes.statement: Let $m \ge k \ge \bar{n}$. We have $(g_k+g_m)/2 \in convex(f_k,f_{k+1},\ldots)$ and it follows since $(r_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is nondecreasing that $\phi((g_k+g_m)/2) \ge A - \varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Midpoints lie in a forward hull, so $\phi$ there is at least $A-\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Convexity gap below delta
nodes.statement: Hence due to the ordering of $m,k,\bar{n}$, \begin{align*} \phi(g_k)/2 + \phi(g_m)/2 - \phi((g_k+g_m)/2) &\le 2(A + \frac{1}{\bar{n}}) - 2(A - \varepsilon) \\ &\le 4 \varepsilon \\ &< \delta \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The convexity gap is at most $4\varepsilon < \delta$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Thus, for $n, m \ge \bar{n}$, $(g_n, g_m) \notin S_\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Pairs beyond $\bar n$ avoid $S_\delta$.

nodes.name: Komlòs lemma in Hilbert space
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space and $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ a bounded sequence in $H$. Then there exist functions $g_n\in convex(f_n,f_{n+1},\cdots)$ such that $(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ converges in $H$.
assumptions: $H$ be a Hilbert space
$(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ a bounded sequence in $H$
conclusions: there exist functions $g_n\in convex(f_n,f_{n+1},\cdots)$ such that $(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ converges in $H$
nodes.label: lem:komlos_norm

nodes.name: Proof of Komlòs lemma in Hilbert space
nodes.statement: Consider $\phi : H \to \mathbb{R}_+$ defined by $\phi(f) = \|f\|_2^2$, which is convex. Then Lemma \ref{lem:komlos_convex} applied to $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $\phi$ gives us functions $g_n\in convex(f_n,f_{n+1},\cdots)$ such that for every $\delta>0$ there exists $N$ such that for $n,m\geq N$, $(g_n,g_m)\notin S_\delta$. Thus for every $\delta>0$ there exists $N$ such that for $n,m\geq N$, \begin{align*} \|g_n\|_2^2/2 + \|g_m\|_2^2/2 - \|(g_n+g_m)/2\|_2^2 &< \delta \: . \end{align*} But the left-hand side is equal to $\|g_n - g_m\|_2^2/4$ by the parallelogram identity, hence $(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $H$ and thus converges in $H$ by completeness.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the abstract Komlòs lemma to $\phi = \|\cdot\|^2$; the parallelogram identity turns small convexity gaps into a Cauchy sequence.

nodes.name: Apply abstract Komlòs lemma to the squared norm
nodes.statement: Consider $\phi : H \to \mathbb{R}_+$ defined by $\phi(f) = \|f\|_2^2$, which is convex. Then Lemma \ref{lem:komlos_convex} applied to $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $\phi$ gives us functions $g_n\in convex(f_n,f_{n+1},\cdots)$ such that for every $\delta>0$ there exists $N$ such that for $n,m\geq N$, $(g_n,g_m)\notin S_\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the abstract lemma with $\phi = \|\cdot\|_2^2$.

nodes.name: Small convexity gaps
nodes.statement: Thus for every $\delta>0$ there exists $N$ such that for $n,m\geq N$, \begin{align*} \|g_n\|_2^2/2 + \|g_m\|_2^2/2 - \|(g_n+g_m)/2\|_2^2 &< \delta \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Convexity gaps of the squared norm are eventually below $\delta$.

nodes.name: Cauchy by parallelogram identity
nodes.statement: But the left-hand side is equal to $\|g_n - g_m\|_2^2/4$ by the parallelogram identity, hence $(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $H$ and thus converges in $H$ by completeness.
nodes.statement_short: The gap equals $\|g_n-g_m\|^2/4$, so $(g_n)$ is Cauchy and converges.

nodes.name: Convex combinations of a convergent sequence converge uniformly
nodes.statement: Let $(x_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in a real vector space converging to $x$. Let $\mathcal{C}((x_n))$ be the set of sequences $(y_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n$, $y_n \in convex(x_n, x_{n+1}, \ldots)$. Then we have uniform convergence over $\mathcal{C}((x_n))$: for all $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\bar{n}$ such that for all $n \ge \bar{n}$, for all $(y_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \in \mathcal{C}((x_n))$, $\Vert y_n - x \Vert \le \varepsilon$;
assumptions: $(x_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in a real vector space converging to $x$
Let $\mathcal{C}((x_n))$ be the set of sequences $(y_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all $n$, $y_n \in convex(x_n, x_{n+1}, \ldots)$.
conclusions: we have uniform convergence over $\mathcal{C}((x_n))$: for all $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\bar{n}$ such that for all $n \ge \bar{n}$, for all $(y_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \in \mathcal{C}((x_n))$, $\Vert y_n - x \Vert \le \varepsilon$
nodes.label: lem:convex_of_converg_seq_is_converg

nodes.name: Proof of Convex combinations of a convergent sequence converge uniformly
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon>0$. By convergence of $x_n$, there exists $\bar{n}$ such that for all $n \ge \bar{n}$, $\Vert x_n-x \Vert \le \varepsilon$. Let $a_{n, m}$ be convex weights such that $y_n = \sum_{m = n}^{N_n} a_{n, m} x_m$. By triangular inequality it follows that for $n \ge \bar{n}$, \begin{align*} \Vert y_n - x \Vert = \left\Vert \sum_{m = n}^{N_n} a_{n, m} x_m - x \right\Vert = \left\Vert \sum_{m = n}^{N_n} a_{n, m} (x_m - x) \right\Vert \le \sum_{m = n}^{N_n} a_{n, m} \Vert x_m - x \Vert \le \varepsilon \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality: a convex combination of terms within $\varepsilon$ of $x$ is within $\varepsilon$ of $x$.

nodes.name: Tail of the sequence close to x
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon>0$. By convergence of $x_n$, there exists $\bar{n}$ such that for all $n \ge \bar{n}$, $\Vert x_n-x \Vert \le \varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\bar n$ with $\|x_n - x\| \le \varepsilon$ beyond it.

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
nodes.statement: Let $a_{n, m}$ be convex weights such that $y_n = \sum_{m = n}^{N_n} a_{n, m} x_m$. By triangular inequality it follows that for $n \ge \bar{n}$, \begin{align*} \Vert y_n - x \Vert = \left\Vert \sum_{m = n}^{N_n} a_{n, m} x_m - x \right\Vert = \left\Vert \sum_{m = n}^{N_n} a_{n, m} (x_m - x) \right\Vert \le \sum_{m = n}^{N_n} a_{n, m} \Vert x_m - x \Vert \le \varepsilon \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $y_n$ with convex weights and bound by the triangle inequality.

nodes.name: Convex weights
differentia: with finitely many nonzero entries
such that $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}} a_n = 1$
nodes.statement: By convex weights on $\mathbb{N}$, we mean a sequence of non-negative real numbers $(a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with finitely many nonzero entries such that $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}} a_n = 1$.

nodes.name: Product of convex weights
nodes.statement: If $(a_m)_{m \in \mathbb{N}}$ are convex weights and $(b^n_m)_{n,m \in \mathbb{N}}$ is such that for all $n$, the $(b^n_m)$ are convex weights, then we denote by $(a_\cdot) * (b^\cdot_\cdot)$ the convex weights defined by $((a_\cdot) * (b^\cdot_\cdot))_m = \sum_{k} a_k b^k_m$.
nodes.statement_short: Composition of convex weights: $((a)*(b))_m = \sum_k a_k b^k_m$.
nodes.label: def:convex_weights_product

nodes.name: Komlòs lemma for countably many sequences (iterated weights)
nodes.statement: Let $E$ be a Hilbert space and for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, let $(x_n^{(i)})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $E$. Then there exists a sequence of convex weights $(\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot)_{k, n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $\lambda^{k,n}_m = 0$ for $m < n$ such that for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $\left(\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(k)}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges.
nodes.statement_short: Iterated convex weights make the $k$-th sequence's forward convex combinations converge, for every $k$.
assumptions: $E$ be a Hilbert space
for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, let $(x_n^{(i)})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $E$
conclusions: there exists a sequence of convex weights $(\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot)_{k, n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $\lambda^{k,n}_m = 0$ for $m < n$ such that for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $\left(\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(k)}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges
nodes.label: lem:komlos_convex_weights

nodes.name: Proof of Komlòs lemma for countably many sequences (iterated weights)
nodes.statement: First by Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_norm} applied to $(x_n^{(1)})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in the Hilbert space $E$, there exist $g_n^1 \in convex(x_n^{(1)}, x_{n+1}^{(1)}, \ldots)$ (call its weights $\lambda^{1,n}_n,\cdots,\lambda^{1,n}_{N^1_n}$) such that $g_n^1$ converges to some $g^1$. Secondly define $\tilde{g}_n^1$, convex combination of $x_n^{(2)}, x_{n+1}^{(2)}, \ldots$ with weights $\lambda^{1,n}_n,\cdots,\lambda^{1,n}_{N^1_n}$. Applying lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_norm} to $(\tilde{g}_n^1)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ gives us $g_n^2 \in convex(\tilde{g}_n^1, \tilde{g}_{n+1}^1, \ldots)$ (call its weights $\lambda^{2,n}_n,\cdots,\lambda^{2,n}_{N^2_n}$) such that $g_n^2$ converges to some $g^2$. $g_n^2$ is a convex combination of $x_n^{(2)}, x_{n+1}^{(2)}, \ldots$ with weights $(\lambda^{2,n}_\cdot) * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)$. We continue iterating this process inductively. At iteration $k$ we have weights $(\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)$. We define $\tilde{g}_n^k$ as the convex combination of $x_n^{(k+1)}, x_{n+1}^{(k+1)}, \ldots$ with those weights: \[ \tilde{g}_n^k = \sum_{l} (\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)_l x^{(k+1)}_l \] We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_norm} to $(\tilde{g}_n^k)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ to get $g_n^{k+1} \in convex(\tilde{g}_n^k, \tilde{g}_{n+1}^k, \ldots)$ such that $g_n^{k+1}$ converges to some $g^{k+1}$. We denote its weights by $\lambda^{k+1,n}_n,\cdots,\lambda^{k+1,n}_{N^{k+1}_n}$ and can then write: \begin{align*} g_n^{k+1} & = \sum_{m} \lambda^{k+1,n}_m \tilde{g}_m^k = \sum_{m} \lambda^{k+1,n}_m \left( \sum_{l} (\lambda^{k,m}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)_l x_l^{(k+1)} \right) \\ & = \sum_{l} \left( \sum_{m} \lambda^{k+1,n}_m (\lambda^{k,m}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)_l \right) x_l^{(k+1)} \\ & = \sum_{l} (\lambda^{k+1,n}_{\cdot} * (\lambda^{k,\cdot}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot))_l x_l^{(k+1)} \end{align*} We have thus defined, for all $k, n \in \mathbb{N}$, convex weights $(\lambda^{k,n}_m)$ (that are zero for $m < n$) such that $\sum_{m \ge n}((\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1, \cdot}_\cdot))_m x_m^{(k)}$ converges to $g^k$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$: apply the Hilbert-space Komlòs lemma to the $k$-th sequence reweighted by the previously composed weights.

nodes.name: First sequence
nodes.statement: First by Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_norm} applied to $(x_n^{(1)})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in the Hilbert space $E$, there exist $g_n^1 \in convex(x_n^{(1)}, x_{n+1}^{(1)}, \ldots)$ (call its weights $\lambda^{1,n}_n,\cdots,\lambda^{1,n}_{N^1_n}$) such that $g_n^1$ converges to some $g^1$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Hilbert-space Komlòs lemma to the first sequence.

nodes.name: Second sequence
nodes.statement: Secondly define $\tilde{g}_n^1$, convex combination of $x_n^{(2)}, x_{n+1}^{(2)}, \ldots$ with weights $\lambda^{1,n}_n,\cdots,\lambda^{1,n}_{N^1_n}$. Applying lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_norm} to $(\tilde{g}_n^1)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ gives us $g_n^2 \in convex(\tilde{g}_n^1, \tilde{g}_{n+1}^1, \ldots)$ (call its weights $\lambda^{2,n}_n,\cdots,\lambda^{2,n}_{N^2_n}$) such that $g_n^2$ converges to some $g^2$. $g_n^2$ is a convex combination of $x_n^{(2)}, x_{n+1}^{(2)}, \ldots$ with weights $(\lambda^{2,n}_\cdot) * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reweight the second sequence and apply the lemma again; weights compose.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: We continue iterating this process inductively. At iteration $k$ we have weights $(\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)$. We define $\tilde{g}_n^k$ as the convex combination of $x_n^{(k+1)}, x_{n+1}^{(k+1)}, \ldots$ with those weights: \[ \tilde{g}_n^k = \sum_{l} (\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)_l x^{(k+1)}_l \] We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_norm} to $(\tilde{g}_n^k)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ to get $g_n^{k+1} \in convex(\tilde{g}_n^k, \tilde{g}_{n+1}^k, \ldots)$ such that $g_n^{k+1}$ converges to some $g^{k+1}$. We denote its weights by $\lambda^{k+1,n}_n,\cdots,\lambda^{k+1,n}_{N^{k+1}_n}$ and can then write: \begin{align*} g_n^{k+1} & = \sum_{m} \lambda^{k+1,n}_m \tilde{g}_m^k = \sum_{m} \lambda^{k+1,n}_m \left( \sum_{l} (\lambda^{k,m}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)_l x_l^{(k+1)} \right) \\ & = \sum_{l} \left( \sum_{m} \lambda^{k+1,n}_m (\lambda^{k,m}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)_l \right) x_l^{(k+1)} \\ & = \sum_{l} (\lambda^{k+1,n}_{\cdot} * (\lambda^{k,\cdot}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot))_l x_l^{(k+1)} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: At step $k+1$ reweight by the composed weights and apply the lemma; compute the composed weights.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: We have thus defined, for all $k, n \in \mathbb{N}$, convex weights $(\lambda^{k,n}_m)$ (that are zero for $m < n$) such that $\sum_{m \ge n}((\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1, \cdot}_\cdot))_m x_m^{(k)}$ converges to $g^k$.
nodes.statement_short: This defines the required convex weights for all $k$.

nodes.name: Iterated Komlòs weights converge uniformly in k
nodes.statement: Let $E$ be a Hilbert space and for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, let $(x_n^{(i)})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $E$. Let $(\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot)_{k, n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be convex weights satisfying the conclusion of Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_convex_weights}, and let $(g^i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$ be the sequence of limits of the sums. Then for every $k \ge i$, the sequence $\left(\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(i)}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges to $g^i$, uniformly in $k$.
assumptions: $E$ be a Hilbert space
for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, let $(x_n^{(i)})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $E$

Let $(\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot)_{k, n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be convex weights satisfying the conclusion of Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_convex_weights}, and let $(g^i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$ be the sequence of limits of the sums.
conclusions: for every $k \ge i$, the sequence $\left(\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(i)}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges to $g^i$, uniformly in $k$
nodes.label: lem:komlos_convex_weights_tendsto

nodes.name: Proof of Iterated Komlòs weights converge uniformly in k
nodes.statement: Let $i \in \mathbb{N}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:convex_of_converg_seq_is_converg}, there is uniform convergence over all convex combinations of the sequence $\left(\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{i,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(i)}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ to $g^i$. All sums $\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(i)}$ for $k \ge i$ are convex combinations of $\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{i,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(i)}$, hence they converge to $g^i$ uniformly in $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Later weighted sums are convex combinations of the $i$-th ones, so uniform convergence of convex combinations applies.

nodes.name: Uniform convergence of convex combinations
nodes.statement: Let $i \in \mathbb{N}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:convex_of_converg_seq_is_converg}, there is uniform convergence over all convex combinations of the sequence $\left(\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{i,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(i)}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ to $g^i$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply uniform convergence of convex combinations to the $i$-th weighted sums.

nodes.name: Later sums are convex combinations
nodes.statement: All sums $\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(i)}$ for $k \ge i$ are convex combinations of $\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{i,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(i)}$, hence they converge to $g^i$ uniformly in $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Sums for $k \ge i$ are convex combinations of those, hence converge uniformly in $k$.

nodes.name: Diagonal Komlòs weights
nodes.statement: Let $E$ be a Hilbert space and for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, let $(x_n^{(i)})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $E$. Then there exists a sequence of convex weights $(\eta^n_\cdot)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $\eta^n_m = 0$ for $m < n$ such that for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the sequence $\left(\sum_{m \ge n} \eta^n_m x_m^{(i)}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges.
nodes.statement_short: A single diagonal family of convex weights makes all countably many sequences converge simultaneously.
assumptions: $E$ be a Hilbert space
for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, let $(x_n^{(i)})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $E$
conclusions: there exists a sequence of convex weights $(\eta^n_\cdot)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $\eta^n_m = 0$ for $m < n$ such that for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the sequence $\left(\sum_{m \ge n} \eta^n_m x_m^{(i)}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges
nodes.label: lem:komlos_convex_weights_diagonal

nodes.name: Proof of Diagonal Komlòs weights
nodes.statement: Let $(\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot)_{k, n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be convex weights satisfying the conclusion of Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_convex_weights}, and let $(g^i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$ be the sequence of limits of the sums. Let $\eta^n_m = (\lambda^{n,n}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)_m$. We show that for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the sequence $\left(\sum_{m \ge n} \eta^n_m x_m^{(i)}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges to $g^i$. Let $i \in \mathbb{N}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_convex_weights_tendsto}, for all $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\bar{n}$ such that for all $n \ge \bar{n}$, for all $k \ge i$, $\left\Vert\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(i)} - g^i\right\Vert \le \varepsilon$. Hence for $n \ge \max(\bar{n}, i)$, \begin{align*} \left\Vert\sum_{m \ge n} \eta^n_m x_m^{(i)} - g^i\right\Vert &= \left\Vert\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{n,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(i)} - g^i\right\Vert \le \varepsilon \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal argument: take $\eta^n = \lambda^{n,n} * \dots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}$ and use uniform convergence in $k$.

nodes.name: Diagonal weights
nodes.statement: Let $(\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot)_{k, n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be convex weights satisfying the conclusion of Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_convex_weights}, and let $(g^i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$ be the sequence of limits of the sums. Let $\eta^n_m = (\lambda^{n,n}_\cdot * \ldots * \lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)_m$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the iterated weights and define the diagonal weights $\eta^n$.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We show that for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the sequence $\left(\sum_{m \ge n} \eta^n_m x_m^{(i)}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges to $g^i$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to show convergence to $g^i$ for each $i$.

nodes.name: Uniform convergence in k
nodes.statement: Let $i \in \mathbb{N}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_convex_weights_tendsto}, for all $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\bar{n}$ such that for all $n \ge \bar{n}$, for all $k \ge i$, $\left\Vert\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{k,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(i)} - g^i\right\Vert \le \varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform convergence in $k$ gives $\bar n$ independent of $k$.

nodes.name: Diagonal estimate
nodes.statement: Hence for $n \ge \max(\bar{n}, i)$, \begin{align*} \left\Vert\sum_{m \ge n} \eta^n_m x_m^{(i)} - g^i\right\Vert &= \left\Vert\sum_{m \ge n} \left((\lambda^{n,n}_\cdot) * \ldots * (\lambda^{1,\cdot}_\cdot)\right)_m x_m^{(i)} - g^i\right\Vert \le \varepsilon \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Take $k = n$ to bound the diagonal sums.

nodes.name: Komlòs lemma for truncations in L2
nodes.statement: Let $E$ be a Hilbert space and let $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $\Omega \to E$. For $i \in \mathbb{N}$, set $f_n^{(i)} = f_n \mathbb{1}_{(\Vert f_n \Vert \le i)}$, such that $f_n^{(i)} \in L^2(E)$. Then there exists a sequence of convex weights $\lambda_n^{n}, \ldots, \lambda_{N_n}^{n}$ such that the functions $\left(\lambda_n^{n} f_n^{(i)} + \ldots + \lambda_{N_n}^{n} f_{N_n}^{(i)} \right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ converge in $L^2(E)$ for every $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
assumptions: $E$ be a Hilbert space
let $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $\Omega \to E$
For $i \in \mathbb{N}$, set $f_n^{(i)} = f_n \mathbb{1}_{(\Vert f_n \Vert \le i)}$, such that $f_n^{(i)} \in L^2(E)$.
conclusions: there exists a sequence of convex weights $\lambda_n^{n}, \ldots, \lambda_{N_n}^{n}$ such that the functions $\left(\lambda_n^{n} f_n^{(i)} + \ldots + \lambda_{N_n}^{n} f_{N_n}^{(i)} \right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ converge in $L^2(E)$ for every $i \in \mathbb{N}$
nodes.label: lem:komlos_convex_aux

nodes.name: Proof of Komlòs lemma for truncations in L2
nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_convex_weights_diagonal} in the Hilbert space $L^2(E)$ with the sequence of sequences $(f_n^{(i)})$, which are bounded in $L^2(E)$ for each $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the diagonal Komlòs lemma in $L^2(E)$ to the bounded truncated sequences.

nodes.name: Komlòs Lemma
nodes.statement: Let $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a uniformly integrable sequence of functions $\Omega \to E$, for $E$ a Hilbert space. Then there exist functions $g_n \in convex(f_n, f_{n+1}, \cdots)$ such that $(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ converges in $L^1$.
assumptions: $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a uniformly integrable sequence of functions $\Omega \to E$, for $E$ a Hilbert space
conclusions: there exist functions $g_n \in convex(f_n, f_{n+1}, \cdots)$ such that $(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ converges in $L^1$
nodes.label: lem:komlos

nodes.name: Proof of Komlòs Lemma
nodes.statement: For $i,n\in\mathbb{N}$ set $f_{n}^{(i)}:=f_n \mathbb{1}_{(|f_n|\leq i)}$ such that $f_{n}^{(i)}\in L^2$. Using \ref{lem:komlos_convex_aux} there exist for every $n$ convex weights $\lambda_n^{n}, \ldots, \lambda_{N_n}^{n}$ such that the functions $ \lambda_n^{n} f_n^{(i)} + \ldots+\lambda_{N_n}^{n} f_{N_n}^{(i)}$ converge in $L^2$ for every $i\in\mathbb{N}$. By uniform integrability, $\lim_{i\to \infty}\| f^{(i)}_n- f_n\|_1=0$, uniformly with respect to $n$. Hence, once again, uniformly with respect to $n$, $$ \textstyle\lim_{i\to\infty}\| (\lambda_n^{n} f_n^{(i)} + \ldots+\lambda_{N_n}^{n} f_{N_n}^{(i)})-(\lambda_n^{n} f_n + \ldots+\lambda_{N_n}^{n} f_{N_n})\|_1= 0.$$ Thus $(\lambda_n^{n} f_n + \ldots+\lambda_{N_n}^{n} f_{N_n})_{n\geq 1}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L^1$.
nodes.statement_short: Truncate at level $i$, get $L^2$-convergent convex combinations for all $i$, and use uniform integrability to pass to $L^1$ Cauchy.

nodes.name: Truncations
nodes.statement: For $i,n\in\mathbb{N}$ set $f_{n}^{(i)}:=f_n \mathbb{1}_{(|f_n|\leq i)}$ such that $f_{n}^{(i)}\in L^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Truncate $f_n$ at level $i$ to get $L^2$ functions.

nodes.name: Common convex weights
nodes.statement: Using \ref{lem:komlos_convex_aux} there exist for every $n$ convex weights $\lambda_n^{n}, \ldots, \lambda_{N_n}^{n}$ such that the functions $ \lambda_n^{n} f_n^{(i)} + \ldots+\lambda_{N_n}^{n} f_{N_n}^{(i)}$ converge in $L^2$ for every $i\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Get convex weights making all truncated combinations converge in $L^2$.

nodes.name: Truncation error
nodes.statement: By uniform integrability, $\lim_{i\to \infty}\| f^{(i)}_n- f_n\|_1=0$, uniformly with respect to $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform integrability makes truncation errors small uniformly in $n$.

nodes.name: Truncation error of combinations
nodes.statement: Hence, once again, uniformly with respect to $n$, $$ \textstyle\lim_{i\to\infty}\| (\lambda_n^{n} f_n^{(i)} + \ldots+\lambda_{N_n}^{n} f_{N_n}^{(i)})-(\lambda_n^{n} f_n + \ldots+\lambda_{N_n}^{n} f_{N_n})\|_1= 0.$$
nodes.statement_short: The same holds for the convex combinations.

nodes.name: Cauchy in L1
nodes.statement: Thus $(\lambda_n^{n} f_n + \ldots+\lambda_{N_n}^{n} f_{N_n})_{n\geq 1}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L^1$.
nodes.statement_short: The untruncated combinations are Cauchy in $L^1$.

nodes.name: Komlòs lemma for nonnegative random variables
nodes.statement: Let $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of random variables with values in $[0, \infty]$. Then there exist random variables $g_n \in convex( f_n, f_{n+1}, \cdots)$ such that $(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ converges almost surely to a random variable $g$.
assumptions: $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of random variables with values in $[0, \infty]$
conclusions: there exist random variables $g_n \in convex( f_n, f_{n+1}, \cdots)$ such that $(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ converges almost surely to a random variable $g$
nodes.label: lem:komlos_ennreal

nodes.name: Proof of Komlòs lemma for nonnegative random variables
nodes.statement: Let $\phi : (\Omega \to [0, \infty]) \to [0, \infty]$ be defined by $\phi(X) = \mathbb{E}[e^{-X}]$. Then $\phi$ is convex and $\phi(f_n) \le 1$ for all $n$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_convex}, there exist $g_n \in convex( f_n, f_{n+1}, \cdots)$ such that for all $\delta>0$, for $N$ large enough and $n, m \ge N$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[e^{-g_n}]/2 + \mathbb{E}[e^{-g_m}]/2 - \mathbb{E}[e^{-(g_n + g_m)/2}] < \delta \: . \end{align*} For $\varepsilon > 0$, let $B_\varepsilon = \{(x, y) \in [0, \infty]^2 \mid \vert x - y \vert \ge \varepsilon \text{ and } \min\{x, y\} \le 1/\varepsilon \}$. Then for all $x, y$, \begin{align*} \left\vert e^{-x} - e^{-y} \right\vert &\le \varepsilon + 2 e^{-1/\varepsilon} + 2 \mathbb{1}_{B_\varepsilon}(x, y) \: . \end{align*} Hence for any pair of random variables $(X, Y)$ with values in $[0, \infty]$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\left\vert e^{-X} - e^{-Y} \right\vert\right] &\le \varepsilon + 2 e^{-1/\varepsilon} + 2 P((X, Y) \in B_\varepsilon) \: . \end{align*} On the other hand, for $(x, y) \in B_\varepsilon$, there exists $\delta_\varepsilon > 0$ such that \begin{align*} e^{-x}/2 + e^{-y}/2 - e^{-(x + y)/2} \ge \delta_\varepsilon \: . \end{align*} Thus, \begin{align*} P((X, Y) \in B_\varepsilon) &\le \frac{1}{\delta_\varepsilon} \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{-X}/2 + e^{-Y}/2 - e^{-(X + Y)/2} \right] \: . \end{align*} For $n, m \ge N$ large enough so that we can apply the first inequality of this proof with $\delta = \varepsilon \delta_\varepsilon$, we deduce that \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\left\vert e^{-g_n} - e^{-g_m} \right\vert\right] &\le \varepsilon + 2 e^{-1/\varepsilon} + \frac{2}{\delta_\varepsilon} \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{-g_n}/2 + e^{-g_m}/2 - e^{-(g_n + g_m)/2} \right] \\ &\le \varepsilon + 2 e^{-1/\varepsilon} + 2 \varepsilon \: . \end{align*} As $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, we deduce that $(e^{-g_n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L^1$ and thus converges in $L^1$ to some random variable $h$. Therefore, it has a subsequence $(e^{-g_{n_k}})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ converging almost surely to $h$. Finally, the subsequence of $g_n$ converges almost surely to $g = -\log(h)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the abstract Komlòs lemma to $\phi(X)=\mathbb{E}[e^{-X}]$; bound $\mathbb{E}|e^{-g_n}-e^{-g_m}|$ to get $L^1$-Cauchy, then extract an a.s. subsequence.

nodes.name: Functional E[exp(-X)]
nodes.statement: Let $\phi : (\Omega \to [0, \infty]) \to [0, \infty]$ be defined by $\phi(X) = \mathbb{E}[e^{-X}]$. Then $\phi$ is convex and $\phi(f_n) \le 1$ for all $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the convex bounded functional $\phi(X) = \mathbb{E}[e^{-X}]$.

nodes.name: Apply abstract Komlòs lemma
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:komlos_convex}, there exist $g_n \in convex( f_n, f_{n+1}, \cdots)$ such that for all $\delta>0$, for $N$ large enough and $n, m \ge N$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[e^{-g_n}]/2 + \mathbb{E}[e^{-g_m}]/2 - \mathbb{E}[e^{-(g_n + g_m)/2}] < \delta \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Get $g_n$ with eventually small convexity gaps of $\phi$.

nodes.name: Pointwise bound via B_eps
nodes.statement: For $\varepsilon > 0$, let $B_\varepsilon = \{(x, y) \in [0, \infty]^2 \mid \vert x - y \vert \ge \varepsilon \text{ and } \min\{x, y\} \le 1/\varepsilon \}$. Then for all $x, y$, \begin{align*} \left\vert e^{-x} - e^{-y} \right\vert &\le \varepsilon + 2 e^{-1/\varepsilon} + 2 \mathbb{1}_{B_\varepsilon}(x, y) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|e^{-x}-e^{-y}|$ using the set $B_\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Bound in expectation
nodes.statement: Hence for any pair of random variables $(X, Y)$ with values in $[0, \infty]$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\left\vert e^{-X} - e^{-Y} \right\vert\right] &\le \varepsilon + 2 e^{-1/\varepsilon} + 2 P((X, Y) \in B_\varepsilon) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Take expectations of the pointwise bound.

nodes.name: Gap on B_eps
nodes.statement: On the other hand, for $(x, y) \in B_\varepsilon$, there exists $\delta_\varepsilon > 0$ such that \begin{align*} e^{-x}/2 + e^{-y}/2 - e^{-(x + y)/2} \ge \delta_\varepsilon \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: On $B_\varepsilon$ the midpoint convexity gap of $e^{-x}$ is at least $\delta_\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Markov bound on B_eps
nodes.statement: Thus, \begin{align*} P((X, Y) \in B_\varepsilon) &\le \frac{1}{\delta_\varepsilon} \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{-X}/2 + e^{-Y}/2 - e^{-(X + Y)/2} \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the probability of $B_\varepsilon$ by the expected gap.

nodes.name: Combine estimates
nodes.statement: For $n, m \ge N$ large enough so that we can apply the first inequality of this proof with $\delta = \varepsilon \delta_\varepsilon$, we deduce that \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\left\vert e^{-g_n} - e^{-g_m} \right\vert\right] &\le \varepsilon + 2 e^{-1/\varepsilon} + \frac{2}{\delta_\varepsilon} \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{-g_n}/2 + e^{-g_m}/2 - e^{-(g_n + g_m)/2} \right] \\ &\le \varepsilon + 2 e^{-1/\varepsilon} + 2 \varepsilon \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Combine to bound $\mathbb{E}|e^{-g_n}-e^{-g_m}|$ by $3\varepsilon + 2e^{-1/\varepsilon}$.

nodes.name: Cauchy in L1
nodes.statement: As $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, we deduce that $(e^{-g_n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L^1$ and thus converges in $L^1$ to some random variable $h$.
nodes.statement_short: $(e^{-g_n})$ is Cauchy in $L^1$ and converges to some $h$.

nodes.name: Almost sure limit
nodes.statement: Therefore, it has a subsequence $(e^{-g_{n_k}})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ converging almost surely to $h$. Finally, the subsequence of $g_n$ converges almost surely to $g = -\log(h)$.
nodes.statement_short: Extract an a.s. convergent subsequence and set $g = -\log h$.

nodes.name: Predictable part
nodes.statement: Let $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to E$ be a process indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, for $E$ a Banach space. Let $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration on $\Omega$. The predictable part of $X$ is the process $A : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to E$ defined for $n \ge 0$ by $$A_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \mathbb{E}[X_{k+1}-X_k \mid \mathcal{F}_k].$$
nodes.statement_short: Predictable part of the Doob decomposition: $A_n = \sum_{k<n} \mathbb{E}[X_{k+1}-X_k \mid \mathcal{F}_k]$.
nodes.label: def:predictablePart

nodes.name: Martingale part
nodes.statement: Let $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to E$ be a process indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, for $E$ a Banach space. Let $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration on $\Omega$ and let $A$ be the predictable part of $X$ for that filtration. The martingale part of $X$ is the process $M : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to E$ defined by $M_n = X_n - A_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Martingale part of the Doob decomposition: $M = X - A$.
nodes.label: def:martingalePart

nodes.name: Standing notation for the Doob decomposition
nodes.statement: In what follows, we fix a process $X : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to E$ and a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, and denote by $A$ the predictable part of $X$ and by $M$ its martingale part.

nodes.name: Predictable part starts at zero
nodes.statement: We have $A_0 = 0$.
nodes.label: lem:predictablePart_zero

nodes.name: Proof of Predictable part starts at zero
nodes.statement: By definition.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition (empty sum).

nodes.name: Proof of Martingale part starts at X_0
nodes.statement: By definition of the martingale part, $M = X - A$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_zero}, $A_0 = 0$, thus $M_0 = X_0 - A_0 = X_0$.

nodes.name: Recursion for the predictable part
nodes.statement: For any integer $n \ge 0$, $A_{n+1} = A_n + \mathbb{E}[X_{n+1} - X_n \mid \mathcal{F}_n]$.
assumptions: For any integer $n \ge 0$
conclusions: $A_{n+1} = A_n + \mathbb{E}[X_{n+1} - X_n \mid \mathcal{F}_n]$
nodes.label: lem:predictablePart_add_one

nodes.name: Proof of Recursion for the predictable part
nodes.statement: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then \begin{align*} A_{n+1} & = \sum_{k=0}^n \mathbb{E}[X_{k+1}-X_k \mid \mathcal{F}_k] \\ & = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \mathbb{E}[X_{k+1}-X_k \mid \mathcal{F}_k] + \mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}-X_n \mid \mathcal{F}_n] \\ & = A_n + \mathbb{E}[X_{n+1} - X_n \mid \mathcal{F}_n], \end{align*} which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Split off the last term of the defining sum.

nodes.name: Recursion for the martingale part
nodes.statement: $M_{n+1} = M_n + X_{n+1} - X_n - \mathbb{E}[X_{n+1} - X_n \mid \mathcal{F}_n]$.
conclusions: $M_{n+1} = M_n + X_{n+1} - X_n - \mathbb{E}[X_{n+1} - X_n \mid \mathcal{F}_n]$
nodes.label: lem:martingalePart_add_one

nodes.name: Proof of Recursion for the martingale part
nodes.statement: Using Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_add_one}, we have for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, \begin{align*} M_{n+1} & = X_{n+1} - A_{n+1} \\ & = X_{n+1} - A_n - \mathbb{E}[X_{n+1} - X_n \mid \mathcal{F}_n] \\ & = M_n + X_{n+1} - X_n - \mathbb{E}[X_{n+1} - X_n \mid \mathcal{F}_n] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the predictable-part recursion into $M = X - A$.

nodes.name: Predictable part of a martingale vanishes
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a martingale, then $A = 0$ almost surely.
assumptions: $X$ is a martingale
conclusions: $A = 0$ almost surely
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.predictablePart_eq_zero

nodes.name: Proof of Predictable part of a martingale vanishes
nodes.statement: By the martingale property, each conditional expectation in the definition of $A$ is zero.
nodes.statement_short: Each conditional increment vanishes by the martingale property.

nodes.name: Predictable part of a predictable process
nodes.statement: If $X$ is predictable, then $A = X - X_0$ almost surely.
assumptions: $X$ is predictable
conclusions: $A = X - X_0$ almost surely
nodes.label: lem:isStronglyPredictable.predictablePart_eq

nodes.name: Proof of Predictable part of a predictable process
nodes.statement: Since $X$ is predictable, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $X_{n+1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable and thus $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1} - X_n \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = X_{n+1} - X_n$ a.s.. We get a telescoping sum in the definition of $A$ and thus $A_n = X_n - X_0$ a.s. for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Predictability makes each conditional increment equal to the increment, giving a telescoping sum.

nodes.name: Martingale part of a predictable process
nodes.statement: If $X$ is predictable, then $M = X_0$ almost surely.
assumptions: $X$ is predictable
conclusions: $M = X_0$ almost surely
nodes.label: lem:martingalePart_eq_zero

nodes.name: Proof of Martingale part of a predictable process
nodes.statement: By definition of the martingale part, $M = X - A$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:isStronglyPredictable.predictablePart_eq}, $A = X - X_0$ almost surely, thus $M = X_0$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: $M = X - A$ with $A = X - X_0$.

nodes.name: Martingale part of a martingale
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a martingale, then $M = X$ almost surely.
assumptions: $X$ is a martingale
conclusions: $M = X$ almost surely
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.martingalePart_eq

nodes.name: Proof of Martingale part of a martingale
nodes.statement: By definition of the martingale part, $M = X - A$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:Martingale.predictablePart_eq_zero}, $A = 0$ almost surely, thus $M = X$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: $M = X - A$ with $A = 0$.

nodes.name: Predictable part is homogeneous
nodes.statement: For any scalar $c$, the predictable part of $c X$ is $c A$.
assumptions: For any scalar $c$
conclusions: the predictable part of $c X$ is $c A$
nodes.label: lem:predictablePart_smul

nodes.name: Proof of Predictable part is homogeneous
nodes.statement: Linearity of the conditional expectation.
nodes.statement_short: Linearity of conditional expectation.

nodes.name: Martingale part is homogeneous
nodes.statement: For any scalar $c$, the martingale part of $c X$ is $c M$.
assumptions: For any scalar $c$
conclusions: the martingale part of $c X$ is $c M$
nodes.label: lem:martingalePart_smul

nodes.name: Proof of Martingale part is homogeneous
nodes.statement: By definition of the martingale part, $M = X - A$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_smul}, the predictable part of $c X$ is $c A$. Therefore, the martingale part of $c X$ is $c X - c A = c M$.
nodes.statement_short: From $M = X - A$ and homogeneity of the predictable part.

nodes.name: Recall definition
nodes.statement: By definition of the martingale part, $M = X - A$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall $M = X - A$.

nodes.name: Homogeneity of predictable part
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_smul}, the predictable part of $c X$ is $c A$.
nodes.statement_short: The predictable part of $cX$ is $cA$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Therefore, the martingale part of $c X$ is $c X - c A = c M$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence the martingale part of $cX$ is $cM$.

nodes.name: Predictable part is additive
nodes.statement: The predictable part of $X + Y$ is the sum of the predictable part of $X$ and the predictable part of $Y$.
conclusions: The predictable part of $X + Y$ is the sum of the predictable part of $X$ and the predictable part of $Y$.
nodes.label: lem:predictablePart_add

nodes.name: Proof of Predictable part is additive
nodes.statement: Linearity of the conditional expectation.
nodes.statement_short: Linearity of conditional expectation.

nodes.name: Martingale part is additive
nodes.statement: The martingale part of $X + Y$ is the sum of the martingale part of $X$ and the martingale part of $Y$.
conclusions: The martingale part of $X + Y$ is the sum of the martingale part of $X$ and the martingale part of $Y$.
nodes.label: lem:martingalePart_add

nodes.name: Proof of Martingale part is additive
nodes.statement: By definition of the martingale part, $M = X - A$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_add}, the predictable part of $X + Y$ is $A + B$. Therefore, the martingale part of $X + Y$ is $(X + Y) - (A + B) = M + N$.
nodes.statement_short: From $M = X - A$ and additivity of the predictable part.

nodes.name: Recall definition
nodes.statement: By definition of the martingale part, $M = X - A$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall $M = X - A$.

nodes.name: Additivity of predictable part
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_add}, the predictable part of $X + Y$ is $A + B$.
nodes.statement_short: The predictable part of $X+Y$ is $A+B$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Therefore, the martingale part of $X + Y$ is $(X + Y) - (A + B) = M + N$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence the martingale part of $X+Y$ is $M+N$.

nodes.name: Predictable part is adapted to the shifted filtration
nodes.statement: The predictable part $A$ is adapted to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{n+1})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$.
conclusions: The predictable part $A$ is adapted to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{n+1})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$.
nodes.label: lem:adapted_predictablePart

nodes.name: Predictable part is predictable
nodes.statement: The predictable part of a process is predictable.
conclusions: The predictable part of a process is predictable.
nodes.label: lem:predictable_predictablePart

nodes.name: Proof of Predictable part is predictable
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_nat_iff}, the process $A$ is predictable if $A_0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable and for all integer $n$, $A_{n+1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable. As $A_0 = 0$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_zero}, it is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable. Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted_predictablePart} allows to conclude the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Use the discrete-time characterization of predictability, $A_0 = 0$, and adaptedness of $A_{n+1}$ to $\mathcal{F}_n$.

nodes.name: Discrete predictability criterion
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:predictable_nat_iff}, the process $A$ is predictable if $A_0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable and for all integer $n$, $A_{n+1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce predictability to measurability of $A_0$ and of $A_{n+1}$ w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}_n$.

nodes.name: Initial value
nodes.statement: As $A_0 = 0$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_zero}, it is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable.
nodes.statement_short: $A_0 = 0$ is $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable.

nodes.name: Adaptedness to the shifted filtration
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:adapted_predictablePart} allows to conclude the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Adaptedness of $A$ to $(\mathcal{F}_{n+1})$ concludes.

nodes.name: Martingale part is a martingale
nodes.statement: Suppose that the filtration is $\sigma$-finite and that $X$ is adapted, with $X_n$ integrable for all $n$. Then the martingale part of $X$ is a martingale.
assumptions: the filtration is $\sigma$-finite
$X$ is adapted, with $X_n$ integrable for all $n$
conclusions: the martingale part of $X$ is a martingale
nodes.label: lem:martingale_martingalePart

nodes.name: Predictable part of a submartingale is nondecreasing
nodes.statement: The predictable part of a real-valued submartingale is an almost surely nondecreasing process.
conclusions: The predictable part of a real-valued submartingale is an almost surely nondecreasing process.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.monotone_predictablePart

nodes.name: Proof of Predictable part of a submartingale is nondecreasing
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a submartingale and let $A$ be its predictable part. Then for all $n \geq 0$, from Lemma~\ref{lem:condExp_sub_nonneg} we have that almost surely \begin{align*} A_{n+1} &= A_n + \mathbb{E}\left[ X_{n+1} - X_n | \mathcal{F}_n \right] \ge A_n \: . \end{align*} The first equality comes from Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_add_one}. As $\mathbb{N}$ is countable, we deduce that almost surely, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $A_{n+1} \ge A_n$. Thus, $(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is almost surely nondecreasing.
nodes.statement_short: Submartingale increments have nonnegative conditional expectation; combine with the recursion and countability of $\mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Increments are nonnegative
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a submartingale and let $A$ be its predictable part. Then for all $n \geq 0$, from Lemma~\ref{lem:condExp_sub_nonneg} we have that almost surely \begin{align*} A_{n+1} &= A_n + \mathbb{E}\left[ X_{n+1} - X_n | \mathcal{F}_n \right] \ge A_n \: . \end{align*} The first equality comes from Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_add_one}.
nodes.statement_short: Each step $A_{n+1} - A_n$ is a.s. nonnegative by the recursion and the submartingale property.

nodes.name: Countable intersection
nodes.statement: As $\mathbb{N}$ is countable, we deduce that almost surely, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $A_{n+1} \ge A_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Countability gives a single a.s. event for all $n$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Thus, $(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is almost surely nondecreasing.
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is a.s. nondecreasing.

nodes.name: Predictable part of a submartingale is nonnegative
nodes.statement: The predictable part of a real-valued submartingale is almost surely nonnegative.
conclusions: The predictable part of a real-valued submartingale is almost surely nonnegative.
nodes.label: lem:Submartingale.predictablePart_nonneg

nodes.name: Proof of Predictable part of a submartingale is nonnegative
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.monotone_predictablePart}, the predictable part $A$ is almost surely nondecreasing. By Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_zero}, $A_0 = 0$. Therefore, $A_n \ge 0$ almost surely for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Nondecreasing and starting at $0$.

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.monotone_predictablePart}, the predictable part $A$ is almost surely nondecreasing.
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is a.s. nondecreasing.

nodes.name: Initial value
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_zero}, $A_0 = 0$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Therefore, $A_n \ge 0$ almost surely for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $A_n \ge 0$ a.s.

nodes.name: Hitting time of the shifted predictable part is a stopping time
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a real adapted process and let $A$ be its predictable part. Let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. The hitting time $\tau_{A_{n + 1} > c}$ of Definition~\ref{def:leastGT} is a stopping time.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a real adapted process and let $A$ be its predictable part.
Let $c \in \mathbb{R}$.
conclusions: The hitting time $\tau_{A_{n + 1} > c}$ of Definition~\ref{def:leastGT} is a stopping time.
nodes.label: lem:IsStoppingTime_leastGT_predictablePart

nodes.name: Proof of Hitting time of the shifted predictable part is a stopping time
nodes.statement: Since $A_{n}$ is predictable, $A_{n + 1}$ is adapted. The hitting time of an adapted process is a stopping time (we use the discrete time version of that result here, not the full Début theorem).
nodes.statement_short: $A_{n+1}$ is adapted, and hitting times of adapted processes are stopping times (discrete time).

nodes.name: Predictable part at its hitting time
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a real adapted process and let $A$ be its predictable part. Let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $A_{\tau_{A_{n + 1} > c}} \le c$ and if $\tau_{A_{n + 1} > c} < \infty$ then $A_{\tau_{A_{n + 1} > c} + 1} > c$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a real adapted process and let $A$ be its predictable part.
Let $c \in \mathbb{R}$.
conclusions: if $\tau_{A_{n + 1} > c} < \infty$ then $A_{\tau_{A_{n + 1} > c} + 1} > c$
nodes.label: lem:leastGT_predictablePart_le

nodes.name: Increment of the predictable part between hitting times
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a real adapted process and let $A$ be its predictable part. Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. If $\tau_{A_{n + 1} > b} < \infty$ then $A_{\tau_{A_{n + 1} > b}+1} - A_{\tau_{A_{n + 1} > a}} \ge b - a$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a real adapted process and let $A$ be its predictable part.
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$.
$\tau_{A_{n + 1} > b} < \infty$
nodes.label: lem:leastGT_predictablePart_sub_ge

nodes.name: Stopped values when X_T = 0
nodes.statement: Let $T \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $X$ be an adapted process with $X_n$ integrable for all $n$ and such that $X_T = 0$. Then for a stopping time $\tau \le T$, almost surely, $M_\tau = -\mathbb{E}[A_T \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau]$ and $X_\tau = A_\tau - \mathbb{E}[A_T \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau]$.
assumptions: Let $T \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $X$ be an adapted process with $X_n$ integrable for all $n$ and such that $X_T = 0$.
for a stopping time $\tau \le T$
conclusions: $M_\tau = -\mathbb{E}[A_T \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau]$
$X_\tau = A_\tau - \mathbb{E}[A_T \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau]$
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux1

nodes.name: Proof of Stopped values when X_T = 0
nodes.statement: By definition and since $X_T = 0$, $M_T = X_T - A_T = - A_T$. Since $M$ is a martingale it follows by optional sampling that for any stopping time $\tau \le T$ \begin{align*} M_\tau = \mathbb{E}[M_T \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau] = -\mathbb{E}[A_T \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau] \: . \end{align*} And then $X_\tau = M_\tau + A_\tau = A_\tau - \mathbb{E}[A_T \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau]$.
nodes.statement_short: $M_T = -A_T$, then optional sampling for the martingale part gives $M_\tau$ and hence $X_\tau$.

nodes.name: Terminal value of M
nodes.statement: By definition and since $X_T = 0$, $M_T = X_T - A_T = - A_T$.

nodes.name: Optional sampling
nodes.statement: Since $M$ is a martingale it follows by optional sampling that for any stopping time $\tau \le T$ \begin{align*} M_\tau = \mathbb{E}[M_T \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau] = -\mathbb{E}[A_T \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Optional sampling gives $M_\tau = -\mathbb{E}[A_T \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau]$.

nodes.name: Stopped value of X
nodes.statement: And then $X_\tau = M_\tau + A_\tau = A_\tau - \mathbb{E}[A_T \mid \mathcal{F}_\tau]$.
nodes.statement_short: Add $A_\tau$ to get $X_\tau$.

nodes.name: Hitting time capped at T
nodes.statement: TODO: define $\tau^T_{A_{n+1}>c}$ as the hitting time of $A_{n+1} > c$ but with the convention that it is equal to $T$ if the hitting time is greater than $T$ (\texttt{hittingBtwn}).

nodes.name: Shorthand tau^T(c)
nodes.statement: In the next lemmas, we write $\tau^T(c) = \tau^T_{A_{n+1}>c}$ for brevity.

nodes.name: Predictable part exceeds c iff hitting time before T
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is a submartingale and let $T \ge 1$, $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $A_T > c \iff \tau^T(c) < T$.
assumptions: $X$ is a submartingale
let $T \ge 1$, $c \in \mathbb{R}$
conclusions: $A_T > c \iff \tau^T(c) < T$
equivalent_conditions: $A_T > c
\tau^T(c) < T$
nodes.label: lem:predictablePart_gt_iff_leastGT_lt

nodes.name: Proof of Predictable part exceeds c iff hitting time before T
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:leastGT_lt_iff}, $\tau^T(c) < T \iff \exists s < T, A_{s+1} > c$, which is equivalent to $\exists s \in \{1, \ldots, T\}, A_s > c$. By monotonicity of $A$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:Submartingale.monotone_predictablePart}), this is equivalent to $A_T > c$.
nodes.statement_short: Characterize $\tau^T(c) < T$ by an exceedance before $T$, then use monotonicity of $A$.

nodes.name: Tail bound for the predictable part, first estimate
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is a submartingale with $X_T = 0$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[A_T \mathbb{I}\{A_T > c\} \right] \le c \mathbb{P}(\tau^T(c) < T) - \int_{\tau^T(c) < T} X_{\tau^T(c)} dP \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: $X$ is a submartingale with $X_T = 0$
conclusions: \mathbb{E}\left[A_T \mathbb{I}\{A_T > c\} \right] \le c \mathbb{P}(\tau^T(c) < T) - \int_{\tau^T(c) < T} X_{\tau^T(c)} dP
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux2

nodes.name: Proof of Tail bound for the predictable part, first estimate
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_gt_iff_leastGT_lt}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[A_T \mathbb{I}\{A_T > c\} \right] = \mathbb{E}\left[A_T \mathbb{I}\{\tau^T(c) < T\} \right] \end{align*} Since that last event is $\mathcal{F}_{\tau^T(c)}$-measurable, we can apply the tower property of conditional expectation to get \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[A_T \mathbb{I}\{\tau^T(c) < T\} \right] = \int_{\tau^T(c) < T} \mathbb{E}[A_T \mid \mathcal{F}_{\tau^T(c)}] dP \end{align*} Now by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux1} and Lemma~\ref{lem:leastGT_predictablePart_le}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[A_T \mathbb{I}\{\tau^T(c) < T\} \right] &= \int_{\tau^T(c) < T} A_{\tau^T(c)} - X_{\tau^T(c)} dP \\ &\le c \mathbb{P}(\tau^T(c) < T) - \int_{\tau^T(c) < T} X_{\tau^T(c)} dP \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the event via the hitting time, condition on $\mathcal{F}_{\tau^T(c)}$, and use the stopped-value identity and $A_{\tau} \le c$.

nodes.name: Rewrite the event
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_gt_iff_leastGT_lt}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[A_T \mathbb{I}\{A_T > c\} \right] = \mathbb{E}\left[A_T \mathbb{I}\{\tau^T(c) < T\} \right] \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Replace $\{A_T > c\}$ by $\{\tau^T(c) < T\}$.

nodes.name: Tower property
nodes.statement: Since that last event is $\mathcal{F}_{\tau^T(c)}$-measurable, we can apply the tower property of conditional expectation to get \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[A_T \mathbb{I}\{\tau^T(c) < T\} \right] = \int_{\tau^T(c) < T} \mathbb{E}[A_T \mid \mathcal{F}_{\tau^T(c)}] dP \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Condition on $\mathcal{F}_{\tau^T(c)}$.

nodes.name: Stopped-value identity and bound
nodes.statement: Now by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux1} and Lemma~\ref{lem:leastGT_predictablePart_le}, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[A_T \mathbb{I}\{\tau^T(c) < T\} \right] &= \int_{\tau^T(c) < T} A_{\tau^T(c)} - X_{\tau^T(c)} dP \\ &\le c \mathbb{P}(\tau^T(c) < T) - \int_{\tau^T(c) < T} X_{\tau^T(c)} dP \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Use $\mathbb{E}[A_T\mid\mathcal{F}_\tau] = A_\tau - X_\tau$ and $A_\tau \le c$.

nodes.name: Probability bound for the hitting time
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is a submartingale with $X_T = 0$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}(\tau^T(c) < T) &\le - \frac{2}{c} \int_{\tau^T(c/2) < T} X_{\tau^T(c/2)} dP \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: $X$ is a submartingale with $X_T = 0$
conclusions: \mathbb{P}(\tau^T(c) < T) &\le - \frac{2}{c} \int_{\tau^T(c/2) < T} X_{\tau^T(c/2)} dP
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux3

nodes.name: Proof of Probability bound for the hitting time
nodes.statement: Notice that $\{\tau^T(c)<T\}\subseteq \{\tau^T(c/2)<T\}$, thus \begin{align*} \int_{\tau^T(c/2)<T} -X_{\tau^T(c/2)}dP &=\int_{\tau^T(c/2)<T}\mathbb{E}[A_T \mid \mathcal{F}_{\tau^T(c/2)}] - A_{\tau^T(c/2)} dP \\ &= \int_{\tau^T(c/2)<T}A_T - A_{\tau^T(c/2)}dP \\ &\geq \int_{\tau^T(c)<T}A_T - A_{\tau^T(c/2)}dP \\ \intertext{(over the event $\{\tau^T(c)<T\}$ $A_T\geq c$ and $A_{\tau^T(c/2)}\leq c/2$, thus $A_T - A_{\tau^T(c/2)}\geq c/2$)} &\ge \frac{c}{2}P(\tau^T(c)<T) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate $A_T - A_{\tau^T(c/2)} \ge c/2$ over $\{\tau^T(c)<T\}$.

nodes.name: Tail bound for the predictable part, combined
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is a submartingale with $X_T = 0$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[A_T \mathbb{I}\{A_T > c\} \right] \le - 2 \int_{\tau^T(c/2) < T} X_{\tau^T(c/2)} dP - \int_{\tau^T(c) < T} X_{\tau^T(c)} dP \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: $X$ is a submartingale with $X_T = 0$
conclusions: \mathbb{E}\left[A_T \mathbb{I}\{A_T > c\} \right] \le - 2 \int_{\tau^T(c/2) < T} X_{\tau^T(c/2)} dP - \int_{\tau^T(c) < T} X_{\tau^T(c)} dP
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux4

nodes.name: Proof of Tail bound for the predictable part, combined
nodes.statement: Put together the bounds of Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux2} and Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux3}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the two previous bounds.

nodes.name: Markov bound for the hitting time
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is a submartingale with $X_T = 0$. Then \begin{align*} P(\tau^T(c) < T) \le -\frac{\mathbb{E}[X_0]}{c} \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: $X$ is a submartingale with $X_T = 0$
conclusions: P(\tau^T(c) < T) \le -\frac{\mathbb{E}[X_0]}{c}
nodes.label: lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux5

nodes.name: Proof of Markov bound for the hitting time
nodes.statement: Starting with Lemma~\ref{lem:predictablePart_gt_iff_leastGT_lt}, \begin{align*} P(\tau^T(c)<T) =P(A_T>c) \stackrel{Markov}{\leq}\frac{\mathbb{E}[A_T]}{c} =-\frac{\mathbb{E}[M_T]}{c} \stackrel{mg}{=}-\frac{\mathbb{E}[X_0]}{c} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Markov's inequality on $A_T$ and $\mathbb{E}[A_T] = -\mathbb{E}[M_T] = -\mathbb{E}[X_0]$.

nodes.name: Dyadics
nodes.statement: For $T>0$, let $\mathcal{D}_n^T = \left\lbrace \frac{k}{2^n}T \mid k=0,\cdots 2^n\right\rbrace$ be the set of dyadics at scale $n$ and let $\mathcal{D}^T=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{D}_n^T$ be the set of all dyadics of $[0,T]$.
nodes.label: def:dyadics

nodes.name: Cadlag submartingale S of class D
nodes.statement: Let $S : [0,T] \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a cadlag submartingale of class D on $[0,T]$.

nodes.name: S, A, M
nodes.statement: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the restriction of $S$ to $\mathcal{D}_n^T$ is a discrete time submartingale $S^n : \mathbb{N} \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}^n_k = \mathcal{F}_{k2^{-n}T}$, with $S^n_k = S_{k2^{-n}T}$ (and constant equal to $S_T$ for $k > 2^n$; similarly for the filtration), and we can apply the construction of the previous section to it. Let $A^n$ and $M^n$ be the predictable and martingale parts of $S^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Discretize $S$ on the dyadics of scale $n$ and take its discrete Doob decomposition $S^n = M^n + A^n$.
nodes.label: def:SAM

nodes.name: Uniform integrability of the discrete predictable parts
nodes.statement: The sequence $(A^n_{2^n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable (bounded in $L^1$ norm).
conclusions: The sequence $(A^n_{2^n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable (bounded in $L^1$ norm).
nodes.label: lem:A_uniform_integrable

nodes.name: Interpretation of A^n at time T
nodes.statement: Remark: $A^n_{2^n}$ is the predictable part of $S$ at time $T$ for the discrete time filtration given by the dyadics at scale $n$.

WLOG $S^n_{2^n} = S_T=0$ and $S_t\leq 0$ (else consider $S_t-\mathbb{E}\left[S_T\vert\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]$). We write $\tau_n(c)$ for the hitting time $\tau^T_{A^n_{k+1}>c}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux4}, $$ \int_{(A^n_{2^n}>c)} A^n_{2^n} dP \le -2 \int_{\tau_n(c/2)< 2^n} S^n_{\tau_n(c/2)} dP - \int_{\tau_n(c) < 2^n} S^n_{\tau_n(c)} dP. $$ On the other hand, by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux5}, $$ P(\tau_n(c)<2^n) \le -\frac{\mathbb{E}[S_0]}{c} $$ which goes to $0$ uniformly in $n$ as $c$ goes to infinity. The integrals in the upper bound on $\int_{(A^n_{2^n}>c)} A^n_{2^n} dP$ are integrals of uniformly integrable random variables (by the class D assumption) over sets whose probability goes to zero uniformly. Therefore, these integrals go to zero uniformly in $n$ as $c$ goes to infinity. This implies that $\int_{(A^n_{2^n}>c)} A^n_{2^n} dP$ goes to 0 uniformly in $n$ as $c \to +\infty$. Hence, the $L^1$ norm is uniformly bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $S_T = 0$, $S \le 0$; bound the tail integrals of $A^n_{2^n}$ via hitting times and the class D property, uniformly in $n$.

nodes.name: Reduction to S_T = 0
nodes.statement: WLOG $S^n_{2^n} = S_T=0$ and $S_t\leq 0$ (else consider $S_t-\mathbb{E}\left[S_T\vert\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]$).
nodes.statement_short: Without loss of generality $S_T = 0$ and $S \le 0$.

nodes.name: Hitting times
nodes.statement: We write $\tau_n(c)$ for the hitting time $\tau^T_{A^n_{k+1}>c}$.
nodes.statement_short: Notation $\tau_n(c)$ for the hitting times of $A^n$.

nodes.name: Tail integral bound
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux4}, $$ \int_{(A^n_{2^n}>c)} A^n_{2^n} dP \le -2 \int_{\tau_n(c/2)< 2^n} S^n_{\tau_n(c/2)} dP - \int_{\tau_n(c) < 2^n} S^n_{\tau_n(c)} dP. $$
nodes.statement_short: Bound the tail integral of $A^n_{2^n}$ by stopped values of $S^n$.

nodes.name: Hitting probability bound
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformIntegrable_predictablePart_aux5}, $$ P(\tau_n(c)<2^n) \le -\frac{\mathbb{E}[S_0]}{c} $$ which goes to $0$ uniformly in $n$ as $c$ goes to infinity.
nodes.statement_short: The hitting probabilities go to $0$ uniformly in $n$.

nodes.name: Class D estimate
nodes.statement: The integrals in the upper bound on $\int_{(A^n_{2^n}>c)} A^n_{2^n} dP$ are integrals of uniformly integrable random variables (by the class D assumption) over sets whose probability goes to zero uniformly. Therefore, these integrals go to zero uniformly in $n$ as $c$ goes to infinity.
nodes.statement_short: By class D, the integrals over small sets go to zero uniformly.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: This implies that $\int_{(A^n_{2^n}>c)} A^n_{2^n} dP$ goes to 0 uniformly in $n$ as $c \to +\infty$. Hence, the $L^1$ norm is uniformly bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Tail integrals vanish uniformly, so the family is uniformly integrable.

nodes.name: Uniform integrability of the discrete martingale parts
nodes.statement: The sequence $(M^n_{2^n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable (bounded in $L^1$ norm).
conclusions: The sequence $(M^n_{2^n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly integrable (bounded in $L^1$ norm).
nodes.label: lem:M_uniform_integrable

nodes.name: Proof of Uniform integrability of the discrete martingale parts
nodes.statement: $M^n_{2^n} = S_{2^n} - A^n_{2^n}$, also $S$ is of class $D$ hence uniformly integrable and $A^n_{2^n}$ is uniformly integrable by Lemma~\ref{lem:A_uniform_integrable}.
nodes.statement_short: $M^n = S - A^n$ with both terms uniformly integrable.

nodes.name: Cadlag modification of the discrete martingale parts
nodes.statement: The martingale on $[0, T]$ defined by $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[M^n_{2^n}\vert\mathcal{F}_t]$ admits a modification which is a cadlag martingale.
conclusions: The martingale on $[0, T]$ defined by $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[M^n_{2^n}\vert\mathcal{F}_t]$ admits a modification which is a cadlag martingale.
nodes.label: lem:M_n_cadlag_mg

nodes.name: Proof of Cadlag modification of the discrete martingale parts
nodes.statement: By theorem \ref{thm:Martingale.exists_cadlag_modification}
nodes.statement_short: Existence of cadlag modifications of martingales.

nodes.name: Cadlag martingale extension of M^n
nodes.statement: For $t\in[0,T]$ let $\overline{M}^n_t$ be the cadlag modification of $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[M^n_{2^n} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$ from lemma \ref{lem:M_n_cadlag_mg}.
nodes.label: def:barM

nodes.name: Komlòs limit of the martingale parts
nodes.statement: There exists an $M : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ and convex weights $\lambda^n_n,\cdots,\lambda^n_{N_n}$ such that $\mathcal{M}^n_T\stackrel{L^1}{\rightarrow}M$, where $\mathcal{M}^n_T := \lambda^n_n \overline{M}^n_T+ \cdots + \lambda^n_{N_n} \overline{M}^{N_n}_T$~.
conclusions: There exists an $M : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ and convex weights $\lambda^n_n,\cdots,\lambda^n_{N_n}$ such that $\mathcal{M}^n_T\stackrel{L^1}{\rightarrow}M$
nodes.label: lem:M_cal_converges_L1

nodes.name: Proof of Komlòs limit of the martingale parts
nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lem:M_uniform_integrable} $(M^n_T)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is uniformly bounded in $L^1$, thus by lemma \ref{lem:komlos} there are convex weights $\lambda^n_n,\cdots,\lambda^n_{N_n}$ such that $\mathcal{M}^n_T\stackrel{L^1}{\rightarrow}M$, where $\mathcal{M}^n_T := \lambda^n_n \overline{M}^n_T+ \cdots + \lambda^n_{N_n} \overline{M}^{N_n}_T$~.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform integrability of $M^n_T$ plus the Komlòs lemma.

nodes.name: Convex combinations of the martingales
nodes.statement: For $t\in[0,T]$ let $\mathcal{M}^n_t=\lambda^n_n \overline{M}^n_t+\cdots +\lambda^n_{N_n} \overline{M}^{N_n}_t$ be the convex combination of the $\overline{M}^n_t$'s with the weights from Lemma~\ref{lem:M_cal_converges_L1} and let $M$ be the limit of $\mathcal{M}^n_T$ from the same lemma.
nodes.label: def:calM

nodes.name: Convex combinations of the martingales are cadlag
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{M}^n$ is cadlag.
conclusions: $\mathcal{M}^n$ is cadlag.
nodes.label: lem:M_cal_cadlag

nodes.name: Proof of Convex combinations of the martingales are cadlag
nodes.statement: By construction and \ref{lem:M_n_cadlag_mg}
nodes.statement_short: A finite convex combination of cadlag processes is cadlag.

nodes.name: Limit martingale M
nodes.statement: Let $M_t$ be a cadlag modification of $\mathbb{E}[M \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$, obtained by applying Theorem~\ref{thm:Martingale.exists_cadlag_modification} to the martingale $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}[M \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$.
nodes.label: def:M

nodes.name: L1 convergence of the convex combinations at each time
nodes.statement: For every $t\in[0,T]$ we have $\mathcal{M}^n_t\stackrel{L^1}{\rightarrow}M_t$.
assumptions: For every $t\in[0,T]$
conclusions: $\mathcal{M}^n_t\stackrel{L^1}{\rightarrow}M_t$
nodes.label: lem:M1_komlos

nodes.name: Proof of L1 convergence of the convex combinations at each time
nodes.statement: By Jensen's inequality, the tower lemma and lemma \ref{lem:M_cal_converges_L1} \begin{gather}\nonumber \mathbb{E}[|\mathcal{M}^n_t-M_t|] = \mathbb{E}[|\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{M}^n_T-M\vert\mathcal{F}_t]|] \le \mathbb{E}[|\mathcal{M}^n_T-M|]\rightarrow0 \: , \\ \Rightarrow \mathcal{M}^n_t\stackrel{L^1}{\rightarrow} M_t,\quad \forall t\in[0,T]. \end{gather}
nodes.statement_short: Jensen's inequality and the tower property reduce convergence at $t$ to convergence at $T$.

nodes.name: L1 convergence at time t
nodes.statement: \nonumber \mathbb{E}[|\mathcal{M}^n_t-M_t|] = \mathbb{E}[|\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{M}^n_T-M\vert\mathcal{F}_t]|] \le \mathbb{E}[|\mathcal{M}^n_T-M|]\rightarrow0 \: , \\ \Rightarrow \mathcal{M}^n_t\stackrel{L^1}{\rightarrow} M_t,\quad \forall t\in[0,T].
nodes.label: equation_DM_e7

nodes.name: Left-continuous step extension of A^n
nodes.statement: For $t\in[0,T]$ let $\overline{A}^n_t$ be process defined by \begin{align*} \overline{A}^n_s := \sum_{m < 2^n} A^n_{m+1} \mathbb{1}_{(m2^{-n}T, (m+1)2^{-n}T]}(s) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:barA

nodes.name: Step extension agrees with A^n on dyadics
nodes.statement: For $s \in \mathcal{D}^T_n$, $\overline{A}^n_s = A^n_m$ where $m$ is such that $s = m2^{-n}T$.
assumptions: For $s \in \mathcal{D}^T_n$
conclusions: $\overline{A}^n_s = A^n_m$ where $m$ is such that $s = m2^{-n}T$
nodes.label: lem:barA_eq

nodes.name: Step extension is left continuous
nodes.statement: $\overline{A}^n$ is left continuous.
conclusions: $\overline{A}^n$ is left continuous.
nodes.label: lem:leftContinuous_barA

nodes.name: Step extension is predictable
nodes.statement: $\overline{A}^n$ is predictable.
conclusions: $\overline{A}^n$ is predictable.
nodes.label: lem:predictable_barA

nodes.name: Proof of Step extension is predictable
nodes.statement: Since $\overline{A}^n$ is left continuous and adapted, it is predictable (Lemma~\ref{lem:Adapted.isPredictable_of_leftContinuous}).
nodes.statement_short: Left continuous and adapted processes are predictable.

nodes.name: Convex combinations of the step processes
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{A}^n := \lambda^n_n \overline{A}^n+\cdots +\lambda^n_{N_n}\overline{A}^{N_n}$, in which the $\lambda^n_n,\cdots,\lambda^n_{N_n}$ are the convex weights from Lemma~\ref{lem:M_cal_converges_L1}.
nodes.label: def:calA

nodes.name: Convex combinations of step processes are left continuous
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{A}^n$ is left continuous.
conclusions: $\mathcal{A}^n$ is left continuous.
nodes.label: lem:leftContinuous_calA

nodes.name: Convex combinations of step processes are predictable
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{A}^n$ is predictable.
conclusions: $\mathcal{A}^n$ is predictable.
nodes.label: lem:predictable_calA

nodes.name: Proof of Convex combinations of step processes are predictable
nodes.statement: Either use that it is left continuous and adapted, or that it is a convex combination of predictable processes.
nodes.statement_short: Left continuous and adapted, or a convex combination of predictable processes.

nodes.name: Convex combinations of step processes are non-decreasing
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{A}^n$ is non-decreasing on $[0,T]$.
conclusions: $\mathcal{A}^n$ is non-decreasing on $[0,T]$.
nodes.label: lem:calA_mono

nodes.name: Compensator candidate A = S - M
nodes.statement: Let $A_t = S_t - M_t$ for $t \in [0, T]$.
nodes.label: def:A

nodes.name: A is cadlag
nodes.statement: $A$ is cadlag.
conclusions: $A$ is cadlag.
nodes.label: lem:cadlag_A

nodes.name: Proof of A is cadlag
nodes.statement: Since $S$ and $M$ are cadlag, their difference $A = S - M$ is also cadlag.
nodes.statement_short: Difference of cadlag processes.

nodes.name: L1 convergence of the step processes on dyadics
nodes.statement: For every $t\in \mathcal{D}^T$, $\mathcal{A}^n_t$ converges to $A_t$ in $L^1$.
assumptions: For every $t\in \mathcal{D}^T$
conclusions: $\mathcal{A}^n_t$ converges to $A_t$ in $L^1$
nodes.label: lem:tendsto_calA_A_L1

nodes.name: Proof of L1 convergence of the step processes on dyadics
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:M1_komlos}, for all $t\in\mathcal{D}^T$, \begin{align*} \mathcal{A}^n_t = S_t - \mathcal{M}^n_t \stackrel{L^1}{\rightarrow} S_t-M_t = A_t \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{A}^n_t = S_t - \mathcal{M}^n_t$ and $L^1$ convergence of $\mathcal{M}^n_t$.

nodes.name: Almost sure convergence along a subsequence on dyadics
nodes.statement: For every $t\in \mathcal{D}^T$, there exists a subsequence $(k_n)$ such that $\mathcal{A}^{k_n}_t$ converges to $A_t$ almost surely.
assumptions: For every $t\in \mathcal{D}^T$
conclusions: there exists a subsequence $(k_n)$ such that $\mathcal{A}^{k_n}_t$ converges to $A_t$ almost surely
nodes.label: lem:tendsto_calA_A_ae

nodes.name: Proof of Almost sure convergence along a subsequence on dyadics
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:tendsto_calA_A_L1}, we have convergence in $L^1$ for every $t\in \mathcal{D}^T$, which implies that there exists a subsequence $(k_n)$ such that $\mathcal{A}^{k_n}_t$ converges to $A_t$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: $L^1$ convergence implies a.s. convergence along a subsequence.

nodes.name: A is non-decreasing on dyadics
nodes.statement: $A$ is almost surely non-decreasing on $\mathcal{D}^T$.
conclusions: $A$ is almost surely non-decreasing on $\mathcal{D}^T$.
nodes.label: lem:A_mono_dyadics

nodes.name: Proof of A is non-decreasing on dyadics
nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal{D}^T$ is countable, to prove that $A$ is almost surely non-decreasing on $\mathcal{D}^T$ it is enough to show that for all $s \le t$ in $\mathcal{D}^T$, $A_s \le A_t$ almost surely. Let $s \le t$ be two elements of $\mathcal{D}^T$. By Lemma \ref{lem:tendsto_calA_A_ae}, there exists a subsequence $(k_n)$ such that $\mathcal{A}^{k_n}_t$ converges to $A_t$ almost surely. The subsequence $\mathcal{A}_s^{k_n}$ converges to $A_s$ in $L^1$ and thus it has a further subsequence $(k'_n)$ that converges almost surely for $s$ and $t$. By Lemma \ref{lem:calA_mono}, $\mathcal{A}^{k'_n}_s \le \mathcal{A}^{k'_n}_t$ for all $n$, thus by taking the limit we get $A_s \le A_t$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to pairs $s \le t$ by countability, extract a common a.s.-convergent subsequence, and pass monotonicity of $\mathcal{A}^n$ to the limit.

nodes.name: Reduction to pairs
nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal{D}^T$ is countable, to prove that $A$ is almost surely non-decreasing on $\mathcal{D}^T$ it is enough to show that for all $s \le t$ in $\mathcal{D}^T$, $A_s \le A_t$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: By countability it suffices to compare $A_s$ and $A_t$ for each pair.

nodes.name: A.s. subsequence at t
nodes.statement: Let $s \le t$ be two elements of $\mathcal{D}^T$. By Lemma \ref{lem:tendsto_calA_A_ae}, there exists a subsequence $(k_n)$ such that $\mathcal{A}^{k_n}_t$ converges to $A_t$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: Take a subsequence along which $\mathcal{A}^{k_n}_t \to A_t$ a.s.

nodes.name: Common subsequence
nodes.statement: The subsequence $\mathcal{A}_s^{k_n}$ converges to $A_s$ in $L^1$ and thus it has a further subsequence $(k'_n)$ that converges almost surely for $s$ and $t$.
nodes.statement_short: Extract a further subsequence converging a.s. at both $s$ and $t$.

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:calA_mono}, $\mathcal{A}^{k'_n}_s \le \mathcal{A}^{k'_n}_t$ for all $n$, thus by taking the limit we get $A_s \le A_t$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of $\mathcal{A}^n$ passes to the limit.

nodes.name: A is non-decreasing
nodes.statement: $(A_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is almost surely non-decreasing.
conclusions: $(A_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is almost surely non-decreasing.
nodes.label: lem:A_increasing

nodes.name: Proof of A is non-decreasing
nodes.statement: $A$ is almost surely non-decreasing on $\mathcal{D}^T$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:A_mono_dyadics}. Since $A$ is cadlag (thus right-continuous) by Lemma~\ref{lem:cadlag_A}, it follows that $A$ must be non-decreasing on $[0,T]$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotone on the dense dyadics and right-continuous.

nodes.name: Jumps of A are caught by hitting times
nodes.statement: For $q,k \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\tau_{q, k}$ be the $q$-th time that the process $A_t$ has a jump higher than $1/(k+1)$ (this is a hitting time). Then if $A(\omega)$ is discontinuous at $t$, then there exists $q,k$ such that $\tau_{q, k}(\omega) = t$.
assumptions: For $q,k \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\tau_{q, k}$ be the $q$-th time that the process $A_t$ has a jump higher than $1/(k+1)$ (this is a hitting time).
$A(\omega)$ is discontinuous at $t$
conclusions: there exists $q,k$ such that $\tau_{q, k}(\omega) = t$
nodes.label: lem:jump_A

nodes.name: Proof of Jumps of A are caught by hitting times
nodes.statement: Since $A$ is non-decreasing it has finitely many jumps of size higher than $1/(k+1)$ for each $k$. Thus, if $A$ is discontinuous at $t$, there exists $k$ such that the jump of $A$ at $t$ is higher than $1/(k+1)$, and thus there exists $q$ such that $\tau_{q, k} = t$.
nodes.statement_short: A non-decreasing function has finitely many jumps above each threshold.

nodes.name: Limsup inequality for increasing functions converging on dyadics
nodes.statement: If $f_n, f : [0, 1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ are increasing functions such that $f$ is right continuous and $\lim_n f_n(t) = f (t)$ for $t \in\mathcal{D}^T$, then $\limsup_n f_n(t) \leq f (t)$ for all $t \in [0, T]$.
assumptions: $f_n, f : [0, 1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ are increasing functions such that $f$ is right continuous
$\lim_n f_n(t) = f (t)$ for $t \in\mathcal{D}^T$
conclusions: $\limsup_n  f_n(t) \leq f (t)$ for all $t \in [0, T]$
nodes.label: lem:incr_fun_lim_right_cont_limsup_ineq

nodes.name: Proof of Limsup inequality for increasing functions converging on dyadics
nodes.statement: Let $t\in[0,T]$ and $s\in\mathcal{D}^T$ such that $t<s$. We have $$ \limsup_n f_n(t)\leq \limsup_n f_n(s)=f(s). $$ Since the above is true uniformly in $s$ in particular since $f$ is right-continuous $$ \limsup_n f_n(t)\leq\lim_{\stackrel{s\rightarrow t^+}{s\in\mathcal{D}^T}}f(s)=f(t). $$
nodes.statement_short: Bound by dyadic points to the right and use right continuity.

nodes.name: Compare with a dyadic to the right
nodes.statement: Let $t\in[0,T]$ and $s\in\mathcal{D}^T$ such that $t<s$. We have $$ \limsup_n f_n(t)\leq \limsup_n f_n(s)=f(s). $$
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\limsup f_n(t)$ by $f(s)$ for dyadic $s > t$.

nodes.name: Right continuity
nodes.statement: Since the above is true uniformly in $s$ in particular since $f$ is right-continuous $$ \limsup_n f_n(t)\leq\lim_{\stackrel{s\rightarrow t^+}{s\in\mathcal{D}^T}}f(s)=f(t). $$
nodes.statement_short: Let $s \downarrow t$ and use right continuity.

nodes.name: Convergence at continuity points for increasing functions
nodes.statement: If $f_n, f : [0, 1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ are increasing functions such that $f$ is right continuous and $\lim_n f_n(t) = f (t)$ for $t \in\mathcal{D^T}$, if $f$ is continuous in $t\in[0,T]$ then $\lim_n f_n(t) = f (t)$.
assumptions: $f_n, f : [0, 1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ are increasing functions such that $f$ is right continuous
$\lim_n f_n(t) = f (t)$ for $t \in\mathcal{D^T}$
$f$ is continuous in $t\in[0,T]$
conclusions: $\lim_n  f_n(t) = f (t)$
nodes.label: lem:incr_fun_lim_right_cont_lim_eq

nodes.name: Proof of Convergence at continuity points for increasing functions
nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lem:incr_fun_lim_right_cont_limsup_ineq} it is enough to show that $\liminf_n f_n(t)\geq f(t)$. Let $s\in\mathcal{D}^T$ such that $t>s$. We have $$ \liminf_n f_n(t)\geq \liminf_n f_n(s)=f(s). $$ Since the above is true uniformly in $s$ in particular since $f$ is continuous in $t$ $$ \liminf_n f_n(t)\geq\lim_{\stackrel{s\rightarrow t^-}{s\in\mathcal{D}^T}}f(s)=f(t). $$
nodes.statement_short: Limsup bound from the previous lemma; liminf bound from dyadic points to the left and continuity at $t$.

nodes.name: Reduction to liminf
nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lem:incr_fun_lim_right_cont_limsup_ineq} it is enough to show that $\liminf_n f_n(t)\geq f(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: By the limsup inequality it suffices to bound the liminf from below.

nodes.name: Compare with a dyadic to the left
nodes.statement: Let $s\in\mathcal{D}^T$ such that $t>s$. We have $$ \liminf_n f_n(t)\geq \liminf_n f_n(s)=f(s). $$
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\liminf f_n(t)$ below by $f(s)$ for dyadic $s < t$.

nodes.name: Continuity at t
nodes.statement: Since the above is true uniformly in $s$ in particular since $f$ is continuous in $t$ $$ \liminf_n f_n(t)\geq\lim_{\stackrel{s\rightarrow t^-}{s\in\mathcal{D}^T}}f(s)=f(t). $$
nodes.statement_short: Let $s \uparrow t$ and use continuity at $t$.

nodes.name: Convergence of expected discrete compensators at stopping times
nodes.statement: Let $\tau$ be an $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ stopping time. We have $\lim_n\mathbb{E}[A^n_\tau]=\mathbb{E}[A_\tau]$.
assumptions: Let $\tau$ be an $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ stopping time.
conclusions: $\lim_n\mathbb{E}[A^n_\tau]=\mathbb{E}[A_\tau]$
nodes.label: lem:lim_Exp_A_n_tau_is_Exp_A_tau

nodes.name: Proof of Convergence of expected discrete compensators at stopping times
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma_n:=\inf\left(t\in\mathcal{D}^T_n\vert t>\tau\right)$. By construction of $A^n$ we have $A^n_\tau=A^n_{\sigma_n}$. Also $\sigma_n\searrow\tau$. Since $S$ is of class $D$ and cadlag we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[A^n_\tau]&=\mathbb{E}[A^n_{\sigma_n}]=\mathbb{E}[S_{\sigma_n}]-\mathbb{E}[M^n_{\sigma_n}]=\mathbb{E}[S_{\sigma_n}]-\mathbb{E}[M^n_0]=\\ &=\mathbb{E}[S_{\sigma_n}]-\mathbb{E}[S_0]\rightarrow \mathbb{E}[S_\tau]-\mathbb{E}[M_0]=\mathbb{E}[S_\tau]-\mathbb{E}[M_\tau]=\mathbb{E}[A_\tau]. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $\tau$ from the right by dyadic stopping times $\sigma_n$ and use class D, right continuity and the martingale property.

nodes.name: Dyadic approximations of tau
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma_n:=\inf\left(t\in\mathcal{D}^T_n\vert t>\tau\right)$. By construction of $A^n$ we have $A^n_\tau=A^n_{\sigma_n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\sigma_n$, the next dyadic after $\tau$, with $A^n_\tau = A^n_{\sigma_n}$.
