nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: Also $\sigma_n\searrow\tau$. Since $S$ is of class $D$ and cadlag we have \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[A^n_\tau]&=\mathbb{E}[A^n_{\sigma_n}]=\mathbb{E}[S_{\sigma_n}]-\mathbb{E}[M^n_{\sigma_n}]=\mathbb{E}[S_{\sigma_n}]-\mathbb{E}[M^n_0]=\\ &=\mathbb{E}[S_{\sigma_n}]-\mathbb{E}[S_0]\rightarrow \mathbb{E}[S_\tau]-\mathbb{E}[M_0]=\mathbb{E}[S_\tau]-\mathbb{E}[M_\tau]=\mathbb{E}[A_\tau]. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Since $\sigma_n \downarrow \tau$, class D and right continuity give the limit of expectations.

nodes.name: Limsup of the convex combinations at stopping times
nodes.statement: Let $\tau$ be an $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ stopping time. We have $\limsup_n \mathcal{A}_\tau^n = A_\tau$.
assumptions: Let $\tau$ be an $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ stopping time.
conclusions: $\limsup_n \mathcal{A}_\tau^n = A_\tau$
nodes.label: lem:limsup_A_n_tau_is_A_tau_ae

nodes.name: Proof of Limsup of the convex combinations at stopping times
nodes.statement: Firstly we notice that $\liminf_n \mathbb{E}[A_\tau^n] \leq \limsup_n \mathbb{E} [\mathcal{A}_\tau^n ] \leq \mathbb{E}[\limsup_n \mathcal{A}_\tau^n ] \leq \mathbb{E}[ A_\tau ]$, where the first inequality is justified by the definition of limsup and liminf and the fact that $$ \sup_{k\geq n}\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^k_\tau]\geq \sum_{m=k}^{N_k}\lambda^k_m\mathbb{E}[A^m_\tau]\geq \sum_{m=k}^{N_k}\lambda^k_m\inf_{j\geq n}\mathbb{E}[A^j_\tau]=\inf_{k\geq n}\mathbb{E}[A^k_\tau] $$ the third inequality by \ref{lem:incr_fun_lim_right_cont_limsup_ineq}. Let's prove the second inequality: observe that $$ \mathcal{A}^n_\tau= A_1+\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1\leq A_1+(\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1)_+, $$ thus it follows that $\mathcal{A}^n_\tau - (\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1)_+\leq A_1$; since $A_1$ is an integrable guardian the inverse Fatou Lemma may be applied to show together with limsup properties that \begin{align*} \limsup_n\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^n_\tau]+0 &= \limsup_n\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^n_\tau]+\liminf_n-\mathbb{E}[(\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1)_+] \leq \limsup_n\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-(\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1)_+]\leq\\ &\leq \mathbb{E}[\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-(\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1)_+]\leq \mathbb{E}[\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_\tau]-\mathbb{E}[\liminf_n(\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1)_+]\leq\mathbb{E}[\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_\tau], \end{align*} where the first equality is justified by the fact that $\mathcal{A}^n_\tau\leq\mathcal{A}^n_1\rightarrow A_1$ almost surely. Due to lemma \ref{lem:lim_Exp_A_n_tau_is_Exp_A_tau} and \ref{lem:incr_fun_lim_right_cont_limsup_ineq} the first sequence of inequalities is a sequence of equalities, thus we know that $A_\tau- \limsup_n \mathcal{A}_\tau^n $ is an a.s. nonnegative function with null expected value, and thus it must be almost everywhere null.
nodes.statement_short: Squeeze a chain of inequalities between $\liminf \mathbb{E}[A^n_\tau]$ and $\mathbb{E}[A_\tau]$; reverse Fatou gives the middle step, and equal expectations force a.s. equality.

nodes.name: Chain of inequalities
nodes.statement: Firstly we notice that $\liminf_n \mathbb{E}[A_\tau^n] \leq \limsup_n \mathbb{E} [\mathcal{A}_\tau^n ] \leq \mathbb{E}[\limsup_n \mathcal{A}_\tau^n ] \leq \mathbb{E}[ A_\tau ]$, where the first inequality is justified by the definition of limsup and liminf and the fact that $$ \sup_{k\geq n}\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^k_\tau]\geq \sum_{m=k}^{N_k}\lambda^k_m\mathbb{E}[A^m_\tau]\geq \sum_{m=k}^{N_k}\lambda^k_m\inf_{j\geq n}\mathbb{E}[A^j_\tau]=\inf_{k\geq n}\mathbb{E}[A^k_\tau] $$ the third inequality by \ref{lem:incr_fun_lim_right_cont_limsup_ineq}.
nodes.statement_short: Set up $\liminf \mathbb{E}[A^n_\tau] \le \limsup \mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^n_\tau] \le \mathbb{E}[\limsup \mathcal{A}^n_\tau] \le \mathbb{E}[A_\tau]$, justifying the first and third.

nodes.name: Reverse Fatou
nodes.statement: Let's prove the second inequality: observe that $$ \mathcal{A}^n_\tau= A_1+\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1\leq A_1+(\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1)_+, $$ thus it follows that $\mathcal{A}^n_\tau - (\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1)_+\leq A_1$; since $A_1$ is an integrable guardian the inverse Fatou Lemma may be applied to show together with limsup properties that \begin{align*} \limsup_n\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^n_\tau]+0 &= \limsup_n\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^n_\tau]+\liminf_n-\mathbb{E}[(\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1)_+] \leq \limsup_n\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-(\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1)_+]\leq\\ &\leq \mathbb{E}[\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-(\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1)_+]\leq \mathbb{E}[\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_\tau]-\mathbb{E}[\liminf_n(\mathcal{A}^n_\tau-A_1)_+]\leq\mathbb{E}[\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_\tau], \end{align*} where the first equality is justified by the fact that $\mathcal{A}^n_\tau\leq\mathcal{A}^n_1\rightarrow A_1$ almost surely.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the second inequality with the reverse Fatou lemma, dominated by $A_1$.

nodes.name: Equalities force a.s. equality
nodes.statement: Due to lemma \ref{lem:lim_Exp_A_n_tau_is_Exp_A_tau} and \ref{lem:incr_fun_lim_right_cont_limsup_ineq} the first sequence of inequalities is a sequence of equalities, thus we know that $A_\tau- \limsup_n \mathcal{A}_\tau^n $ is an a.s. nonnegative function with null expected value, and thus it must be almost everywhere null.
nodes.statement_short: The ends agree, so $A_\tau - \limsup \mathcal{A}^n_\tau$ is a.s. nonnegative with zero mean, hence zero.

nodes.name: Doob-Meyer decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $S = (S_t )_{0\leq t\leq T}$ be a cadlag submartingale of class $D$. Then, $S$ can be written in a unique way in the form $S = M + A$ where $M$ is a cadlag martingale and $A$ is a predictable increasing process starting at $0$.
assumptions: Let $S = (S_t )_{0\leq t\leq T}$ be a cadlag submartingale of class $D$.
conclusions: $S$ can be written in a unique way in the form  $S = M + A$ where $M$ is a cadlag martingale and $A$ is a predictable increasing process starting at $0$
nodes.origin_citation: Doob-Meyer; proof following Beiglböck, Schachermayer & Veliyev 2012
nodes.label: thm:Doob_Meyer

nodes.name: Proof of Doob-Meyer decomposition
nodes.statement: By construction $M$ is a cadlag martingale and $A_0=0$ and by lemma \ref{lem:A_increasing} $A$ is increasing. It suffices to show that $A$ is predictable. $A^n,\mathcal{A}^n$ are left continuous and adapted, and thus they are predictable (Lemma~\ref{lem:Adapted.isPredictable_of_leftContinuous}). It is enough to show that $\omega-a.e.$, $\forall t\in[0,T]$, $\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_t(\omega)=A_t(\omega)$. By lemma \ref{lem:incr_fun_lim_right_cont_lim_eq} that is true for any continuity point of $A$. Since $A$ is increasing it can only have a finite amount of jumps larger than $1/k$ for any $k\in\mathbb{N}$. Consider now $\tau_{q,k}$ the family of stopping times equal to the $q$-th time that the process $A_t$ has a jump higher than $1/k$. This is a countable family. Given a time $t$ and a trajectory $\omega$ there are only two possibilities: either $A$ is continuous or not at time $t$ along $\omega$. If $A$ is continuous at time $t$ we have $\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_t(\omega)=A_t(\omega)$, if it jumps there exists $q(\omega),k(\omega)$ such that $t=\tau_{q(\omega),k(\omega)}(\omega)$. Due to lemma \ref{lem:limsup_A_n_tau_is_A_tau_ae} we know that $\limsup_n A^n_{\tau_{q,k}} = A_{\tau_{q,k}}$ for each $q,k$ almost surely. Thus, since it is an intersection of a countable amount of almost sure events $\forall\omega\in\Omega'$ with $P(\Omega')=1$, for each $q,k$ $\limsup_n A^n_{\tau_{q,k}}(\omega) = A_{\tau_{q,k}}(\omega)$ ($\omega$ does not depend upon $q,k$). Consequently, $\forall\omega\in\Omega'$ we have $\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_t(\omega)=\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_{\tau_{q(\omega),k(\omega)}}(\omega)=A_{\tau_{q(\omega),k(\omega)}}(\omega)=A_t(\omega)$
nodes.statement_short: With the constructed $M$ and $A$, it remains to show $A$ is predictable: $\limsup_n \mathcal{A}^n_t = A_t$ at continuity points and, via countably many jump stopping times, at jumps.

nodes.name: Properties already established
nodes.statement: By construction $M$ is a cadlag martingale and $A_0=0$ and by lemma \ref{lem:A_increasing} $A$ is increasing.
nodes.statement_short: $M$ is a cadlag martingale, $A_0 = 0$ and $A$ is increasing.

nodes.name: Reduction to predictability
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that $A$ is predictable.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show that $A$ is predictable.

nodes.name: Approximants are predictable
nodes.statement: $A^n,\mathcal{A}^n$ are left continuous and adapted, and thus they are predictable (Lemma~\ref{lem:Adapted.isPredictable_of_leftContinuous}).
nodes.statement_short: The approximants are left continuous and adapted, hence predictable.

nodes.name: Reduction to limsup identity
nodes.statement: It is enough to show that $\omega-a.e.$, $\forall t\in[0,T]$, $\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_t(\omega)=A_t(\omega)$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices that $\limsup_n \mathcal{A}^n_t = A_t$ for all $t$, a.s.

nodes.name: Continuity points
nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lem:incr_fun_lim_right_cont_lim_eq} that is true for any continuity point of $A$.
nodes.statement_short: The identity holds at continuity points of $A$.

nodes.name: Jump stopping times
nodes.statement: Since $A$ is increasing it can only have a finite amount of jumps larger than $1/k$ for any $k\in\mathbb{N}$. Consider now $\tau_{q,k}$ the family of stopping times equal to the $q$-th time that the process $A_t$ has a jump higher than $1/k$. This is a countable family.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the countable family $\tau_{q,k}$ of jump times.

nodes.name: Continuous or jump
nodes.statement: Given a time $t$ and a trajectory $\omega$ there are only two possibilities: either $A$ is continuous or not at time $t$ along $\omega$. If $A$ is continuous at time $t$ we have $\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_t(\omega)=A_t(\omega)$, if it jumps there exists $q(\omega),k(\omega)$ such that $t=\tau_{q(\omega),k(\omega)}(\omega)$.
nodes.statement_short: Either $A$ is continuous at $t$, or $t$ is one of the jump times.

nodes.name: Jump times
nodes.statement: Due to lemma \ref{lem:limsup_A_n_tau_is_A_tau_ae} we know that $\limsup_n A^n_{\tau_{q,k}} = A_{\tau_{q,k}}$ for each $q,k$ almost surely. Thus, since it is an intersection of a countable amount of almost sure events $\forall\omega\in\Omega'$ with $P(\Omega')=1$, for each $q,k$ $\limsup_n A^n_{\tau_{q,k}}(\omega) = A_{\tau_{q,k}}(\omega)$ ($\omega$ does not depend upon $q,k$).
nodes.statement_short: At each jump stopping time the identity holds a.s.; intersect countably many events.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Consequently, $\forall\omega\in\Omega'$ we have $\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_t(\omega)=\limsup_n\mathcal{A}^n_{\tau_{q(\omega),k(\omega)}}(\omega)=A_{\tau_{q(\omega),k(\omega)}}(\omega)=A_t(\omega)$
nodes.statement_short: Hence the identity holds at every $t$ on $\Omega'$.

nodes.name: Local Doob-Meyer decomposition
nodes.statement: An adapted process $X$ is a cadlag local submartingale iff $X = M + A$ where $M$ is a cadlag local martingale and $A$ is a predictable, cadlag, locally integrable and increasing process starting at $0$. The processes $M$ and $A$ are uniquely determined by $X$ a.s.
nodes.section: 12.4 Local version of the Doob-Meyer decomposition
assumptions: An adapted process $X$
conclusions: $X$ is a cadlag local submartingale iff $X = M + A$ where $M$ is a cadlag local martingale and $A$ is a predictable, cadlag, locally integrable and increasing process starting at $0$
The processes $M$ and $A$ are uniquely determined by $X$ a.s.
equivalent_conditions: $X$ is a cadlag local submartingale
$X = M + A$ where $M$ is a cadlag local martingale and $A$ is a predictable, cadlag, locally integrable and increasing process starting at $0$
nodes.label: thm:local_doobMeyer

nodes.name: Increasing process is a submartingale iff integrable
nodes.statement: An adapted increasing process $A$ is a submartingale iff it is integrable.
nodes.section: 12.4 Local version of the Doob-Meyer decomposition
assumptions: An adapted increasing process $A$
conclusions: is a submartingale iff it is integrable
equivalent_conditions: is a submartingale
it is integrable
nodes.label: lem:submartingale_iff_integrable

nodes.name: Doob-Meyer decomposition of a locally integrable increasing process
nodes.statement: An adapted locally integrable increasing process $A$ can be written as a sum of a local martingale and a predictable locally integrable increasing process.
nodes.section: 12.4 Local version of the Doob-Meyer decomposition
assumptions: An adapted locally integrable increasing process $A$
conclusions: can be written as a sum of a local martingale and a predictable locally integrable increasing process
nodes.label: lem:local_doobMeyer_increasing

nodes.name: Proof of Doob-Meyer decomposition of a locally integrable increasing process
nodes.statement: A locally integrable increasing process is a local submartingale, thus we can apply Theorem~\ref{thm:local_doobMeyer}.
nodes.section: 12.4 Local version of the Doob-Meyer decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Such a process is a local submartingale; apply the local Doob-Meyer decomposition.

nodes.name: Notations for classes of processes
nodes.statement:
Notations for classes of processes:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $\mathcal{V}$: finite variation processes (Definition~\ref{def:HasFiniteVariation})
  \item $\mathcal{V}^+$: non-decreasing finite variation processes
  \item $\mathcal{A}$: adapted processes with integrable variation (Definition~\ref{def:HasIntegrableVariation})
  \item $\mathcal{A}^+$: non-decreasing adapted integrable processes
  \item $\mathcal{M}$: càdlàg martingales (TODO: \cite{he2019semimartingale} add uniform integrability)
  \item $\mathcal{M}^c$: continuous martingales
  \item $\mathcal{M}^2$: square-integrable martingales (Definition~\ref{def:IsSquareIntegrable})
  \item $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for a class $\mathcal{C}$: processes that are locally in $\mathcal{C}$
\end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Notation for classes of processes: $\mathcal{V}$, $\mathcal{V}^+$, $\mathcal{A}$, $\mathcal{A}^+$, $\mathcal{M}$, $\mathcal{M}^c$, $\mathcal{M}^2$ and local classes $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
nodes.section: 13 Classes of martingales and related processes

nodes.name: Jumps of a process
nodes.statement: The jumps of a process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is the process $\Delta X : T \to \Omega \to E$ defined by $(t, \omega) \mapsto X_t(\omega) - X_{t^-}(\omega)$~.
nodes.label: def:jump

nodes.name: Jump part
nodes.statement: The jump part (or purely discontinuous part) of a process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is the process $T \to \Omega \to E$ defined by $(t, \omega) \mapsto \sum_{0 < s \le t} \Delta X_s(\omega)$~.
nodes.label: def:jumpPart

nodes.name: Continuous part
nodes.statement: The continuous part of a process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is the process $X^c : T \to \Omega \to E$ defined by $(t, \omega) \mapsto X_t(\omega) - \sum_{0 < s \le t} \Delta X_s(\omega)$~.
nodes.label: def:continuousPart

nodes.name: Large jumps
nodes.statement: The large jump part of a process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ at level $\varepsilon$ is the process $X^{d, \varepsilon} : T \to \Omega \to E$ defined by $(t, \omega) \mapsto \sum_{0 < s \le t} \Delta X_s(\omega) \mathbb{1}_{\{\Vert \Delta X_s(\omega) \Vert > \varepsilon\}}$~.
nodes.label: def:largeJump

nodes.name: Extended variation
nodes.statement: The (extended-real-valued) variation of a function $f : T \to E$ on a set $s$ inside a linear order is the supremum of $\sum_i \mathrm{edist}(f(u_{i+1}, f(u_i)))$ over all finite increasing sequences $u : N \to T$ in $s$. We denote it by $V_f(s)$~.
nodes.statement_short: Variation of $f$ on $s$: supremum over finite increasing sequences of summed extended distances.
nodes.label: def:eVariationOn

nodes.name: Bounded variation
nodes.statement: A function $f : T \to E$ is of bounded variation on a set $s$ if its variation $V_f(s)$ is finite.
differentia: its variation $V_f(s)$ is finite
nodes.label: def:BoundedVariationOn

nodes.name: Locally bounded variation
nodes.statement: A function $f : T \to E$ is of locally bounded variation on a set $s$ if for every $a, b$ in $s$, the variation $V_f(s \cap [a, b])$ is finite.
nodes.label: def:LocallyBoundedVariationOn

nodes.name: Discontinuities of locally bounded variation functions are countable
nodes.statement: The set of points of discontinuity of a function of locally bounded variation is at most countable.
conclusions: The set of points of discontinuity of a function of locally bounded variation is at most countable.
nodes.label: lem:LocallyBoundedVariationOn.countable_not_continuous_at

nodes.name: Proof of Discontinuities of locally bounded variation functions are countable
nodes.statement: Mathlib has the result for monotone functions and has the fact that a function of locally bounded variation is the difference of two monotone functions.
nodes.statement_short: Write the function as a difference of monotone functions and use the monotone case.

nodes.name: Finite variation process, $\mathcal{V}$
nodes.statement: A process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is of finite variation if it is right-continuous and for every $\omega \in \Omega$, the path $t \mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is of locally bounded variation on $T$~. We denote by $\mathcal{V}$ the class of finite variation processes.
differentia: it is right-continuous
for every $\omega \in \Omega$, the path $t \mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is of locally bounded variation on $T$
nodes.label: def:HasFiniteVariation

nodes.name: Finite variation processes are cadlag
nodes.statement: A finite variation process is càdlàg.
conclusions: A finite variation process is càdlàg.
nodes.label: lem:HasFiniteVariation.isCadlag

nodes.name: Proof of Finite variation processes are cadlag
nodes.statement: Right-continuity is by definition. Left limits exist because a function of locally bounded variation has left limits (that should be in Mathlib's file about locally bounded variation).
nodes.statement_short: Right-continuity by definition; left limits from locally bounded variation.

nodes.name: Variation process
nodes.statement: The variation of a process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is the process $V_X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $(t, \omega) \mapsto V_{X(\omega)}([0,t])$~.
nodes.label: def:variationProcess

nodes.name: Variation process is non-decreasing
nodes.statement: The variation process $V_X$ of a process $X$ is non-decreasing.
conclusions: The variation process $V_X$ of a process $X$ is non-decreasing.
nodes.label: lem:monotone_variationProcess

nodes.name: Variation process is right-continuous
nodes.statement: The variation process $V_X$ of a right-continuous process $X$ is right-continuous.
assumptions: a right-continuous process $X$
conclusions: The variation process $V_X$ of a right-continuous process $X$ is right-continuous.
nodes.label: lem:rightContinuous_variationProcess

nodes.name: Integrable variation, $\mathcal{A}$
nodes.statement: We say that a stochastic process $X$ has integrable variation if its variation process $V_X$ (Definition~\ref{def:variationProcess}) is integrable (Definition~\ref{def:HasIntegrableSup}). We denote by $\mathcal{A}$ the class of adapted processes with integrable variation.
nodes.label: def:HasIntegrableVariation

nodes.name: Class A+
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{A}^+$ the class of non-decreasing adapted integrable processes.

nodes.name: Class V+
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{V}^+$ the class of non-decreasing adapted processes.

nodes.name: Integrable variation as difference of increasing processes
nodes.statement: A process with integrable variation can be written as the difference of two non-decreasing adapted integrable processes.
conclusions: A process with integrable variation can be written as the difference of two non-decreasing adapted integrable processes.
nodes.label: lem:HasIntegrableVariation.eq_sub_monotone

nodes.name: Doob-Meyer decomposition for locally integrable variation
nodes.statement: A process in $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ (locally integrable variation) can be written as a sum of a local martingale and a predictable locally integrable process.
assumptions: A process in $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ (locally integrable variation)
conclusions: can be written as a sum of a local martingale and a predictable locally integrable process
nodes.label: lem:local_doobMeyer_integrable_variation

nodes.name: Proof of Doob-Meyer decomposition for locally integrable variation
nodes.statement: We write the process as a difference of two non-decreasing locally integrable processes, and then apply Lemma~\ref{lem:local_doobMeyer_increasing} to each of them. We take the difference of the two resulting local martingales and the difference of the two resulting predictable locally integrable processes.
nodes.statement_short: Split into two increasing locally integrable processes, decompose each by local Doob-Meyer, and subtract.

nodes.name: Martingale with integrable variation is its compensated jump part
nodes.statement: Let $M \in \mathcal{M} \cap \mathcal{A}$ be a martingale with integrable variation. Then the jump part $A = \sum_{0 < s \le \cdot} \Delta M_s$ is an adapted process with integrable variation. Let $A_m$ be the martingale part of the Doob decomposition of $A$. Then $M = M_0 + A_m$. Finally, the predictable part of the decomposition of $A$ is continuous.
assumptions: Let $M \in \mathcal{M} \cap \mathcal{A}$ be a martingale with integrable variation.
conclusions: the jump part $A = \sum_{0 < s \le \cdot} \Delta M_s$ is an adapted process with integrable variation
the predictable part of the decomposition of $A$ is continuous

nodes.name: Predictable uniformly integrable martingales are continuous
nodes.statement: A predictable uniformly integrable martingale is continuous.
conclusions: A predictable uniformly integrable martingale is continuous.
nodes.label: lem:Martingale.continuous_of_isStronglyPredictable_of_uniformIntegrable

nodes.name: Standing assumption on E
nodes.statement: In this section, $E$ denotes a complete normed space.

nodes.name: Square integrable martingales
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a linear order with bottom element 0, on which we have a filtration $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying the usual conditions. We say that a martingale $M : T \to \Omega \to E$ is square integrable if it is càdlàg and $\sup_{t \in T} \Vert M_t \Vert_{L^2} < \infty$ (Lean remark: use \texttt{eLpNorm (M t) 2}).
differentia: it is càdlàg
$\sup_{t \in T} \Vert M_t \Vert_{L^2} < \infty$

nodes.name: Proof of Square integrable martingales are uniformly integrable

nodes.name: L2 norm of a square integrable martingale is non-decreasing
nodes.statement: For $M$ a square integrable martingale, the function $t \mapsto \Vert M_t \Vert_{L^2}$ is non-decreasing.

nodes.name: Proof of L2 norm of a square integrable martingale is non-decreasing
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:IsSquareIntegrable.submartingale_sq}, $\Vert M_t \Vert^2$ is a submartingale. Thus, for $s \le t$~, \begin{align*} \Vert M_s \Vert_{L^2}^2 &= \mathbb{E}[\Vert M_s \Vert^2] \\ &\le \mathbb{E}[\Vert M_t \Vert^2] \\ &= \Vert M_t \Vert_{L^2}^2 \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 13.3.1 The Hilbert space of square integrable martingales
nodes.statement_short: Expectations of the submartingale $\Vert M_t\Vert^2$ are non-decreasing.

nodes.statement: A càdlàg and uniformly integrable martingale $M$ is square integrable if and only if $M_\infty$ is in $\mathrm L^2$.

nodes.name: Stopped square integrable martingale is square integrable
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a square integrable martingale and $\tau$ is a stopping time, then $M^\tau$ is a square integrable martingale.

assumptions: $M$ is a square integrable martingale and $\tau$ is a stopping time
conclusions: $M^\tau$ is a square integrable martingale

nodes.name: Proof of Stopped square integrable martingale is square integrable
nodes.statement: We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:isSquareIntegrable_of_limitProcess}. First, $M^\tau$ is a martingale. Moreover, $M$ is uniformly integrable by Lemma~\ref{lem:IsSquareIntegrable.uniformIntegrable}, thus it is of class D by Lemma~\ref{lem:Martingale.classD_iff_uniformIntegrable}, thus $M^\tau$ is uniformly integrable. Finally, we have \begin{align*} \|M^\tau_\infty\|_2^2 & = \|M_\tau\|^2 \\ & \le \int (\sup_t \|M_t(\omega)\|)^2 P(\mathrm d\omega) \\ & \le 4 \|M_\infty\|^2_2 \\ & < \infty. \end{align*} The first equality follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_stoppedProcess}. The first inequality is obtained as follows: if $\tau(\omega) = \infty$, then $M_\tau = M_\infty$ and $M_t \longrightarrow M_\infty$ almost surely so $\|M_\infty(\omega)\| \le \sup_t \|M_t(\omega)\|$. Otherwise the inequality is obvious. The second inequality is Corollary~\ref{cor:doob_lp_norm_top}.

nodes.statement_short: Use the limit criterion: $M^\tau$ is a uniformly integrable martingale (class D), and Doob's $L^2$ inequality bounds $\Vert M_\tau\Vert_2$.

nodes.name: Use the limit criterion

nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the square-integrability criterion via the limit.

nodes.statement: Finally, we have \begin{align*} \|M^\tau_\infty\|_2^2 & = \|M_\tau\|^2 \\ & \le \int (\sup_t \|M_t(\omega)\|)^2 P(\mathrm d\omega) \\ & \le 4 \|M_\infty\|^2_2 \\ & < \infty. \end{align*} The first equality follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_stoppedProcess}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\Vert M^\tau_\infty\Vert_2^2$ by $4\Vert M_\infty\Vert_2^2$.

nodes.name: Proof of Doob L2 bound for the running supremum
nodes.statement: Combine Corollary~\ref{cor:doob_lp_norm_top}, the fact that suprema commute with power, and Lemma~\ref{lem:IsSquareIntegrable.sup_eLpNorm_eq_eLpNorm_limitProcess}.

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:IsSquareIntegrable.sup_eLpNorm_eq_eLpNorm_limitProcess}, $\Vert M \Vert = 0$ if and only if for all $t \in T$, $\Vert M_t \Vert_{L^2} = 0$~. Because $M$ is càdlàg, this implies that $M$ is indistinguishable from $0$.

nodes.name: Proof of M^2 is a Hilbert space
nodes.statement: We show that the map \begin{align*} \phi : \mathcal{M}^2 & \to \left\{f \in L^2(E, P) | f \text{ is } \left(\bigsqcup_t, \mathcal{F}_t\right)\text{-strongly measurable}\right\} \\ M & \mapsto M_\infty \end{align*} is a bijective isometry. It is an isometry by Definition~\ref{def:L2Martingales.norm}. We define the inverse $\psi$ as the map which to $f$ associates a càdlàg martingale that is a modification of $t \mapsto P[f | \mathcal{F}_t]$, given by Lemma~\ref{lem:exists_cadlag_mod_of_local_mg}. Let $M$ be a square integrable martingale. Then for any $t$, $M_t$ is a.e. equal to $P[M_\infty | \mathcal{F}_t]$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:condExp_limitProcess}, thus $M$ is a càdlàg modification of $t \mapsto P[f | \mathcal{F}_t]$, thus it is indistinguishable from $\psi(M_\infty)$. Let $f \in L^2(E, P)$ be a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup_t \mathcal{F}_t$. Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:tendsto_ae_condExp} we know that almost surely $P[f | \mathcal{F}_t]$ converges to $f$. Because $T$ is separable we can consider $(t_n)$ a sequence of points that tends to infinity. Because $\psi(f)$ and $P[f | \mathcal{F}_t]$ are modifications of each other, we have that almost surely, for all $n \in \mathcal{N}$, $\psi(f)_{t_n} = P[f | \mathcal{F}_{t_n}]$. But we also know that $\psi(f)_{t_n}$ converges to $\psi(f)_\infty$ so we conclude that $\psi(f)_\infty$ is a.e. equal to f.

nodes.name: Isometry

nodes.statement: Let $f \in L^2(E, P)$ be a.e. strongly measurable with respect to $\bigsqcup_t \mathcal{F}_t$. Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:tendsto_ae_condExp} we know that almost surely $P[f | \mathcal{F}_t]$ converges to $f$. But we also know that $\psi(f)_{t_n}$ converges to $\psi(f)_\infty$ so we conclude that $\psi(f)_\infty$ is a.e. equal to f.
