nodes.name: L2 bound for elementary stochastic integrals
nodes.statement: For $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, F}$ bounded by a constant $D$, $M \in \mathcal{M}^2(E)$ and a continuous bilinear map $B: E \times F \to G$, \begin{align*} \Vert (V \bullet_B M)_t \Vert_{L^2} \le 2 D \: \Vert B \Vert \: \sup_t \Vert M_t \Vert_{L^2} \end{align*} TODO: this can be improved to $D \: \Vert B \Vert \: \Vert M_t \Vert_{L^2}$?
assumptions: For $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, F}$ bounded by a constant $D$, $M \in \mathcal{M}^2(E)$ and a continuous bilinear map $B: E \times F \to G$
conclusions: \Vert (V \bullet_B M)_t \Vert_{L^2} \le 2 D \: \Vert B \Vert \: \sup_t \Vert M_t \Vert_{L^2}
nodes.label: lem:eLpNorm_elemStochIntegralBilin_le

nodes.name: Proof of L2 bound for elementary stochastic integrals
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a bound on $\Vert M_t \Vert_{L^2}$ for all $t \in T$~. Let $(s_k < t_k)_{k \in \{1, ..., n\}}$ and $\eta_k$ be the intervals and random variables defining $V$~. Let $D$ be a bound on $\Vert\eta_k\Vert$. Then, for all $t$~, \begin{align*} \Vert (V \bullet_B M)_t \Vert_{L^2} &\le \sum_{k=1}^n \Vert B(M^t_{t_k} - M^t_{s_k}, \eta_k) \Vert_{L^2} \: . \end{align*} Since only at most one term of that sum is non-zero for each fixed $t$~, we can bound the sum by the maximum of its terms. It suffices then to bound each term of that sum. TODO: here we supposed that the intervals of the simple process are disjoint. Check with our Lean def. For each $k$~, \begin{align*} \Vert B(M^t_{t_k} - M^t_{s_k}, \eta_k) \Vert_{L^2} &\le \left\Vert \Vert B \Vert \: \Vert M^t_{t_k} - M^t_{s_k} \Vert \: \Vert \eta_k \Vert \right\Vert_{L^2} \\ &\le \Vert B \Vert \: \Vert M^t_{t_k} - M^t_{s_k} \Vert_{L^2} \: D \\ &\le 2 \Vert B \Vert \: C \: D \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: At most one term of the elementary integral is nonzero at each time; bound each term by $2\Vert B\Vert C D$.

nodes.name: Bounds and data of V
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a bound on $\Vert M_t \Vert_{L^2}$ for all $t \in T$~. Let $(s_k < t_k)_{k \in \{1, ..., n\}}$ and $\eta_k$ be the intervals and random variables defining $V$~. Let $D$ be a bound on $\Vert\eta_k\Vert$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the bound $C$, the intervals and coefficients of $V$, and the bound $D$.

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
nodes.statement: Then, for all $t$~, \begin{align*} \Vert (V \bullet_B M)_t \Vert_{L^2} &\le \sum_{k=1}^n \Vert B(M^t_{t_k} - M^t_{s_k}, \eta_k) \Vert_{L^2} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the integral by the sum of its terms.

nodes.name: Disjoint intervals
nodes.statement: Since only at most one term of that sum is non-zero for each fixed $t$~, we can bound the sum by the maximum of its terms.
nodes.statement_short: At most one term is nonzero, so the sum is a maximum.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It suffices then to bound each term of that sum.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to bound each term.

nodes.name: Disjointness caveat
nodes.statement: TODO: here we supposed that the intervals of the simple process are disjoint. Check with our Lean def.
nodes.statement_short: Note: assumes disjoint intervals.

nodes.name: Bound each term
nodes.statement: For each $k$~, \begin{align*} \Vert B(M^t_{t_k} - M^t_{s_k}, \eta_k) \Vert_{L^2} &\le \left\Vert \Vert B \Vert \: \Vert M^t_{t_k} - M^t_{s_k} \Vert \: \Vert \eta_k \Vert \right\Vert_{L^2} \\ &\le \Vert B \Vert \: \Vert M^t_{t_k} - M^t_{s_k} \Vert_{L^2} \: D \\ &\le 2 \Vert B \Vert \: C \: D \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Each term is at most $2\Vert B\Vert C D$.

nodes.name: Elementary stochastic integrals are square integrable
nodes.statement: For $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, F}$, $M \in \mathcal{M}^2(E)$ and a continuous bilinear map $B: E \times F \to G$, the elementary stochastic integral $V \bullet_B M$ is in $\mathcal{M}^2(G)$.
assumptions: For $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, F}$, $M \in \mathcal{M}^2(E)$ and a continuous bilinear map $B: E \times F \to G$
conclusions: the elementary stochastic integral $V \bullet_B M$ is in $\mathcal{M}^2(G)$
nodes.label: lem:isSquareIntegrable_elemStochIntegralBilin

nodes.name: Proof of Elementary stochastic integrals are square integrable
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:cadlag_elemStochIntegralBilin}, $V \bullet_B M$ is càdlàg, and we know that it is a martingale by Lemma~\ref{lem:Martingale.elemStochIntegral}~. It remains to show that $\sup_{t \in T} \Vert (V \bullet_B M)_t \Vert_{L^2} < \infty$~. By Lemma~\ref{lem:eLpNorm_elemStochIntegralBilin_le}, this supremum is bounded by $2 D \Vert B \Vert \sup_{t \in T} \Vert M_t \Vert_{L^2}$, which is finite since $M \in \mathcal{M}^2(E)$ and $V$ is bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Càdlàg and martingale by earlier lemmas; the $L^2$ bound gives finiteness of the supremum.

nodes.name: Cadlag martingale
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:cadlag_elemStochIntegralBilin}, $V \bullet_B M$ is càdlàg, and we know that it is a martingale by Lemma~\ref{lem:Martingale.elemStochIntegral}~.
nodes.statement_short: The integral is a càdlàg martingale.

nodes.name: Remaining bound
nodes.statement: It remains to show that $\sup_{t \in T} \Vert (V \bullet_B M)_t \Vert_{L^2} < \infty$~.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to bound the $L^2$ norms.

nodes.name: Apply the L2 bound
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:eLpNorm_elemStochIntegralBilin_le}, this supremum is bounded by $2 D \Vert B \Vert \sup_{t \in T} \Vert M_t \Vert_{L^2}$, which is finite since $M \in \mathcal{M}^2(E)$ and $V$ is bounded.
nodes.statement_short: The supremum is bounded by $2D\Vert B\Vert \sup_t \Vert M_t\Vert_{L^2} < \infty$.

nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{M}^{2,c}$ the submodule of $\mathcal{M}^2$ made of continuous square integrable martingales.
nodes.label: def:continuousSquareIntegrable

nodes.name: L2 convergence of limits gives a.s. uniform convergence along a subsequence
nodes.statement: Let $(M^{(n)})$ be a sequence of square integrable martingales and $N$ be a square integrable martingale such that $\|M^{(n)}_\infty - N_\infty\|_2 \longrightarrow_{n \to +\infty} 0$. Then there exists $\phi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ increasing such that, almost surely, $M^{(\phi(n))}_\cdot(\omega)$ converges uniformly to $N_\cdot(\omega)$ as $n$ goes to infinity.
assumptions: Let $(M^{(n)})$ be a sequence of square integrable martingales and $N$ be a square integrable martingale such that $\|M^{(n)}_\infty - N_\infty\|_2 \longrightarrow_{n \to +\infty} 0$.
conclusions: there exists $\phi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ increasing such that, almost surely, $M^{(\phi(n))}_\cdot(\omega)$ converges uniformly to $N_\cdot(\omega)$ as $n$ goes to infinity
nodes.label: lem:exists_subsequence_ae_tendsto_uniformly

nodes.name: Proof of L2 convergence of limits gives a.s. uniform convergence along a subsequence
nodes.statement: We can find $\phi$ increasing such that $\|M^{(\phi(n))}_\infty - N_\infty\|_2 \le 1/2^n$. Then, \begin{align*} P[\sum_n \sup_t \|M^{(\phi(n))}_t - N_t\|] & = \sum_n P[\sup_t \|M^{(\phi(n))}_t - N_t\|] \\ & \le \sqrt{P(\Omega)} \sum_n P[(\sup_t \|M^{(\phi(n))}_t - N_t\|)^2]^{1/2} \\ & \le 2 \sqrt{P(\Omega)} \|M^{(\phi(n))}_\infty - N_\infty\|_2 < \infty, \end{align*} Where the second inequality is Lemma~\ref{lem:IsSquareIntegrable.integral_iSup_norm_rpow_rpow_inv_le_limitProcess}. In particular, almost surely, $\sum_n \sup_t \|M^{(\phi(n))}_t - N_t\| < \infty$ and thus $\sup_t \|M^{(\phi(n))}_t - N_t\| \longrightarrow_{n \to +\infty} 0$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a fast subsequence and bound the expected sum of sup-distances via Doob's $L^2$ inequality (Borel-Cantelli type argument).

nodes.name: Fast subsequence
nodes.statement: We can find $\phi$ increasing such that $\|M^{(\phi(n))}_\infty - N_\infty\|_2 \le 1/2^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\phi$ with $\Vert M^{(\phi(n))}_\infty - N_\infty\Vert_2 \le 2^{-n}$.

nodes.name: Summable sup-distances
nodes.statement: Then, \begin{align*} P[\sum_n \sup_t \|M^{(\phi(n))}_t - N_t\|] & = \sum_n P[\sup_t \|M^{(\phi(n))}_t - N_t\|] \\ & \le \sqrt{P(\Omega)} \sum_n P[(\sup_t \|M^{(\phi(n))}_t - N_t\|)^2]^{1/2} \\ & \le 2 \sqrt{P(\Omega)} \|M^{(\phi(n))}_\infty - N_\infty\|_2 < \infty, \end{align*} Where the second inequality is Lemma~\ref{lem:IsSquareIntegrable.integral_iSup_norm_rpow_rpow_inv_le_limitProcess}.
nodes.statement_short: The expected sum of sup-distances is finite by Doob's $L^2$ bound.

nodes.name: Uniform convergence
nodes.statement: In particular, almost surely, $\sum_n \sup_t \|M^{(\phi(n))}_t - N_t\| < \infty$ and thus $\sup_t \|M^{(\phi(n))}_t - N_t\| \longrightarrow_{n \to +\infty} 0$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: A.s. summability gives uniform convergence.

nodes.name: Continuous square integrable martingales form a closed subspace
nodes.statement: The submodule $\mathcal{M}^{2,c}$ is closed in the Hilbert space $\mathcal{M}^2$.
conclusions: The submodule $\mathcal{M}^{2,c}$ is closed in the Hilbert space $\mathcal{M}^2$.
nodes.label: lem:isClosed_continuousSquareIntegrable

nodes.name: Proof of Continuous square integrable martingales form a closed subspace
nodes.statement: Take $M^{(n)}$ a sequence of continuous square integrable martingales that converges to $N$ in $\mathcal{M}^2$. This means that $\|M^{(n)}_\infty - N_\infty\|$ goes to zero as $n$ goes to infinity, which means that there exists $\phi$ increasing such that, almost surely, $M^{(\phi(n))}_\cdot(\omega)$ converges uniformly to $N_\cdot(\omega)$ as $n$ goes to infinity (Lemma~\ref{lem:exists_subsequence_ae_tendsto_uniformly}). As each $M^{(\phi(n))}(\omega)$ is continuous, $N(\omega)$ is also continuous.
nodes.statement_short: A limit in $\mathcal{M}^2$ is an a.s. uniform limit along a subsequence, so continuity passes to the limit.

nodes.name: Uniformly convergent subsequence
nodes.statement: Take $M^{(n)}$ a sequence of continuous square integrable martingales that converges to $N$ in $\mathcal{M}^2$. This means that $\|M^{(n)}_\infty - N_\infty\|$ goes to zero as $n$ goes to infinity, which means that there exists $\phi$ increasing such that, almost surely, $M^{(\phi(n))}_\cdot(\omega)$ converges uniformly to $N_\cdot(\omega)$ as $n$ goes to infinity (Lemma~\ref{lem:exists_subsequence_ae_tendsto_uniformly}).
nodes.statement_short: Convergence in $\mathcal{M}^2$ gives an a.s. uniformly convergent subsequence.

nodes.name: Continuity of the limit
nodes.statement: As each $M^{(\phi(n))}(\omega)$ is continuous, $N(\omega)$ is also continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform limits of continuous paths are continuous.

nodes.statement: If $M$ is a square integrable martingale, we define its \emph{continuous part} as the orthogonal projection of $M$ onto the closed subspace $\mathcal{M}^{2,c}$. We denote it by $M^c$.
nodes.label: def:continuousPartSquareIntegrable

nodes.name: Continuous part is continuous
nodes.statement: The continuous part of a square integrable martingale is continuous.
conclusions: The continuous part of a square integrable martingale is continuous.
nodes.label: lem:continuous_continuousPart

nodes.name: Proof of Continuous part is continuous
nodes.statement: By definition of the orthogonal projection.
nodes.statement_short: By definition of the orthogonal projection.

nodes.name: Continuous part is square integrable
nodes.statement: The continuous part of a square integrable martingale is a square integrable martingale.
conclusions: The continuous part of a square integrable martingale is a square integrable martingale.
nodes.label: lem:isSquareIntegrable_continuousPart

nodes.name: Proof of Continuous part is square integrable
nodes.statement: By definition of the orthogonal projection.
nodes.statement_short: By definition of the orthogonal projection.

nodes.statement: If $M$ is a square integrable martingale, we define its \emph{discontinuous part} by $M^d := M - M^c$.
nodes.label: def:discontinuousPart

nodes.name: Discontinuous part is square integrable
nodes.statement: The discontinuous part of a square integrable martingale is a square integrable martingale.
conclusions: The discontinuous part of a square integrable martingale is a square integrable martingale.
nodes.label: lem:isSquareIntegrable_discontinuousPart

nodes.name: Proof of Discontinuous part is square integrable
nodes.statement: By definition.
nodes.statement_short: By definition.

nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{M}^{2,d}$ the orthogonal of $\mathcal{M}^{2,c}$ and call its elements purely discontinuous square integrable martingales.
nodes.label: def:discontinuousSquareIntegrable

nodes.name: Purely discontinuous martingales lie in M^{2,d}
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a purely discontinuous martingale in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:IsPurelyDiscontinuous}, then it belongs to $\mathcal{M}^{2,d}$.
assumptions: $M$ is a purely discontinuous martingale in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:IsPurelyDiscontinuous}
conclusions: it belongs to $\mathcal{M}^{2,d}$
nodes.label: lem:mem_discontinuousSquareIntegrable

nodes.name: Proof of Purely discontinuous martingales lie in M^{2,d}
nodes.statement: By definition of the orthogonal projection.
nodes.statement_short: By definition of the orthogonal projection.

nodes.name: Discontinuous part is purely discontinuous
nodes.statement: The discontinuous part of square integrable martingale is purely discontinuous.
conclusions: The discontinuous part of square integrable martingale is purely discontinuous.
nodes.label: lem:isPurelyDiscontinuous_discontinuousPart

nodes.name: Proof of Discontinuous part is purely discontinuous
nodes.statement: By definition of the orthogonal projection.
nodes.statement_short: By definition of the orthogonal projection.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the continuous / purely discontinuous decomposition
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a square integrable martingale, then the decomposition $M = M^c + M^d$ as the sum of a continuous and a purely discontinuous square integrable martingales is unique up to indistinguishability.
assumptions: $M$ is a square integrable martingale
conclusions: the decomposition $M = M^c + M^d$ as the sum of a continuous and a purely discontinuous square integrable martingales is unique up to indistinguishability
nodes.label: lem:unique_continuousPart

nodes.name: Proof of Uniqueness of the continuous / purely discontinuous decomposition
nodes.statement: A closed subspace is the complement of its orthogonal subspace.
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonal decomposition with respect to a closed subspace.

nodes.name: Stopped purely discontinuous martingale is purely discontinuous
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a purely discontinuous martingale and $\tau$ is a stopping time, then $M^\tau$ is a purely discontinuous martingale.
assumptions: $M$ is a purely discontinuous martingale and $\tau$ is a stopping time
conclusions: $M^\tau$ is a purely discontinuous martingale
nodes.label: lem:IsPurelyDiscontinuous.stoppedProcess

nodes.name: Proof of Stopped purely discontinuous martingale is purely discontinuous
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:IsSquareIntegrable.stoppedProcess} $M^\tau$ is a square integrable martingale. Let $N$ be a continuous square integrable martingale. Then again by Lemma~\ref{lem:IsSquareIntegrable.stoppedProcess}, $N^\tau$ is a continuous square integrable martingale. We thus have \begin{align*} P[\langle M^\tau_\infty, N_\infty\rangle] & = P[\langle M_\tau, N_\infty\rangle] \\ & = P[\langle M_\tau, P[M_\infty | \mathcal{F}_\tau]\rangle] \\ & = P[\langle M_\tau, N_\tau\rangle] \\ & = P[\langle M_\infty, N_\tau\rangle] \\ & = 0. \end{align*} The first equality is Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_stoppedProcess}, the second is the pull-out property of the conditional expectation, the third one is Lemma~\ref{lem:condExp_limitProcess_stopped}, the fourth one is the same as before and the last one is the fact that $M$ is purely discontinuous while $N^\tau$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $P[\langle M^\tau_\infty, N_\infty\rangle]$ by stopping and conditioning, reducing to orthogonality of $M$ and the continuous $N^\tau$.

nodes.name: Stopped process is square integrable
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:IsSquareIntegrable.stoppedProcess} $M^\tau$ is a square integrable martingale.
nodes.statement_short: $M^\tau$ is square integrable.

nodes.name: Stopped continuous martingale
nodes.statement: Let $N$ be a continuous square integrable martingale. Then again by Lemma~\ref{lem:IsSquareIntegrable.stoppedProcess}, $N^\tau$ is a continuous square integrable martingale.
nodes.statement_short: For continuous $N$, $N^\tau$ is a continuous square integrable martingale.

nodes.name: Orthogonality computation
nodes.statement: We thus have \begin{align*} P[\langle M^\tau_\infty, N_\infty\rangle] & = P[\langle M_\tau, N_\infty\rangle] \\ & = P[\langle M_\tau, P[M_\infty | \mathcal{F}_\tau]\rangle] \\ & = P[\langle M_\tau, N_\tau\rangle] \\ & = P[\langle M_\infty, N_\tau\rangle] \\ & = 0. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Chain of equalities ending in $0$.

nodes.name: Justify the equalities
nodes.statement: The first equality is Lemma~\ref{lem:limitProcess_stoppedProcess}, the second is the pull-out property of the conditional expectation, the third one is Lemma~\ref{lem:condExp_limitProcess_stopped}, the fourth one is the same as before and the last one is the fact that $M$ is purely discontinuous while $N^\tau$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Each equality by stopping, pull-out, conditioning and pure discontinuity of $M$.

nodes.name: Continuous and discontinuous parts commute with stopping
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a square integrable martingale and $\tau$ is a stopping time, then $(M^\tau)^c = (M^c)^\tau$ and $(M^\tau)^d = (M^d)^\tau$.
assumptions: $M$ is a square integrable martingale and $\tau$ is a stopping time
conclusions: $(M^\tau)^c = (M^c)^\tau$ and $(M^\tau)^d = (M^d)^\tau$
nodes.label: lem:continuousPart_stoppedProcess

nodes.name: Proof of Continuous and discontinuous parts commute with stopping
nodes.statement: We can write $M^\tau = (M^c + M^d)^\tau = (M^c)^\tau + (M^d)^\tau$. We conclude by Lemma~\ref{lem:unique_continuousPart} thanks to Lemma~\ref{lem:IsPurelyDiscontinuous.stoppedProcess}.
nodes.statement_short: Stop the decomposition and use its uniqueness.

nodes.name: Inner product with an elementary stochastic integral
nodes.statement: For $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, \mathbb{R}}$ and $M, N \in \mathcal{M}^2$, we have \begin{align*} \langle V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} M, N \rangle_{\mathcal{M}^2} &= V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} \langle M, N \rangle_{\mathcal{M}^2} \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, \mathbb{R}}$ and $M, N \in \mathcal{M}^2$
conclusions: \langle V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} M, N \rangle_{\mathcal{M}^2} &= V \bullet_{\mathbb{R}} \langle M, N \rangle_{\mathcal{M}^2}
nodes.label: lem:inner_elemStochIntegral

nodes.name: Locally square-integrable martingales
nodes.statement: A process is locally square-integrable if it locally satisfies the square-integrable martingale property. We denote that class of processes by $\mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$~.
nodes.label: def:IsLocallySquareIntegrable

nodes.name: Square integrable implies locally square integrable
nodes.statement: Every square-integrable martingale is locally square-integrable: $\mathcal{M}^2 \subseteq \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$~.
conclusions: Every square-integrable martingale is locally square-integrable: $\mathcal{M}^2 \subseteq \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$~.
nodes.label: lem:IsSquareIntegrable.isLocallySquareIntegrable

nodes.name: Proof of Square integrable implies locally square integrable
nodes.statement: This follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:implies_locally}.
nodes.statement_short: A property implies its local version.

nodes.name: Squared norm of a locally square integrable martingale is a local submartingale
nodes.statement: If $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$, then $\Vert M \Vert^2$ is a càdlàg local submartingale.
assumptions: $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$
conclusions: $\Vert M \Vert^2$ is a càdlàg local submartingale
nodes.label: lem:IsLocallySquareIntegrable.isLocalSubmartingale_sq_norm

nodes.name: Continuous local martingales are locally square integrable
nodes.statement: A continuous local martingale is locally square-integrable: $\mathcal{M}^c_{\mathrm{loc}} \subseteq \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$~.
conclusions: A continuous local martingale is locally square-integrable: $\mathcal{M}^c_{\mathrm{loc}} \subseteq \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$~.
nodes.label: lem:IsLocalMartingale.isLocallySquareIntegrable_of_continuous

nodes.name: Predictable quadratic variation
nodes.statement: For $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with càdlàg paths, the predictable quadratic variation of $M$ is defined as the predictable part of the Doob-Meyer decomposition of the local submartingale $\Vert M \Vert^2$~. We denote it by $\langle M \rangle$~.
nodes.label: def:quadraticVariation

nodes.name: Predictable quadratic variation is predictable
nodes.statement: The predictable quadratic variation $\langle M \rangle$ of $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is a predictable process.
conclusions: The predictable quadratic variation $\langle M \rangle$ of $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is a predictable process.
nodes.label: lem:predictable_quadraticVariation

nodes.name: Predictable quadratic variation is cadlag
nodes.statement: The predictable quadratic variation $\langle M \rangle$ of $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is càdlàg.
conclusions: The predictable quadratic variation $\langle M \rangle$ of $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is càdlàg.
nodes.label: lem:cadlag_quadraticVariation

nodes.name: Predictable quadratic variation is locally integrable
nodes.statement: The predictable quadratic variation $\langle M \rangle$ of $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is locally integrable.
conclusions: The predictable quadratic variation $\langle M \rangle$ of $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is locally integrable.
nodes.label: lem:locallyIntegrable_quadraticVariation

nodes.name: Predictable quadratic variation starts at zero
nodes.statement: $\langle M \rangle_0 = 0$~.
conclusions: $\langle M \rangle_0 = 0$
nodes.label: lem:quadraticVariation_zero

nodes.name: Predictable quadratic variation is non-decreasing
nodes.statement: The predictable quadratic variation $\langle M \rangle$ of $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is non-decreasing.
conclusions: The predictable quadratic variation $\langle M \rangle$ of $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is non-decreasing.
nodes.label: lem:monotone_quadraticVariation

nodes.name: Squared norm minus quadratic variation is a local martingale
nodes.statement: For $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$, the process $\Vert M_t \Vert^2 - \langle M \rangle_t$ is a local martingale.
assumptions: For $M \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$
conclusions: the process $\Vert M_t \Vert^2 - \langle M \rangle_t$ is a local martingale
nodes.label: lem:local_martingale_sub_quadraticVariation

nodes.name: Predictable covariation
nodes.statement: For $M, N \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$, the predictable covariation $\langle M, N \rangle$ is a stochastic process defined by polarization of the predictable quadratic variation: \begin{align*} \langle M, N \rangle_t = \frac{1}{2}\left(\langle M+N \rangle_t - \langle M \rangle_t - \langle N \rangle_t \right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Predictable covariation by polarization of the predictable quadratic variation.
nodes.label: def:covariation

nodes.name: Predictable covariation is predictable
nodes.statement: The predictable covariation $\langle M, N \rangle$ of $M, N \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is a predictable process.
conclusions: The predictable covariation $\langle M, N \rangle$ of $M, N \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is a predictable process.
nodes.label: lem:predictable_covariation

nodes.name: Predictable covariation is cadlag
nodes.statement: The predictable covariation $\langle M, N \rangle$ of $M, N \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is càdlàg.
conclusions: The predictable covariation $\langle M, N \rangle$ of $M, N \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is càdlàg.
nodes.label: lem:cadlag_covariation

nodes.name: Predictable covariation starts at zero
nodes.statement: $\langle M, N \rangle_0 = 0$~.
conclusions: $\langle M, N \rangle_0 = 0$
nodes.label: lem:covariation_zero

nodes.name: Inner product minus covariation is a local martingale
nodes.statement: For $M, N \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$, the process $\langle M_t, N_t \rangle_E - \langle M, N \rangle_t$ is a local martingale.
assumptions: For $M, N \in \mathcal{M}^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$
conclusions: the process $\langle M_t, N_t \rangle_E - \langle M, N \rangle_t$ is a local martingale
nodes.label: lem:local_martingale_sub_covariation

nodes.name: Proof of Inner product minus covariation is a local martingale
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} &\langle M_t, N_t \rangle_E - \langle M, N \rangle_t \\ &= \frac{1}{4}\left( \left(\Vert M_t + N_t \Vert^2 - \langle M+N \rangle_t\right) - \left(\Vert M_t - N_t \Vert^2 - \langle M-N \rangle_t\right) \right) \: . \end{align*} The two differences are local martingales by Lemma~\ref{lem:local_martingale_sub_quadraticVariation}, so their linear combination is also a local martingale.
nodes.statement_short: Polarization: write the difference as a combination of two local martingales $\Vert M\pm N\Vert^2 - \langle M \pm N\rangle$.

nodes.name: Expected covariation equals M^2 inner product
nodes.statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be square integrable martingales. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\langle M,N \rangle_\infty\right] = \langle M - M_0, N - N_0 \rangle_{\mathcal{M}^2} \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $M$ and $N$ be square integrable martingales.
conclusions: \mathbb{E}\left[\langle M,N \rangle_\infty\right] = \langle M - M_0, N - N_0 \rangle_{\mathcal{M}^2}
nodes.label: lem:covariation_eq_inner

nodes.name: Quadratic variation of Brownian motion
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion. Then the quadratic variation of $B$ is given by $\langle B \rangle_t = t$~.
assumptions: Let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion.
conclusions: the quadratic variation of $B$ is given by $\langle B \rangle_t = t$
nodes.label: lem:quadraticVariation_brownian

nodes.name: Large jumps of a local martingale have locally integrable variation
nodes.statement: The large jump process of a local martingale is a process with locally integrable variation (it's in $(\mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{M})_{\mathrm{loc}}$).
conclusions: The large jump process of a local martingale is a process with locally integrable variation (it's in $(\mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{M})_{\mathrm{loc}}$).
nodes.label: lem:IsLocalMartingale.locally_hasIntegrableVariation_largeJumps

nodes.name: Fundamental decomposition of local martingales
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a local martingale. Then for any $\varepsilon > 0$, $M$ can be decomposed as $M = M_0 + U + V$, where $U$ is a locally bounded martingale (local version of both bounded and martingale) with $\vert \Delta U \vert \le \varepsilon$ and $U_0 = 0$ and $V$ is a local martingale with locally integrable variation ($V \in (\mathcal{M} \cap \mathcal{A})_{\mathrm{loc}}$) and $V_0 = 0$.
assumptions: Let $M$ be a local martingale.
for any $\varepsilon > 0$
conclusions: $M$ can be decomposed as $M = M_0 + U + V$, where $U$ is a locally bounded martingale (local version of both bounded and martingale) with $\vert \Delta U \vert \le \varepsilon$ and $U_0 = 0$ and $V$ is a local martingale with locally integrable variation ($V \in (\mathcal{M} \cap \mathcal{A})_{\mathrm{loc}}$) and $V_0 = 0$
nodes.label: thm:local_martingale_decomposition

nodes.name: Proof of Fundamental decomposition of local martingales
nodes.statement: See \cite{he2019semimartingale}, 7.17
nodes.statement_short: Cited from He, Wang and Yan, Theorem 7.17.

nodes.name: Use of the local martingale decomposition for integration
nodes.statement:
Remark:
$U$ is locally bounded, hence locally square integrable, so we can use the integration machinery for those to define an integral.
$V$ has locally integrable variation so we can integrate it with Stieltjes integrals.

nodes.name: Semimartingale
nodes.statement: A process $X$ is a semimartingale if it can be decomposed as $X = M + A$, where $M$ is a local martingale ($M \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}$) and $A$ is an adapted process with finite variation.
differentia: it can be decomposed as $X = M + A$, where $M$ is a local martingale ($M \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}$) and $A$ is an adapted process with finite variation
nodes.label: def:IsSemimartingale

nodes.name: Semimartingale decomposition with bounded jumps
nodes.statement: A semimartingale $X$ can be decomposed as $X = M + A$, where $M$ is a locally bounded martingale with bounded jumps and $A$ is an adapted process with finite variation.
assumptions: A semimartingale $X$
conclusions: can be decomposed as $X = M + A$, where $M$ is a locally bounded martingale with bounded jumps and $A$ is an adapted process with finite variation
nodes.label: lem:IsSemimartingale.decomposition

nodes.name: Proof of Semimartingale decomposition with bounded jumps
nodes.statement: Decompose $X = M + A$ as in Definition~\ref{def:IsSemimartingale}. Then decompose $M$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:local_martingale_decomposition} with $\varepsilon = 1$. Then $M = M_0 + U + V$ with $U$ a locally bounded martingale with $\vert \Delta U \vert \le 1$ and $V$ a local martingale with locally integrable variation. Then $X = (M_0 + U) + (A + V)$, with $U$ a locally bounded martingale with bounded jumps and $A + V$ an adapted process of finite variation (since $V$ has locally integrable variation, hence finite variation).
nodes.statement_short: Decompose the local martingale part with the fundamental decomposition at $\varepsilon=1$ and regroup terms.

nodes.name: Semimartingale decomposition
nodes.statement: Decompose $X = M + A$ as in Definition~\ref{def:IsSemimartingale}.
nodes.statement_short: Start from $X = M + A$.

nodes.name: Decompose the local martingale
nodes.statement: Then decompose $M$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:local_martingale_decomposition} with $\varepsilon = 1$. Then $M = M_0 + U + V$ with $U$ a locally bounded martingale with $\vert \Delta U \vert \le 1$ and $V$ a local martingale with locally integrable variation.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the fundamental decomposition with $\varepsilon = 1$.

nodes.name: Regroup
nodes.statement: Then $X = (M_0 + U) + (A + V)$, with $U$ a locally bounded martingale with bounded jumps and $A + V$ an adapted process of finite variation (since $V$ has locally integrable variation, hence finite variation).
nodes.statement_short: Regroup into a locally bounded martingale with bounded jumps plus a finite variation process.

nodes.name: Continuous martingale part
nodes.statement: TODO. Denoted by $X^c$.
nodes.label: def:IsSemimartingale.continuousMartingalePart

nodes.name: Quadratic covariation of semimartingales
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be semimartingales. Their quadratic covariation $[X, Y]$ is defined as \begin{align*} [X, Y]_t = X_0 Y_0 + \langle X^c, Y^c \rangle_t + \sum_{0 < s \le t} \Delta X_s \Delta Y_s \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:quadCovariation

nodes.name: Quadratic variation of a semimartingale
nodes.statement: The quadratic variation of a semimartingale $X$ is defined as $[X] = [X, X]$~.
nodes.label: def:quadVariation

nodes.name: Special semimartingale
nodes.statement: A semimartingale $X$ is a special semimartingale if it can be decomposed as $X = M + A$, where $M$ is a local martingale and $A$ is an adapted process with locally integrable variation.
nodes.label: def:IsSpecialSemimartingale

nodes.name: Canonical decomposition of special semimartingales
nodes.statement: A special semimartingale $X$ can be decomposed as $X = M + A$, where $M$ is a local martingale and $A$ is a predictable process with finite variation and $A_0 = 0$.
assumptions: A special semimartingale $X$
conclusions: can be decomposed as $X = M + A$, where $M$ is a local martingale and $A$ is a predictable process with finite variation and $A_0 = 0$
nodes.label: lem:IsSpecialSemimartingale.decomposition

nodes.name: Additive content
nodes.statement: Let $E$ be a commutative monoid and $\mathcal{A}$ be a family of sets. An \emph{additive content} is a set function $\lambda : \mathcal{A} \to E$ with value $0$ at the empty set which is finitely additive on $\mathcal{A}$~.
differentia: with value $0$ at the empty set
which is finitely additive on $\mathcal{A}$
nodes.label: def:addContent

nodes.name: Extension of an additive content to the generated ring
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda$ be an additive content on a semi-ring of sets $C$~. Then $\lambda$ admits a unique additive extension to the ring of sets generated by $C$~.
assumptions: Let $\lambda$ be an additive content on a semi-ring of sets $C$~.
conclusions: $\lambda$ admits a unique additive extension to the ring of sets generated by $C$
nodes.label: lem:addContent_extension

nodes.name: Content associated with a process
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$, where $E$ is a Banach space, be an adapted process with $X_t \in L^1$ for every $t \in T$~. The \emph{content} $\lambda_X$ associated with $X$ is an $E$-valued additive content on elementary predictable sets, given on predictable rectangles by \begin{align*} \lambda_X((s, t] \times F) &= \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_F (X_t - X_s)], & s < t \text{ in } T,\ F \in \mathcal{F}_s, \\ \lambda_X(\{0\} \times F) &= 0, & F \in \mathcal{F}_0 \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Content of an integrable adapted process: $\lambda_X((s,t]\times F) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_F (X_t - X_s)]$ on predictable rectangles.
nodes.label: def:contentAssociatedWithProcess

nodes.name: Content of a process is well defined
nodes.statement: The content $\lambda_X$ associated with $X$ is uniquely defined.
conclusions: The content $\lambda_X$ associated with $X$ is uniquely defined.
nodes.label: lem:contentAssociatedWithProcess_wellDefined

nodes.name: Proof of Content of a process is well defined
nodes.statement: The uniqueness of $\lambda_X$ is guaranteed by Lemma~\ref{lem:addContent_extension}, since the predictable rectangles form a semi-ring of sets (Lemma~\ref{lem:predictableRectangles_isSetSemiring}), one that generates the ring of elementary predictable sets (Lemma~\ref{lem:elementaryPredictableSets_isSetRing_of}).
nodes.statement_short: Predictable rectangles form a semi-ring generating the elementary predictable sets, so the extension is unique.

nodes.name: Partition of a set
nodes.statement: An \emph{partition} of a set $A$ is a family of pairwise disjoint sets, which does not contain the empty set, and whose union is $A$~. For a family of sets $C$, a \emph{$C$-partition} of $A$ is a partition of $A$ consisting of sets in $C$~.
nodes.label: def:partitionOfSet

nodes.name: Bounded variation of a content
nodes.statement: An additive content $\lambda$ on a ring $\mathcal{A}$ of sets, with values in a normed space $E$, has \emph{bounded variation} on a set $A \in \mathcal{A}$ if \begin{align*} \vert \lambda \vert(A) := \sup \Big\{ \sum_{i=1}^n \| \lambda(A_i) \| \:\Big|\: (A_i)_{i=1}^n \text{ finite } \mathcal{A}\text{-partition of } A \Big\} < \infty \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: A content has bounded variation on $A$ if the supremum of summed norms over finite partitions of $A$ is finite.
nodes.label: def:contentBoundedVariation

nodes.name: Variation of a content via generator partitions
nodes.statement: We can equivalently take supremum over $C$-partitions of $A$ in the above definition, when $\mathcal{A}$ is generated by the semi-ring $C$~.
assumptions: when $\mathcal{A}$ is generated by the semi-ring $C$
conclusions: We can equivalently take supremum over $C$-partitions of $A$ in the above definition
nodes.label: lem:contentBoundedVariation_equivOnGenerator

nodes.name: Proof of Variation of a content via generator partitions
nodes.statement: This follows (by triangle inequality and additivity of the content) from the Definition~\ref{def:partitionOfSet}, and from the Lemmata~\ref{lem:semiRingOfSets_disjoint_of_union}, \ref{lem:setRing_of_finiteUnions}.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality and additivity, refining partitions into semi-ring pieces.

nodes.name: Content equals expected elementary integral of an indicator
nodes.statement: The content $\lambda_X$ associated with a process $X$ satisfies, for every elementary predictable set $A\subseteq (0, t] \times \Omega$, \begin{align*} \lambda_X(A) = \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: for every elementary predictable set $A\subseteq (0, t] \times \Omega$
conclusions: \lambda_X(A) = \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t]
nodes.label: lem:contentEquivElementaryIntegral

nodes.name: Proof of Content equals expected elementary integral of an indicator
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:elementaryPredictableSet_iff_indicator}, the process $\mathbb{1}_A$ is a simple one, \begin{align*} (\mathbb{1}_A)_t = \mathbb{1}_{F_0}\mathbb{1}_{\{0\}}(t) + \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}_{F_i} \mathbb{1}_{(s_i, t_i]}(t) \:, \end{align*} where $(s_i, t_i]$ may be taken to be pairwise disjoint, thanks to the Lemma \ref{lem:simpleProcess_admitsDisjointIntervals}. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}_{F_i} (X_{t \wedge t_i} - X_{t \wedge s_i})\right] \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{1}_{F_i} (X_{t \wedge t_i} - X_{t \wedge s_i})\right] \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_X((s_i, t_i] \times F_i) = \lambda_X(A), \end{align*} taking into account that for all $i$ we have $t\wedge t_i = t_i$, $t\wedge s_i = s_i$, as $A\subseteq (0, t] \times \Omega$~.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\mathbb{1}_A$ as a simple process with disjoint intervals and expand the expectation of the elementary integral.

nodes.name: Quasi-martingale
nodes.statement: Let $E$ be a Banach space. An adapted integrable process $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ is called a \emph{quasi-martingale} if the additive content $\lambda_X$ (on elementary predictable sets) associated with $X$ has bounded variation on every set $(0, t] \times \Omega$ with $t \in T$~, that is, \begin{align*} \forall t \in T, \quad \vert \lambda_X \vert\big((0, t] \times \Omega\big) < \infty \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:Quasimartingale

nodes.name: Quasi-martingales via bounded elementary integrals
nodes.statement: The content $\lambda_X$ associated with a real-valued process $X$ has bounded variation on $(0, t] \times \Omega$ if and only if the set $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \mid A \text{ elementary predictable}\}$ is bounded. In particular, an adapted integrable process $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral}, iff it is a quasi-martingale.
assumptions: The content $\lambda_X$ associated with a real-valued process $X$
conclusions: has bounded variation on $(0, t] \times \Omega$ if and only if the set $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \mid A \text{ elementary predictable}\}$ is bounded

In particular, an adapted integrable process $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:exists_rightContinuous_modification_of_bounded_elemStochIntegral}, iff it is a quasi-martingale.
equivalent_conditions: has bounded variation on $(0, t] \times \Omega$
the set $\{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t] \mid A \text{ elementary predictable}\}$ is bounded
nodes.label: lem:realContentBoundedVariation_equivalent_definition

nodes.name: Proof of Quasi-martingales via bounded elementary integrals
nodes.statement: The above boundedness condition, \[ \sup \Big\{ |\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t]| \:\Big|\: A \text{ elementary predictable} \Big\} <\infty \quad\text{for all } t\in T, \] does not change after restricting the above supremum to sets $A$ contained in $(0, t] \times \Omega$, since by Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegral_stoppedIntegrator}, \[ (\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t = (\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)^t_t = ((\mathbb{1}_{[0, t]}\mathbb{1}_A) \bullet X)_t = ((\mathbb{1}_{(0, t]}\mathbb{1}_A) \bullet X)_t \:. \] Moreover, for those $A$ the Lemma~\ref{lem:contentEquivElementaryIntegral} is applicable; in effect, we can express the boundedness condition as \[ \sup \Big\{ |\lambda_X(A)| \:\Big|\: A \text{ elementary predictable},\: A\subset(0,t]\times\Omega \Big\} <\infty \quad\text{for all } t\in T. \] Let $\mathcal{A}$ be the class of predictable rectangles, and let us use it in the definition of bounded variation of $\lambda_X$ (see Lemma~\ref{lem:contentBoundedVariation_equivOnGenerator}). Fix $t\in T$~. We aim to show that \[ \vert \lambda_X \vert((0,t]\times\Omega) = \sup\Big\{ \sum_{i=1}^n | \lambda_X(A_i)| \:\Big|\: (A_i)_{i=1}^n \text{ finite } \mathcal{A}\text{-partition of } (0,t]\times\Omega \Big\} <\infty \] holds if and only if \[ \sup \Big\{ |\lambda_X(A)| \:\Big|\: A \text{ elementary predictable},\: A\subset(0,t]\times\Omega \Big\} <\infty. \] Take an elementary predictable $A\subset B:=(0,t]\times\Omega$; choose $A_1$, \ldots, $A_m\in\mathcal{A}$ to be pairwise disjoint and such that (Corollary~\ref{cor:semiRingOfSets_subtract_ringElem}) \[ B\setminus A = \bigcup_{j=1}^m A_j. \] Express $A$ as a disjoint union of some $A_{m+1}$, \ldots, $A_n\in\mathcal{A}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:elementaryPredictableSets_asDisjointUnions}). Clearly, $(A_i)_{i=1}^n$ is a finite $\mathcal{A}$-partition of $B=(0,t]\times\Omega$, so, by content's additivity, \[ |\lambda_X(A)| = \left| \sum_{i=m+1}^n \lambda_X(A_i) \right| \le \sum_{i=1}^n |\lambda_X(A_i)|. \] This shows the "only if" part. For the "if" direction, take a sequence $((A_i^k)_{i=1}^{n_k})_{k=1}^\infty$ of finite $\mathcal{A}$-partitions of $(0,t]\times\Omega$ such that \[ \lim_{k\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^{n_k} | \lambda_X(A_i^k)| =\infty. \] Let \[ J_k = \{i \mid 1\le i\le n_k, \: \lambda_X(A_i^k) > 0\}, \] and note that $A_k = \bigcup_{i\in J_k} A_i^k$ is an elementary predictable subset of $(0,t]\times\Omega$~. Without loss of generality, we may assume that \[ \limsup_{k\to\infty} \sum_{i\in J_k} \lambda_X(A_i^k) = \infty, \] which by additivity means \[ \limsup_{k\to\infty} \lambda_X(A_k) = \infty. \]
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to sets in $(0,t]\times\Omega$ and pass to contents; 'only if' by completing a set to a partition, 'if' by collecting positive pieces of partitions with exploding sums (argument left incomplete).

nodes.name: Restrict to subsets of (0,t] x Omega
nodes.statement: The above boundedness condition, \[ \sup \Big\{ |\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t]| \:\Big|\: A \text{ elementary predictable} \Big\} <\infty \quad\text{for all } t\in T, \] does not change after restricting the above supremum to sets $A$ contained in $(0, t] \times \Omega$, since by Lemma~\ref{lem:elemStochIntegral_stoppedIntegrator}, \[ (\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)_t = (\mathbb{1}_A \bullet X)^t_t = ((\mathbb{1}_{[0, t]}\mathbb{1}_A) \bullet X)_t = ((\mathbb{1}_{(0, t]}\mathbb{1}_A) \bullet X)_t \:. \]
nodes.statement_short: The boundedness condition may be restricted to sets inside $(0,t]\times\Omega$.

nodes.name: Express via the content
nodes.statement: Moreover, for those $A$ the Lemma~\ref{lem:contentEquivElementaryIntegral} is applicable; in effect, we can express the boundedness condition as \[ \sup \Big\{ |\lambda_X(A)| \:\Big|\: A \text{ elementary predictable},\: A\subset(0,t]\times\Omega \Big\} <\infty \quad\text{for all } t\in T. \]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the condition in terms of $\lambda_X$.

nodes.name: Use rectangle partitions
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be the class of predictable rectangles, and let us use it in the definition of bounded variation of $\lambda_X$ (see Lemma~\ref{lem:contentBoundedVariation_equivOnGenerator}).
nodes.statement_short: Use predictable-rectangle partitions in the variation.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Fix $t\in T$~. We aim to show that \[ \vert \lambda_X \vert((0,t]\times\Omega) = \sup\Big\{ \sum_{i=1}^n | \lambda_X(A_i)| \:\Big|\: (A_i)_{i=1}^n \text{ finite } \mathcal{A}\text{-partition of } (0,t]\times\Omega \Big\} <\infty \] holds if and only if \[ \sup \Big\{ |\lambda_X(A)| \:\Big|\: A \text{ elementary predictable},\: A\subset(0,t]\times\Omega \Big\} <\infty. \]
nodes.statement_short: State the equivalence to prove for fixed $t$.

nodes.name: Only if direction
nodes.statement: Take an elementary predictable $A\subset B:=(0,t]\times\Omega$; choose $A_1$, \ldots, $A_m\in\mathcal{A}$ to be pairwise disjoint and such that (Corollary~\ref{cor:semiRingOfSets_subtract_ringElem}) \[ B\setminus A = \bigcup_{j=1}^m A_j. \] Express $A$ as a disjoint union of some $A_{m+1}$, \ldots, $A_n\in\mathcal{A}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:elementaryPredictableSets_asDisjointUnions}). Clearly, $(A_i)_{i=1}^n$ is a finite $\mathcal{A}$-partition of $B=(0,t]\times\Omega$, so, by content's additivity, \[ |\lambda_X(A)| = \left| \sum_{i=m+1}^n \lambda_X(A_i) \right| \le \sum_{i=1}^n |\lambda_X(A_i)|. \] This shows the "only if" part.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|\lambda_X(A)|$ by a partition sum.

nodes.name: Complete A to a partition
nodes.statement: Take an elementary predictable $A\subset B:=(0,t]\times\Omega$; choose $A_1$, \ldots, $A_m\in\mathcal{A}$ to be pairwise disjoint and such that (Corollary~\ref{cor:semiRingOfSets_subtract_ringElem}) \[ B\setminus A = \bigcup_{j=1}^m A_j. \]
nodes.statement_short: Partition $B \setminus A$ into rectangles.

nodes.name: Partition A
nodes.statement: Express $A$ as a disjoint union of some $A_{m+1}$, \ldots, $A_n\in\mathcal{A}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:elementaryPredictableSets_asDisjointUnions}).
nodes.statement_short: Partition $A$ into rectangles.

nodes.name: Additivity bound
nodes.statement: Clearly, $(A_i)_{i=1}^n$ is a finite $\mathcal{A}$-partition of $B=(0,t]\times\Omega$, so, by content's additivity, \[ |\lambda_X(A)| = \left| \sum_{i=m+1}^n \lambda_X(A_i) \right| \le \sum_{i=1}^n |\lambda_X(A_i)|. \]
nodes.statement_short: Additivity bounds $|\lambda_X(A)|$ by the partition sum.

nodes.name: Conclude only if
nodes.statement: This shows the "only if" part.
nodes.statement_short: This gives the 'only if' part.

nodes.name: If direction
nodes.statement: For the "if" direction, take a sequence $((A_i^k)_{i=1}^{n_k})_{k=1}^\infty$ of finite $\mathcal{A}$-partitions of $(0,t]\times\Omega$ such that \[ \lim_{k\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^{n_k} | \lambda_X(A_i^k)| =\infty. \] Let \[ J_k = \{i \mid 1\le i\le n_k, \: \lambda_X(A_i^k) > 0\}, \] and note that $A_k = \bigcup_{i\in J_k} A_i^k$ is an elementary predictable subset of $(0,t]\times\Omega$~. Without loss of generality, we may assume that \[ \limsup_{k\to\infty} \sum_{i\in J_k} \lambda_X(A_i^k) = \infty, \] which by additivity means \[ \limsup_{k\to\infty} \lambda_X(A_k) = \infty. \]
nodes.statement_short: Take partitions with exploding sums and collect the positive pieces.

nodes.name: Exploding partitions
nodes.statement: For the "if" direction, take a sequence $((A_i^k)_{i=1}^{n_k})_{k=1}^\infty$ of finite $\mathcal{A}$-partitions of $(0,t]\times\Omega$ such that \[ \lim_{k\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^{n_k} | \lambda_X(A_i^k)| =\infty. \]
nodes.statement_short: Take partitions with sums tending to infinity.

nodes.name: Positive pieces
nodes.statement: Let \[ J_k = \{i \mid 1\le i\le n_k, \: \lambda_X(A_i^k) > 0\}, \] and note that $A_k = \bigcup_{i\in J_k} A_i^k$ is an elementary predictable subset of $(0,t]\times\Omega$~.
nodes.statement_short: Collect the pieces with positive content into $A_k$.

nodes.name: Unbounded contents
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we may assume that \[ \limsup_{k\to\infty} \sum_{i\in J_k} \lambda_X(A_i^k) = \infty, \] which by additivity means \[ \limsup_{k\to\infty} \lambda_X(A_k) = \infty. \]
nodes.statement_short: WLOG the positive parts explode, so $\lambda_X(A_k)$ is unbounded.

nodes.name: Stieltjes measure of a monotone function
nodes.statement: Let $f : T \to \mathbb{R}$ be a right-continuous monotone function on a conditionally complete linear order $T$. We denote by $d_+ f$ the measure on $T$ defined by $d_+ f((a, b]) = f(b) - f(a)$ for all $a, b \in T$~.
nodes.label: def:StieltjesFunction.measure

nodes.name: Measurability of the Stieltjes measure of a monotone process
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a right-continuous adapted process which is monotone in the time variable. Then the measure $d_+ X_\omega$ is measurable in $\omega$~.
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a right-continuous adapted process which is monotone in the time variable.
conclusions: the measure $d_+ X_\omega$ is measurable in $\omega$
nodes.label: lem:StieltjesFunction.measurable_measure

nodes.name: Vector measure of a bounded variation function
nodes.statement: Let $f : T \to E$ be a function of bounded variation on a suitable order $T$, with $E$ a complete normed additive group. Then there exists a signed measure $df$ on $T$ defined by $df((a, b]) = f(b^+) - f(a^+)$~.
nodes.label: def:BoundedVariationOn.vectorMeasure

nodes.name: Measurability of the vector measure of a bounded variation process
nodes.statement: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be an adapted process which is of bounded variation in the time variable. Then the measure $dX_\omega$ is measurable in $\omega$~.
assumptions: Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be an adapted process which is of bounded variation in the time variable.
conclusions: the measure $dX_\omega$ is measurable in $\omega$
nodes.label: lem:BoundedVariationOn.measurable_vectorMeasure

nodes.name: Variation equals total variation of the measure
nodes.statement: Denoting by $\vert df \vert$ the total variation of the measure $df$~, $V_f([a, b]) = \vert df \vert([a, b])$~.
assumptions: Denoting by $\vert df \vert$ the total variation of the measure $df$~
conclusions: $V_f([a, b]) = \vert df \vert([a, b])$
nodes.label: lem:eVariationOn_eq_totalVariation

nodes.name: Vector measure of a monotone function is its Stieltjes measure
nodes.statement: If $f : T \to \mathbb{R}$ is a right-continuous monotone function, then the measure $df$ coincides with the measure $d_+ f$~.
assumptions: $f : T \to \mathbb{R}$ is a right-continuous monotone function
conclusions: the measure $df$ coincides with the measure $d_+ f$
nodes.label: lem:BoundedVariationOn.vectorMeasure_of_monotone

nodes.name: Content mu_X of an integrable process
nodes.statement:
Let $X : T \to \Omega \to E$ be a stochastic process such that $X_t$ is integrable for all $t$~.
For $s < t$ and $A \in \mathcal{F}_s$, let
\begin{align*}
  \mu_X((s, t] \times A) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_A (X_t - X_s)]
  \: .
\end{align*}
Set $\mu_X(\{0\} \times A) = 0$~.

nodes.name: mu_X extends to a content on the generated ring
conclusions: $\mu_X$ is a content on the predictable rectangles, which can be extended to the ring of sets it generates
nodes.statement: Then $\mu_X$ is a content on the predictable rectangles, which can be extended to the ring of sets it generates.

nodes.name: Measure d<M> induced by the quadratic variation
nodes.statement: For all $\omega \in \Omega$, $\langle M \rangle(\omega)$ is a right-continuous non-decreasing function (called a Stieltjes function in Mathlib) so it defines a measure on $\mathbb{R}_+$, denoted by $d\langle M \rangle$~.

nodes.name: Pathwise integral against d<M>
nodes.statement: By $\int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s$, we mean the random variable $\omega \mapsto \int_0^t X_s(\omega) \: d\langle M \rangle(\omega)$~.

nodes.name: Predictable sigma-algebra is contained in the product sigma-algebra
nodes.statement: The predictable $\sigma$-algebra on $T \times \Omega$ is a sub-$\sigma$-algebra of the product $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}(T) \otimes \mathcal{F}$~.
conclusions: The predictable $\sigma$-algebra on $T \times \Omega$ is a sub-$\sigma$-algebra of the product $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}(T) \otimes \mathcal{F}$~.
nodes.label: lem:Filtration.predictable_le_prod

nodes.name: L2 space of predictable processes
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $T$ and $P$ a measure on $\Omega$. We denote by $L^2(\mu, P)$ the space $L^2(T \times \Omega, \mathcal{P}, \mu \times P)$, in which $\mathcal{P}$ is the predictable $\sigma$-algebra, and the measure $\mu \times P$ is the restriction of the product measure on $\mathcal{B}(T) \otimes \mathcal{F}$ to $\mathcal{P}$~.
nodes.label: def:L2Predictable

nodes.name: Inner product in L2 of predictable processes
nodes.statement: For $X, Y \in L^2(\mu, P)$, we have \begin{align*} \langle X, Y \rangle_{L^2(\mu, P)} = P\left[ \int_0^{\infty} \langle X_t, Y_t\rangle \: d\mu \right] \: . \end{align*} The norm is $\Vert X \Vert_{L^2(\mu, P)}^2 = P\left[ \int_0^{\infty} \Vert X_t \Vert^2 \: d\mu \right]$~.
assumptions: For $X, Y \in L^2(\mu, P)$
conclusions: \langle X, Y \rangle_{L^2(\mu, P)} = P\left[ \int_0^{\infty} \langle X_t, Y_t\rangle \: d\mu \right]
The norm is $\Vert X \Vert_{L^2(\mu, P)}^2 = P\left[ \int_0^{\infty} \Vert X_t \Vert^2 \: d\mu \right]$~.
nodes.label: lem:L2Predictable.inner_eq

nodes.name: Proof of Inner product in L2 of predictable processes
nodes.statement: The inner product in $L^2$ spaces is defined as the integral of the pointwise inner products. \begin{align*} \langle X, Y \rangle_{L^2(\mu, P)} &= \int_{T \times \Omega} \langle X_t(\omega), Y_t(\omega) \rangle \: d(\mu \times P)(t, \omega) \\ &= P\left[ \int_0^{\infty} \langle X_t, Y_t\rangle \: d\mu \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Unfold the $L^2$ inner product and apply Fubini.

nodes.name: Simple processes are in L2(mu, P)
nodes.statement: Any simple process in $\mathcal{E}_{T, E}$ is in $L^2(\mu, P)$~. (Lean remark: we mean that the uncurried version of its coercion to a function satisfies \texttt{MemLp})
conclusions: Any simple process in $\mathcal{E}_{T, E}$ is in $L^2(\mu, P)$~.
nodes.label: lem:simpleProcess_mem_L2Predictable

nodes.name: Proof of Simple processes are in L2(mu, P)
nodes.statement: A simple process is bounded by definition.
nodes.statement_short: Simple processes are bounded.

nodes.name: L2 norm of a simple process
nodes.statement: Let $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, E}$ and $\mu$ a measure on $T$~. Let $f$ be a right-continuous non-decreasing function such that for all $s < t$, $\mu((s,t]) = f(t) - f(s)$ (the CDF of $\mu$, but that's only defined for $\mathbb{R}$ in Lean). Then \begin{align*} \Vert V \Vert^2_{L^2(\mu, P)} &= P\left[ \sum_{k=1}^n \Vert \eta_k \Vert^2 \: (f(t_k) - f(s_k)) \right] \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, E}$ and $\mu$ a measure on $T$~.
Let $f$ be a right-continuous non-decreasing function such that for all $s < t$, $\mu((s,t]) = f(t) - f(s)$ (the CDF of $\mu$, but that's only defined for $\mathbb{R}$ in Lean).
conclusions: \Vert V \Vert^2_{L^2(\mu, P)} &= P\left[ \sum_{k=1}^n \Vert \eta_k \Vert^2 \: (f(t_k) - f(s_k)) \right]
nodes.label: lem:L2Predictable.sq_norm_simpleProcess

nodes.name: Proof of L2 norm of a simple process
nodes.statement: TODO: this proof (and the result of the lemma) assumes that the intervals defining the simple process are disjoint. Let $V \in \mathcal{E}_{T, E}$~, with $V_t(\omega) = \sum_{k=1}^n \eta_k(\omega) \mathbb{1}_{(s_k, t_k]}(t)$~. \begin{align*} \Vert V \Vert^2_{L^2(\mu, P)} &= P\left[ \int_0^{\infty} \Vert V_t \Vert^2 \: d\mu \right] \\ &= P\left[ \int_0^{\infty} \left\Vert \sum_{k=1}^n \eta_k \mathbb{1}_{(s_k, t_k]}(t) \right\Vert^2 \: d\mu \right] \\ &= P\left[ \int_0^{\infty} \sum_{k=1}^n \Vert \eta_k \Vert^2 \mathbb{1}_{(s_k, t_k]}(t) \: d\mu \right] \\ &= P\left[ \sum_{k=1}^n \Vert \eta_k \Vert^2 \: \mu((s_k, t_k]) \right] \\ &= P\left[ \sum_{k=1}^n \Vert \eta_k \Vert^2 \: (f(t_k) - f(s_k)) \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the norm, use disjointness of the intervals, and integrate indicators against $\mu$.

nodes.name: L2 space with respect to a square integrable martingale
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a square integrable martingale. We define \begin{align*} L^2(M) = L^2(d\langle M \rangle, P) = L^2(T \times \Omega, \mathcal{P}, d\langle M \rangle \times P) \end{align*} in which $\mathcal{P}$ is the predictable $\sigma$-algebra and $d\langle M \rangle$ is the measure induced by the quadratic variation of $M$.
nodes.label: def:L2M

nodes.name: Itô isometry for elementary integrals
nodes.statement: For $V \in \mathcal{E}$ and $M \in \mathcal{M}^2$, then $V \bullet M \in \mathcal{M}^2$ (by Lemma~\ref{lem:isSquareIntegrable_elemStochIntegralBilin}) and \begin{align*} \Vert V \bullet M \Vert_{\mathcal{M}^2}^2 &= \Vert V \Vert_{L^2(M)}^2 \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For $V \in \mathcal{E}$ and $M \in \mathcal{M}^2$
conclusions: $V \bullet M \in \mathcal{M}^2$
\Vert V \bullet M \Vert_{\mathcal{M}^2}^2 &= \Vert V \Vert_{L^2(M)}^2
nodes.label: lem:sq_norm_elemStochIntegral

nodes.name: Proof of Itô isometry for elementary integrals
nodes.statement: There are two steps to the proof. First, in order to make sense of $\Vert V \Vert_{L^2(M)}$, we define the natural linear map from $\mathcal{E}$ to $L^2(M)$ via \texttt{SimpleProcess.toFun}. (Informally, this is identifying $\mathcal{E}$ as a subset $\mathcal{E} \subseteq L^2(M)$.) This induces the $L^2(M)$-norm on $\mathcal{E}$, using something like \texttt{NormedSpace.induced}. Next, we show that integration $V \mapsto V \bullet M$ is an isometry from $\mathcal{E}$ with the $L^2(M)$-norm, to $\mathcal{M}^2$. The proof is TODO.
nodes.statement_short: Embed simple processes in $L^2(M)$ to define the norm, then show the elementary integral is an isometry (left TODO).

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: There are two steps to the proof.
nodes.statement_short: The proof has two steps.

nodes.name: Embed simple processes in L2(M)
nodes.statement: First, in order to make sense of $\Vert V \Vert_{L^2(M)}$, we define the natural linear map from $\mathcal{E}$ to $L^2(M)$ via \texttt{SimpleProcess.toFun}. (Informally, this is identifying $\mathcal{E}$ as a subset $\mathcal{E} \subseteq L^2(M)$.) This induces the $L^2(M)$-norm on $\mathcal{E}$, using something like \texttt{NormedSpace.induced}.
nodes.statement_short: Map simple processes into $L^2(M)$ and induce the norm.

nodes.name: Isometry (TODO)
nodes.statement: Next, we show that integration $V \mapsto V \bullet M$ is an isometry from $\mathcal{E}$ with the $L^2(M)$-norm, to $\mathcal{M}^2$. The proof is TODO.

nodes.name: Vanishing integrals force the integrand to vanish
nodes.statement: Let $X\in L^2(M)$ such that $\int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s = 0$ for all $t \ge 0$ a.s.. Then $X = 0$ $(\mathbb{P} \times d\langle M \rangle)$-almost everywhere.
assumptions: Let $X\in L^2(M)$ such that $\int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s = 0$ for all $t \ge 0$ a.s..
conclusions: $X = 0$ $(\mathbb{P} \times d\langle M \rangle)$-almost everywhere
nodes.label: lem:integral_process_eq_zero

nodes.name: Proof of Vanishing integrals force the integrand to vanish
nodes.statement:
For $B$ a measurable set of $\mathbb{R}_+$ and $\omega \in \Omega$, let $
u_\omega(B) = \int_B X_s(\omega) \: d\langle M angle_s(\omega)$~. This is a signed measure on $\mathbb{R}_+$~. Then if for all $t$, $\int_0^t X_s(\omega) \: d\langle M angle_s(\omega) = 0$ then $
u_\omega([0,t]) = 0$ for all $t$. Those intervals generate the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathbb{R}_+$, so $
u_\omega$ is the zero measure. Thus, for almost all $\omega$, $
u_\omega$ is the zero measure. The measure $
u_\omega$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the measure $d\langle M angle(\omega)$~, and its Radon-Nikodym derivative is $X(\omega)$~. Since $
u_\omega$ is the zero measure for almost all $\omega$, we have that $X(\omega) = 0$ $d\langle M angle(\omega)$-almost everywhere for almost all $\omega$~. Equivalently, $X = 0$ $(\mathbb{P} 	imes d\langle M angle)$-almost everywhere.
nodes.statement_short: The signed measures $\nu_\omega$ vanish on intervals hence everywhere; their Radon-Nikodym derivative $X(\omega)$ is then a.e. zero.

nodes.name: Signed measures nu_omega
nodes.statement: For $B$ a measurable set of $\mathbb{R}_+$ and $\omega \in \Omega$, let $\nu_\omega(B) = \int_B X_s(\omega) \: d\langle M \rangle_s(\omega)$~. This is a signed measure on $\mathbb{R}_+$~.
nodes.statement_short: Define the signed measures $\nu_\omega$.

nodes.name: Vanishing on intervals
nodes.statement: Then if for all $t$, $\int_0^t X_s(\omega) \: d\langle M \rangle_s(\omega) = 0$ then $\nu_\omega([0,t]) = 0$ for all $t$.
nodes.statement_short: $\nu_\omega$ vanishes on all $[0,t]$.

nodes.name: Zero measure
nodes.statement: Those intervals generate the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathbb{R}_+$, so $\nu_\omega$ is the zero measure. Thus, for almost all $\omega$, $\nu_\omega$ is the zero measure.
nodes.statement_short: Intervals generate the Borel sets, so $\nu_\omega = 0$ for almost all $\omega$.

nodes.name: Radon-Nikodym derivative
nodes.statement: The measure $\nu_\omega$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the measure $d\langle M \rangle(\omega)$~, and its Radon-Nikodym derivative is $X(\omega)$~.
nodes.statement_short: $\nu_\omega$ has density $X(\omega)$ w.r.t. $d\langle M\rangle(\omega)$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Since $\nu_\omega$ is the zero measure for almost all $\omega$, we have that $X(\omega) = 0$ $d\langle M \rangle(\omega)$-almost everywhere for almost all $\omega$~. Equivalently, $X = 0$ $(\mathbb{P} \times d\langle M \rangle)$-almost everywhere.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $X = 0$ almost everywhere for the product measure.

nodes.name: Injectivity of the integral
nodes.statement: Let $X, Y \in L^2(M)$ such that $\int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s = \int_0^t Y_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s$ for all $t \ge 0$ a.s.. Then $X = Y$ almost everywhere.
assumptions: Let $X, Y \in L^2(M)$ such that $\int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s = \int_0^t Y_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s$ for all $t \ge 0$ a.s..
conclusions: $X = Y$ almost everywhere
nodes.label: lem:integral_process_injective

nodes.name: Proof of Injectivity of the integral
nodes.statement: By linearity of the integral, we have $\int_0^t (X_s - Y_s) \: d\langle M \rangle_s = 0$ for all $t \ge 0$ a.s.. Then apply Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_process_eq_zero} to $X - Y$~.
nodes.statement_short: Linearity, then apply the vanishing lemma to $X - Y$.

nodes.name: Integral of an integrand orthogonal to simple processes is a martingale
nodes.statement: Let $X \in L^2(M)$ such that $\langle X, V\rangle = 0$ for any simple process $V$. Let $A_t = \int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s$. Then $A_t$ is a martingale.
assumptions: Let $X \in L^2(M)$ such that $\langle X, V\rangle = 0$ for any simple process $V$.
Let $A_t = \int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s$.
conclusions: $A_t$ is a martingale
nodes.label: lem:martingale_integral_of_forall_eq_zero

nodes.name: Proof of Integral of an integrand orthogonal to simple processes is a martingale
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_iff_integral_elemStochIntegral_eq_zero}, it is enough to show that for any bounded real simple process $V$, $\mathbb{E}[(V \bullet A)_\infty] = 0$~. \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[(V \bullet A)_\infty\right] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^{\infty} V_t X_t \: d\langle M \rangle_t \right] \\ &= \langle X, V \rangle \\ &= 0 \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Martingale criterion via elementary integrals: $\mathbb{E}[(V\bullet A)_\infty] = \langle X, V\rangle = 0$.

nodes.name: Integral of an integrand orthogonal to simple processes vanishes
nodes.statement: Let $X \in L^2(M)$ such that $\langle X, V\rangle = 0$ for any simple process $V$. Then for all $t$, $\int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s = 0$.
assumptions: Let $X \in L^2(M)$ such that $\langle X, V\rangle = 0$ for any simple process $V$.
conclusions: for all $t$, $\int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s = 0$
nodes.label: lem:integral_eq_zero_of_forall_eq_zero

nodes.name: Proof of Integral of an integrand orthogonal to simple processes vanishes
nodes.statement: $A_t := \int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s$ is a finite variation process such that $A_t$ is integrable for all $t \ge 0$~. By Theorem~\ref{thm:IsLocalMartingale.eq_zero_of_finiteVariation}, it is enough to show that $A$ is a local martingale. We have by Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_integral_of_forall_eq_zero} that $A$ is a martingale, and hence a local martingale (Lemma~\ref{lem:Martingale.IsLocalMartingale}).
nodes.statement_short: A finite variation local martingale vanishes; the integral is a martingale, hence a local martingale.

nodes.name: Integral process
nodes.statement: $A_t := \int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s$ is a finite variation process such that $A_t$ is integrable for all $t \ge 0$~.
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is an integrable finite variation process.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:IsLocalMartingale.eq_zero_of_finiteVariation}, it is enough to show that $A$ is a local martingale.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to show $A$ is a local martingale.

nodes.name: Martingale
nodes.statement: We have by Lemma~\ref{lem:martingale_integral_of_forall_eq_zero} that $A$ is a martingale, and hence a local martingale (Lemma~\ref{lem:Martingale.IsLocalMartingale}).
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is a martingale, hence a local martingale.

nodes.name: Simple processes are dense in L2(M)
nodes.statement: The set of simple processes is dense in $L^2(M)$.
conclusions: The set of simple processes is dense in $L^2(M)$.
nodes.label: lem:dense_simpleProcess

nodes.name: Proof of Simple processes are dense in L2(M)
nodes.statement: Since $L^2(M)$ is a Hilbert space, it is enough to show that if $X \in L^2(M)$ is orthogonal to all simple processes, then $X = 0$~. Let $X \in L^2(M)$ such that for any simple process $V$, $\mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^{\infty} X_t V_t \: d\langle M \rangle_t \right] = 0$~. Let $A_t = \int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s$. It suffices to show that $A = 0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_process_eq_zero}~. This is proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_eq_zero_of_forall_eq_zero}~. In Lean, this is stated as: the natural linear map \texttt{toFun} from $\mathcal{E}$ to $L^2(M)$ is \texttt{IsDenseInducing}. The Itô isometry is then defined using \texttt{IsDenseInducing.extend}.
nodes.statement_short: In a Hilbert space, density follows if only zero is orthogonal to all simple processes; this reduces to vanishing of the integral process.

nodes.name: Reduction to orthogonal complement
nodes.statement: Since $L^2(M)$ is a Hilbert space, it is enough to show that if $X \in L^2(M)$ is orthogonal to all simple processes, then $X = 0$~.
nodes.statement_short: Density follows if only $0$ is orthogonal to all simple processes.

nodes.name: Orthogonal integrand
nodes.statement: Let $X \in L^2(M)$ such that for any simple process $V$, $\mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^{\infty} X_t V_t \: d\langle M \rangle_t \right] = 0$~. Let $A_t = \int_0^t X_s \: d\langle M \rangle_s$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $X$ orthogonal to simple processes and its integral process $A$.

nodes.name: Reduction to A = 0
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that $A = 0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_process_eq_zero}~.
nodes.statement_short: By the vanishing lemma it suffices that $A = 0$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: This is proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:integral_eq_zero_of_forall_eq_zero}~.
nodes.statement_short: Proved by the previous lemma.

nodes.name: Lean remark
nodes.statement: In Lean, this is stated as: the natural linear map \texttt{toFun} from $\mathcal{E}$ to $L^2(M)$ is \texttt{IsDenseInducing}. The Itô isometry is then defined using \texttt{IsDenseInducing.extend}.
nodes.statement_short: In Lean: dense inducing map, Itô isometry via extension.

nodes.name: Itô isometry
nodes.statement: Let $M \in \mathcal{M}^2$. Then the elementary stochastic integral map $\mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{M}^2$ defined by $V \mapsto V \bullet M$ extends to an isometry $L^2(M) \to \mathcal{M}^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend $V \mapsto V \bullet M$ from simple processes to an isometry $L^2(M) \to \mathcal{M}^2$.
nodes.label: def:itoIsometry

nodes.name: Inner product of Itô integrals
nodes.statement: $\langle X \cdot M, Y \cdot M \rangle_{\mathcal{M}^2} = (XY) \cdot \langle M, N \rangle_{\mathcal{M}^2}$.
conclusions: $\langle X \cdot M, Y \cdot M \rangle_{\mathcal{M}^2} = (XY) \cdot \langle M, N \rangle_{\mathcal{M}^2}$
nodes.label: lem:inner_itoIsometry

nodes.name: $L^2_{loc}(M)$
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a continuous local martingale. We define $L^2_{loc}(M)$ as the space of predictable processes $X$ such that for all $t \ge 0$, $\mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^t X_s^2 \: d\langle M \rangle_s \right] < \infty$.
nodes.label: def:L2locM

nodes.name: Stochastic integral for continuous local martingales
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a continuous local martingale and let $X \in L^2_{loc}(M)$. We define the local stochastic integral $X \cdot M$ as the unique continuous local martingale with $(X \cdot M)_0 = 0$ such that for any continuous local martingale $N$, almost surely, \begin{align*} \langle X \cdot M, N \rangle = X \cdot \langle M, N \rangle \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The stochastic integral $X\cdot M$ is the unique continuous local martingale started at 0 with $\langle X\cdot M, N\rangle = X\cdot\langle M,N\rangle$.
nodes.label: def:locStochIntegral

nodes.name: Stochastic integral for continuous semimartingales
nodes.statement: For a continuous semi-martingale $X = M + A$ and $V \in L^2_{semi}(X)$ (to be defined) we define the stochastic integral as \begin{align*} V \cdot X = V \cdot M + V \cdot A \: , \end{align*} in which $V \cdot M$ is the local stochastic integral defined in \ref{def:locStochIntegral} and $V \cdot A$ is the Lebesgue-Stieltjes integral with respect to the locally finite variation process $A$.
nodes.label: def:stochIntegral

nodes.name: Covariation of continuous semimartingales
Integration by parts
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous semi-martingales. Then we have almost surely \begin{align*} X_t Y_t - X_0 Y_0 = (X \cdot Y)_t + (Y \cdot X)_t + [X,Y]_t \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous semi-martingales.
conclusions: X_t Y_t - X_0 Y_0 = (X \cdot Y)_t + (Y \cdot X)_t + [X,Y]_t
nodes.label: thm:integration_by_parts

nodes.name: Itô's formula
nodes.statement: Let $X^1, \ldots, X^d$ be continuous semi-martingales and let $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ be a twice continuously differentiable function. Then, writing $X = (X^1, \ldots, X^d)$, the process $f(X)$ is a semi-martingale and we have \begin{align*} f(X_t) &= f(X_0) + \sum_{i=1}^d \int_0^t \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(X_s) \: dX^i_s + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^d \int_0^t \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(X_s) \: d[X^i, X^j]_s \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Itô's formula for a $C^2$ function of continuous semimartingales.
assumptions: Let $X^1, \ldots, X^d$ be continuous semi-martingales and let $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ be a twice continuously differentiable function.
conclusions: the process $f(X)$ is a semi-martingale
f(X_t) &= f(X_0) + \sum_{i=1}^d \int_0^t \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(X_s) \: dX^i_s + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^d \int_0^t \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(X_s) \: d[X^i, X^j]_s
nodes.label: thm:Ito_formula
